docs.text: Byrgenwerth Bloodborne Paleblood is a decompilation of Bloodborne with its own runtime, one verified function at a time We are born of the blood, made men by the blood, undone by the blood. Our eyes are yet to open… Fear the old blood. Master Willem / The Blood Minister Read the devlog Join the hunt Paleblood rewrites Bloodborne ( PS4 , CUSA03173, version 1.09) function by function as readable C++ that does exactly what the original did, and builds a runtime of its own for that code to run on. Where the hunt stands The game doesn't run on Paleblood yet: 21 of 157,757 functions are verified (0.01%). On our own runtime the executable's boot gets as far as the run's time limit, still running (no call stopped it), with 683 of 686 system imports provided. 100% of imports System imports provided 683 of 686 imports the boot needs are provided. 219 come from the game's own modules and 464 from the runtime. Boot milestone: first flip (8 of 8). Start here The hunt Devlog What changed each week, mistakes included. Read Numbers Progress Replaced and verified functions, by system and address. See progress How it works Runtime Our own runtime and how far the game boots on it. Explore For hunters Contributing Your first pull request, and the rules that keep it clean. Get started A place to learn No console, dump or game files are needed to learn here: every page explains how the game's code works in our own words and our own code. How a console game fits together The executable, its libraries, the frame loop and the two tracks. Architecture The first system, step by step How the frame limiter paces the game, and how it was replaced. Frame limiter Reverse engineering in practice Reading disassembly, and the traps in the tools. Ghidra & PS4 quirks Every term, explained Hover a dotted term anywhere for its meaning. Glossary More about the project Why we do this, and the goal Because we love this game. Yharnam deserves to outlive the hardware it was made for, and to be understood as well as it is loved: every function of the original, read, named, rewritten and proved to behave exactly as it did, so that one day it runs natively, at any frame rate, for as long as there are hunters to play it. The goal is a complete source port of Bloodborne for the PC. When the hunt is over, every function of the game's 1.09 executable will have been rewritten as readable C++ and proved to behave exactly like the original, and the game will run natively on Paleblood's own runtime : no PS4 , no emulator, no original executable, only the game's data from your own copy. Because it will be source, the game can be read, understood, preserved, fixed and modded like any other program, at any frame rate and resolution. Two tracks get there, side by side: Decompilation: functions rewritten as readable C++ and proved against the original in the verification harness , on inputs recorded earlier and on generated edge cases . Tiny functions the compiler emitted many times over share one replacement per function family , which moves the function count far more than the byte count. Runtime: our own loader (done), input capture (a game run can now record a function's inputs by tracing the original), kernel, threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and the graphics, rebuilt at the engine's own level rather than by emulating the PS4 's GPU ( Runtime ). The game does not run on Paleblood until the runtime is far enough along that road. Today merged main boots through all eight milestones to first flip (8 of 8): the game starts its threads, reads its files, sets up input, starts its sound system, opens its display and hands its first frame to the screen (4 November 2026). Since 6 November no system call stops the boot any more: it keeps running until the harness 's time limit ( #408 , #443 , #536 ). Since then too, in the maintainer's local runs with the display on, Paleblood's own renderer draws the studio logos and the title screen ( #441 , #442 ), and with scripted input ( #447 ) it gets past the title: the game creates its save data, shows its main menu, New Game reaches the first-run Brightness and Controls screens, and on 10 November the opening cinematic plays in 3D and the game reaches character creation ( Milestones ). The playable game has not run yet. The runtime checklist is done: every system import the boot reaches is answered, and the last three of the executable's, by contributor @EzequielRindello , merged on 11 November ( #555 ; Runtime ). The runtime also plays the game's movies and sound and reads a keyboard or gamepad ( #419 , #398 , #406 , #431 ). Full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed; the Runtime page shows how far a boot gets. How a function becomes verified Analyze. Ghidra with the GhidraOrbis loader finds the function in your own dump; its callers, callees and the memory it touches are read from the disassembly, not only the decompiler. Name. It gets a name and a system in the shared function table, so every contributor's Ghidra shows the same names. Rewrite. A readable C++ version: named structures instead of raw offsets, named calls instead of addresses, named constants, faithful to what the original does. Verify. The harness runs the original and the replacement on equivalent recorded and generated inputs, comparing ABI-selected results, preserved registers, declared memory state, and scripted library calls. Optional instruction tracing adds bounded access and control-flow observations; its limits are described in Architecture . Deliberately wrong versions must fail. Review. An independent reviewer checks the verification and the readability. A function whose code no recording reaches yet is edge-verified until one does. Key documents Document What it covers Architecture The two tracks, the verification harness , the frame pipeline Runtime Our own runtime : the roadmap and how far the game's executable boots on it How the Frame Limiter Works The first system replaced , step by step Glossary PS4 and project terms explained Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the ABI Contributing Joining, the first pull request, the rules The executable's code, slice by slice, is on the Address Map ; every tracked function with its status is on its system page . The devlog tells the story as it happened, mistakes included. Legal, and the target this project is built for This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Sony Interactive Entertainment or FromSoftware in any way. Tools and source only: no game files, no extracted assets, no decompiler dumps. Everything starts from your own console and your own copy: to contribute or verify you need Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. How to read it Density is relative to the densest slice. Hover a cell for its address range, function count and bytes. Only code is mapped. The code is one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not on the map. Addresses are not systems. The game's systems are spread across the executable; the system pages say which functions belong where. Small replacements stay visible. A slice with replaced code always gets a bar at least a little wide. Layout of the executable Range What 0x00400000 … Code ( .text ): every function the map shows after the code Read-only data, .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr (unwind tables) after that Writable data and zero-initialized data The exact block boundaries are the GhidraOrbis loader 's; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks for how they were checked against the unwind tables.

docs.title: Address Map

docs.text: Density is relative to the densest slice. Hover a cell for its address range, function count and bytes. Only code is mapped. The code is one block from 0x00400000 ; read-only data, the exception tables and the writable data follow it and are not on the map. Addresses are not systems. The game's systems are spread across the executable; the system pages say which functions belong where. Small replacements stay visible. A slice with replaced code always gets a bar at least a little wide.
docs.title: How to read it

docs.text: Range What 0x00400000 … Code ( .text ): every function the map shows after the code Read-only data, .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr (unwind tables) after that Writable data and zero-initialized data The exact block boundaries are the GhidraOrbis loader 's; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks for how they were checked against the unwind tables.

docs.text: Architecture How Paleblood fits together: two tracks, decompilation and runtime, and how a function moves from original code to verified, readable C++. Runtime track Runtime The loader, the boot harness and how far the game boots. Read Runtime track Runtime system calls Each implemented call and the evidence behind it. Read First system The Frame Limiter How each frame is paced, and how it was replaced. Read Map Address Map The executable's code, slice by slice, and what is replaced. Read Reference Target The exact game version and executables the project works on. Read At a glance Decompilation The game's code rewritten, function by function, as readable C++ proved to behave like the original. Runtime Paleblood's own loader and a growing set of PS4 system-call implementations. Game runs The game does not run on Paleblood's runtime yet; full runs still use an external host scaffold. Merge rule A function reaches main only when verified and readable, checked by an independent reviewer. Your own pkgs base + 1.09 update prepare_dump.sh extract, merge, SELF to ELF, hash check Ghidra + GhidraOrbis eboot.elf: names and sizes into symbols/ Paleblood's loader map, relocate, bind every import Boot harness the entry on our runtime, to the first gap Verification harness original and replacement, same inputs Runtime libraries kernel, files, input, audio, video, GNM Readable C++ verified and independently reviewed The game runs on Paleblood once the runtime is far enough along Paleblood is a decompilation with its own runtime . The decompilation rewrites the game's code, function by function, as readable C++ that is proved to behave like the original. The runtime is what that code, and the original executable while it is being replaced , runs on: Paleblood's own loader and a growing set of PS4 system-call implementations. The renderer draws the game's frames with Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS, by hooking the game's own drawing layer and translating its shaders, not by emulating the PS4 's GPU. Its plan and progress are on the Runtime page. The game does not run on Paleblood's runtime yet; the Runtime page has the roadmap, implemented calls, and the latest saved boot result. What runs where today Full game runs still use an external host scaffold while the project-owned runtime is completed. The verification harness independently maps the executable and replays recorded inputs. A game run can now record a hooked function's inputs as a case: with BB_CAPTURE_TRACE=1 , the runtime traces the original function once, instruction by instruction, before handing the call to the replacement, and scripts any system call it makes on the way ( #133 , #134 , #135 ). Its tests use synthetic guest functions; no recording from a real game run has verified a function yet. Paleblood also has a project-owned implementation of the version-1 hook callback. A synthetic executable-memory test verifies that its jump reaches a replacement, but the callback is not yet wired into the full game-run scaffold and does not establish full-run equivalence. What the executable is made of Not all of the game's code is FromSoftware's own. Its assertion messages keep the source path of each file they were compiled from, and since #480 Paleblood tags every function with the file and library it most likely came from ( symbols/source_files.csv , generated by tools/source_files.py ). The lead came from @sweetbbak in issue #453 : the engine is FromSoftware's Dantelion2, with Havok 2014.1 and HavokScript, FMOD Ex 4.44.50, Silicon Studio's YEBIS and Sony's gnmx linked in. Library Functions Share of the 157,757 Engine (Dantelion2 and the game's own code) 84,215 53% Havok 21,098 13% FMOD (sound) 4,272 3% YEBIS (post-processing) 2,183 1% HavokScript (scripting) 1,278 1% Sony gnmx (GPU helper library) 113 0.1% Not tagged 44,598 28% Counts from Paleblood's docs/FUNCTION_CATALOG.md at the merge of #480. Only about 1,700 functions are tagged directly, because they load a file's path; the rest are filled in between two tags of the same file or library, so the split is an estimate, strongest where tags are dense. The game was built with Sony's PS4 Clang, so this says which library a function belongs to, not how to rebuild it byte for byte. It helps tell the engine's own code from middleware when choosing what to study and decompile next. The decompilation track A replacement lives in the code repository's game/<system>/ and follows its style rules: the objects a function touches are structures with named fields; the original's other functions and globals are reached through named declarations, not addresses; constants are named; there is no test plumbing inside the game's code. A function reaches the main branch only when it is both verified and readable, and an independent reviewer, not the author, has checked both. How a replacement takes over. Replacements are registered in a hook table. When the runtime runs the game, each registered function's entry will jump to its replacement, so every caller lands in the new code. It is a 14-byte jump, which is why a function shorter than that cannot be hooked this way, except where the compiler's padding after it leaves room: that is how the tiny, repeated functions of a function family are hooked, many at once, with one replacement per family. The runtime track Load. Paleblood's loader maps the game's executable, together with the game's own C library and file system modules. Link. It applies every relocation and binds every system import, to one of those modules or to the runtime 's own implementation. Boot. The boot harness starts the guest startup sequence. It stops at the first system function the runtime does not implement yet, naming it, or runs until its time limit. Implement. The next piece of runtime work implements what the boot stopped at, written clean-room from public documentation and our own reverse engineering. The latest saved trace ( #536 , 10 November 2026) reaches all eight boot milestones and runs until the time limit: no system call stops it, and all but three of the executable's system imports are bound (those three merged the next day, #555 ). With the display on, the maintainer's local runs draw the studio logos and the title screen, and with scripted input they get past the title, through the menus and the opening cinematic to character creation ( Runtime ). The frame pipeline The first system decompiled. Solid boxes are verified C++; dashed boxes are still original code. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Once per frame, the frame step: checks that the window is running; creates the SprjFlipper on the first frame (its constructor reads Game.FlipMode ); lets the flipper's limiter wait out the frame; runs the game's task update. The full walk-through is in How the Frame Limiter Works . Verification Earlier game runs inputs recorded while the game ran Edge-case generators what a recording does not reach Capture library captures/ / _NNNN.json harness.py our loader; original and replacement, same inputs verify.py compare returns, registers, bytes, calls Mutation test wrong variants must fail edge-verified, verified plus the independent review A replacement is checked against the original outside the game. Map. The harness maps the executable from your own dump with Paleblood's loader , and scripts every library call the function makes. Feed. The inputs are cases recorded in earlier game runs (the capture library) and edge cases generated for the corners. Run both. The original and the replacement run on the same inputs. Compare. ABI-selected return values, callee-saved registers, final bytes in declared memory regions, and scripted library calls must match. Break it on purpose. Deliberately wrong versions of the replacement must fail; if one passes, the cases are too weak and get fixed first. Status Meaning edge-verified Passes, but no recording reaches the function's code yet. verified Recordings for it exist and pass, and the independent review has approved it. What the automated tools can establish The merged differential engine adds deterministic fixture replay, bounded input exploration, mismatch minimization, and portable evidence reports. Its tests prove infrastructure behavior using synthetic instructions; they do not establish a new game function's semantics or promote a function automatically. Instruction tracing (optional, Linux) watches supported guest memory reads and writes at byte granularity, including unaligned accesses, aliased pointers, and writes that leave the same value. For each access it records: the instruction; the access range; the bytes before and after; the register context. Reading a difference. The first differing recorded memory event is a bounded diagnostic. Original and replacement code may take different instruction paths, so an internal trace difference with equal observable results is not treated as a behavior mismatch. Limits of instruction tracing The support matrix defines its limits: classified string/repeat, vector-memory, atomic, and system instructions fail closed; host code outside the instrumented ranges leaves an explicit gap. Capstone does not identify every architectural implicit-memory operation, so completeness applies only to the audited instruction families. The tool does not claim an exact first divergence of every register at every instruction. Coverage and the candidate pipeline Supported instruction traces record executed basic blocks and outgoing edges per fixture. Complete traces can prioritize seeds that found new edges, or a conditional outcome whose other outcome is still unseen. Partial and unavailable coverage remain explicit and cannot feed that ranking. This describes observed fixture paths, not a complete static map of every possible path. The opt-in automation prototype connects catalog qualification to an isolated worktree, local recorded fixtures, both compiler builds, differential tests, repository checks, and a reviewable draft pull request. It accepts a prewritten clean-room replacement patch; source generation is not automated. Each gate needs its evidence, and missing evidence rejects the run: Gate Evidence required Candidate Fresh ownership checks, replacement-development qualification, exact executable identity, and documented ABI. Fixtures Recorded-game provenance and sufficient matching cases; generated boundary cases supplement those recordings. Execution Matching observable results, complete supported instruction traces, valid memory accesses, and eligible CFG coverage. Delivery Compiler and repository checks, a reproducible evidence report, then GitHub CI and human review. What the pipeline has not shown Missing evidence rejects the run. Dry-run mode performs local work only, and a regression canary cannot open a function PR. No complete real-game candidate-to-PR run has been established by the merged evidence. Synthetic pipeline success does not change the verification counts . Addresses Every address in this wiki is a PS4 virtual address with the executable at 0x400000 , the convention of the community patches. See Ghidra & PS4 Quirks . What comes next The queues live in the code repository's NEXT.md : one for the decompilation track, one for the runtime track. Import-boundary observations PR #85 takes bounded snapshots of registers and selected stack/fixture-buffer bytes when the harness enters and returns from a recognized import. They show the net change at that boundary, and nothing more. What import-boundary snapshots do not show Merged PR #85 adds bounded snapshots of registers and selected stack/fixture-buffer bytes at recognized harness import entry and return. They expose net changes at that boundary; they do not trace host instructions, establish argument types, observe every memory access, or prove host control-flow coverage. Comparison, automation acceptance and coverage feedback continue to reject external-execution evidence even if another label incorrectly calls the trace complete. These diagnostics cannot qualify a function for verification, and the import-dependent clock regression remains incomplete.

docs.text: CI Setup Both repositories run GitHub Actions on every push and pull request. Neither ever sees game data: nothing from a dump is in the repositories, and CI does not need it. At a glance Code repository Build matrix (GCC, Clang), policy, and a session report on pull requests. Wiki Rejects game data, checks generated files, builds with --strict . Merge-blocking The four code repository checks, including the readable-code check. Runs locally only Function-level verification against the real game: it needs your dump. Code repository ( Paleblood ) .github/workflows/ci.yml runs three jobs: Job What it checks build (gcc) , build (clang) CMake build, the syslib CTest (RT_SYSLIB), the rest of CTest, and the Python suites. policy No game data, valid function tables, README progress, readable code, pre-commit hooks . session report On pull requests: picks the right report from the changed file paths. What each job does in full build (gcc) and build (clang) — install the pinned optional Capstone dependency, configure and build with CMake, run the syslib CTest (the RT_SYSLIB unit test), then run the remaining CTest suite. The workflow also runs the harness /instruction-trace and differential-engine Python suites with each compiler and its built loader . It includes hook -table and loader tests, the plug-in contract test, synthetic executable-memory hook tests, and synthetic tracing, CFG, and mutation regressions. These tests do not run the full game-run scaffold or establish native game-run equivalence. policy — rejects anything that looks like game data; validates the function tables; checks that runtime and tools name nothing specific to the game; checks that the README progress matches tools/progress.py ; runs the readable-code check (addresses, raw offsets, magic numbers, and recording code); and exercises the pre-commit hooks . session report — on pull requests, CI selects the concise report for runtime -only changes, the documentation report, or the full decompilation/mixed report from changed file paths. Unknown code paths fail closed to the full report. Runtime changes cannot downgrade a mixed PR. The build and policy jobs still apply to every path. These four checks are required by Paleblood's current main branch protection. Readability and independent review tools/check_readable.py (in policy ) is required and merge-blocking. A reviewer who did not write a function must approve it before it is verified . Function-level verification runs locally, not in CI. Readability check and review record The policy job's tools/check_readable.py step is a required, merge-blocking check. It rejects mechanical transcription patterns in game/ , and CI refuses any growth in the grandfathered-file list. The check does not judge whether names, structure, complexity, or comments are easy for people to follow. Before a function is marked verified , a reviewer who did not write it must assess both its verification evidence and readability; the approval is recorded in symbols/reviews.csv and the promotion tools validate that record. Paleblood's current branch protection does not require a blanket approving review on every pull request. Local verification, runtime PRs and promotion Function-level verification against the real game cannot run in CI, because it needs your dump. It remains required for decompilation changes and runs locally ( tools/verify.py run , tools/smoke.sh ). The full session report must include every replacement status change recorded for the PR and matching, non-empty, passing verify.py evidence for each replaced , edge-verified , or verified function. Runtime-only contributions do not require a dump, captures , or function-level verification. After a runtime PR merges, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts its result on the PR. tools/promote.py checks existing recorded and edge cases locally and requires an approved review before promotion. Comparison result files go to temporary storage; the capture library remains input-only. --dry-run leaves verification metadata and function status unchanged. Wiki ( Byrgenwerth ) .github/workflows/ci.yml installs MkDocs, rejects game data, checks that every generated file (progress data, tables, visuals) agrees with the data it comes from and that no page has a hand-typed count, builds the site with --strict , and exercises the pre-commit hooks . Local workflow (no CI needed) Shell tools/install_hooks.sh # both repositories tools/smoke.sh # code repository: the pipeline on a known function export BB_PORT_DIR = /absolute/path/to/clean-paleblood-main-at-merged-sha tools/end_session.sh # wiki: pull numbers from the code repository, build, check python3 -m mkdocs serve # wiki: preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 Pin BB_PORT_DIR for wiki validation For wiki validation and publication, pin BB_PORT_DIR to a clean worktree at the exact merged Paleblood revision and record its absolute path and full SHA in the shared checkpoint. docs.text: .github/workflows/ci.yml runs three jobs: Job What it checks build (gcc) , build (clang) CMake build, the syslib CTest (RT_SYSLIB), the rest of CTest, and the Python suites. policy No game data, valid function tables, README progress, readable code, pre-commit hooks . session report On pull requests: picks the right report from the changed file paths. What each job does in full build (gcc) and build (clang) — install the pinned optional Capstone dependency, configure and build with CMake, run the syslib CTest (the RT_SYSLIB unit test), then run the remaining CTest suite. The workflow also runs the harness /instruction-trace and differential-engine Python suites with each compiler and its built loader . It includes hook -table and loader tests, the plug-in contract test, synthetic executable-memory hook tests, and synthetic tracing, CFG, and mutation regressions. These tests do not run the full game-run scaffold or establish native game-run equivalence. policy — rejects anything that looks like game data; validates the function tables; checks that runtime and tools name nothing specific to the game; checks that the README progress matches tools/progress.py ; runs the readable-code check (addresses, raw offsets, magic numbers, and recording code); and exercises the pre-commit hooks . session report — on pull requests, CI selects the concise report for runtime -only changes, the documentation report, or the full decompilation/mixed report from changed file paths. Unknown code paths fail closed to the full report. Runtime changes cannot downgrade a mixed PR. The build and policy jobs still apply to every path. These four checks are required by Paleblood's current main branch protection.
docs.title: Code repository (Paleblood)

docs.text: tools/check_readable.py (in policy ) is required and merge-blocking. A reviewer who did not write a function must approve it before it is verified . Function-level verification runs locally, not in CI. Readability check and review record The policy job's tools/check_readable.py step is a required, merge-blocking check. It rejects mechanical transcription patterns in game/ , and CI refuses any growth in the grandfathered-file list. The check does not judge whether names, structure, complexity, or comments are easy for people to follow. Before a function is marked verified , a reviewer who did not write it must assess both its verification evidence and readability; the approval is recorded in symbols/reviews.csv and the promotion tools validate that record. Paleblood's current branch protection does not require a blanket approving review on every pull request. Local verification, runtime PRs and promotion Function-level verification against the real game cannot run in CI, because it needs your dump. It remains required for decompilation changes and runs locally ( tools/verify.py run , tools/smoke.sh ). The full session report must include every replacement status change recorded for the PR and matching, non-empty, passing verify.py evidence for each replaced , edge-verified , or verified function. Runtime-only contributions do not require a dump, captures , or function-level verification. After a runtime PR merges, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts its result on the PR. tools/promote.py checks existing recorded and edge cases locally and requires an approved review before promotion. Comparison result files go to temporary storage; the capture library remains input-only. --dry-run leaves verification metadata and function status unchanged.

docs.text: Contributing Tonight, Gehrman joins the hunt. Gehrman, the First Hunter Paleblood is open to everyone. This is the short version: how to help, your first pull request, and the rules. Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Read Glossary PS4 and project terms explained. Read CI Setup What runs on every push and pull request. Read Credits The tools and contributors the project stands on. Read Evidence & Media Review How claims are labelled and media is reviewed. Read Full rules: the code repository's CONTRIBUTING.md . Setup: its ONBOARDING.md . Questions: Discussions . Ways to help Track What you do Name functions Good first issues: name small, clear functions in the shared function table. Document a system One page here per system. Replace functions Readable C++ replacements, verified and reviewed. Build the runtime Implement PS4 system calls in RT_SYSLIB . No dump needed. Tooling The harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. More on each track Name functions — the good first issues: small functions with a clear purpose, identified from their callers and the library calls they make, named in the shared function table. Document a system — a page here per system: summary, key functions, structures, patch points, open questions. Replace functions — readable C++ replacements, verified against the original with the harness and reviewed independently. Build the runtime — claim a call or tightly related group in its system issue ( #34–#41 ), then use a runtime/<function> branch to implement it in runtime/syslib/<group>.c , registered with RT_SYSLIB . Its tests go in a file of their own, test/syslib/<group>.c , as SYSLIB_TEST(name) { ... } blocks, so parallel pull requests do not edit the same lines ( #407 ); the PR checks count those files as runtime tests ( #430 ). Runtime-only work is clean-room, needs no game dump or captures , and receives maintainer boot verification after merge. Independent reverse engineering may include the system libraries of your own console's firmware: name each by its SHA-256 in the runtime report, take only facts from it, write your own code, and never copy, attach or link the files ( #356 ). See the runtime syscall notes and the full workflow in Paleblood's contribution guide. Tooling — the harness , the capture library, the Ghidra scripts. Your first pull request Fork. Fork Paleblood and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. Set up. Decompilation: follow ONBOARDING.md. Runtime: claim a function in its system issue (#34–#41) on a runtime/<function> branch. Keep it small. One function or tightly related group per PR, with its tests in test/syslib/<group>.c and a runtime report. Merge. CI runs without a dump. After merge, a maintainer boot-tests it and posts the result. Each step in full Fork Paleblood on GitHub and run tools/install_hooks.sh in your clone. For decompilation, follow ONBOARDING.md from your own dump to Ghidra . A draft from tools/draft.sh is a starting point; it marks with ; GAP: and decodes the code Ghidra leaves out after a call it wrongly treats as not returning ( #189 ). For runtime work, read the syscall notes and claim one function or related group in its system issue (#34–#41); use a branch named runtime/<function> . Keep one function or tightly related group per PR. Put its RT_SYSLIB tests in their own file, test/syslib/<group>.c ( test/syslib/np_trophy.c is an example; cases already in test/test_syslib.c may be updated there), and include evidence, confirmed behavior, unresolved questions, and test results in the runtime report. For a decompilation PR, tools/session_report.py --verify takes the output folder of a tools/verify.py run (or the summary.json it writes there) and adds its results to the session report ( #417 ). A change to a function family takes the summary.json of a clean tools/verify.py family run the same way: the report lists each changed family, and CI refuses a family change without one ( #515 ). To bring your branch up to date, merge origin/main into it; the push gate checks only the commits main does not have yet ( #407 ). Runtime-only PRs run the compiler matrix, RT_SYSLIB tests, and repository policy checks without requiring a dump, captures , or function-level verify.py . CI also builds and tests each pull request merged with every other open one (the combined job, #136 ), so two changes that break only together are caught before either merges. After merge, a maintainer runs tools/boot.py locally and posts the result on the PR. However you work, the workflow is the same; tools/handoff.py writes a shareable handoff of where a piece of work stands, so someone else can pick it up ( #93 ). Your own copy Decompilation needs your own PS4 and your own copy of the game. Runtime work needs no game files. The project never provides them. Your own copy in full Decompilation work starts from your own console and your own copy of the game: Bloodborne (CUSA03173, EU) with the 1.09 update, dumped from your own PS4 . Runtime-only contributions do not need a dump, captures , or any game files. The project does not provide or point to game files, pkgs, firmware, keys or decryption tools. Requests for game files, or links to them, are removed wherever they are posted, and may lead to a ban. Ground rules No game files. Ever. No game media in the code repository. Verified and readable before it is done. Say how you know. One pull request per function or cluster. The ground rules in full No game files. Ever. No executables, assets, decompiler output or extracted data in commits, issues, pull requests or Discussions. Keep game media out of Paleblood's code repository and its issues, pull requests, and Discussions. The hook and CI refuse image and video files (by extension and by contents). The only images allowed there are under docs/assets/ and listed in docs/assets/ALLOWLIST with the command that produced them, and they are our own work: recordings of our tools' output, and frames drawn by Paleblood's own renderer, at full resolution, added by the maintainer with attribution (such as the README's title screen, #445 ). Every file there is capped at 2 MiB; an allowlisted image may be up to 8 MiB, so a frame is posted whole ( #550 ). Contributors do not add game frames themselves; propose one in an issue instead. The documentation site follows a separate, asset-by-asset review process for technical and critical context; attribution or educational purpose alone does not establish permission. See Evidence & Media Review . Verified and readable. A replacement that "looks right" is not done until the harness finds no difference on recorded and edge cases , deliberately wrong versions fail, it reads well (the code repository's STYLE.md), and an independent reviewer has approved it. The local promotion tool reruns the recorded and edge suites before changing a function to verified ; its comparison output is temporary and kept away from the capture library. Case data stays on the contributor's machine. Say how you know. When you name a function, say how you inferred what it does: its callers, its library calls, the memory it touches. A name says what is known and no more. One pull request per function or cluster , with the disclosures CONTRIBUTING.md asks for.

docs.text: Evidence & Media Review How pages label evidence, and how any image or clip gets reviewed before it appears on this site. At a glance Label it Name the evidence type behind each claim, and link the exact source. Not evidence Merging a pull request or closing an issue does not show that game execution advanced. Review each asset Every image or clip needs its own provenance and rights review before it is copied or published. Credit ≠ permission Attribution and educational intent are context; neither alone grants permission. Code repository Only our own work: tool recordings and frames drawn by Paleblood's renderer, added by the maintainer. No extracted game assets. How to read a claim Byrgenwerth explains how Bloodborne works from evidence gathered by Paleblood and its contributors. A test result, a trace, and a gameplay observation answer different questions, so pages label them separately. Evidence label What it supports What it does not establish by itself Verified original-game behavior A Paleblood replacement matched the original on the recorded and edge cases listed in its verification record, with independent review. Every possible input or every game state. Direct static analysis A behavior or relationship visible in disassembly, callers, data references, or a readable replacement. That a code path ran in an observed play session. Recorded original-game observation What happened in an original-game run or captured call, for the recorded conditions. Unobserved states or the reason behind an outcome. Synthetic Paleblood test The tested Paleblood infrastructure or function behavior under the synthetic fixture. Original-game execution or a real production capture . Paleblood-owned infrastructure A project-created loader , host interface, diagnostic, test, or tool and its demonstrated behavior. That the full game uses or reaches it. External research A cited fact or interpretation from a named outside source. Independent confirmation by Paleblood. Hypothesis / open question A plausible interpretation that guides further investigation. A confirmed function purpose or game rule. When a claim combines evidence types, say which part each type supports. Combining and citing evidence When a claim combines evidence types, state which part each type supports. Link to the exact source revision, test record, or published source that supports it. Merging a pull request or closing an issue is not evidence that game execution advanced. Screenshots, clips, and other media Use as little as possible: the smallest portion that explains the point. Frames drawn by Paleblood's own renderer are our own work and are shown whole, at full resolution, never downscaled (maintainer decision, 2026-11-06). Such a frame may be up to 8 MiB, here and in the code repository; code, data and every other file keep the 2 MiB cap (maintainer decision, 2026-11-10; tools/check_policy.py and tools/check_publish.py enforce it). Never publish extracted assets, proprietary captures , bulk game text, secrets, or unsourced material. No retired or borrowed images presented as Paleblood output. The media rule in full The public documentation site may use an individual image or short clip when it materially helps explain a technical point, or supports criticism, research, or commentary. Each proposed asset needs its own provenance and rights review before it is copied into this private source or published. Attribution and educational intent are relevant context; neither alone grants permission. The review must identify the source, creator and rights holder where known, intended use, amount shown, attribution terms, permission or license (or a reasoned, asset-specific legal basis for the proposed use), privacy and security concerns, accessibility text, resizing or redaction, and maintainer approval. Use only the smallest portion that explains the point; frames drawn by Paleblood's own renderer are shown at full resolution. Do not publish extracted assets, proprietary captures , bulk game text, secrets, or material whose source cannot be established. Do not republish retired image collections or describe another project's screenshots as Paleblood output. The code repository's own rule The Paleblood code repository has its own rule: extracted game assets, game files and decompiler output never belong there, and contributors do not add game screenshots or clips. The only images it holds are our own work, added by the maintainer: recordings of our tools, and frames drawn by Paleblood's own renderer at full resolution, with attribution (its CONTRIBUTING.md, Rules). A media review for this site does not by itself place media in the code repository. Current media record Asset Status Bloodborne menu artwork in the sidebar Displayed with maintainer approval; rights unresolved Original SVG diagram Paleblood-owned, no game imagery Thirteen frames drawn by Paleblood's renderer ( Milestones ), from the first non-black frame to character creation Our own captures , full resolution (shown small in a grid, opened whole), maintainer-approved 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-10; each reviewed privately; rights holders credited Retired gallery Absent Attribution and a link to the source entry are on the Credits page. The sidebar artwork: display, provenance and rights The site menu shows the 256×256 Bloodborne menu artwork credited to r_dsgnd on SteamGridDB. It appears once per page as a small image at the top of the sidebar, above the section's links (on the homepage, above the Home link), shown as a banner 120 pixels tall cropped from the square picture, with descriptive alt text. Its contributor/source attribution and a link to the source entry are on the Credits page. The private asset record explains the supplied file's provenance and pixel match to the former wiki icon, intended display size, copyright rationale, and unresolved rights status. No license for redistribution of the underlying game artwork was found; contributor credit and the educational/research context are not treated as permission or as a guarantee of an exception. The maintainer approved this specific display through the review-and-merge workflow; the unresolved rights assessment remains recorded privately. The retired gallery remains absent. An original SVG diagram elsewhere in the encyclopedia is Paleblood-owned and contains no game imagery. Where the detailed records are kept Maintainers keep the detailed per-asset record privately; those records are not included in the generated website.

docs.text: Ghidra & PS4 Quirks Grant us eyes, grant us eyes! Plant eyes on our brains, to cleanse our beastly idiocy! Micolash, Host of the Nightmare Traps in the tools and the PS4 ABI that cost time. This page is the code repository's QUIRKS.md , copied in by tools/sync_progress.py , so the two never disagree. Traps in Ghidra and the PS4 ABI that cost time. Entries marked unconfirmed come from general PS4 / Orbis knowledge and have not been checked on this target yet; confirm or correct them when you hit them. The converted executable The ELF has no section headers (confirmed). The Orbis loader ( GhidraOrbis ) synthesizes blocks from the program headers: the executable PT_LOAD becomes .text , and its own heuristic splits .rodata , .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr off the end of it. The progress denominator is the functions Ghidra finds in that .text block, so it depends on the loader and the analysis. progress.py ties its numbers to the hash of the committed export, and the export prints how many functions fell outside .text . .eh_frame and .eh_frame_hdr are marked executable by the loader ; they are data. e_type is 0xfe10 (confirmed), not ET_EXEC or ET_DYN . The first PT_LOAD has p_vaddr 0, so the file does not say where the game lives; the convention below does. Optimized code splits and merges functions (tail calls, shared epilogues, cold paths in the same range). A "function" boundary in Ghidra may be wrong. Check the call sites before you claim a size. Ghidra shows stubs. Names come from public NID databases, not from the binary. Unconfirmed for this target's import layout. Shorter functions cannot be hooked that way, except function family members, whose jump overwrites only the compiler's NOP padding up to the next function ( docs/FAMILIES.md ). Example: kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) returns -3 after the EINVAL report. Since #189, tools/draft.sh marks each such span with ; GAP: and decodes it. Example: 0x01ea4a10 (#188) re-reads an entry at 0x01ea4b17 after the report and goes on to keep it. A five-byte call write at 0x02715d71 is partly overwritten by a later write starting at 0x02715d75 . The resulting instruction calls 0xffffffff917166f7 ; analyzing the first write alone gives the wrong target. A still later edit at 0x02713d76 replaces the incoming stock branch with a live path that loads SprjFlipper::frame_seconds , applies scalar min with 1/30 s, and jumps past the malformed residual code to 0x02715d79 . Direct intraprocedural control-flow walking finds no reachable incoming edge to the malformed call. This does not establish the absence of unknown external jumps. The invalid-owner route instead reads 0x0575a908 , initialized by this patch to bits 0x3c088889 (1/120 s). A replacement must reproduce the reachable patched routes, including their float operand order, rather than keep the stock time step because one isolated edit looks invalid. Retain the exact XML revision and replay all its writes before reasoning about option coverage; other revisions may differ. The file at that commit has SHA-256 cb85bec1aa772b1092327b231bcf81e42b8670d73a0a7032cf061e6da9d29e00 : check yours before tools/patch_overlap.py or tools/verify.py --patch . docs.text: Function families Tens of thousands of the game's functions are tiny copies of the same few bytes. A family replaces each such shape once, with one readable body, and proves it on every copy. Families move the function count far more than the byte count, so this page always shows both. At a glance What Empty methods, functions that return 0 or a fixed number, getters and setters of one field: each family is one exact byte shape, and every function with exactly that shape is a member. Proof Every member runs its edge cases on the original and on the replacement, compared as strictly as any hand-written function, and deliberately wrong versions must fail. Members are edge-verified : no in-game recording has reached them yet. Honest numbers Members are a large share of the functions but a very small share of the code's bytes (the table below). Most of the game's code is still ahead. Source Paleblood's docs/FAMILIES.md , merged in #515 , #527 , #529 and #531 (10 November 2026). Why the executable is full of tiny functions C++ code is full of small virtual methods and accessors. When a class overrides a method to do nothing, the compiler still emits a function for it: a lone ret . A getter that returns a pointer kept some way into an object becomes mov rax, [rdi+K]; ret , where rdi holds the object and K is where the field sits. The compiler emits these bodies again for every class, so the executable holds thousands of identical copies. Each is a real function in the export, so each counts in the function total, but each is only one to a few bytes long. Writing and proving each copy by hand would be pointless work, and leaving them out would leave the game's call graph full of unreplaced leaves. A family does them all at once. What makes a function a member A family is defined by its exact bytes, with at most one parameter (the field offset, or the constant returned). Paleblood's tools/family_scan.py reads your own copy of the executable and takes a function only when: its bytes are exactly the family's shape, from its start to its exported end; everything after it up to the next function is the compiler's padding, and there is enough room for the hook 's 14-byte jump, so installing the replacement overwrites only padding and never the next function (see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks ); nothing patches it: no relocation, no community frame-rate patch line, no other replacement or observation hook names it. Shapes are kept deliberately narrow. A body that reads a global, calls anything, or writes only part of a register (which would keep the caller's upper bytes) is not a family: no synthetic case could stand in for the value it depends on. The member count and bytes are written down before the member table is generated, and the generator refuses a table that differs, so a family cannot quietly grow. How a family is proved Every member runs its edge cases on the original machine code and on the replacement, with registers and memory compared exactly as for a single hand-written function. The cases seed the return register and the argument registers with values no replacement could guess, point every argument at a probe buffer, and compare all writable memory afterwards. On a sample of members, at least one per parameter value, every listed wrong version (a mutant) must fail, and for a parameterized family so must the replacement for a neighbouring value. A run with any failure or surviving mutant records nothing. Members become verified only the way any function does: with in-game recordings and an independent review. docs.text: C++ code is full of small virtual methods and accessors. When a class overrides a method to do nothing, the compiler still emits a function for it: a lone ret . A getter that returns a pointer kept some way into an object becomes mov rax, [rdi+K]; ret , where rdi holds the object and K is where the field sits. The compiler emits these bodies again for every class, so the executable holds thousands of identical copies. Each is a real function in the export, so each counts in the function total, but each is only one to a few bytes long. Writing and proving each copy by hand would be pointless work, and leaving them out would leave the game's call graph full of unreplaced leaves. A family does them all at once.

docs.text: Glossary: PS4 and port terms A running glossary for terms used across the devlog and the system pages. Hover any of them on another page for a short definition. The project Functional decompilation Rewriting the game's code as readable source that behaves exactly like the original, checked by running both on the same inputs. A matching decompilation goes further and requires the rebuilt bytes to be identical; this project does not, because the goal is a native port, not the original binary. What it does require is that every replaced function does the same thing: the same return value, the same memory written, the same calls made. Source port The game rebuilt from source to run natively somewhere else, here on a PC. It is where Paleblood is headed, not what it is today: the game does not run on Paleblood until its own runtime is far enough along. Hook A 14-byte jump written over the first bytes of an original function, pointing at the replacement. Every caller still calls the original address and lands in the replacement. A function shorter than the jump cannot be hooked this way. The hook table is installed by the runtime once it runs the game; the verification harness calls replacements directly. Thunk A tiny piece of code that only forwards a call. The game calls each PS4 library function through a thunk ; our replacements call the same thunks , so whatever answers the original's calls (the harness 's scripted stubs, or the runtime ) answers the replacement's the same way. Verification Replaced, edge-verified and verified A function is replaced once it is registered for hooking and the game library builds. It is edge-verified once its generated edge cases match the original instructions. It is verified once matching recorded-game cases also pass, mutation tests reject known wrong versions, and an independent reviewer approves the evidence and readability. These labels describe the recorded evidence, not every possible input or game state. tools/promote.py reruns the required cases and checks the review record before promotion; it does not create captures or supply approval. Harness, captures and edge cases The harness runs the original function from your own dump and its replacement, natively, outside the game, on the same inputs. Captures are inputs recorded while the game ran (the existing library was recorded on the old borrowed runtime ; Paleblood's own recorder now has a stable, self-identifying output format, but still needs production call sites); edge cases are generated for situations a short run does not reach. Mutation test Deliberately wrong versions of a replacement go through verification too: each must fail. If one passes, the cases cannot see that difference, and they are fixed before anything is called verified . Instruction trace and CFG coverage An instruction trace records supported memory accesses made while single-stepping a bounded fixture. A control-flow graph (CFG) describes blocks and the edges between them; dynamic CFG coverage records only the blocks and edges that the fixture actually reached. Complete supported coverage, partial coverage, and unavailable coverage are different outcomes. A skipped host call or unsupported instruction cannot be treated as a complete trace. See Architecture: Verification for the guarantees and limits. Runtime Runtime and loader The runtime is what the game's code runs on: Paleblood's own loader , which maps the executable and the game's own C library and file system modules and binds every system import, and its own versions of the PS4 system libraries, written clean-room. The project-owned runtime does not yet run the full game; see Runtime . Boot milestone and import coverage The runtime track measures how far the game's executable gets on Paleblood's own runtime . Import coverage distinguishes imports supplied by bundled guest modules, imports implemented by Paleblood, registered unresolved diagnostics, and unbound imports. The dashboard reports the last saved boot; registry changes alone do not refresh it. A boot milestone records a reached stage in startup, such as entry, threads, files, input, audio, video out, GPU, or first flip. The boot harness names the first unresolved call or execution failure. PS4 platform PS4, Orbis The PlayStation 4 runs an AMD x86-64 CPU (Jaguar) and Orbis OS, derived from FreeBSD. Because the CPU is x86-64 like a PC's, the game's code can run directly on a PC once something provides the operating system around it. SELF, ELF, PRX, eboot An ELF is the standard executable format of Linux and FreeBSD. The PS4 wraps executables in a SELF (signed ELF ); ours are fake-signed and unencrypted, so turning them back into ELFs only unwraps them. The main executable is eboot.bin ; PRX files are the PS4 's shared libraries. NID PS4 programs link to library functions by NID : a hash of the function's name. GhidraOrbis carries a database that turns NIDs back into names, so sceKernelUsleep shows up instead of a hash. FDE A Frame Description Entry: one function's unwind record in the executable's .eh_frame . Counting them gave an independent check on how many functions Ghidra found. GNM, PM4, GCN GNM is the PS4 's low-level graphics API; the game builds PM4 command packets for its AMD GCN graphics chip. Paleblood does not plan to emulate that chip: the graphics are to be rebuilt at the level of the game's own graphics layer, on Vulkan. vblank and flip The screen refreshes at a fixed rate; the gap between two refreshes is the vertical blank. A flip shows a finished frame at a vblank . The frame limiter can flip every vblank (60 frames a second on a 60 Hz screen) or every other one (30).

docs.text: How the Frame Limiter Works The first system of Bloodborne replaced in C++ is the one that decides how long each frame lasts. This page walks through it as the original does it, and as the replacement now does it, exactly the same way. At a glance When At the start of every frame, before the game's frame of work. Job Make sure the previous frame took long enough. Input One configuration value, Game.FlipMode . How it waits By spinning on the clock: precise, and it keeps one CPU core busy. next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work Where it sits Every frame, frame_timing_frame_step runs this sequence: Check. It asks the window whether the game is still running. Create, once. On the very first frame it creates the game's frame-pacing object, the SprjFlipper . Its constructor, frame_timing_flipper_init , reads one value from the game's configuration: Game.FlipMode . Pace. It calls the flipper's limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame . Work. Only after the limiter returns does the game do its frame of work. So the limiter runs at the start of every frame, and its job is to make sure the previous frame took long enough. Choosing the pace The flip mode picks one of five settings. Each sets two things in the flipper: the frame interval : a float, in seconds; the sync interval : how many vblanks a flip waits for. Mode Frame interval Sync interval 0, 1 1/30 s 2 2 1/60 s 1 3, 4 1/30 s 1 A pending mode can replace the current one at the start of a frame; a few flags reset the pacing state, for example after a load. Waiting out the frame The limiter reads the time with gettimeofday , works out how much of the frame's budget is left, and waits. The game carries two ways of waiting: Wait How it works Sleep, then spin Sleeps in chunks and spins the last few milliseconds. Spin only Reads the clock again and again until the time is up. A switch compiled into this build always picks the spinning one. That is why a quick frame can read the clock hundreds of thousands of times. It is precise, and it keeps one CPU core busy. The budget adapts. It is not always the full interval. The flipper keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring, marking the frames that ran late. If recent frames ran over, the next budget is shortened to catch up, but never below a third of the interval. Afterwards Once the wait is over, the limiter: records the frame's time in the ring; decides whether this frame counts as late, and if so drops the sync interval to 0 so the next flip does not wait for a vblank ; keeps a 16-frame history, from which it computes the frame rate the game reports; if a flag asks for it, tells another object that the game now targets 60 frames a second. The replacement The C++ version follows the original instruction by instruction, including how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats a value that is not a number. It also carries the port's first setting, BB_TARGET_FPS : BB_TARGET_FPS Effect unset Nothing changes. 30 A fixed interval of 1/30 s, no overrides. 60 A fixed interval of 1/60 s, no overrides. uncapped A fixed interval of 1/240 s, no overrides. The set values do what the community frame-rate patches do here, and the frame step passes the game the real frame time, as those patches do. See the frame timing page . How the replacement was checked It was compared with the original on every frame recorded in two game runs, including frames that spin on the clock for hundreds of thousands of reads, and on hand-written cases for every mode and flag; four deliberately wrong versions all failed. Each part of BB_TARGET_FPS is checked against the patch itself.

docs.text: Milestones The project's milestones in pictures: how far the game gets on Paleblood's own runtime, from the first recorded boot to the latest. First, the frames Paleblood's own renderer has drawn, in the order they first appeared; then the boot journey, generated from the saved boot records by tools/sync_progress.py . Visual history: frames from Paleblood's renderer These are the game's own frames, drawn on a PC by Paleblood's runtime and renderer from the maintainer's own copy, at full resolution as rendered (1920x1080), oldest first. Select a frame to see it at full size with its full caption (arrow keys move between frames, Esc closes). Each passed the media review on its own. Nothing here comes from another project, and no extracted game assets appear on this page. Bloodborne and its logos and art are © Sony Interactive Entertainment / FromSoftware; they are shown as evidence of technical milestones. Times are UTC: when the pull request that made each frame possible merged or, for local runs, when the frame was captured. Before 6 November 2026: black. The game ran its frames and flipped them ( #310 ), and the display showed them ( #313 ), but nothing drew into them. From #369 (6 November, 07:20) the renderer was wired into the running game, waiting for the game's drawing calls to reach it. After the title: local runs. Frames marked local run come from the maintainer's own runs of main with scripted input and with pull requests that were still in review applied; each caption names them. They are not saved boot records. 6 Nov, 18:18 First non-black frame 6 November, 18:18 ( #433 ): the first non-black frame. The game's compute pass clears its image to grey and its full-screen colour pass carries it to the screen; grey is the correct output of that pass. It proved the whole path: compute, the PS4's tiled image layouts, descriptors read from game memory, texture sampling, the draw and the flip. 6 Nov, 20:26 First logo 6 November, 20:26 ( #441 ): the first logo. The game's own logo pass, with its indexed draws, vertex colours and a BC7 texture, drawn through the renderer. 6 Nov, 20:46 JAPAN Studio card 6 November, 20:46 ( #442 ): once the renderer ran about 22 times faster, the boot reached the later logos. The JAPAN Studio card matches a reference capture pixel for pixel in the maintainer's local runs. 6 Nov, 20:46 FROM SOFTWARE card The FROM SOFTWARE card, from the same runs ( #442 ), also identical to the reference. 6 Nov, 20:46 Title screen The title screen, from the same runs ( #442 ). It differs from the reference only in the animated menu highlight (0.7% of pixels ). 6 Nov, ~22:05 Play Offline selected (local run) 6 November, about 22:05 (local run): "Play Offline" selected by scripted controller input, which presses buttons on a timetable so an unattended boot can get past the title ( #447 , merged 22:17). 6 Nov, ~22:05 Creating save data (local run) Same run: after "Play Offline" the game creates its save data, which Paleblood keeps in a host folder ( #402 ). The file writes in this run came from #444 (sceKernelWrite and sceKernelPwrite, by @EzequielRindello ), then in review and applied locally; it merged on 10 November at 08:11. 6 Nov, ~22:50 Main menu (local run) 6 November, about 22:50 (local run): the main menu (New Game, System, Log In). The save's next calls, sceKernelFtruncate and sceKernelRename, are answered by #449 (merged 22:39); the menu's draws needed 8- and 16-bit buffer formats, applied from the work that merged on 10 November as #457 , with #444 again applied locally. 10 Nov, ~07:30 Brightness screen (local run) 10 November, about 07:30 (local run): after New Game, the first-run Brightness screen. The run used #457 (8- and 16-bit format buffer loads, merged 07:06) with #470 (compute queues' buffers, in review), #471 (depth and stencil tests that read the buffer, merged later at 07:59) and #444 (which merged at 08:11) applied. 10 Nov, ~07:52 Controls screen (local run) 10 November, about 07:52 (local run): the next screen, Controls, on main after the 10 November runtime batch ( #458 to #469 ), again with #470 (in review), #471 and #444 applied (both merged soon after, 07:59 and 08:11). 10 Nov, ~08:20 First 3D scene: the opening cinematic (local run) 10 November, about 08:20 (local run): past the Controls screen, the first 3D scene the renderer draws, the game's opening cinematic with its subtitle. Its draws needed image descriptors loaded behind a branch, two-channel 8-bit images and samplers with anisotropy fields, which merged later that morning as #474 , #476 and #477 and were applied from review, with #470 (in review). 10 Nov, ~10:03 The opening cinematic, lit (local run) 10 November, about 10:03 (local run): further into the opening cinematic, the old man who offers the contract, drawn with his lighting, hair and lantern glow. By then the renderer recorded each buffer's work as one batch ( #463 ) and tiled its images on the GPU ( #472 , which brought the logos and title to the game's 30 fps cap). Renderer work then still in review was applied; the 3D features it needed merged later that day ( #494 to #540 , on the Runtime page). 10 Nov, ~11:34 Character creation (local run) 10 November, about 11:34 (local run): after the cinematic, character creation, the game's contract screen, drawn in full with its menu, default choices, starting attributes and button hints. It hands the GPU 70 command buffers in one submission, which the runtime had capped at 64 ( #504 ); renderer work then still in review was applied. The character preview on the right draws into float render targets ( #534 , #547 , merged that evening) and is still empty here. Later milestones (the first playable scene) are added here as they are reached. docs.text: These are the game's own frames, drawn on a PC by Paleblood's runtime and renderer from the maintainer's own copy, at full resolution as rendered (1920x1080), oldest first. Nothing here comes from another project, and no extracted game assets appear on this page. Bloodborne and its logos and art are © Sony Interactive Entertainment / FromSoftware; they are shown as evidence of technical milestones. Times are UTC: when the pull request that made each frame possible merged or, for local runs, when the frame was captured. Before 6 November 2026: black. The game ran its frames and flipped them ( #310 ), and the display showed them ( #313 ), but nothing drew into them. From #369 (6 November, 07:20) the renderer was wired into the running game, waiting for the game's drawing calls to reach it. After the title: local runs. Frames marked local run come from the maintainer's own runs of main with scripted input and with pull requests that were still in review applied; each caption names them. They are not saved boot records. 6 Nov, 18:18 First non-black frame 6 November, 18:18 ( #433 ): the first non-black frame. The game's compute pass clears its image to grey and its full-screen colour pass carries it to the screen; grey is the correct output of that pass. It proved the whole path: compute, the PS4's tiled image layouts, descriptors read from game memory, texture sampling, the draw and the flip. 6 Nov, 20:26 First logo 6 November, 20:26 ( #441 ): the first logo.
