docs.text: Runtime call reference The runtime's own detailed notes on each system call: the evidence, the exact behavior and what stops by name. This page is copied from Paleblood's docs/runtime-syscalls.md every time the wiki syncs, so it always matches the code. For the reader-friendly explanation of the same calls, start with Runtime system calls . This page records contracts used to implement small runtime calls in issues #34 and #41 . Public standards and manuals describe portable or platform-specific API behavior; they do not by themselves prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. Keep the distinction below, and leave unresolved behavior unresolved until public documentation, our own reverse engineering, or observed behavior settles it. Evidence in this repository The runtime registry distinguishes behavior it implements from diagnostics for behavior that is still unknown. RT_SYSLIB entries are callable implementations and count toward coverage; RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED entries remain callable so a reached import can fail with a useful name, but do not count as implemented or as supplied imports in progress reports. symbols/imports.csv records getpagesize and gettimeofday as imports of eboot from libScePosix ; libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . Import rows establish that the names are required, not their arguments, return values at every call site, or all clock IDs. The eight hash- verified target images ( eboot.elf and the seven modules, tools/check_target.py ) all state p_align 0x4000 for every PT_LOAD segment, with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000 (the difference is exactly 0x4000 in each; readelf -l prints the headers). The decompiled frame limiter calls gettimeofday with a null timezone argument. A separate verified clock helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , named CLOCK_MONOTONIC in that code. This confirms one monotonic clock request in the game; it does not establish every ID passed through the imported clock_gettime wrapper, or that no other ID is used in unexamined code. The sceKernelGetCompiledSdkVersion contract describes the observed libkernel getter, the runtime 's provider of mapped executable process-parameter metadata, and the dedicated synthetic registry tests. It also distinguishes that metadata provider from the unresolved console kernel syscall behavior. Interfaces and known behavior Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 getpagesize(void) No arguments. Returns the target's page size in bytes. The numeric value is platform-specific. getpagesize is not in current POSIX; portable code is directed to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . Linux and FreeBSD document the byte count; their manuals do not define a general error return for this function. Linux exposes it as a libc interface, not necessarily a dedicated kernel syscall. FreeBSD notes the system page size may differ from the underlying hardware page size. The import is present twice ( eboot from libScePosix , libc.elf from libkernel ), and both library names are registered against one implementation that answers 16384 , by the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c , #528). It is a ruling, not a measurement: the target images bound the value without picking one (every PT_LOAD of the eight hash- verified ELFs has p_align 0x4000 with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000, so the ELF ABI's congruence rule limits the page size to a divisor of 16384), stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096, and no public source names the console's own value; every PS4 runtime and port we can cite answers 16 KiB. See "getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown" below. What would still confirm it: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console. getpid(void) No arguments. Returns a pid_t naming the calling process. POSIX specifies that it succeeds and has no error return. Linux process IDs are scoped by PID namespaces; other systems have their own process-ID scope and lifecycle rules. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel ; libunwind passes the result to sysctl . The runtime answers a fixed id, 1000 , by the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c , #528, see "Process and input" below): runs stay reproducible, and the host's process id is not the guest's. The console's own value and its scope are not established. clock_gettime(clock_id, tp) clock_id selects a clock; tp points to a struct timespec . On the POSIX interface, tv_sec is seconds and tv_nsec is nanoseconds in [0, 1,000,000,000) . The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. POSIX uses 0 for success and -1 with errno for failure. An unsupported clock ID is an EINVAL case. Linux and BSD manuals document additional pointer-error details; use the target contract rather than assuming the host's errno mapping. The imported wrapper is present. The verified sceKernelClockGettime call requests ID 4 ( CLOCK_MONOTONIC ). That is evidence for the SCE entry point only, not proof of the libc wrapper's IDs. Other IDs and exact PS4 error and pointer handling remain unresolved. Unknown IDs must not silently return a fabricated time. gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds in [0, 1,000,000) . The historical timezone argument is passed as null at the confirmed game call site. The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. The wall clock can jump and is not a monotonic elapsed-time source. Historical POSIX specified a zero return on success and left errors undefined; Linux documents -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores the timezone argument. POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The imported wrapper and game call sites are present; the game passes null for the second argument. Exact target behavior for bad pointers, non-null timezone arguments, and error mapping is not established. Do not silently ignore an error without evidence. sched_yield(void) No arguments. Returns int . POSIX: the calling thread gives up the processor until it is again at the head of its thread list; 0 on success, -1 with errno otherwise, and POSIX defines no error case for it. FreeBSD documents the same call. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel . Implemented: a guest thread runs on a host thread, so the runtime yields the host thread and returns 0 ( runtime/syslib/kernel_thread.c ). A host failure has no FreeBSD error number to report, so it stops by name. Not observable in a unit test: that the host scheduler actually ran another thread. scePthreadYield Asks for the same yield through the thread library. The PS4 -visible signature is not established. FreeBSD's pthread_yield(3) is void ; Linux's is int (always 0 ). No PS4 -specific public source gives the SCE name's declaration. Imported by eboot and libc.elf from libkernel ; no call site in this repository shows whether the caller reads a result. Registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED : the entry stops by name and does not count as implemented. What would settle it: a guest call site showing whether the return register is read after the call, or a PS4 -specific public declaration. Do not assume an int or 0 from the FreeBSD or Linux analogues. memcpy(dest, src, n) , memset(dest, c, n) (libSceLibcInternal) void *memcpy(void *, const void *, size_t) and void *memset(void *, int, size_t) , the ISO C declarations. ISO C 7.24.2.1 and 7.24.6.1: memcpy copies n bytes from src to dest ; memset writes c converted to unsigned char into the first n bytes; both return dest . Overlapping memcpy regions and null pointers are undefined behaviour. Imported by libSceFios2.elf from libSceLibcInternal ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the host's own functions, since the standard fixes the whole result and no target-specific value is involved ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not modelled: what the PS4 C library does for the undefined cases; no public source or call site establishes it. sceKernelUsleep(microseconds) (libkernel), usleep(microseconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned 32-bit count of microseconds, returning int . For sceKernelUsleep the guest fixes the shape: the verified call sites in game/frame_timing/frame_limiter.cpp and game/render/swap_chain_present.cpp declare it as int(uint32_t microseconds) , and their cases expect 0 . FreeBSD's useconds_t is 32-bit unsigned. FreeBSD usleep(3) : suspends the thread for the given microseconds, 0 on success, -1 with EINTR if a signal interrupts it. SUSv2 also let usleep fail with EINVAL from 1,000,000 on; FreeBSD and POSIX.1-2008 (which removed usleep ) have no such limit. sceKernelUsleep is imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf , usleep by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: usleep with 1,000,000 or more, which stops by name because no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest sleeps or gets EINVAL ; and the SCE error, if any, for sceKernelUsleep , which the guest's sites never check. sleep(seconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned count of seconds, returning unsigned int : unsigned sleep(unsigned seconds) in POSIX and FreeBSD's sleep(3) . No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: suspends the thread until the seconds have elapsed or a caught signal arrives; returns 0 when the time has elapsed, otherwise the unslept seconds; no errors are defined. FreeBSD's libc ( lib/libc/gen/sleep.c ) is a nanosleep that rounds the unslept remainder up to whole seconds; above INT_MAX it sleeps INT_MAX seconds and returns seconds - INT_MAX without any signal. Imported by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested seconds and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left, as for usleep ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: more than INT_MAX seconds, which stops by name because POSIX has no early return without a signal and no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest gets the full sleep or FreeBSD's remainder. nanosleep(rqtp, rmtp) (libkernel) int nanosleep(const struct timespec *rqtp, struct timespec *rmtp) in POSIX and FreeBSD's nanosleep(2) , with FreeBSD amd64's struct timespec (two 64-bit fields, seconds and nanoseconds), the layout the clock_gettime entry uses. No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: suspends the thread until the requested time has elapsed and returns 0 ; a caught signal returns -1 with EINTR and writes the time left through a non-null rmtp ; nanoseconds outside [0, 1,000,000,000) are -1 with EINVAL ; rqtp and rmtp may point to the same object. A negative second count is not defined. FreeBSD's kern_time.c (same in stable/9 and main): the EINVAL check first, then a zero or negative time returns 0 at once without sleeping; nanosleep(2) adds EFAULT for a pointer it cannot use. Imported by libc.elf . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left and rmtp is never written, as for usleep and sleep ; the request is copied first, so rqtp and rmtp may be the same ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Stops by name: the errno cases (no rqtp , nanoseconds out of range), since errno is not modelled, as for clock_gettime . Open: a negative second count, which stops by name because POSIX does not define it, FreeBSD returns 0 at once and the host answers EINVAL , and no PS4 -specific source says which answer the guest gets. scePthreadRwlockInit(rwlock, attr, name) , scePthreadRwlockDestroy(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockRdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockWrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTryrdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTrywrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockUnlock(rwlock) (libkernel) A pointer to the guest's rwlock variable ( Init also an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); each returns int32_t . No call site in this repository shows these shapes; they come from the public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declarations, supporting evidence for the shapes only, and match FreeBSD's pthread_rwlock_* . POSIX pthread_rwlock_* , as FreeBSD libthr ( thr_rwlock.c ) and the kernel's umtx read-write lock ( kern_umtx.c ) implement it: a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use and a destroyed rwlock holding 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed rwlock; EBUSY from the try forms when the lock is not available; destroying does not check whether the lock is held, and leaves an unused initializer in place; unlocking is EPERM when another thread holds the write lock or when nobody holds the lock, and readers are counted, not named; a thread that locks again while holding the write lock is not given an error, it waits forever (no owner check in do_rw_wrlock or do_rw_rdlock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. Imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf ( Tryrdlock by libSceFios2.elf only; symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented on a host rwlock that also records the writer and the reader count, which the host does not expose, for the unlock answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_rwlock.c ). A missing variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do; unlocking a never-used initializer is EPERM , as for the mutex. Stops by name: Rdlock or Wrlock while the caller holds the write lock (the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK ; neither is useful to return), and an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock and Timedwrlock are under Timed locks . Not part of this entry: the libScePosix names. __stack_chk_fail(void) (libkernel) No arguments, no result: void __stack_chk_fail(void) , and it never returns (LSB; FreeBSD libc declares it __dead2 ). Compiler-generated code calls it, not application code. LSB Core: the function that called it is aborted with a message that a stack overflow was detected, and the program then exits. FreeBSD libc logs "stack overflow detected; terminated" and ends the process with SIGABRT . Imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented as a stop by name ( rt_fatal , which aborts): ending the program is the whole guest-visible contract, so the entry counts as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not covered: the PS4 's own message or crash report, which the guest cannot observe after it ends; and __stack_chk_guard , a separate data import whose PS4 value is not established (an unbound data import gets a zeroed page, runtime/boot.c ). _exit(status) (libkernel) One int , no result: void _exit(int status) , and it never returns (POSIX; FreeBSD's _exit(2) has the same shape and declares it __dead2 ). No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: the process ends at once; functions registered with atexit are not called and open streams are not flushed; the low 8 bits of status ( status & 0377 ) are available to the waiting parent, and the full value to waitid and SIGCHLD handlers. FreeBSD _exit(2) : the same, the C library's exit(3) runs the atexit handlers and flushes, then calls _exit . Imported by libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented: the host's _exit with the guest's status, which has the same contract ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Under the boot harness , rt_exit_observer records the run's outcome first, as rt_fatal_observer does for a stop: pbboot reports "exited with code" and the full status, from any guest thread, and still writes the boot record ( runtime/boot.c ). Not covered: what the PS4 shows the player when a game ends this way, which the guest cannot observe after it ends. scePthreadCondInit(cond, attr, name) , scePthreadCondDestroy(cond) , scePthreadCondSignal(cond) , scePthreadCondBroadcast(cond) , scePthreadCondWait(cond, mutex) , scePthreadCondTimedwait(cond, mutex, microseconds) (libkernel) Pointers to the guest's cond and mutex variables; each returns int32_t . The guest fixes the wait shapes: the verified game/kernel/condition_wait.cpp declares Wait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex) and Timedwait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex, uint32_t timeout_us) , a relative timeout in microseconds, not POSIX's absolute timespec . The public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares all six with these shapes ( Init with an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); it is supporting evidence for the shapes only. POSIX pthread_cond_* , as FreeBSD libthr implements it ( thr_cond.c ): a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use; a destroyed cond holds 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed cond; EBUSY to destroy one with waiters; destroying an unused initializer succeeds and leaves it in place; EPERM when the waiter does not own the mutex, for every mutex type, EINVAL when the mutex is destroyed ( _mutex_owned , thr_mutex.c ); ETIMEDOUT when a timed wait expires; a recursive mutex is released completely for the wait and its count restored after ( _mutex_cv_unlock , _mutex_cv_lock ). Clock IDs and platform differences The only clock ID confirmed by a decompiled game call in this repository is 4 , used with sceKernelClockGettime and identified there as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . This does not prove that the game passes 4 to the imported clock_gettime wrapper. POSIX defines clock identifiers symbolically; their numeric values are implementation-specific. Linux adds clocks such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Their names and numeric values are not interchangeable evidence for PS4 behavior. CLOCK_MONOTONIC represents elapsed time from an unspecified starting point and is not the wall clock. The precise effects of suspend, rate correction, and resolution vary by implementation. gettimeofday and CLOCK_REALTIME represent wall time tied to the Epoch and can move when system time changes. No source examined here establishes that the game asks the imported clock_gettime wrapper for CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or another ID. The standard byte-order contract converts host order to network (big-endian) order for hton* , and reverses that conversion for ntoh* ; this is documented by the FreeBSD byte-order manual . Paleblood's guest ABI is AMD64, so these four conversions are byte reversals. Their implementations do not call host networking APIs or depend on host socket state. All sixteen PT_LOAD segments of those eight images have p_align 0x4000 , and in every one p_offset - p_vaddr is exactly 0x4000 . Three guest call sites share one shape: 0x00e04168 , 0x00e04939 and 0x00e05cf9 , each inside functions 0x00e04140 , 0x00e045c0 and 0x00e05a80 . Each is a lazy initialiser: a guard tests 0x05859ec0 , the call is made, the result is cltq -extended, blsr %rax,%rcx with jne rejects it unless it is a power of two, and the value is cached in 0x05859ec8 beside three fixed siblings ( 0x10000 , 0x40000 , 0x200000 ). 0x05859ec8 has exactly five cross-references in the executable: the three writes above and two reads, all inside those same three functions. Inferred, and the premise each inference needs : The ELF ABI takes p_align of a loadable segment to be a multiple of the system page size, and requires p_offset and p_vaddr to be congruent modulo the page size. If the PS4 loader follows both rules for these segments , a page size larger than 0x4000 could not map them at their fixed addresses, while any power-of-two divisor of 0x4000 could. Restricting that to 0x1000 , 0x2000 and 0x4000 adds a second assumption - that the page size is at least 4096 - which is ours, not observed. The guest's own blsr check is consistent with every power of two and selects none of them. So p_align bounds the candidate set under our premises; it does not measure the value the kernel returns, and none of the three candidates is established. Unknown : the number the PS4 reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096 ( PAGE_SHIFT 12 , sys/amd64/include/param.h ), and Sony's open-source page confirms a FreeBSD kernel but publishes the upstream sources rather than the console's modifications, so that value describes the ancestor and not the target. Our own loader does not depend on a page size either: it copies PT_LOAD segments at byte-exact p_vaddr into one image buffer ( runtime/loader.c , rt_elf_map ) and uses p_align only for TLS, and the 4096 s in runtime/boot.c are host allocation sizes. A size other than 16 and a missing structure stop by name. 0 is the success value, the convention public SCE-family documentation states for these calls (the @return 0 on success lines in psp2/error.h of vita-headers). libSceNetCtl's own error codes have no public source, so no path in runtime/syslib/netctl.c returns one: a case that would need an error value stops the boot by name instead. Thread attribute detach state ( scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate , issue #34) eboot and libSceFios2.elf import scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate from libkernel , and eboot imports pthread_attr_setdetachstate from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ). Each source below establishes a different part: What the call does: POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate . A thread created with the attribute starts detached for PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and joinable for PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE . Invalid detach state: POSIX and FreeBSD's pthread_attr(3) both make any other value EINVAL . Invalid attribute variable: POSIX leaves a null or uninitialised attribute undefined and only recommends EINVAL , and the FreeBSD manual lists no error for it. The behaviour comes from FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_setdetachstate ( lib/libthr/thread/thr_attr.c ), which returns EINVAL when the variable is null or holds no attribute object. The numbers: FreeBSD's <pthread.h> defines the two states as 0 and 1 . The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK header ( include/orbis/_types/pthread.h ) defines ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE and ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED with the same values. That header follows FreeBSD's text, so it corroborates the numbers rather than measuring them independently. As with the mutex functions ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ), the SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number, and the POSIX name returns the number itself. Still open: the detach state a fresh attribute starts with, and the one scePthreadAttrGet copies from a running thread. Both are values the system supplies. POSIX makes joinable the default, but nothing we can cite confirms what the PS4 reports. In FreeBSD libthr, _pthread_create ( thr_create.c ) uses that same default ( _pthread_attr_default ) when it is given no attribute variable or an empty one. The runtime treats both cases as the unknown default, so the outcome, a fatal, does not depend on the PS4 matching libthr there. How the runtime keeps that open: The attribute records a state only when one is set ( has_detach_state ). scePthreadAttrGet replaces the whole attribute, as libthr's pthread_attr_get_np does, so a state set before the copy is dropped. By convention, thread creation reads the state through rt_thread_attr_detach_state ( runtime/include/runtime/process.h ) and never from the field. A fresh attribute's field holds zero, which is the joinable value, so reading the field directly would assume joinable silently. For no variable, an empty variable, or a state nobody set, the reader stops the process ( rt_fatal ), names the call that asked, and says which of those cases it hit. What would settle it: an observed scePthreadAttrGetdetachstate result on a console, for a fresh attribute and for one filled by scePthreadAttrGet from the main thread. Guest call sites would also settle it: a thread created without a detach state being set, then joined or detached ( scePthreadJoin , pthread_join and scePthreadDetach are imported). POSIX names of the thread self and attribute calls ( libScePosix , issue #34) eboot imports pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ), next to the libkernel SCE names the runtime already implements. They are the same calls with the POSIX error convention, as for the mutex and detach-state calls: pthread_self has no error return (POSIX), so it answers what scePthreadSelf answers: the calling thread's own variable value. With no guest thread registered on the host thread it stops by the name the guest used. pthread_attr_init allocates the attribute object and stores it in the variable; ENOMEM when it cannot (POSIX; FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_init ). pthread_attr_destroy frees it and empties the variable; EINVAL for a missing or empty variable (libthr's _pthread_attr_destroy ). The POSIX names return the error number itself, the SCE names 0x80020000 plus it, and an object made under one name is freed under the other. A missing variable passed to pthread_attr_init is undefined in POSIX and unchecked in libthr. The runtime answers EINVAL under both names, as the SCE name already did; no PS4 source or call site says otherwise. Mutex ownership ( scePthreadMutexUnlock , issue #132) A mutex belongs to the thread that locked it. FreeBSD libthr ( thr_mutex.c , the same in stable/9 and main) checks that for every mutex type: Unlocking a mutex the caller does not own is EPERM , whether it is free or another thread holds it ( mutex_unlock_common ); so is a condition wait with it ( _mutex_owned ). The owner locking again gets EDEADLK for the error-checking (default) and adaptive types, and waits forever for the normal type, on purpose ( mutex_self_lock ). Its trylock is EBUSY for all three ( mutex_self_trylock ). A recursive mutex counts one more level. The host (glibc) checks the owner only for its error-checking and recursive types, and its adaptive type waits forever when the owner locks again. So the runtime makes every non-recursive guest mutex an error-checking host mutex, and keeps the guest type for its own answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ): scePthreadMutexUnlock , pthread_mutex_unlock and the condition waits answer EPERM for a caller that does not own the mutex, for the normal and adaptive types too. The adaptive type locked again by its owner answers EDEADLK , as in libthr. The normal type locked again by its owner stops by the name the guest used ( scePthreadMutexLock or pthread_mutex_lock ): the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK , and neither is useful to return. The SCE names return 0x80020000 plus the error number, the libScePosix names the number itself. One difference left: the adaptive type no longer spins before it sleeps, as libthr's and glibc's do; that changes timing only, not an answer. Timed locks ( scePthreadMutexTimedlock , scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock , scePthreadRwlockTimedwrlock , issue #34) Each takes the lock variable and the most it may wait, in microseconds from now (OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares an OrbisKernelUseconds ; shadPS4 binds the three names to libthr's relative-time calls, pthread_mutex_reltimedlock_np and pthread_rwlock_reltimed*lock_np , facts only). The executable's lock wrappers take them for any timeout but -1, which uses the untimed call: 0x02484119 (mutex) tells EDEADLK , EINVAL , EAGAIN and ETIMEDOUT apart, and 0x0247f681 and 0x0247f411 (rwlock) EDEADLK , EINVAL and ETIMEDOUT . What the runtime does: - The wait ends with the lock, or with ETIMEDOUT once the time has passed, on the monotonic clock (as for scePthreadCondTimedwait ). - The owner asking again. With a timeout, libthr's mutex_self_lock sleeps the whole time and answers ETIMEDOUT for the error-checking, adaptive and normal types; a recursive mutex takes one more level. The kernel's umtx rwlock has no owner check, so a thread holding the write lock that asks again waits out the time too ( do_rw_rdlock , do_rw_wrlock ). The host would answer EDEADLK at once, so the runtime sleeps the time itself. - A destroyed lock or a missing variable is EINVAL , and the static initializers are set up on first use, as for the untimed calls. Direct memory ( libkernel , issue #34) eboot imports sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize , sceKernelAllocateDirectMemory , sceKernelMapDirectMemory and sceKernelReleaseDirectMemory ( symbols/imports.csv ). Its first use is the startup heap, at 0x02481a80 : It asks for the size. It allocates 0x7400000 bytes, aligned to 0x200000 , anywhere from 0 to that size, with memory type 0. It maps the range read/write (protection 3) with flags 0, so the system picks the address, at the same alignment. If the map fails, it releases the range. On any failure it logs an error and builds its heap from a null base, so these calls have to succeed. The signatures match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h , as supporting evidence only. The pool. Direct memory is a host memory file. An allocation is a range of it and a map is a host mapping of that range, so two maps of one range see the same bytes. The size. sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize answers the size of that pool (5 GiB), a choice of the runtime . The PS4 's value is not established here. A title that sizes its allocations from the answer sizes them from the runtime 's pool. Allocation. It takes the lowest start at or above the search start that fits before the search end. GPU access. The executable maps with protection 3 and 0x33 , CPU and GPU read/write ( 0x10 and 0x20 in the public SDK list). The host mapping takes the CPU bits. Where a map goes. Without an address hint, the system chooses: A GPU-visible map goes at a fixed base ( 0x2000000000 ) plus its offset in the pool. Every such address is then a fixed distance from the same byte of the pool, which is how the renderer's GPU will reach guest memory: it gets the whole pool as one buffer ( runtime/gpu_memory.h , docs/RENDERER.md ). Other maps go anywhere free in the map window above that region. A second GPU-visible map of a range would need the same place, so it stops by name. A boot doesn't make one: every range it maps, it maps once. With a hint, a map goes where the hint says (below). What stops by name. Every case whose PS4 answer is not established stops with the function's name: lengths, starts or alignments that are not multiples of 16 KiB (the granularity the executable's calls use); memory types other than 0, 3 and 10; map flags other than no-overwrite ( 0x80 , shadPS4's kernel memory.h ). No-overwrite keeps a map off memory already mapped, and the runtime never replaces a mapping, so it changes nothing. The movie code ( 0x02d032b9 ) passes it with no address, to map part of its own direct memory a second time; protection other than CPU and GPU read and write; a range that does not fit or was not allocated; releasing part of a range or a mapped one; the error values. Measured with a local boot that let the libc affinity probe return (not committed): with these four calls the executable's heap setup succeeds and the boot reaches entry . It stops next at scePthreadRwlockInit . Range arithmetic The existing sceKernelAllocateDirectMemory and sceKernelMapDirectMemory implementations validate lengths by subtraction after checking the starting address. This prevents a full-width length from wrapping an end address and passing the allocation or containment check. An allocation must fit wholly inside its end-exclusive search range; a map must fit inside one live allocation. Misaligned address hints still stop by the API name before mapping. test_direct_memory_bounds exercises the registered calls with exact boundaries, overlong and wrapping ranges, a misaligned hint and a valid writable map. These are host validation limits, without a claim about native error codes. What the title's C library imports (libc.elf and libSceFios2, issue #34) libc.elf is Sony's FreeBSD-derived libc, with HP libunwind for C++ exceptions. These call sites are in libc.elf unless marked; libSceFios2 imports from libSceLibcInternal . Data - __progname points at "eboot.bin" (shadPS4, the deadinside28 port). - _Stdout ( libSceLibcInternal ) is a 456-byte object, the size of libc.elf 's own _Stdout . libSceFios2 only passes its address to fflush . - Need_sceLibcInternal is an int holding 1. libSceFios2 stores its address and never reads it. A signal outside 1 to 128, or a handler other than SIG_DFL for SIGKILL or SIGSTOP, answers SIG_ERR with EINVAL (FreeBSD's rules). - __cxa_finalize ( libSceFios2 ) does nothing: the module registers no handlers. Other descriptors stop by name. - fflush ( libSceFios2 ) flushes the host's standard output for &_Stdout , and every host stream for NULL. Memory - mmap . Anonymous private read-write maps ( +0x52fac and others) are flexible memory, rounded up to 16 KiB (shadPS4's posix_mmap , and a native port family). - EINVAL for a zero length, a descriptor other than -1, or a non-zero offset. - File maps, hints, and other flags or protections stop by name. - munmap is sceKernelMunmap with -1 and errno. - msync is libunwind's mapped-memory probe ( +0x541a5 ). A semaphore is a runtime object behind the handle. Wait blocks until the units are there. Waiters are served in the order they arrived, or with attr 2 by thread priority: - the best priority goes first, which is the smallest number (OpenOrbis _types/user.h : 0x100 highest, 0x2FF lowest); - equal priorities are served in arrival order; - each waiter is placed by the priority its thread has when it starts to wait. Ending a thread ( scePthreadExit ) scePthreadExit(void *value) ends the calling thread with value , as a return from its entry would: the value kept for a join, then the thread's key destructors, then the end (FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_exit , and shadPS4's posix_pthread_exit ). The runtime does not unwind the guest's frames, which were not built for the host's unwinder. Instead the thread's host side marks where it starts the guest's entry ( setjmp ), and an exit returns there ( longjmp ). It then ends exactly as a return does. Thread attributes: stack size and scheduling policy (issue #34) The executable's thread wrapper ( 0x02a3b324 – 0x02a3b46e ) sets up each thread like this: It initializes an attribute. It sets the stack size: the caller's size, or 64 KiB by default. If that is refused, it retries with 16 KiB and reports a fatal error if that fails too. It sets detach state 0 and scheduling policy 1. It creates the thread with (&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) , comparing a failure with EPERM, EINVAL and EAGAIN as SCE codes. It destroys the attribute and sets the new thread's affinity to a mask of the six bits 0x3f . What the runtime does: scePthreadAttrSetstacksize and pthread_attr_setstacksize record the size. The stack's address is left to the system, as libthr keeps one address and size per attribute. Sizes below 16 KiB are refused with EINVAL. libthr refuses sizes below its minimum that way, and the executable's wrapper names the PS4 's minimum: its callers pass smaller sizes, and when one is refused it asks again for exactly 16 KiB ( 0x02a3b383 ). scePthreadAttrSetschedpolicy records one of FreeBSD's three policies (FIFO 1, OTHER 2, RR 3). libthr refuses any other with ENOTSUP, whose SCE value is not established, so another policy stops by name. A missing attribute answers EINVAL (as an SCE code under the SCE names). It is registered, so scePthreadSelf answers the new thread's handle. entry(argument) is called with the guest's convention. A return ends the thread (POSIX). The attribute's detach state decides whether the host thread is joinable. The scheduling policy is recorded, but the host schedules the thread: guest priorities are not modelled. The variable's first int is its state: 0 never done (the static initializer), 1 done, 2 in progress, 3 in progress with waiters. A caller that finds it in progress waits for the end; any other state is EINVAL . libc.elf calls it five times ( +0xad02 , +0x1b292 , +0x54ecb and two tail calls) with a static variable and a routine. Nothing cancels a guest thread, so a routine always runs to its end. scePthreadRename(thread, name) records a thread's name (OpenOrbis libkernel.h ; libthr's pthread_set_name_np , to which shadPS4 binds it, facts only). The executable's job threads rename themselves with it (a tail call at 0x00466834 ). The runtime keeps the first 31 bytes, as for the name scePthreadCreate takes, names the host thread with the first 15 (the host's limit; debuggers and the host's thread list show it), and answers 0. Stops by name: a thread the runtime does not know or has collected, and a missing name. PlayGo ( libScePlayGo ) PlayGo lets a title start before all of its package is installed: the title asks which chunks of the package are present. On this runtime the whole title is always present, so every chunk is reported installed ( runtime/syslib/playgo.c ). The user service's start-up calls ( libSceUserService , issue #36) eboot imports sceUserServiceInitialize , sceUserServiceTerminate , sceUserServiceGetInitialUser and sceUserServiceGetLoginUserIdList , among others. The shapes match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's UserService.h and _types/user.h (supporting evidence only): - the parameter block holds a uint32_t priority; - the login list is four user ids, an unused slot holding -1; - id 0xFF is the system's. The executable initializes the service twice: - once at 0x024e1e69 , with priority 0x2bc ; - again at 0x010ba1ac , where it accepts success or exactly 0x80960003 . So a second initialize answers 0x80960003 , the "already initialized" code. What the runtime does. It models one user, the person running it, logged in from the start: - GetInitialUser answers that user's id; - the login list holds it, then three -1 slots; - the id is a handle the runtime hands out, never -1 or 0xFF , because the PS4 's ids are the system's and a title only passes them back. What stops by name: a call before initialize, a missing argument, and the other error values. The user's name ( sceUserServiceGetUserName(int32_t, char *, const size_t) , in OpenOrbis UserService.h ; a name is at most 16 characters). The executable asks with 17 bytes ( 0x02561cd7 ) or a size it computed ( 0x0111bdfe ), and goes on only on 0. The name is the runtime 's choice, Hunter , written with its terminating zero. A user the runtime did not hand out, or a buffer too small for the name, stops by name. Login and logout events ( sceUserServiceGetEvent(OrbisUserServiceEvent *) , the event being a type, 0 login or 1 logout, and a user id; "no event" is 0x80960007 , OpenOrbis errors.h ). No user logs in or out during a run, so every call answers 0x80960007 and writes nothing. The executable's one caller ( 0x025628e4 ) is a polling thread: after any non-zero answer it sleeps 33 ms ( sceKernelUsleep(0x80e8) ) and asks again, and it handles a login or logout only when one comes. It never waits for the first user's login to be reported; whether the PS4 reports that login is not public. The real-time clock ( libSceRtc ) The runtime gives the host's local time, and keeps ticks as its own convention ( runtime/syslib/rtc.c ). Sources. - Signatures: OpenOrbis Rtc.h gives sceRtcGetCurrentClockLocalTime(date and time *) , sceRtcGetTick(const date and time *, uint64_t *) and sceRtcSetTick(date and time *, const uint64_t *) . It names sceRtcGetTickResolution without a signature; the executable's one call ( 0x010b70ea ) takes no argument and uses the int32_t answer as ticks per second, a negative one being a failure. - The date and time is six 16-bit fields (year, month, day, hour, minute, second), then a 32-bit microsecond at offset 12, 16 bytes in all. Rtc.h gives the microsecond 16 bits, which cannot hold 999999. The Vita homebrew SDK's SceDateTime , of the same library family, gives it 32 bits in a 16-byte structure, and the executable copies the whole structure as 16 bytes. - Ticks: the executable compares ticks, takes their differences and asks for the resolution. It holds no constant relating them to another epoch (neither the span from 0001 to 1970 in microseconds or seconds, nor its negation). About 60 sites ask for the local time; those reached pass it straight to sceRtcGetTick . What the runtime does. - The local time is the host's, in the time zone of the person running the runtime , as the console gives the one its owner set. A leap second shows as :59 . - A tick is the runtime 's own convention, the same in every call: microseconds since 0001-01-01 00:00:00 (proleptic Gregorian), 1000000 per second. sceRtcSetTick reverses sceRtcGetTick exactly. - Stops by name: a date out of range (including February 30 and February 29 of a non-leap century), a tick past the year 9999, a missing argument, and every error value. Day of the week: sceRtcGetDayOfWeek(year, month, day) ( 0x024ee2a9 , its answer packed into 3 bits) answers 0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday. The PS4Recomp project's libSceRtc numbers the days so, and notes that a real PS4 's ticks count from year 1, as these do; both are used as facts only. (The PSP SDK documents 0 as Monday, for an older library.) A date out of range stops by name. Unix time, time zones, RFC 2822 and the network tick (issue #40) These five calls relate ticks to Unix time and to UTC ( runtime/syslib/rtc.c , tests in test/syslib/rtc_time_zones.c ). Ticks and Unix time: a tick counts microseconds from year 1, so 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC is tick 62135596800000000. PS4Recomp's libSceRtc and shadPS4's rtc.cpp both relate them so (facts only). sceRtcSetTime_t(date and time *, time_t) ( 0x010b70a6 : seconds parsed from text, then sceRtcGetTick on the result, going on only on 0) gives the UTC date and time that many seconds after 1970. Both sources say the answer depends on the SDK the title was built with: before SDK 3.00 only the low 32 bits count, from 3.00 a negative count is an error. Counts from 0 to 0xffffffff mean the same either way; others stop by name. sceRtcConvertUtcToLocalTime(const tick *, tick *) and sceRtcConvertLocalTimeToUtc (11 and 2 call sites, such as 0x01969648 and 0x019696ae ; each passes a local copy of the tick and treats anything but 0 as no time) use the host's time zone, as the local time above does, with its daylight saving rule at that instant. A local time that the clock skips or shows twice at a daylight saving change stops by name, because the PS4 's choice there is not established. sceRtcFormatRFC2822LocalTime(char *, const tick *utc) ( 0x023e5ca9 , with no tick, which means now) writes RFC 2822 section 3.3's date and time in the host's local time, such as Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:05:09 +0100 : 31 characters and a NUL, the day of the month in two digits as both sources write it. sceRtcGetCurrentNetworkTick(tick *) ( 0x01086f50 , 0x010b70cf ; 0 is success, and the first treats a failure as no time) answers the current UTC tick from the host's clock, as both sources do. The host's wall clock stands for the network clock. Stops by name: a missing argument, and a time before year 1 or past the year 9999. The controller ( libScePad ) The runtime models one standard controller, the one user's, always connected ( runtime/syslib/pad.c ). Its state comes from the input backend ( runtime/input_host.h , runtime/input/ ): by default ( pbboot --input none , tools/boot.py --input none ) none is installed and the pad is at rest, so CI and recorded boots read the same state as before. With --input host the host's first gamepad and the window's keyboard drive it, and the title's vibration rumbles the gamepad. Sources. - Signatures and layouts: the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Pad.h , _types/pad.h and _types/errors.h . They give the 120-byte OrbisPadData (touch data at 0x34 : a count, seven reserved bytes, then two 8-byte touches of x, y and an id), the 28-byte OrbisPadInformation , the two-byte vibration block (large motor, then small), port type 0 (standard), and ALREADY_OPENED 0x80920004 . - Button bits: OpenOrbis' OrbisPadButton ; shadPS4's OrbisPadButtonDataOffset ( src/core/libraries/pad/pad.h ) agrees: L3 0x2 , R3 0x4 , options 0x8 , up 0x10 , right 0x20 , down 0x40 , left 0x80 , L2 0x100 , R2 0x200 , L1 0x400 , R1 0x800 , triangle 0x1000 , circle 0x2000 , cross 0x4000 , square 0x8000 , touch pad 0x100000 . - The executable's own calls agree: - before each scePadReadState ( 0x02a90168 , 0x02a91948 ) it clears exactly 120 bytes, and afterwards it tests connected at offset 0x4c ; - scePadGetControllerInformation gets a cleared 28-byte block. The title reads the touch resolution, dividing a non-zero touch point by it, and the stick deadzones: a stick within 0x80 ± the deadzone counts as centred; - scePadInit is called once ( 0x02fa6182 ), and the result is not read; - scePadOpen(initial user, 0, 0, NULL) keeps any handle ≥ 0, and the title closes before it opens again; - scePadSetVibration is called with the title's speeds ( 0x02a9c7c1 ) or with both 0 to stop ( 0x02a9c822 ), and 0 counts as success. - The DualShock 4: the touch pad is 1920 × 942 ( DS4_TOUCHPAD_WIDTH and _HEIGHT in the Linux kernel's drivers/hid/hid-playstation.c ); each stick axis is a byte, 0 at the left and at the top; a touch carries a 7-bit id that changes for each new touch; the left motor is the strong one (a force-feedback effect's strong magnitude goes to motor_left ). - SDL3: stick axes run -32768 (left, up) to 32767 (right, down) and triggers 0 to 32767 ( SDL_GetGamepadAxis ); touch fingers are 0..1 of the pad ( SDL_GetGamepadTouchpadFinger ); scancodes are USB HID keyboard usages ( SDL_scancode.h ); SDL_RumbleGamepad 's low-frequency motor is the left one. - The timestamp is the process time in microseconds when the state is read, as shadPS4 stamps it ( src/input/controller.cpp ); the title does not read it. Call Runtime scePadInit 0 scePadOpen handle 1, the runtime 's choice; a second open while it is open answers 0x80920004 scePadClose 0; the pad can be opened again scePadReadState the backend's buttons, sticks, triggers and touches, the timestamp, connected 1; no motion, identity orientation. At rest without a backend: no button, sticks 0x80 , triggers 0, no touch, timestamp 0 scePadGetControllerInformation touch pad 1920 × 942; stick deadzones 13 (the runtime 's choice); connected; a local pad scePadSetVibration 0; the speeds are kept ( rt_pad_vibration ) and passed to the backend: with --input host , the large motor to SDL's low-frequency rumble, the small one to the high-frequency rumble Host input ( pbboot --input host , tools/boot.py --input host ). It needs a build with SDL3 (the window's) and --display window , since the window's event loop reads the devices: SDL's events are pumped on the display's thread ( display_vulkan.c ), never from a guest thread, and after each pump rt_input_host_pump samples the gamepad and keyboard there ( runtime/input/input_host_sdl.c ). The state therefore changes once per presented frame. For example: Text Only python3 tools/boot.py --display window --audio host --input host The first connected SDL gamepad is used, and the next one when it is removed. Its buttons map by position: south cross, east circle, west square, north triangle, start options, back and the touch pad click the touch pad, the shoulders L1 and R1, the stick clicks L3 and R3, the D-pad the D-pad. A DualShock 4 or DualSense touch pad reports up to two touches. Stick bytes are the axis' top eight bits after the offset; the triggers are scaled to 0..255. The keyboard works with or without a gamepad; a key's stick direction overrides the gamepad's stick, both keys of an axis cancel out, and buttons combine. The default layout ( rt_default_keys , runtime/input/input.c ): Keys Pad W A S D left stick up, left, down, right (full deflection) arrow keys right stick I J K L D-pad up, left, down, right Return, Space cross Backspace circle R square F triangle Q / E L1 / R1 Z / C L2 / R2, fully pressed left Shift / Tab L3 / R3 Escape options T touch pad click The runtime 's choices: the L2 and R2 bits are set while their trigger is off zero; touch ids count 0..127 and wrap, down fingers listed first; a held vibration is sent to SDL again every 30 seconds, as SDL's rumble lasts at most about 65. Scripted input ( pbboot --input-script SPEC , tools/boot.py --no-record --input-script SPEC ). For unattended boots, a timed script plays the controller through the same backend interface ( runtime/input/input_script.c ); it works with any --display mode and cannot be combined with --input host . SPEC is the script, or @FILE to read it from a file. Events are separated by commas, semicolons or new lines, and # starts a comment. Each event is WHEN:CONTROLS[*HOLD] : WHEN is seconds since the process started ( 45 , 45.5s ) or frames presented by video out's first port ( 700f ). Frames follow the game's own progress, so they suit a slow boot; seconds need no display. CONTROLS are names joined by + : cross circle square triangle up down left right l1 r1 l2 r2 l3 r3 options touch , and the stick directions lstick-up lstick-down lstick-left lstick-right and rstick-up ... rstick-right at full deflection. A scripted trigger is fully pressed. The controls are held from WHEN for HOLD , on the same clock (default 0.25 s or 4 frames), then released; overlapping events combine. pbboot writes pbboot: input script: event N starts (S s, frame F) when the title first reads the pad during an event, so a run's log shows when each press landed. For example: Text Only python3 tools/boot.py --no-record --display headless --input-script "45:down,47:cross" A malformed event, an unknown control, a hold on the other clock, more than 256 events or a script file over 64 KiB is refused before the boot, naming the event. Fields the executable does not read are left zero. Not modelled: motion. The accelerometer and gyroscope are not forwarded, because the units and axes the system reports them in are not established here (shadPS4 scales SDL's m/s² by 0.098 without a source); acceleration and angular velocity stay 0 and the orientation the identity. Stops by name: a second initialize, a call before initialize, another user, port type, index or open parameters, an unknown handle, a missing argument, and the other error values. The motion settings (issue #36). scePadResetOrientation(handle) (OpenOrbis Pad.h ) makes the pad's present attitude the reference its orientation is reported from; scePadSetAngularVelocityDeadbandState(handle, bool) and scePadSetTiltCorrectionState(handle, bool) (named in Pad.h without a signature; shadPS4's pad.cpp declares (int32_t handle, bool enable) , used as a fact) switch the motion sensors' deadband and tilt correction. The executable calls each through a small wrapper ( 0x02a9082e , 0x02a90852 , 0x02a90882 ) with its open handle, and a bool for the two settings, and counts 0 as success. Since motion is not modelled, a reset leaves the reported orientation the identity, neither setting changes a reading with no motion, and each call answers 0 ( test/syslib/pad_motion_settings.c ). An unknown handle and a setting other than 0 or 1 stop by name. The on-screen keyboard, canceled ( libSceImeDialog , issue #36) Facts. OpenOrbis ImeDialog.h and _types/ime_dialog.h give: - the shapes: sceImeDialogInit(setting, extended) , GetStatus() , GetResult(result) and Term() ; - the statuses: NONE 0, RUNNING 1, STOPPED 2; - the result: an end status (OK 0, CANCEL 1, ABORT 2) followed by 12 reserved bytes. shadPS4's ime_dialog.cpp (facts only) gives the states: Init from NONE to RUNNING, Abort from RUNNING to finished with ABORT, and Term from finished to NONE. The executable's keyboard ( 0x02d03f80 ): - Opening. It fills a setting with a text buffer that holds the initial text, calls Init with no extended setting, and takes 0 as open. - Polling. Each frame, 0x02d03df0 asks GetStatus. On 2 it reads the result: end status 0 takes the buffer's text; 1 and 2 (or a failed GetResult) take none. - Closing. 0x02d03e70 then calls Term. 0x02d04300 calls Abort while the keyboard is open and takes 0 as closed. What the runtime does: - Cancel. Init opens the keyboard, and the first GetStatus finds it closed with CANCEL, as if the user backed out at once. The title takes no text, the buffer is left as given, and nothing is shown. - Abort and Term. Abort of an open keyboard closes it with ABORT, and Term closes the library. What stops by name: - Init without a setting, or while a keyboard is open or not yet terminated (shadPS4 answers busy, 0x80bc0001 ; this is not confirmed); - GetResult before the keyboard closed, or with no structure; - Abort when no keyboard is open; - Term before the keyboard closed. An extended setting is ignored. The mouse, not connected ( libSceMouse , issue #36) The runtime has no host mouse, so it answers as a console with no mouse plugged in ( runtime/syslib/mouse.c , tests in test/syslib/mouse_not_connected.c ). Sources. shadPS4's libSceMouse ( mouse.h , mouse.cpp , mouse_error.h ; facts only) gives the shapes: sceMouseInit(void) , sceMouseOpen(user, type, index, param) , sceMouseRead(handle, data, count) answering how many records it wrote (1 to 64 asked for), sceMouseClose(handle) , the 40-byte record { uint64_t timestamp, bool connected, uint32_t buttons, int32_t x, y, wheel, tilt, 8 reserved } and 0x80DF0004 for a mouse already open. With no mouse it answers one record, not connected, all zero. OpenOrbis Mouse.h only names the calls. The executable's calls agree. It loads the library's system module ( 0x02a8bce1 ), then calls Init (six sites, such as 0x02a8bcea ) and counts 0 as success. Two input objects each open the mouse with (the initial user, 0, 0, NULL) ( 0x02a8bf75 , 0x02a8c465 ), keep the answer as their handle only when it is above 0, and close a handle above 0 before opening again. Read ( 0x02a8c07f , 0x02a8c56f ) asks for one record into the 40 bytes the object clears: below 0 is a failure, and a record that is not connected ends the poll. What the runtime does. Init answers 0 every time, as shadPS4 does. Open gives handle 1 (the runtime 's choice; the title keeps only handles above 0) and 0x80DF0004 while it is open. Read writes one all-zero record (not connected) and answers 1. Close frees the handle. Stops by name: a call before Init, another user, type, index or open parameters, an unknown handle, a count outside 1 to 64, and a missing record. The common dialog's initialize ( libSceCommonDialog , issue #40) sceCommonDialogInitialize is the only call eboot imports from libSceCommonDialog . It takes no arguments (OpenOrbis CommonDialog.h , as supporting evidence). The executable calls it twice: - at 0x024e1e8c , logging a failure; - at 0x02023fbb , accepting success or exactly 0x80b80002 . So the first call succeeds and a repeat answers 0x80b80002 , the "already initialized" code. No dialog is shown: each dialog library's own calls do that (next section). The common dialogs, closed at once ( libSceMsgDialog , libSceSaveDataDialog , libSceNpProfileDialog , libSceNpCommerce , issues #35 and #40) The executable uses four of the console's common dialogs. It never reads a choice from three of them: the message, save data and commerce dialogs do not import GetResult . It reads the profile dialog's result but does not use it. So the runtime models each dialog as one the user closes at once. Facts: - Statuses and the base block. NONE 0, INITIALIZED 1, RUNNING 2, FINISHED 3, and the parameter block's base: 0x30 bytes, with a magic number 0xC0D1A109 at 0x2c (OpenOrbis _types/common_dialog.h ). Every call site stores the magic as 0xC0D1A109 plus the low 32 bits of the base's own address. - Errors and states. 0x80b80003 (not initialized) and 0x80b80004 (already initialized), and the states: Initialize from NONE, Open from INITIALIZED or FINISHED, Terminate back to NONE (shadPS4's commondialog.h , msgdialog.cpp , np_commerce.cpp and np_profile_dialog.cpp , facts only). The executable's uses: - Message dialog. One system message, mode 3 with type 2 (the PSN user-generated content restriction notice, built at 0x020233b3 ). Its start-up ( 0x02023e95 ) accepts 0 or exactly 0x80b80004 . It polls UpdateStatus while RUNNING ( 0x02023d6b ) and terminates on FINISHED. - Save data dialog. Shown when a save mount fails with 0x809f000a (no space, 0x02c425e7 ). It initializes, retrying while the answer is busy ( 0x80b80008 ), opens a system message (mode 3, size 0x98), polls while RUNNING and terminates. - Profile dialog. 0x010b85e0 opens a profile (mode 1, size 0x80) for an online id and polls. On FINISHED it reads the result, which it does not use, and then terminates. - Commerce dialog. 0x02040350 opens the PlayStation Plus offer (mode 5, size 0x80), ignoring Initialize's answer. 0x02040244 polls while RUNNING. Terminate's answer is ignored. What the runtime does: - Opening. Open checks the block (base size 0x30, the address-based magic, the library's own size field) and starts the dialog. - Closing. The first UpdateStatus after Open finishes it. Nothing is shown. - Terminating. A Terminate before any Initialize answers 0x80b80003 , which every caller ignores. - The profile result. It is result 0, user action 1 (canceled) and the caller's user data ( OrbisNpProfileDialogResult , 0x30 bytes, in shadPS4's np_profile_dialog.h ). What stops by name: an Open outside INITIALIZED or FINISHED; a NULL or malformed block; a profile result before FINISHED or with no structure. One dialog at a time (the console's busy answer, 0x80b80008 ) is not enforced: each runtime dialog finishes on its first status update. The splash screen and system status ( sceSystemServiceHideSplashScreen , sceSystemServiceGetStatus ) sceSystemServiceHideSplashScreen() : the title tells the system it may take down the boot splash, because its own screens follow. It answers 0, and the runtime keeps the fact ( rt_splash_hidden ), a sign of how far a boot got. The executable calls it through a function pointer ( 0x01d5d995 ) and reads no result. sceSystemServiceGetStatus(status) : polled for system events. The status is {int32_t pending events, then one byte each: system UI overlaid, in background execution, CPU mode 7 normal, live streaming, out of the VR play area} , and a missing pointer answers 0x80A10003 . The runtime has no system UI and no system events, so the answer is: no events, nothing overlaid, in the foreground, CPU mode normal, not streaming, not in VR. Only these 9 bytes are written. Facts from shadPS4's libSceSystemService ( systemservice.cpp , systemservice.h , systemservice_error.h ). The web browser, not opened ( sceSystemServiceLaunchWebBrowser , issue #40) The executable calls it in three places and discards the answer each time. Each call passes a URL string and NULL; OpenOrbis SystemService.h names the function without a shape. The three places: - the official site link at 0x02437039 ; - a debug BROWSER_TEST command at 0x01d5eeeb , with the same URL; - a URL it builds at 0x02437112 . The runtime opens no browser, as if the user closed it at once. It notes the URL on stderr and answers 0 (shadPS4 also answers 0, facts only). No URL stops by name. The setting ids and the language codes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's _types/sys_service.h (id 1 is the language, and 1 there is English (United States)). A setting is the console owner's choice, so the runtime answers what the person running it chose: - tools/boot.py passes --system-param ID=VALUE ; - it defaults the language to 1 (English, United States); - --system-param 1=18 , for example, chooses English (United Kingdom). What stops by name: a setting nobody gave a value, and a missing variable. Sockets, the resolver and HTTP requests, offline ( libSceNet , libSceHttp , issue #41) Sockets are FreeBSD's socket calls under SCE names (shapes from OpenOrbis net.h and shadPS4's net.cpp , facts only). A failure answers 0x80410100 plus the error number, with the number in the network errno. The executable expects exactly that: it compares answers with 0x80410123 , 0x80410139 , 0x80410109 and 0x80410104 at 0x02f9a8d0 , and errno with 35 at 0x011c7c60 . A socket can be created, set up, bound and listened on, as FreeBSD 9 does with only its loopback interface. shadPS4, the droogie bbhost runtime and PS4Recomp also create sockets. A family of native ports refuses every socket call with ENETUNREACH instead, which breaks the executable's Havok code: its bind and listen checks test for -1. Nothing ever connects or arrives: - Connect and send. Connect, or a datagram to a non-loopback address, answers ENETUNREACH at once (FreeBSD 9's in_pcbladdr ). An unconnected stream socket answers ENOTCONN to send and receive. A datagram socket with no destination answers EDESTADDRREQ to send. - Accept and datagram receive. These answer EWOULDBLOCK on a nonblocking socket ( SO_NBIO ). A blocking socket waits until sceNetSocketAbort or sceNetSocketClose (EINTR), or until its accept or receive timeout option passes (EWOULDBLOCK, as shadPS4 does). An abort with no waiter answers ENOTBLK. - Bind and listen. Bind answers EINVAL when the socket is already bound, EADDRNOTAVAIL for an address other than any or loopback, and EADDRINUSE for a port another socket holds, unless the new one set SO_REUSEADDR or SO_REUSEPORT (FreeBSD 9's in_pcbbind ). Listen on a datagram socket answers EOPNOTSUPP. - Options. The executable's options are stored and read back. - Epoll sets. sceNetEpollControl adds a socket to a set (events 1 or 3) or removes it. Answers, from shadPS4: EINVAL for a bad operation or event; EBADF for an unknown set or socket, or for removing a socket the set does not hold; EEXIST for adding one twice. A closed socket leaves every set. Offline nothing ever becomes ready. The resolver. With no DNS server, a name other than localhost answers RESOLVER_ENODNS, 0x804101e1 (shadPS4's offline resolver). An IPv4 literal is converted unless flag 0x10000 is set. A pool that is not live, including the 0 that the HavokScript debugger ( 0x00dfd1b0 ) passes, answers EBADF. HTTP requests. The executable's HTTP manager ( 0x013d2740 ) builds a connection and a request, then sets the content length, timeout and waiting handle. Its state machine ( 0x013d2970 ) sends, and treats any error other than busy, again or timeout as failure. The runtime builds both, with ids from 1 that are never reused: - sceHttpSendRequest answers 0x80431063 (network). PS4Recomp and the native port family answer the same; shadPS4 sends in the background and then answers 0x80431065 . Either way, the job ends failed. - The response calls answer 0x80431065 . - Ids that are not live answer 0x80431100 , a missing URL 0x80433060 , and NULL results 0x804311fe (shadPS4's codes). What stops by name (each needs a maintainer ruling or a real network to settle): - type 6 peer-to-peer sockets and other families; - binding port 0 (the PS4 's ephemeral port is not known); - connect or datagrams to loopback (no loopback stack); - reading an option that was never set (the PS4 's defaults are not known); - asynchronous resolving, listening while unbound, and abort flags; - non-HTTP URLs, methods other than GET, POST and PUT, and full tables. Signal masks ( _sigprocmask , issue #34) _sigprocmask(how, set, old) is FreeBSD's sigprocmask(2) : the calling thread's blocked signals. A FreeBSD sigset_t is four 32-bit words, with signal n at bit n - 1. how is SIG_BLOCK (1), SIG_UNBLOCK (2) or SIG_SETMASK (3), and is ignored when there is no new set. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be blocked, and are dropped silently. The bundled libc's setjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fcb0 ) reads the mask with SIG_BLOCK and no new set, and its longjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fd00 ) puts it back with SIG_SETMASK . What the runtime does. No signal is delivered to the guest yet. So the runtime keeps each guest thread's mask, a new thread starting with its creator's, and does not apply it to the host thread. What stops by name: an unknown how . Its error is reported through the guest's errno , which the runtime does not model. sigprocmask and sigfillset ( libc.elf imports both from libkernel). sigprocmask is the same call under its POSIX name (FreeBSD's libc sigprocmask is the system call itself); its thirteen calls include +0x53f84 , which blocks everything with SIG_SETMASK and a set from sigfillset and keeps the old mask. sigfillset(set) puts every signal in the set, each of the four words all ones (FreeBSD libc's sigsetops.c , POSIX), and answers 0. A missing set stops by name: POSIX defines no error for it. It sets priorities from 256 ( 0x100 ) to 767 ( 0x2ff ), at 0x02a3b63d and 0x0111ab46 . Where a thread's priority comes from: - The main thread. An executable may declare its main thread's settings in its process parameters ( sceUserMainThreadPriority and the like, which homebrew titles define). Contexts, codecs and instances. - Contexts: sceAjmInitialize(0, &context) and sceAjmFinalize(context) . - Codecs: sceAjmModuleRegister(context, codec, 0) and sceAjmModuleUnregister , with 0 MP3, 1 ATRAC9 and 2 AAC. - Instances: sceAjmInstanceCreate(context, codec, flags, &instance) gives an id that is the slot index with the codec at bit 14. Its flags hold a revision (bits 0–2, not 0), the channels (3–6), the sample format (7–9, 0 for 16-bit) and gapless looping (bit 10). - The title's instances: it creates ATRAC9 instances with flags 0x409 to 0x441 : revision 1, 1 to 8 channels, 16-bit, gapless looping ( 0x01118d9a ). Jobs and batches. - Building jobs: sceAjmBatchJobControlBufferRa and sceAjmBatchJobRunBufferRa write a job into the batch and return the next free position. - A job is a sequence of chunks, each with a 32-bit header: an identifier in bits 0–6 and a 20-bit payload. The chunks are the job itself (payload the instance), an optional return address, input and output buffers ( {header, size, pointer} ) and the flags. - Fixed sizes: a control job is 0x30 bytes (0x40 with a return address) and a run job 0x40 (0x50). The title's FMOD lays jobs out at those strides. - Starting and waiting: sceAjmBatchStartBuffer runs the batch (a size that is not a multiple of 8 is malformed, 0x80930011 ). sceAjmBatchWait waits with a timeout in ms; sceAjmBatchCancel and sceAjmBatchErrorDump round it out. Job flags: - run: bit 11 get codec info, bit 12 multiple frames; - control: bit 13 reset, bit 14 initialize, bit 15 resample; - sideband: bit 45 gapless, bit 46 format, bit 47 stream. A job's output control buffer starts with its result, then the stream result, format, gapless state, frame count and codec info, as its flags ask. The ATRAC9 codec info is {superframe bytes, frames per superframe, bytes left in the superframe, samples per frame} . What the runtime does. - When jobs run: when the batch is started, on the calling thread (bbhost does the same for this title). A wait finds the batch finished and frees its id; a cancel of a batch that has run does nothing. - Control jobs are modelled: initialize with the 4-byte ATRAC9 configuration word, reset, and gapless. So is the codec info, derived from the configuration word: 0xFE , a sample rate index, a channel configuration, a 0 bit, the frame bytes minus one, and a superframe index, read most-significant bit first. - Errors: context 0x80930002 , instance 0x80930003 , batch 0x80930004 , parameter 0x80930005 , no batch id left 0x80930006 , no instance left 0x80930007 , already registered 0x80930009 , not registered 0x8093000A , revision 0 0x8093000B . Decoding. ATRAC9 is decoded with LibAtrac9 (MIT, vendored unmodified in third_party/libatrac9 ), behind a small decoder interface ( runtime/ajm.h ). The decode loop answers as shadPS4's does: - Before each frame: too little output room answers "not enough room" ( 0x10 ), and less input than the rest of the superframe "partial input" ( 0x8 ). - Each frame: it drops the gapless skip and stops at the gapless total. A superframe's padding is skipped, and when the gapless window ends mid-superframe the rest of it is decoded and dropped. - Looping and repeats: an instance with gapless looping starts the window again. A job repeats frames only with "multiple frames". - Errors: a decoder error is fatal, with its code as the internal result. The tests use a stand-in decoder, because no ATRAC9 data may be in the repository, plus the real one on junk input. Stops by name: codecs other than ATRAC9, sample formats other than 16-bit, resampling, format inputs and outputs, and the statistics instance. No microphone and no voice chat ( libSceAudioIn , libSceVoice , issue #37) Microphone input. The executable's only user is FMOD's PS4 record driver: - Opening. Its record start ( 0x0111c050 ) opens a port with sceAudioInOpen(user, type 0/1/5, index 0, 256 samples, 16000 Hz, param 0 = 16-bit mono) at 0x0111c11d . A negative answer is an FMOD error. - Reading. Its update thread calls sceAudioInInput at 0x0111beee and uses the answer as a sample count to advance a ring buffer, so an open port must never answer an error there. - Closing. The port is closed at 0x0111c25b , and the answer is ignored. The facts come from shadPS4's audioin.cpp and audioin_error.h (facts only), whose codes match the PS Vita SDK's audioin.h : - A port opens without a device and reads silence. PS4Recomp and the droogie bbhost runtime agree; the bloodborne-native port family answers 0x80260109 (not opened) instead, so the majority answer is used. - The length must be 1 to 2048 samples ( 0x80260102 ), the frequency 16000 or 48000 ( 0x80260103 ), and the param 0 or 1, 16-bit mono or stereo ( 0x80260106 ). - An unknown handle is 0x80260101 , a NULL buffer 0x80260105 . What the runtime does with the microphone: - Open hands out handles from 1. - Input writes the port's samples of silence, waits for the time they last (length / frequency), and answers the sample count. - Close frees the handle. - Stops by name: a type other than 0, 1 and 5; an index other than 0; a full table. Voice chat. At 0x010c8000 the executable initializes the library ( sceVoiceInit(param, 100) ). It then creates a microphone port (type 0) and a speaker port (type 5) for the initial user. Its microphone loop ( 0x010c8a50 ) reads only while sceVoiceGetPortInfo reports bytes. Peer ports, connections, Start and the incoming packet path need an online peer. Teardown ignores every answer. shadPS4 ( voice.cpp , voice.h ), PS4Recomp ( ps4_voice.c ), the droogie bbhost runtime and the bloodborne-native port family all answer success with no audio behind it (facts only). The port info is 0x20 bytes: the byte count is at 0x10, and the frame size at 0x14 is 1 (shadPS4), which the incoming packet path divides by. Their error codes disagree (shadPS4 0x804e08xx , the PS Vita's; PS4Recomp 0x80233xxx ), so misuse stops by name. What the runtime does with voice chat: - Answers 0. Init; CreatePort, which hands out the lowest free id from 0; DeletePort, for any id, since the executable also deletes 0xff ; Connect, Disconnect, Start and Stop; End, which forgets every port. - GetPortInfo writes the type, frame size 1 and byte count 0. - ReadFromOPort reads 0 bytes, and WriteToIPort discards the data. Audio output ( sceAudioOutInit , sceAudioOutOpen , sceAudioOutSetVolume , sceAudioOutOutput , issue #37) The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's AudioOut.h declares int32_t sceAudioOutInit(void) and int32_t sceAudioOutOpen(user, port type, index, length, sample rate, param) . Its _types headers give: - port type 0 (main); - format 4 (float stereo); - the error codes 0x8026000E (already initialized) and 0x8026000F (not initialized). What the executable does: - Its only init call ( 0x0111b665 ) accepts success or exactly 0x8026000E . - Its only open ( 0x0111b69d ) passes user 0xff (the system user in the SDK's user types), the main port, index 0, 256 samples, 48000 Hz and a format. It keeps a non-negative result as the port handle. - The format is the executable's own evidence. Its output callback ( 0x0111b600 ) accepts 2 or 8 channels and passes 4 | (channels == 8) . So 4 is float stereo (as in the SDK) and 5 is float with eight channels. The boot opens eight channels. - A second open ( 0x0111b6fc ) passes port type 1 with the same settings, and does not check the result. The PS4 name of type 1 is not public; the sibling Vita SDK calls it BGM. - The movie player's sound gets a port of its own ( 0x02c225ae , 0x02c22842 ): 1024 samples at 48000 Hz. Its format comes from the movie's channel count: 0, 1 or 2 (16-bit mono, stereo, eight channels) for 48 kHz sound, and 3, 4 or 5 (float) otherwise. The SDK's _types/audio_out.h names 0, 1, 3 and 4; shadPS4's audioout.h adds 2 and 5 as the eight-channel forms. The 6-channel movies open format 2. With --audio host , 16-bit blocks are scaled to -1..1 for the host stream. What the runtime does. It records each open port and hands out handles from 1, the lowest one free, so a closed port's handle is handed out again (shadPS4 also reuses a closed port's slot). Sound output belongs to the output calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: any open other than the observed ones (256 float samples in formats 4 and 5, or 1024 samples in formats 0 to 5, at 48000 Hz), and running out of handles. int32_t sceAudioOutSetVolume(handle, flag, int32_t *volume) , as the SDK declares it, comes next. The executable's only call ( 0x0111b6d6 ) passes its new port, flag 0xff and eight volumes of 32768, and treats nonzero as failure. Flag bit n selects channel n, whose volume is volume[n] . What the runtime does. It records the volumes. What stops by name: - a handle it did not hand out; - a flag naming a channel the port does not have; - a missing array; - a volume outside 0–32768. int32_t sceAudioOutOutput(handle, const void *samples) , as the SDK declares it, hands a port sound. The executable's audio thread ( 0x0111b93c ) hands its port one block at a time ( length samples for every channel). It advances its ring buffer when the result is not negative, and loops with no wait of its own. So the call itself paces the thread: it returns once the port has room for the next block. What the runtime does. It plays nothing yet. - Each port takes one block per length / rate seconds (256 samples at 48000 Hz: 5.33 ms). - A call waits until the block before it would have finished playing, then answers 0 (the caller only checks the sign). - A port that falls behind starts again from now. - No block ( samples NULL) hands nothing over: the call waits until the port has room for the next block and answers 0, without moving the port's timeline on. shadPS4 ( audioout.cpp ) waits for the port's buffer to drain and copies nothing for a null pointer, returning 0 samples; PS4Recomp ( ps4_audioout.c ) waits for room and pushes nothing, returning 0. The movie player's sound thread calls it so when it has no sound to give (found during the opening movie). What stops by name: a handle the runtime did not hand out. int32_t sceAudioOutClose(handle) , as the SDK declares it, closes a port. The movie player's sound ends with it ( 0x02c2276f ): first no block ( sceAudioOutOutput with NULL, which waits for room), then the close, whose negative result it takes as failure. The runtime takes the port back once any output call on it has returned, closes its host stream and answers 0, as shadPS4's audioout.cpp does; the handle is free for the next open. A handle that names no open port stops by name (the error value is not established). int32_t sceAudioOutGetPortState(handle, void *state) , as the SDK declares it, reports a port's state. Its _types/audio_out.h gives the layout (32 bytes): a 16-bit output, an 8-bit channel count, a volume and a 64-bit flag. The executable's only call ( 0x0111bb41 ) asks about its second port, and reads only output, testing it for 0. What the runtime does. It plays nothing on the host, so no port is output anywhere. It answers output 0, and 0 in the fields whose encoding is not established. This must change when the runtime plays sound. What stops by name: an unknown handle, and a missing state. Sound on the host ( pbboot --audio host , tools/boot.py --audio host ). With this option, each port plays through SDL3 on the default playback device ( runtime/audio_host.h , runtime/audio/audio_host_sdl.c ). Without it, or in a build without SDL3, nothing is played and ports keep time on their own as before. Boots are silent by default. Each block: each channel is scaled by its volume (32768 is 0 dB, the level the title sets; until it sets one the port plays at 0 dB, the runtime 's choice) and queued on the port's stream. Pacing: the call returns once no more than four blocks wait to be played, so the title's audio thread runs at the device's pace. Channel order: the title's 8-channel float format (format 5) is passed in SDL's 7.1 order, as shadPS4's SDL backend does; the STD layouts, which are remapped, are not used by the title. Port state: a port playing on the host reports output 1 ( CONNECTED_PRIMARY , shadPS4's audioout.h ). Observed: with ATRAC9 decoding, a boot plays the game's own sound after about 17 seconds. The movie player ( libSceAvPlayer ) The title plays its movies ( /app0/.../movie/*.mp4 : H.264 video, AAC sound in several languages) through the console's movie player. One wrapper in the executable makes every call ( 0x02cfdf33 to 0x02d004a9 ): sceAvPlayerInit gets a 0x78-byte block with the title's memory callbacks and an event callback. The block has no file callbacks, auto start is 0 and the default language is none. sceAvPlayerPostInit gets decoder settings (video decoder type 3). sceAvPlayerAddSource gets the movie's path and sceAvPlayerSetLooping a flag. After the ready event the title counts the streams and reads each one's info. It enables one video stream and the audio stream its language setting picks, then calls sceAvPlayerStart . Each frame, a picture comes from sceAvPlayerGetVideoDataEx and sound from sceAvPlayerGetAudioData on the title's audio thread. The layouts, event numbers and error values are from shadPS4's libSceAvPlayer ( avplayer.h , avplayer_error.h , avplayer_state.cpp , avplayer_source.cpp ), checked against the OpenOrbis AvPlayer.h . The code is the runtime 's own ( runtime/syslib/avplayer.c ). Decoding uses FFmpeg on the host ( runtime/media/ , runtime/media_host.h ), when the runtime is built with it.
