Attribute priority and CPU mask ( scePthreadAttrSetschedparam , scePthreadAttrSetaffinity , issue #34) scePthreadAttrSetschedparam(attr, const struct sched_param *param) sets the priority ( sched_param 's one int) of a thread created with the attribute. OpenOrbis' libkernel.h gives the shape; libthr's _pthread_attr_setschedparam gives the semantics. What the executable does. Its thread wrapper ( 0x0111aafd ) sets it without explicit-scheduling inheritance. So under libthr's default ( PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ), the new thread still starts at its creator's priority. The wrapper then sets the priority itself with scePthreadSetprio ( 0x0111ab46 ). What the runtime does. It records the priority on the attribute. A variable holding no attribute is EINVAL (libthr). What stops by name: a missing param, and a priority outside 256–767. scePthreadAttrSetaffinity(attr, uint64_t mask) is the wrapper's next call ( 0x0111ab0e ), with the CPU mask its caller chose. As for scePthreadSetaffinity , the runtime records the mask (the created thread takes it) and the host schedules. An empty mask stops by name, and a variable holding no attribute is EINVAL . Save data ( libSceSaveData ) The title's saves live in the host folder given to pbboot --savedata . tools/boot.py gives each run a new empty one, so boots start alike, unless --savedata DIR names a folder to keep them in. A mounted save appears to the title as /savedataN (N the lowest free of 16), through the same file calls as /app0 and /data , read-only or writable as mounted. Sources. shadPS4's libSceSaveData ( savedata.cpp , savedata.h , savedata_error.h , save_instance.cpp , save_memory.cpp ), checked against two other Bloodborne ports and the OpenOrbis headers. Where they disagree, shadPS4's answer is taken. The code is the runtime 's own. The title's SDK version decides some answers. The executable says SDK 0x02000071 (firmware 2.00), which the runtime reads through rt_compiled_sdk_version : - "not initialized" is 0x80960002 (it is 0x809F000B before 2.00 and 0x809F0001 from 2.50); - a directory search reports the total hits, the number set and the params (from 1.70); - a mount writes back only the mount point (before 4.50), and mode 0x20 (create or open) does not create; - terminating with saves mounted unmounts them (before 4.00). On the host. <savedata>/<user id>/<directory name>/ holds the title's files, with sce_sys/param.bin (the 1328-byte param) and sce_sys/icon0.png ; a save exists when its sce_sys does. The memory-backed save is <savedata>/<user id>/sce_sdmemory/memory.dat . These are the runtime 's own files, not a console's param.sfo . The executable's one caller ( 0x02c3e765 ) passes no title id and asks again while the answer is 0x809F0014 Stops by name (not modelled): another title's saves (a title id), the free-space check and its required-blocks answer, the backup copy and its "corrupted" marker, sort key 4, and a memory read or write past the size set up, a delete of a save that is not there (shadPS4 answers 0 then, which is not established for the console), and a host failure to remove a save. The save data dialog stays unbound until the boot reaches it. The title's files: /app0 , sceKernelStat , opening and reading (issue #35) The title reads its own data under /app0 , the console's read-only mount of its package. The runtime serves /app0 from your own copy and never writes to it: - tools/boot.py --app0 DIR chooses the copy, defaulting to $BB_APP0 , then $BB_DATA_ROOT/merged . - pbboot takes it as --app0 . - A path under any other mount, and one with a .. component (which could leave the copy), stops by name. sceKernelStat(path, struct stat *) is FreeBSD's stat(2) under its SCE name, which returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. The PS4 's struct stat is FreeBSD 9's amd64 layout, 120 bytes (OpenOrbis' _types/kernel.h , OrbisKernelStat ). What the executable does. Its call at 0x02474519 asks whether /app0/dvdroot_ps4/sound/sprj_mixer.fev exists: - 0 means yes; - exactly 0x80020002 ( ENOENT ) means no; - anything else goes to its error path. What the runtime does. It fills the structure from the host file: - type, size, block count and size, link count and times; - the permission bits without write (the mount is read-only); - device and inode numbers as the host's (they only identify the file); - the birth time as the modification time (the host's stat has none); - owner, group, flags and generation 0. Errors. A missing file answers ENOENT , and a missing directory component ENOTDIR (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux). Any other host error stops by name. POSIX stat and errno . eboot also imports POSIX stat from libScePosix . The runtime gives it the same lookup and answer, the POSIX way: 0, or -1 with the calling thread's errno set to ENOENT (2) or ENOTDIR (20). The executable's one call ( 0x00465431 ) reads the access and modification times and the size on 0, and treats any other answer as no file. errno is libkernel's __error() , FreeBSD's int *__error(void) behind the errno macro. It is imported by eboot , libc and libSceFios2 . Each guest thread runs on its own host thread, so a thread-local int is that thread's errno ; it starts at 0, and success leaves it alone. Truncating by name, and the POSIX mkdir, rmdir and rename sceKernelTruncate(path, length) (imported by eboot and libSceFios2 ) is FreeBSD's truncate(2) under its SCE name: 0, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The shape is OpenOrbis libkernel.h 's; the executable's wrapper ( 0x024733a4 ) passes a 64-bit length and turns each 0x8002xxxx answer into an engine error through a table ( 0x02473530 ). eboot also imports mkdir , rmdir and rename from libScePosix : 0, or -1 with errno set. The executable's calls ( 0x00df0bf4 , 0x00e03e68 , 0x00e03ddb and others) ignore the answer or only compare it with 0. ( sceKernelRename and sceKernelFtruncate are under "Opening and reading".) What the runtime does: - Paths resolve as for opening: /data , the mounted save data, and /app0 . - Errors are FreeBSD's numbers, never the host's: ENOENT , ENOTDIR , EEXIST , EISDIR , EINVAL and ENOTEMPTY (66 on FreeBSD, 39 on Linux). - rmdir of a mount's own root is EBUSY (the man page's "mount point for a mounted file system"). - rename across mounts is EXDEV , after the source and the target's folder are looked up, in FreeBSD's order (stable/9 vfs_syscalls.c , kern_renameat ). A directory over a non-empty one is ENOTEMPTY . - truncate with a negative length is EINVAL before the lookup ( kern_truncate ; Linux checks it first too); a directory is EISDIR . Growing a file fills with zero bytes. - A new directory's mode is mode & 0777 less the host's umask. The PS4 process's umask is not established. What stops by name: - no path; - any change under a read-only mount ( /app0 , save data mounted to read). FreeBSD answers EROFS , but only after lookups whose order the runtime does not model for each call, and the title's callers change only /data and its saves; - renaming a mount's root; - any other host error ( EACCES , ENOSPC , EIO and the rest). Opening and reading sceKernelOpen , sceKernelRead , sceKernelPread , sceKernelLseek , sceKernelFstat and sceKernelClose are FreeBSD's open(2) , read(2) , pread(2) , lseek(2) , fstat(2) and close(2) under their SCE names. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares the shapes. Each returns a result, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The executable opens its data with flags 0 ( O_RDONLY ) and mode 0555. What the runtime does: - Opening. It opens the host file read-only. A request to write, create, truncate or append answers EROFS , as FreeBSD does on a read-only mount. The lookup comes first: a missing file without O_CREAT is ENOENT . Other flag bits stop by name. - Descriptors. A descriptor is the runtime 's own number, from 3 up, standing for a host descriptor (the title only passes it back). One the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . - Seeking. A whence other than 0, 1 or 2 ( SEEK_SET , SEEK_CUR , SEEK_END , the same on FreeBSD and Linux), and a seek before the start, are EINVAL . Writing sceKernelWrite(fd, buf, n) (imported by eboot and libSceFios2 ) and sceKernelPwrite(fd, buf, n, offset) (imported by libSceFios2 ) are FreeBSD's write(2) and pwrite(2) under their SCE names, with the shapes from the same libkernel.h . Each returns the number of bytes written, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. Writes reach files under the writable /data mount, which sceKernelOpen opens with the requested access mode. What the runtime does: - Order of checks. FreeBSD's order (stable/9 sys_generic.c , sys_write , sys_pwrite and kern_pwritev ): the size, then the descriptor, then the offset. - EBADF . write(2) answers it for a descriptor that is not open for writing: one the runtime did not hand out (0 to 2 included, as for reading), and one opened read-only, which is every /app0 file and a /data file opened with O_RDONLY . - EINVAL . A negative pwrite offset, as for pread ( pwrite(2) : "The offset value was negative"). - The position. A pwrite leaves the file position where it was. A write past the end leaves a hole that reads as zero bytes, as the host file system does. A zero count writes nothing and answers 0. - The count. The answer is the host's count, which can be short. Linux writes at most 0x7ffff000 bytes per call, so a request between that and INT_MAX comes back short where FreeBSD would write it all. What stops by name: - More than INT_MAX bytes. FreeBSD answers EINVAL above IOSIZE_MAX . That is INT_MAX while the debug.iosize_max_clamp sysctl is set (its default in FreeBSD 9; current FreeBSD defaults to 0), and SSIZE_MAX otherwise. The FreeBSD 9.0 write(2) page says INT_MAX . The PS4 's setting is not known. - No buffer for a non-zero count, as for reading. - A pwrite on a descriptor opened with O_APPEND . POSIX writes at the offset. FreeBSD's write(2) BUGS section says its pwrite appends instead, and Linux does the same. The PS4 's answer is not established. - Any host write error ( ENOSPC , EIO , EFBIG and the rest). What would settle the stops: guest call sites that pass these cases, or results observed on a console. Truncating and renaming sceKernelFtruncate(fd, length) is FreeBSD's ftruncate(2) under its SCE name (shape from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ). The title reaches it after Play Offline, while it creates its save data: its file object cuts its file at its current position ( 0x02473290 ). The runtime passes the length to the host. A negative length, and a descriptor opened without write permission, are EINVAL (FreeBSD's truncate(2) ; Linux answers the same); one the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . Any other host error stops by name. sceKernelRename(from, to) is FreeBSD's rename(2) (shape from libkernel.h ); the title calls it ( 0x02474a85 ) while it creates its save data. The runtime renames the host file, replacing an existing to as rename(2) does. Paths on two different mounts are EXDEV ( rename(2) : "on different logical devices"); on the read-only /app0 EROFS , after the lookup; a missing file or directory component ENOENT or ENOTDIR . Any other host error stops by name. Directories and flushing sceKernelGetdirentries(fd, buf, nbytes, basep) is FreeBSD's getdirentries(2) and sceKernelFsync(fd) FreeBSD's fsync(2) , under their SCE names (shapes from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ). eboot and libSceFios2 import the first, libSceFios2 the second. How the executable lists a directory. Its directory iterator opens the directory with sceKernelOpen(path, 0x20000, 0555) , that is O_DIRECTORY ( 0x024722d0 ), and treats a negative answer as no listing. Each step ( 0x02472480 ) takes st_blksize from the directory's sceKernelFstat as nbytes , then walks the FreeBSD 9 records: a 32-bit file number, the 16-bit record length, the type, the name length and the NUL-terminated name. It skips . and .. , adds / to a DT_DIR (4) name, and, when it stops partway through a buffer, seeks the descriptor back to *basep so that its next call reads the same records again. What the runtime does: - Opening. O_DIRECTORY alone opens a directory on either mount. A path that is not a directory is ENOTDIR ( open(2) ). - Listing. It lists the host directory in the host's order, as many whole records as fit, each rounded up to 4 bytes (FreeBSD 9's GENERIC_DIRSIZ ), and answers the byte count, 0 at the end. File numbers are the host's inode numbers (they only identify a file). The type is the host's: FreeBSD and Linux share the DT_ numbers. Where the host file system leaves it unknown, the runtime asks fstatat . - Positions. *basep (when not NULL) is the position before the call, and the position afterwards follows the last record listed. So a seek to *basep lists the same records again. A position is a count of entries, the runtime 's own number; FreeBSD's is a byte offset. The title only hands it back to sceKernelLseek , which on a directory accepts SEEK_SET and SEEK_CUR ; a position before the start is EINVAL . - Flushing. sceKernelFsync flushes the host file and answers 0. - Errors. A descriptor the runtime did not hand out is EBADF for both. What stops by name: O_DIRECTORY with any other flag; listing a descriptor that is not a directory, with no buffer, or into fewer than 512 bytes (a directory block: shadPS4 answers EINVAL , the PS4 's answer is not established); SEEK_END on a directory; a host fsync error. An entry added or removed between two calls can move the listing by one entry, as on any file system that lists by position. Directories and removing files sceKernelMkdir(path, mode) , sceKernelRmdir(path) and sceKernelUnlink(path) are FreeBSD's mkdir(2) , rmdir(2) and unlink(2) under their SCE names, 0 or 0x80020000 plus the error number. eboot and libSceFios2.elf import all three from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). The shapes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ( int32_t sceKernelMkdir(const char *, OrbisKernelMode) , OrbisKernelMode a uint16_t like FreeBSD's mode_t ; int32_t sceKernelRmdir(const char *) , int32_t sceKernelUnlink(const char *) ), supporting evidence for the shapes only. No call site in the repository shows them yet. Under /data and a writable mount the host does the work, and its error is translated: - a missing file or directory component is ENOENT or ENOTDIR , and mkdir of an existing name EEXIST (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux); - rmdir of a directory with entries is ENOTEMPTY , 66 on FreeBSD (Linux's is 39), and of a path whose last component is . EINVAL ( rmdir(2) ; Linux answers the same); - unlink of a directory is EPERM . FreeBSD's unlink(2) page lists both EISDIR and EPERM for "the named file is a directory"; the kernel settles it: kern_unlinkat (stable/9) and kern_funlinkat (current) answer EPERM ("POSIX"), and turn the lookup's EINVAL for a last component . into EPERM too. Linux answers EISDIR for both, which the runtime translates. - Any other host error stops by name. The mode of mkdir . FreeBSD gives the new directory (mode & ACCESSPERMS) & ~umask ( kern_mkdirat , stable/9 and current), so bits above 0777 are dropped. The runtime passes mode & 0777 to the host, as sceKernelOpen does for a new file, and the host process's umask then applies. Not established: the PS4 process's umask, so the bits a later sceKernelStat shows are the host's answer, not a console's; and whether the console enforces those bits for the title (a folder made without the owner's write and search bits refuses files on the host, which then stop by name). On a read-only mount ( /app0 , a save mounted read-only) nothing changes, and the answers follow FreeBSD's lookup order ( vfs_lookup.c , stable/9 and current): - a missing component of the path prefix is ENOENT or ENOTDIR first; - mkdir of an existing name is EEXIST (the read-only check is not made for a name that exists), of a new name EROFS ; - rmdir and unlink of an existing name, file or directory, are EROFS , before rmdir 's ENOTDIR and ENOTEMPTY and unlink 's EPERM for a directory; - a last component . is refused by the lookup before that: rmdir EINVAL , unlink EPERM . Stops by name , besides the path checks every file call shares (no path, a path outside the mounts, a .. component, a path longer than the runtime 's buffer): rmdir of a mount point itself ( /data , /app0 , /savedataN ). FreeBSD's rmdir(2) answers EBUSY for the root of a mounted file system, but whether /data is one on the console is not established, and the host would remove the runtime 's own folder. The disc map ( sceDiscMapIsRequestOnHDD , issue #35) The disc map tells the file library whether part of a file is already on the hard disk or still only on the disc ( runtime/syslib/disc_map.c ). Shape: sceDiscMapIsRequestOnHDD(const char *path, int64_t offset, int64_t bytes, int32_t *on_hdd) , as shadPS4's disc_map.cpp declares it (a fact only). The caller: the bundled file library's one call ( libSceFios2.elf+0x2d71c ) passes a variable preset to 0. On 0 it takes a nonzero variable as on the hard disk; on any other answer it treats the request as not mapped and remembers that the map is unavailable. The answer: the runtime serves the title from host files with no disc, so there is no disc bitmap. It answers 0x81100004 ("no bitmap info", numbered in shadPS4's disc_map_codes.h ), as shadPS4 does, and writes nothing. A missing path or variable stops by name. The unnamed import ioKMruft1ek . Its name is not public, so it is registered by its NID with RT_SYSLIB_NID ( runtime/include/runtime/syslib.h ): the loader matches the import's hash directly, and tools/runtime_issues.py checks the row ioKMruft1ek#A#B . The file library calls it as (path, offset, bytes, int *, int *, int *) ( libSceFios2.elf+0x29c6f , +0x2a381 ) and takes any non-zero answer as "no map". It answers 0x81100004 and writes nothing, as shadPS4 and the bloodborne-native ports do (PS4Recomp answers 0x80820001 ); the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 picked 0x81100004 . A missing path or variable stops by name. Memory protection queries ( sceKernelQueryMemoryProtection , issue #34) sceKernelQueryMemoryProtection(void *address, void **start, void **end, int32_t *protection) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares it, gives the protection of the mapping that holds an address. What the executable does. Its helpers ( 0x02abad98 , 0x02abadf8 ) pass no start or end. They test the protection's CPU read bit (1) and GPU read bit ( 0x10 ), on memory the game mapped itself. Another ( 0x02d031df , reached once the movie player runs) passes a start and an end and reads only the protection. What the runtime does. It records every direct and flexible mapping with the protection the guest asked for, GPU bits included, and answers that. A start gets the mapping's start, and an end the address one past its last byte (exclusive), as shadPS4's MemoryManager::QueryProtection and PS4Recomp's ps4_direct_mem.c both answer. What stops by name: - an address outside those mappings (other memory is not tracked yet); - a missing variable. GNM : the tessellation factor ring ( sceGnmGetTheTessellationFactorRingBufferBaseAddress , issue #39) Graphics are rebuilt at the engine level (issue #39), so the GNM calls answer what the engine expects back; the GPU is not emulated. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's GnmDriver.h only names this call. The executable's only call ( 0x02ad3fb4 ) takes a 64-bit address and maps 128 KiB of direct memory there, for the GPU's tessellation factors: sceKernelMapDirectMemory with that address as a hint, protection 0x33 , alignment 0x10000 . What the runtime does. The PS4 answers a fixed address of its own. The runtime answers one it reserves for this, 0xfe00000000 : below 2^40, and clear of the executable, modules and thread objects. It is the runtime 's choice, not the PS4 's value: the engine only maps it and hands it back to the GPU calls. For this, sceKernelMapDirectMemory now takes an address hint as FreeBSD's mmap does without MAP_FIXED : the map goes there when the range is free. A hint in use (where the system then maps is not established) and one off the alignment stop by name. Virtual memory queries ( sceKernelVirtualQuery , issue #34) sceKernelVirtualQuery(address, flags, info *, size) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h and _types/kernel.h ( OrbisKernelVirtualQueryInfo ) declare it, describes the mapping that holds an address. The answer is a 0x48-byte structure: Offset Field 0x00 , 0x08 start and end 0x10 the direct memory offset 0x18 protection 0x1c memory type 0x20 flag bits: flexible 1, direct 2, stack 4, pooled 8, committed 0x10 0x24 a 32-byte name What the executable does. Every call passes flags 0 and size 0x48, and reads the start, the offset or the direct bit: - 0x02d0328c works out an address's place in direct memory as offset + (address - start) ; - 0x02ad3f5e , 0x02ad4066 and 0x02ad423e release the direct memory at the offset. What the runtime does. It answers from its record of direct and flexible mappings: start, offset, protection as asked for, memory type, flexible or direct, committed, and no name. No call reads the end, and whether it is inclusive is not established; the runtime writes the address just past the mapping. What stops by name: - flags other than 0; - a size other than 0x48; - an address outside those mappings (other memory is not tracked yet); - a missing structure. Unmapping, protecting and typing memory ( sceKernelMunmap , sceKernelMprotect , sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType , issue #34) The shapes are OpenOrbis libkernel.h 's: sceKernelMunmap(address, length) , sceKernelMprotect(address, length, protection) and sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType(start, &type, &range_start, &range_end) . What the executable does: - It frees a direct map with sceKernelMunmap and then sceKernelReleaseDirectMemory ( 0x024826fd , 0x0248270c ), the order the release needs. - 0x02d03214 wraps sceKernelMprotect and answers whether the result was 0. - 0x02abae74 passes the pool offset sceKernelVirtualQuery gave for an address to sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType and only tests whether the type is 3 (write-combined garlic). What the runtime does: - Munmap is FreeBSD's munmap(2) . A zero length is EINVAL (FreeBSD's sys_munmap ; shadPS4's sceKernelMunmap answers the same, facts only). As in FreeBSD the range may span several mappings, reserved space and holes: every mapping the runtime made inside it goes (a direct map no longer holds its range, which can then be released), reserved space inside it is given back, and holes stay as they are. A GPU-visible range can be mapped again at its GPU address. The address is not handed out again for other maps. - Mprotect is FreeBSD's mprotect(2) : the mapping takes the new protection, the CPU bits on the host and the GPU bits recorded, as for a map. The queries answer the new protection. - GetDirectMemoryType answers the memory type of the allocated range that holds the pool offset, and that range's start and end (just past it, as for sceKernelVirtualQuery ). What stops by name: - part of a mapping; for munmap, a start off the 16 KiB page, or a range outside the runtime 's map window that touches nothing it mapped or reserved; for mprotect, more than one mapping or memory the runtime did not map (other memory is not tracked yet); - an offset outside every allocated range (shadPS4 answers ENOENT ; no public source settles it); - protection beyond CPU and GPU read and write; - a missing variable. Reserving address space and mapping into it ( sceKernelReserveVirtualRange , sceKernelBatchMap , sceKernelReleaseFlexibleMemory , issue #34) The executable's block allocator ( 0x02d01eb0 ) builds one contiguous view of blocks it got separately. It reserves room for all of them ( sceKernelReserveVirtualRange , flags 0x80 , no overwrite, alignment 0); for each block it asks sceKernelVirtualQuery where the block lies in direct memory, then maps an alias of every block at its place in the reserved range in one sceKernelBatchMap . To free the view (or after a failed batch) it turns every entry into an unmap, runs the batch again, and unmaps the whole reserved range, which by then is holes. sceKernelReserveVirtualRange(&address, length, flags, alignment) reserves inaccessible space in the runtime 's map window (shadPS4 maps it with no access). EINVAL ( 0x80020016 ) for no variable, a length that is 0 or not whole 16 KiB pages, and an alignment that is not 0 or a power-of-two multiple of 16 KiB up to 2 GiB (shadPS4's checks, shared by the bloodborne-native ports). An address hint and flags other than no overwrite stop by name. sceKernelBatchMap(entries, count, &processed) runs 32-byte operations (start 0x00 , offset 0x08 , length 0x10 , protection 0x18 , type 0x19 , operation 0x1c ; shadPS4's memory.h ) in order until one fails, and writes how many succeeded when processed is given. Each map is placed at its start exactly: shadPS4, the bloodborne-native ports and droogie's host agree on the implicit MAP_FIXED . No list, a zero length or an operation above 4 answers EINVAL . Map direct (0) maps the pool range over reserved space, with the CPU bits. Unmap (1) is the munmap above. Protect (2) is sceKernelMprotect . Stops by name: a map outside reserved space (what a fixed map replaces is not modelled), an aliased map with GPU access (the GPU reaches each pool range at one address, runtime/gpu_memory.h ), and the flexible-map and type-protect operations (3, 4), which the executable does not use. sceKernelReleaseFlexibleMemory(address, length) unmaps (maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10; the bloodborne-native ports and droogie's host unmap, shadPS4 keeps the mapping and drops its pages). The allocator frees whole flexible blocks with it ( 0x02482721 ). EINVAL for no address, a zero length or one that is not whole 16 KiB pages; direct memory in the range stops by name. GNM : compute queues ( sceGnmMapComputeQueue , issue #39) OpenOrbis' GnmDriver.h only names this call, so its shape comes from the engine's wrapper ( 0x01489a80 , called from its compute queue setup at 0x0148c7b0 ). What the engine does: - The wrapper passes the pipe and queue from the queue object, the ring buffer, its size in dwords, and the address of the GPU's read pointer. - A negative result is failure. Otherwise the wrapper keeps the result as the queue's id, and sets the read pointer to 0. - The setup then reports success only when that id is not 0. What the runtime does. It does not run the GPU, so the ring is never read. It records each queue for the engine-level graphics layer, and answers ids from 1. What stops by name: mapping the same pipe and queue twice, and a missing ring or read pointer. The renderer and compute queues. sceGnmDingDong completes each indirect buffer the ring points to (the temporary stand-in in runtime/syslib/gnm.c ), then hands it to the renderer, which drops its recorded calls without running them ( rt_renderer_skip ): compute queues do not run on the renderer yet. Dropping them matters because a shader bound in a command buffer is recorded by its address. A compute queue's buffer is never submitted to the graphics queue, so before this its bindings stayed waiting, and a graphics buffer later built in the same memory picked them up: on the main menu after Play Offline, a stale compute shader replaced the one the graphics buffer had just bound. Kernel event queues ( sceKernelCreateEqueue , sceKernelWaitEqueue , sceKernelDeleteEqueue , issue #34) The PS4 kernel is FreeBSD's, whose kqueue delivers struct kevent : ident (64-bit), filter (16-bit), flags (16-bit), fflags (32-bit), data (64-bit) and udata (a pointer), 32 bytes on amd64. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares create and delete; its _types/kernel.h lists the filters (display -13, graphics core -14, ...). What the executable does. Right after asking video out for a flip, it waits with room for one event, a variable for how many came back, and no timeout ( 0x015e41b6 , 0x02ad6f26 ). So the wait blocks until the flip is done. What the runtime does: - The queue is a list of registrations, added and triggered by the runtime 's own event sources ( runtime/include/runtime/equeue.h ; video out is the first). - A wait returns the triggered events, oldest first, and clears them, so each is reported once per trigger. - An event's flags and fflags are 0: what the PS4 sets there is not established, and no caller reads them. What stops by name: - a timeout (no call passes one); - deleting a queue a thread is waiting on; - an event array or count that does not fit; - the error values. Video out ( libSceVideoOut , issue #38) The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's VideoOut.h declares the calls. Its _types/video.h gives: - the 40-byte buffer attribute: format, tiling mode, aspect, width, height, pitch in pixels; - the 64-byte flip status: flip count, two times, the flip argument, pending counts, current buffer; - flip rates (0: 60 Hz, 1: 30 Hz, 2: 20 Hz) and flip modes (1: vsync, 2: hsync). What the executable does. It sets video out up twice, in the same order ( 0x015e488e and 0x02ad61d4 ): 1. open, with (0, 0, 0, no parameter); 2. flip rate 0; 3. an event queue with a flip event; 4. a buffer attribute (format 0x80000000 ; 1920 × 1080 in the first); 5. its buffers. Each frame, it submits a flip with mode 2 and waits on the queue ( 0x015e419a , then 0x015e41b6 ). Its other loop ( 0x02ad6ee9 ) reads the flip status until the flip argument reaches the frame it submitted. What the runtime does. It has no display yet. It keeps each port's buffers and status, and an hsync flip completes at once: - the current buffer and flip argument change, and the flip count grows; - the port's flip events are triggered. The flip event's ident is 0, and its data the flip argument. The PS4 's values are not established, and no caller reads them. What stops by name: - a vsync flip, and other flip modes or rates; - a flip status before the first flip (its initial argument is not established); - other open arguments; - errors. The buffer-attribute setter and buffer registration share the 40-byte rt_video_out_buffer_attribute layout. The setter copies all six input DWORDs without interpreting them and clears the 16 reserved bytes; unaligned output is supported. The public API is void. The independently examined native leaf also leaves the zero-extended pitch in RAX, which this implementation preserves for callers that observe it. A null output stops by the API name before any store. Implementation rule Implement the established contract and test the RT_SYSLIB entry through its library and symbol name. Keep target-specific values separate from host values. When an argument, ID, return value, or error case is unknown, fail loudly with the call name and leave the question open; never choose a value to make tools/boot.py advance. Module TLS ( __tls_get_addr ) Boot assigns TLS module IDs in mapped-object order, beginning at one, and prepares all nonempty templates before module entry. The executable reuses its static TLS block: the base is the thread pointer minus its rounded allocation size. Other blocks copy the relocated initialization bytes, zero-fill the rest and respect alignment. Lookup allocates nothing. Each context belongs to its host thread; unbinding and rebinding retain values, and destruction preserves borrowed storage. scePthreadCreate installs static executable TLS but no module context, so module lookups on those threads stop as __tls_get_addr . Evidence and limits The libkernel library SHA-256 is b3e13917da667d01a353ccf49025d6b1308a32cf86f3f351f96b3a13cd5c7c2f . Its __tls_get_addr export, NID vNe1w4diLCs , begins at ELF address 0x289c0 . The body reads a two-word 64-bit module/offset index, consults TCB/DTV and linker state, masks a slot to 48 bits and adds the full offset without a bounds check. Invalid states can diagnose and execute INT 0x44 . Generation updates, lazy allocation, alternate modes and linker helpers remain unsupported. Adjacent helpers at 0x2a9a0 and 0x2aca0 do not establish a general allocation-residue rule. The title libc template has virtual-address residue 8, while LibcInternal has zero; this implementation aligns the block base to the template's declared alignment. Paleblood accepts full-width IDs and offsets through the template's logical size, including a one-past pointer. Unknown IDs, larger offsets and absent contexts stop by name. These bounds are runtime support limits, not native error behavior. There is no native DTV layout, lazy loading or unloading. The initialization model follows the TLS ABI and Oracle linker documentation . No other PS4 runtime implementation was used. Validation The loader rejects duplicate headers, initialized size beyond logical size, out-of-file bytes, inconsistent segment aliases, invalid alignment and templates outside the mapped image. Zero alignment becomes one; TBSS need not be readable. Boot checks allocation arithmetic and allocates aligned storage. test_module_tls checks the registry, initialization, owned 256- and 4096-byte alignment, zero-fill, stable writes, borrowed storage, separate threads, full-width requests and named stops. test_module_tls_boot.py runs synthetic AMD64 fixtures through boot, checking static/dynamic main-block aliasing, rounded sizes, module-ID relocations, relocated pointers, constructor persistence and rejected IDs. Loader tests cover malformed metadata. FreeBSD libthr thr_cond.c , thr_mutex.c ( _mutex_owned , _mutex_cv_unlock , mutex_unlock_common , mutex_self_lock , mutex_self_trylock ) and thr_private.h ( THR_COND_DESTROYED ); for pthread_cond_timedwait , POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait (the CLOCK_REALTIME default, ETIMEDOUT , EINVAL ), pthread_condattr_getclock , libthr thr_cond.c ( _pthread_cond_timedwait in stable/9 and main, cond_init ) and thr_init.c ( _pthread_condattr_default ) vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/net/netctl.h - PS Vita, a different operating system: shape of the SceNetCtl declarations, never a PS4 value PSP2SDK psp2/net/netctl.h file reference and vitasdk SceNetCtl user group - the same declarations, with no prose describing any return value in this group vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/error.h - 0 on success as the documented SCE-family return convention OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain Sysmodule.h and _types/sysmodule.h - the sceSysmoduleLoadModule , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule declarations and return convention, and the system module ids (after psdevwiki, "Libraries" ) POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate - the detach state semantics, the invalid-value error, and the recommended EINVAL for an uninitialised attribute POSIX pthread_self and pthread_attr_init / pthread_attr_destroy FreeBSD pthread_attr(3) , libthr thr_attr.c ( _pthread_attr_setdetachstate , _pthread_attr_get_np ), thr_create.c ( _pthread_create : the default attribute for a null or empty variable) and include/pthread.h ( PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE , PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED ) OpenOrbis include/orbis/_types/pthread.h - the PS4 homebrew SDK's ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_* values, which follow FreeBSD's FreeBSD 9.0 mkdir(2) , rmdir(2) , unlink(2) and current unlink(2) ; FreeBSD vfs_syscalls.c (stable/9 and main: kern_mkdirat and its mode, kern_rmdirat / kern_frmdirat , kern_unlinkat / kern_funlinkat and EPERM for a directory) and vfs_lookup.c (stable/9 and main: the read-only checks and the . check, and their order); OpenOrbis libkernel.h and _types/kernel.h ( OrbisKernelMode ) for the shapes
docs.title: Runtime call reference

docs.text: The runtime's own detailed notes on each system call: the evidence, the exact behavior and what stops by name. This page is copied from Paleblood's docs/runtime-syscalls.md every time the wiki syncs, so it always matches the code. For the reader-friendly explanation of the same calls, start with Runtime system calls . This page records contracts used to implement small runtime calls in issues #34 and #41 . Public standards and manuals describe portable or platform-specific API behavior; they do not by themselves prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. Keep the distinction below, and leave unresolved behavior unresolved until public documentation, our own reverse engineering, or observed behavior settles it.
docs.title: Runtime call reference

docs.text: The runtime registry distinguishes behavior it implements from diagnostics for behavior that is still unknown. RT_SYSLIB entries are callable implementations and count toward coverage; RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED entries remain callable so a reached import can fail with a useful name, but do not count as implemented or as supplied imports in progress reports. symbols/imports.csv records getpagesize and gettimeofday as imports of eboot from libScePosix ; libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . Import rows establish that the names are required, not their arguments, return values at every call site, or all clock IDs. The eight hash- verified target images ( eboot.elf and the seven modules, tools/check_target.py ) all state p_align 0x4000 for every PT_LOAD segment, with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000 (the difference is exactly 0x4000 in each; readelf -l prints the headers). The decompiled frame limiter calls gettimeofday with a null timezone argument. A separate verified clock helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , named CLOCK_MONOTONIC in that code. This confirms one monotonic clock request in the game; it does not establish every ID passed through the imported clock_gettime wrapper, or that no other ID is used in unexamined code. The sceKernelGetCompiledSdkVersion contract describes the observed libkernel getter, the runtime 's provider of mapped executable process-parameter metadata, and the dedicated synthetic registry tests. It also distinguishes that metadata provider from the unresolved console kernel syscall behavior.
docs.title: Evidence in this repository

docs.text: Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 getpagesize(void) No arguments. Returns the target's page size in bytes. The numeric value is platform-specific. getpagesize is not in current POSIX; portable code is directed to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . Linux and FreeBSD document the byte count; their manuals do not define a general error return for this function. Linux exposes it as a libc interface, not necessarily a dedicated kernel syscall. FreeBSD notes the system page size may differ from the underlying hardware page size. The import is present twice ( eboot from libScePosix , libc.elf from libkernel ), and both library names are registered against one implementation that answers 16384 , by the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c , #528). It is a ruling, not a measurement: the target images bound the value without picking one (every PT_LOAD of the eight hash- verified ELFs has p_align 0x4000 with p_offset congruent to p_vaddr modulo 0x4000, so the ELF ABI's congruence rule limits the page size to a divisor of 16384), stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096, and no public source names the console's own value; every PS4 runtime and port we can cite answers 16 KiB. See "getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown" below. What would still confirm it: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console. getpid(void) No arguments. Returns a pid_t naming the calling process. POSIX specifies that it succeeds and has no error return. Linux process IDs are scoped by PID namespaces; other systems have their own process-ID scope and lifecycle rules. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel ; libunwind passes the result to sysctl . The runtime answers a fixed id, 1000 , by the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c , #528, see "Process and input" below): runs stay reproducible, and the host's process id is not the guest's. The console's own value and its scope are not established. clock_gettime(clock_id, tp) clock_id selects a clock; tp points to a struct timespec . On the POSIX interface, tv_sec is seconds and tv_nsec is nanoseconds in [0, 1,000,000,000) . The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. POSIX uses 0 for success and -1 with errno for failure. An unsupported clock ID is an EINVAL case. Linux and BSD manuals document additional pointer-error details; use the target contract rather than assuming the host's errno mapping. The imported wrapper is present. The verified sceKernelClockGettime call requests ID 4 ( CLOCK_MONOTONIC ). That is evidence for the SCE entry point only, not proof of the libc wrapper's IDs. Other IDs and exact PS4 error and pointer handling remain unresolved. Unknown IDs must not silently return a fabricated time. gettimeofday(tv, tz) tv points to a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds in [0, 1,000,000) . The historical timezone argument is passed as null at the confirmed game call site. The exact target structure layout still needs ABI evidence. The wall clock can jump and is not a monotonic elapsed-time source. Historical POSIX specified a zero return on success and left errors undefined; Linux documents -1 / EFAULT for inaccessible pointers and ignores the timezone argument. POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. The imported wrapper and game call sites are present; the game passes null for the second argument. Exact target behavior for bad pointers, non-null timezone arguments, and error mapping is not established. Do not silently ignore an error without evidence. sched_yield(void) No arguments. Returns int . POSIX: the calling thread gives up the processor until it is again at the head of its thread list; 0 on success, -1 with errno otherwise, and POSIX defines no error case for it. FreeBSD documents the same call. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel . Implemented: a guest thread runs on a host thread, so the runtime yields the host thread and returns 0 ( runtime/syslib/kernel_thread.c ). A host failure has no FreeBSD error number to report, so it stops by name. Not observable in a unit test: that the host scheduler actually ran another thread. scePthreadYield Asks for the same yield through the thread library. The PS4 -visible signature is not established. FreeBSD's pthread_yield(3) is void ; Linux's is int (always 0 ). No PS4 -specific public source gives the SCE name's declaration. Imported by eboot and libc.elf from libkernel ; no call site in this repository shows whether the caller reads a result. Registered with RT_SYSLIB_UNRESOLVED : the entry stops by name and does not count as implemented. What would settle it: a guest call site showing whether the return register is read after the call, or a PS4 -specific public declaration. Do not assume an int or 0 from the FreeBSD or Linux analogues. memcpy(dest, src, n) , memset(dest, c, n) (libSceLibcInternal) void *memcpy(void *, const void *, size_t) and void *memset(void *, int, size_t) , the ISO C declarations. ISO C 7.24.2.1 and 7.24.6.1: memcpy copies n bytes from src to dest ; memset writes c converted to unsigned char into the first n bytes; both return dest . Overlapping memcpy regions and null pointers are undefined behaviour. Imported by libSceFios2.elf from libSceLibcInternal ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the host's own functions, since the standard fixes the whole result and no target-specific value is involved ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not modelled: what the PS4 C library does for the undefined cases; no public source or call site establishes it. sceKernelUsleep(microseconds) (libkernel), usleep(microseconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned 32-bit count of microseconds, returning int . For sceKernelUsleep the guest fixes the shape: the verified call sites in game/frame_timing/frame_limiter.cpp and game/render/swap_chain_present.cpp declare it as int(uint32_t microseconds) , and their cases expect 0 . FreeBSD's useconds_t is 32-bit unsigned. FreeBSD usleep(3) : suspends the thread for the given microseconds, 0 on success, -1 with EINTR if a signal interrupts it. SUSv2 also let usleep fail with EINVAL from 1,000,000 on; FreeBSD and POSIX.1-2008 (which removed usleep ) have no such limit. sceKernelUsleep is imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf , usleep by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: usleep with 1,000,000 or more, which stops by name because no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest sleeps or gets EINVAL ; and the SCE error, if any, for sceKernelUsleep , which the guest's sites never check. sleep(seconds) (libScePosix) One unsigned count of seconds, returning unsigned int : unsigned sleep(unsigned seconds) in POSIX and FreeBSD's sleep(3) . No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: suspends the thread until the seconds have elapsed or a caught signal arrives; returns 0 when the time has elapsed, otherwise the unslept seconds; no errors are defined. FreeBSD's libc ( lib/libc/gen/sleep.c ) is a nanosleep that rounds the unslept remainder up to whole seconds; above INT_MAX it sleeps INT_MAX seconds and returns seconds - INT_MAX without any signal. Imported by eboot . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested seconds and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left, as for usleep ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Open: more than INT_MAX seconds, which stops by name because POSIX has no early return without a signal and no PS4 -specific source says whether the guest gets the full sleep or FreeBSD's remainder. nanosleep(rqtp, rmtp) (libkernel) int nanosleep(const struct timespec *rqtp, struct timespec *rmtp) in POSIX and FreeBSD's nanosleep(2) , with FreeBSD amd64's struct timespec (two 64-bit fields, seconds and nanoseconds), the layout the clock_gettime entry uses. No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: suspends the thread until the requested time has elapsed and returns 0 ; a caught signal returns -1 with EINTR and writes the time left through a non-null rmtp ; nanoseconds outside [0, 1,000,000,000) are -1 with EINVAL ; rqtp and rmtp may point to the same object. A negative second count is not defined. FreeBSD's kern_time.c (same in stable/9 and main): the EINVAL check first, then a zero or negative time returns 0 at once without sleeping; nanosleep(2) adds EFAULT for a pointer it cannot use. Imported by libc.elf . Implemented: the host thread sleeps at least the requested time and the call returns 0 ; a host signal is not a guest event, so the sleep resumes with the time left and rmtp is never written, as for usleep and sleep ; the request is copied first, so rqtp and rmtp may be the same ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Stops by name: the errno cases (no rqtp , nanoseconds out of range), since errno is not modelled, as for clock_gettime . Open: a negative second count, which stops by name because POSIX does not define it, FreeBSD returns 0 at once and the host answers EINVAL , and no PS4 -specific source says which answer the guest gets. scePthreadRwlockInit(rwlock, attr, name) , scePthreadRwlockDestroy(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockRdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockWrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTryrdlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockTrywrlock(rwlock) , scePthreadRwlockUnlock(rwlock) (libkernel) A pointer to the guest's rwlock variable ( Init also an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); each returns int32_t . No call site in this repository shows these shapes; they come from the public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declarations, supporting evidence for the shapes only, and match FreeBSD's pthread_rwlock_* . POSIX pthread_rwlock_* , as FreeBSD libthr ( thr_rwlock.c ) and the kernel's umtx read-write lock ( kern_umtx.c ) implement it: a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use and a destroyed rwlock holding 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed rwlock; EBUSY from the try forms when the lock is not available; destroying does not check whether the lock is held, and leaves an unused initializer in place; unlocking is EPERM when another thread holds the write lock or when nobody holds the lock, and readers are counted, not named; a thread that locks again while holding the write lock is not given an error, it waits forever (no owner check in do_rw_wrlock or do_rw_rdlock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. Imported by eboot and libSceFios2.elf ( Tryrdlock by libSceFios2.elf only; symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented on a host rwlock that also records the writer and the reader count, which the host does not expose, for the unlock answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_rwlock.c ). A missing variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do; unlocking a never-used initializer is EPERM , as for the mutex. Stops by name: Rdlock or Wrlock while the caller holds the write lock (the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK ; neither is useful to return), and an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock and Timedwrlock are under Timed locks . Not part of this entry: the libScePosix names. __stack_chk_fail(void) (libkernel) No arguments, no result: void __stack_chk_fail(void) , and it never returns (LSB; FreeBSD libc declares it __dead2 ). Compiler-generated code calls it, not application code. LSB Core: the function that called it is aborted with a message that a stack overflow was detected, and the program then exits. FreeBSD libc logs "stack overflow detected; terminated" and ends the process with SIGABRT . Imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented as a stop by name ( rt_fatal , which aborts): ending the program is the whole guest-visible contract, so the entry counts as implemented ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Not covered: the PS4 's own message or crash report, which the guest cannot observe after it ends; and __stack_chk_guard , a separate data import whose PS4 value is not established (an unbound data import gets a zeroed page, runtime/boot.c ). _exit(status) (libkernel) One int , no result: void _exit(int status) , and it never returns (POSIX; FreeBSD's _exit(2) has the same shape and declares it __dead2 ). No call site in the repository fixes the shape further. POSIX: the process ends at once; functions registered with atexit are not called and open streams are not flushed; the low 8 bits of status ( status & 0377 ) are available to the waiting parent, and the full value to waitid and SIGCHLD handlers. FreeBSD _exit(2) : the same, the C library's exit(3) runs the atexit handlers and flushes, then calls _exit . Imported by libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented: the host's _exit with the guest's status, which has the same contract ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Under the boot harness , rt_exit_observer records the run's outcome first, as rt_fatal_observer does for a stop: pbboot reports "exited with code" and the full status, from any guest thread, and still writes the boot record ( runtime/boot.c ). Not covered: what the PS4 shows the player when a game ends this way, which the guest cannot observe after it ends. scePthreadCondInit(cond, attr, name) , scePthreadCondDestroy(cond) , scePthreadCondSignal(cond) , scePthreadCondBroadcast(cond) , scePthreadCondWait(cond, mutex) , scePthreadCondTimedwait(cond, mutex, microseconds) (libkernel) Pointers to the guest's cond and mutex variables; each returns int32_t . The guest fixes the wait shapes: the verified game/kernel/condition_wait.cpp declares Wait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex) and Timedwait as int32_t(void *cond, void *mutex, uint32_t timeout_us) , a relative timeout in microseconds, not POSIX's absolute timespec . The public OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares all six with these shapes ( Init with an attribute pointer and a name, as scePthreadMutexInit ); it is supporting evidence for the shapes only. POSIX pthread_cond_* , as FreeBSD libthr implements it ( thr_cond.c ): a static initializer ( NULL ) set up on first use; a destroyed cond holds 1 ( thr_private.h ); EINVAL for a destroyed cond; EBUSY to destroy one with waiters; destroying an unused initializer succeeds and leaves it in place; EPERM when the waiter does not own the mutex, for every mutex type, EINVAL when the mutex is destroyed ( _mutex_owned , thr_mutex.c ); ETIMEDOUT when a timed wait expires; a recursive mutex is released completely for the wait and its count restored after ( _mutex_cv_unlock , _mutex_cv_lock ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. scePthreadCondWait and Timedwait are imported by eboot , libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf , the other four by libSceFios2.elf and libc.elf ( symbols/imports.csv ). The guest's call site checks exactly 0x80020001 (EPERM), 0x80020016 (EINVAL) and 0x8002003c (ETIMEDOUT). Implemented on a host cond on the monotonic clock ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ): the timed wait times out once the given microseconds have passed since the call ( 0 : at once). A missing cond or mutex variable answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do. Stops by name: an attribute object passed to Init (no imported call creates one, so its contents are not established; an empty attribute variable means the defaults, as in libthr). A wait with a recursive mutex releases every level the caller holds and takes them back after, as libthr does: the runtime tracks each recursive mutex's owner and depth, and releases the extra levels itself around the host wait. A wait with a mutex the caller does not own is EPERM for every type, as in libthr (see Mutex ownership ). Open: a woken waiter counts until it has taken the mutex back, so a destroy right after a broadcast can answer EBUSY while libthr's succeeds; no known call site destroys a cond that way. The libScePosix names pthread_cond_init , _destroy , _signal , _broadcast and _wait (imported by eboot ) are the same calls with errno values: the executable's call at 0x0247e6d7 passes (&cond, NULL) and its caller compares the result with bare error numbers (12, 16, 34, 35). pthread_cond_timedwait(cond, mutex, abstime) (imported by eboot ; no call site in the repository) takes an absolute time in FreeBSD amd64's struct timespec , the two 64-bit fields of the clock_gettime entry, measured on the cond's clock: CLOCK_REALTIME unless an attribute set another (POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait ; libthr's cond_init for no attribute). No imported call can set another: nothing imports pthread_condattr_* , and an attribute object stops Init by name. libthr's pthread_cond_timedwait answers EINVAL before touching the mutex for no time, negative seconds and nanoseconds outside [0, 1,000,000,000) ; POSIX names only the nanoseconds case and leaves the other two undefined, and the runtime answers all three as libthr does. Implemented: the wait ends at the monotonic deadline where the wall clock reaches the time, the wall clock read first so it is never early; a time already passed is ETIMEDOUT with the mutex taken back. Open: a change of the wall clock during the wait is not followed, which POSIX's CLOCK_REALTIME wait would do. scePthreadKeyCreate(key, destructor) , scePthreadKeyDelete(key) , scePthreadGetspecific(key) , scePthreadSetspecific(key, value) (libkernel) A key is a pthread_key_t , an int on FreeBSD ( sys/_pthreadtypes.h ); Create takes a pointer to the guest's key variable and a destructor ( void (*)(void *) , may be null), Getspecific returns void * , the others int32_t . These shapes come from the public OpenOrbis libkernel.h , supporting evidence for the shapes only, and match FreeBSD's pthread_key_create , pthread_key_delete , pthread_getspecific and pthread_setspecific . POSIX thread-specific data, as FreeBSD libthr implements it ( thr_spec.c , the same in stable/9): a key is its slot's index plus 1, and Create takes the first free slot; Delete of a key that is out of range or free is EINVAL and calls no destructor; Setspecific of such a key is EINVAL , Getspecific answers NULL , as it does for a key the thread has not set since the key was created (each slot counts its creations). When a thread ends, each non-null value is cleared and, if its key is still the one it was set under, the destructor is called with it, in rounds while values remain ( _thread_cleanupspecific ). The SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. Imported by libc.elf from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the runtime 's own key table and a host thread-local value array per guest thread ( runtime/syslib/kernel_key.c ); a thread created by scePthreadCreate runs its destructors on its guest stack when its entry returns ( runtime/syslib/kernel_thread.c ). A missing key variable for Create (unchecked in libthr) answers EINVAL , as the mutex calls do. Not established: the PS4 's number of keys and of destructor rounds. POSIX guarantees at least 128 keys ( _POSIX_THREAD_KEYS_MAX ) and 4 rounds ( _POSIX_THREAD_DESTRUCTOR_ITERATIONS ), FreeBSD gives 256 and 4 ( <pthread.h> ); the runtime gives what POSIX guarantees and stops by name past it: a 129th live key, and a thread whose destructors still leave values after the 4th round. The main thread's values get no destructors, since it never ends through a thread exit here. | sceSysmoduleLoadModule(id) , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded(id) , sceSysmoduleUnloadModule(id) | One 32-bit system module ID; each returns int32_t . libSceSysmodule uses the complete 32-bit ID; the public OpenOrbis enum is narrower. | Load returns 0x805a1000 when (id & 0x7fffffff) == 0 ; query and unload return that status for ID 0, before locks or state changes. Evidence and library hash: system-module evidence . Other native errors are not established. | Declared 16-bit stub IDs retain the existing load/query/unload policy; other full-width requests stop by name before lookup, without aliasing a low ID. See "Module loading at run time" below. | | time(tloc) (libSceLibcInternal) | time_t time(time_t *tloc) , the ISO C declaration; time_t is a signed 64-bit integer on FreeBSD amd64. | ISO C 7.27.2.4: returns the calendar time, and also stores it in *tloc when tloc is not null; POSIX and FreeBSD time(3) make it the seconds since the Epoch (UTC). FreeBSD's implementation ( lib/libc/gen/time.c ) returns the seconds of clock_gettime(CLOCK_SECOND) since FreeBSD 9, and (time_t)-1 only when that call fails. | Imported by libSceFios2.elf from libSceLibcInternal ( symbols/imports.csv ); the executable's own time import is bound to the bundled libc.elf , whose time() also asks for clock 13 and returns its seconds (see " clock_gettime and sceKernelClockGettime " below). Implemented from the same clock as clock_gettime(13) : the host's wall clock in whole seconds, returned and stored through a non-null tloc ( runtime/syslib/kernel_time_of_day.c ). No -1 path: the runtime 's CLOCK_SECOND read cannot fail. Not established: no call site in this repository shows how libSceFios2.elf uses the result; an invalid non-null tloc is undefined behaviour and not modelled. | | gmtime(timer) , gmtime_s(timer, result) (libSceLibcInternal) | struct tm *gmtime(const time_t *) and C11 Annex K's struct tm *gmtime_s(const time_t *restrict, struct tm *restrict) : libSceFios2 's calls ( +0x2cd73 , +0x2cdf4 , +0x2e494 ) pass a time_t on the stack, and the gmtime_s callers test the answer for null, so it is the Annex K form, not Microsoft's error-number one. The PS4 's struct tm is ISO C's nine int s, 36 bytes, without FreeBSD's tm_gmtoff and tm_zone : the same module's time-zone helper ( +0x2cd15 ) copies exactly 0x24 bytes into a local struct tm that mktime normalizes in place, and its next local starts 0x28 bytes later, so a 56-byte FreeBSD struct tm would not fit. | ISO C 7.27.3.3 and N1570 K.3.8.2.3: the UTC broken-down time; gmtime answers a pointer to the library's own object, which a later call may overwrite, gmtime_s fills the caller's structure and answers its address. | Imported by libSceFios2.elf ( symbols/imports.csv ). Implemented with the host's gmtime_r , writing the nine int s and nothing more; gmtime 's object is one per thread ( runtime/syslib/libc_internal.c ). Stops by name: no time or no result (undefined in ISO C; Annex K's constraint handler is not modelled), and a time whose year does not fit an int (FreeBSD sets errno , which is not modelled for this library). localtime and mktime stay unimplemented: they need the console's time zone, which is not established. | | printf(format, ...) , vprintf(format, ap) , vsnprintf(buffer, size, format, ap) (libSceLibcInternal) | The ISO C declarations. The module's 62 printf calls pass constant formats with %s conversions; its 33 vsnprintf calls pass formats through from their callers. | ISO C 7.21.6.3, 7.21.6.10 and 7.21.6.12. | Imported by libSceFios2.elf ( symbols/imports.csv ). The guest calls with the System V convention the host uses, so its va_list is the host's and the host's functions format; printf and vprintf write to the host's standard output ( runtime/syslib/libc_internal.c ). Each format is checked first, and what the runtime cannot hand to the host unchanged stops by name: %lc and %ls (the PS4 's wchar_t is not established), %n (the host's fortified printf refuses it from writable memory, and no call is known to pass it), any conversion ISO C does not define, no format, and no buffer for a non-zero size. Not implemented: fflush (its stream is the _Stdout data import, which the runtime does not provide). |
docs.title: Interfaces and known behavior

docs.text: Observed in our target : the executable imports sceSysmoduleLoadModule , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule from libSceSysmodule ; its shipped file I/O module imports the load and unload calls too. Neither imports sceKernelLoadStartModule or another loader entry ( symbols/imports.csv ), so a module is asked for by its system module id and nothing else. Five of the seven modules the title ships are listed with action stub in game/modules.csv , which records that the executable imports nothing from them; they are not mapped. Documented publicly : the OpenOrbis toolchain's id list ( include/orbis/_types/sysmodule.h , after psdevwiki's "Libraries" page) names the ids of those five: ORBIS_SYSMODULE_FACE 0x0038 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_SMART 0x0039 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_S3DCONVERSION 0x0086 , ORBIS_SYSMODULE_HAND 0x0093 and ORBIS_SYSMODULE_HEAD_TRACKER 0x00cb . They are recorded in the sysmodule column of game/modules.csv ; the runtime itself names no module ( tools/check_agnostic.py ): tools/boot.py passes each stub to pbboot as --stub-module ID:NAME , and the run's status ( stub_modules in symbols/boot.json ) says which of them the guest loaded. Inferred : if nothing we map imports from a stub (as game/modules.csv records for the executable), answering the load without mapping the module cannot leave a call unbound; an import it would have satisfied still shows up unbound in symbols/imports.csv and stops the boot by name. Whether the executable's sites check the result beyond success, and which ids they pass, is not yet observed: the boot stops before the first load today. System modules the runtime provides : a module the title does not ship but loads by id (it is part of the system) can be listed with action runtime once the runtime implements the functions the executable imports from it. tools/boot.py passes it like a stub, so a load is reported as done, and its imports bind to the runtime 's entries by name. The first is libSceAppContent ( 0x00b4 in the OpenOrbis id list), below. A second load of a loaded module succeeds and is counted; each unload takes one load back, and the module is loaded until the last one (maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10; shadPS4's sysmodule_internal.cpp counts loads the same way, facts only). The message and commerce dialogs load their module on every open, so a refused second load would stop the second dialog. Unknown : the error values (a module not loaded, an id the system does not know). Each is a named fatal until a console measurement or a guest call site settles it. The runtime validates the complete 32-bit module ID before consulting its configured module list. A wider ID such as 0xabcd7f01 does not alias the 16-bit ID 0x7f01 . Unsupported IDs stop by API name before looking up or changing a module record. In libSceSysmodule (SHA-256 43c456e00b59b2bd1303023cbcb463f50c0647854b4837468f8fc6c290b55c23 ), these argument checks precede the lock and the delegated module operation: sceSysmoduleLoadModule returns 0x805a1000 when (id & 0x7fffffff) == 0 , covering IDs 0 and 0x80000000 . sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule return the same status for ID 0. Their handling of 0x80000000 is delegated and remains unknown. These early errors leave every configured module record unchanged, including an explicitly configured zero-ID record. The original load validator distinguishes IDs 0x80 , 0xb0 and 0xb8 from other complete 32-bit IDs before its category checks; narrowing the argument would select a different path. The library functions are at module offsets 0x410 (load), 0x580 (query), 0x520 (unload) and 0x480 (load validation). Their complete instruction spans and unwind entries establish the boundaries. These observations describe this library version; they do not establish behavior on every firmware. The wrappers also propagate lock failures and delegated statuses. Load remaps 0x80020064 to 0x80020016 after a successful lock. Inner loading, category predicates, reference counts and release behavior remain unknown; the runtime stops on requests that would need those answers. The module-ID tests check the early numeric errors, complete-ID diagnostics, unchanged module records on rejection, wider IDs against loaded and unloaded records, and the configured 16-bit module lifecycle. Synthetic configured IDs exercise the runtime 's supported behavior; they do not prove acceptance by the original library's validator.
docs.title: Module loading at run time (libSceSysmodule)

docs.text: An affinity mask identifies the CPUs on which a thread may run. The current startup stop is a query for the main thread's mask. Returning success without the correct output would change the CPU count that the bundled C library stores; it would not implement the query. Observed in the hash-pinned bundled libc.elf : the function at module offset 0x81a80 initializes a thread attribute, obtains the current thread, and copies its attributes. If those operations succeed, its call at libc.elf+0x81ad0 passes the address of that attribute variable in RDI and the address of a zero-initialized eight-byte stack slot in RSI. This is a two-pointer interface, not FreeBSD's three-argument interface with an explicit buffer size. The return site is libc.elf+0x81ad5 , matching the genuine boot diagnostic. The caller does not check the affinity query's return value: after destroying the attribute it reads the slot, counts its set bits across 64 bits, and stores a 32-bit count. This establishes the consumer's memory requirements, not the real query's write width, the actual mask or its complete error contract. The original consumer also ran through the existing harness on nine private constructed fixtures with scripted imports, using each compiler's loader . It produced the expected counts for zero, low-bit, high-bit and all-bit masks, and exercised both earlier failure branches. A scripted nonzero affinity return with a supplied mask still produced that mask's count, corroborating that this caller ignores the return. These are original-consumer observations under synthetic import behavior, not observations of PS4 affinity, recorded gameplay, complete instruction-trace verification or an original-versus-replacement comparison. No function status changes follow from them. Public supporting evidence: the OpenOrbis homebrew header libkernel.h declares a signed 32-bit return and an attribute pointer plus an output pointer. Its comment explicitly leaves the mask type unfinished; the declaration is corroboration, not a measured PS4 contract. The FreeBSD 9.3 affinity manual describes retrieving a stored attribute mask, success/error returns and invalid attributes, but its API includes a size argument absent at this target call. Its errors and CPU-set layout cannot simply be assigned to the SCE interface. Still required before implementation: independently establish the main thread's actual mask, how a fresh attribute differs from one filled by scePthreadAttrGet , the exact output write extent, success/error results, and invalid/null attribute or output handling. Host CPU availability and a guessed console core count establish none of these. No specific affinity implementation is added or registered by this investigation; the import remains unbound. A useful target measurement would record the console/firmware and executable identities, the results of attribute initialization and copying from scePthreadSelf , the getter's return bits, the output bytes with adjacent canaries, and repeated observations without changing affinity. Check current claims in issue #34 before taking implementation work; mentions of the boot blocker are not themselves contributor claims. Generic gameplay capture remains separate contributor-owned work, not a reason to synthesize the missing affinity observation. How the boot gets past it without a value. These are observations from static analysis of the hash-pinned eboot.elf , libc.elf and libSceFios2.elf ( Ghidra 12.0.3 with GhidraOrbis , issue
docs.title: scePthreadAttrGetaffinity: the startup consumer and missing evidence

docs.text: The probe's count is stored at libc.elf+0xd1c54 . That lies past the RW segment's file size, so it starts zero. The probe returns nothing. It is reached only by a tail jump from the initializer at +0x5fad0 , which the module's DT_INIT runs. The count's only reader found is the exported std::thread::hardware_concurrency() at +0x5fac0 . No reference to that function was found in those three objects, none of them imports it, and none imports sceKernelDlsym . So game/module_hooks.csv replaces two functions before any guest code runs: - the probe ( +0x81a80 , 128 bytes) with return , so the affinity query is never made and the count stays zero; - hardware_concurrency ( +0x5fac0 , 7 bytes) with stop , so a caller ends the run by name instead of reading a count nobody established. pbboot --module-hook first compares each function's first bytes, as the mapped and relocated module holds them, with the ones the file gives ( first_bytes ), and refuses the run before any guest code runs if they differ. It then writes each as a five-byte relative jump to a stub in the module's slot. A return stub leaves every register as the caller had it. A stop is reported like an unimplemented import: the status names the hook and its caller in stopped_by_hook . scePthreadAttrGetaffinity stays unbound. The hook guards calls only. A direct read of +0xd1c54 that the analysis missed would see 0, not a measured count. The offsets fit only the pinned libc.elf ( target.sha256 ); another build fails the byte check by name instead of being patched.
docs.title: 34), not guarantees:

docs.text: The only clock ID confirmed by a decompiled game call in this repository is 4 , used with sceKernelClockGettime and identified there as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . This does not prove that the game passes 4 to the imported clock_gettime wrapper. POSIX defines clock identifiers symbolically; their numeric values are implementation-specific. Linux adds clocks such as CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME ; FreeBSD has its own clock set, including CLOCK_UPTIME variants. Their names and numeric values are not interchangeable evidence for PS4 behavior. CLOCK_MONOTONIC represents elapsed time from an unspecified starting point and is not the wall clock. The precise effects of suspend, rate correction, and resolution vary by implementation. gettimeofday and CLOCK_REALTIME represent wall time tied to the Epoch and can move when system time changes. No source examined here establishes that the game asks the imported clock_gettime wrapper for CLOCK_REALTIME , CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW , CLOCK_BOOTTIME , or another ID.
docs.title: Clock IDs and platform differences

docs.text: The four libSceNet imports sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs take and return 32-bit or 16-bit unsigned integers, respectively. Public PSP2SDK API declarations provide those widths for the SCE names. The standard byte-order contract converts host order to network (big-endian) order for hton* , and reverses that conversion for ntoh* ; this is documented by the FreeBSD byte-order manual . Paleblood's guest ABI is AMD64, so these four conversions are byte reversals. Their implementations do not call host networking APIs or depend on host socket state. This evidence supports only the four integer conversions. It says nothing about libSceNet socket, resolver, epoll, offline-state, or error behavior; those imports remain unresolved until their own contracts are established.
docs.title: Network byte-order helpers

docs.text: The executable imports sceNetInetPton from libSceNet . Target call-site inspection found four unconditional call instructions (at 0x0085785e , 0x011c7a7b , 0x02f984f6 , and 0x02df348d ); each passes address family 2 and supplies the result as an IPv4 address. The consumers use a positive return as success. This establishes Bloodborne's observed call shape, not every address family supported by the PS4 library. The import thunk and pointer-table references are not additional call sites. For the observed AF_INET path, the runtime uses the documented BSD inet_pton(3) contract : parse dotted-decimal IPv4 text into four network-order bytes, return 1 for valid input and 0 for malformed input. This conversion does not open a socket or perform network I/O. Other target address families and null-pointer error behavior remain unresolved, so the runtime emits a named diagnostic for those inputs instead of forwarding host-specific errors. sceNetInetNtop(family, source, destination, size) is the reverse, BSD inet_ntop(3) for AF_INET: the four network-order bytes as dotted-decimal text, answering the destination. The executable's one call ( 0x02f982df ) passes family 2 , an address from sceNetHtonl and a 16-byte buffer (enough for 255.255.255.255 and its terminator), and tests the answer for null. A buffer too small for the text answers null with ENOSPC in errno under BSD; the library's errno ( sceNetErrnoLoc ) is not modelled, so that case stops by name, as do other families and missing pointers.
docs.title: IPv4 text conversion (sceNetInetPton, sceNetInetNtop, issue #41)

docs.text: Ruling (maintainer, 2026-11-10): both entries answer 16384 ( runtime/syslib/kernel.c ). Every source we can cite agrees on 16 KiB: shadPS4's kernel, the bloodborne-native port family and the Astrr00 port (facts only), the p_align of every target segment, and the runtime 's own 16 KiB memory granule. The record below is why it is a ruling and not a measurement. Observed in our target (read-only; the eight images verify against target.sha256 and target.image.sha256 ): symbols/imports.csv has exactly two getpagesize rows - eboot from libScePosix and libc.elf from libkernel . No sysconf and no quad-page call is imported, so this is the only page-size query the guest has. All sixteen PT_LOAD segments of those eight images have p_align 0x4000 , and in every one p_offset - p_vaddr is exactly 0x4000 . Three guest call sites share one shape: 0x00e04168 , 0x00e04939 and 0x00e05cf9 , each inside functions 0x00e04140 , 0x00e045c0 and 0x00e05a80 . Each is a lazy initialiser: a guard tests 0x05859ec0 , the call is made, the result is cltq -extended, blsr %rax,%rcx with jne rejects it unless it is a power of two, and the value is cached in 0x05859ec8 beside three fixed siblings ( 0x10000 , 0x40000 , 0x200000 ). 0x05859ec8 has exactly five cross-references in the executable: the three writes above and two reads, all inside those same three functions. None of them compares the cached value against a constant, and no other function reads it. Inferred, and the premise each inference needs : The ELF ABI takes p_align of a loadable segment to be a multiple of the system page size, and requires p_offset and p_vaddr to be congruent modulo the page size. If the PS4 loader follows both rules for these segments , a page size larger than 0x4000 could not map them at their fixed addresses, while any power-of-two divisor of 0x4000 could. Restricting that to 0x1000 , 0x2000 and 0x4000 adds a second assumption - that the page size is at least 4096 - which is ours, not observed. The guest's own blsr check is consistent with every power of two and selects none of them. So p_align bounds the candidate set under our premises; it does not measure the value the kernel returns, and none of the three candidates is established. Unknown : the number the PS4 reports. Stock FreeBSD on AMD64 uses 4096 ( PAGE_SHIFT 12 , sys/amd64/include/param.h ), and Sony's open-source page confirms a FreeBSD kernel but publishes the upstream sources rather than the console's modifications, so that value describes the ancestor and not the target. Our own loader does not depend on a page size either: it copies PT_LOAD segments at byte-exact p_vaddr into one image buffer ( runtime/loader.c , rt_elf_map ) and uses p_align only for TLS, and the 4096 s in runtime/boot.c are host allocation sizes. What would confirm the ruling: one observed getpagesize() or sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) result on a console.
docs.title: getpagesize: observed, inferred, unknown

docs.text: The executable imports exactly six functions from libSceNetCtl and neither sceNetCtlInit nor sceNetCtlTerm ( symbols/imports.csv ), so the runtime answers the connection queries itself and the game takes its offline paths. The public declarations of the same API family on PS Vita ( psp2/net/netctl.h in vitasdk/vita-headers, and the PSP2SDK header reference) give the shape of the calls: a state query through an int * , an information query by an int code into a structure pointer, one NAT query through a structure pointer, and a callback check that takes nothing and returns int . Vita is a different operating system, so those declarations are evidence for the shape only and their numbers are never proof of a PS4 value. Facts from other runtimes are used only where a row cites them (the "not connected" value); elsewhere the guest's own call sites decide. They have settled the state numbers (0 is not up, 3 is connected) and the callback keying (an id handed back, not a state), and everything they do not reach - error codes, structure layouts, the offline answers - stays a fatal that names the question and the evidence that would close it. Function Arguments and representation Publicly documented result and errors Evidence and open questions for PS4 sceNetCtlGetState(int *state) One pointer to a 32-bit int , by the Vita-era declaration. Writes the state the system is in. The Vita-era family names the disconnected state first in its state enum, so 0 there. Public sources give no error return for a query that succeeds. Implemented: an offline runtime reports the disconnected state and succeeds. The guest fixes the numbers for us - one site tests the returned slot against 0 at 0x00dfd260 to decide whether to keep waiting, another bounds it with cmp $0x3; ja before a four-entry table at 0x020413f3 (so the states it can see are {0, 1, 2, 3}), and equality with 3 is the connected branch at 0x010b839f and in its own callback at 0x010b45e5 .
