Still open: what 1 and 2 mean, the PS4 enumerator names, and the error value for a null state pointer (fatal). sceNetCtlCheckCallback(void) No arguments; returns int , by the Vita-era declaration. Runs the callbacks made due by a state change. No public source describes the return value at all, only the declaration. Implemented as 0, the one value both candidate contracts give while nothing is due: the runtime never leaves the disconnected state, so no callback runs. Which reading is the PS4 's (a success code, or the number of callbacks it ran)? It only matters once a state change is possible. sceNetCtlRegisterCallback(void *callback, void *arg, int *cid) A callback pointer, an argument pointer and an out-parameter int *cid , returning int . The guest's own call at 0x010b8352 passes a function in the image, this , and lea -0x78(%rbp) , a slot it never writes, then reads that slot back at 0x010b8428 into its object at +0x130 . Vita-era registration is keyed by a callback id the caller receives back ( func, arg, int *cid ); the guest's sites show the same shape on PS4 . The two public Vita-era sources disagree about the callback's return type, so the pointer stays opaque and no signature is modelled for it - the guest's callback at 0x010b45e0 does show it being dispatched as (state, arg). Implemented: each registration gets a fresh id written through the caller's pointer, numbered from 1 so an id can never look like an unwritten slot, and nothing is ever dispatched while offline. Open: the error values for a null callback or a null id slot, the table's capacity, and whether re-registering the same callback replaces or adds (we add, being keyed by id). sceNetCtlUnregisterCallback(int cid) One int : the id a previous register call handed back. The guest passes the field it stored from that out-parameter ( 0x010b8f8d ). The Vita-era form takes the callback id int cid , which the sites match. Implemented for an id we handed out: remove it and succeed. Fatal for an id we never handed out, or one already removed - no public source gives the PS4 answer and the guest's own paths never reach it. sceNetCtlGetInfo(int code, void *info) Claimed as an int code and a structure pointer, by the Vita-era sceNetCtlInetGetInfo(int code, SceNetCtlInfo *info) ; OpenOrbis NetCtl.h and shadPS4's netctl.h name code 14 ORBIS_NET_CTL_INFO_IP_ADDRESS . shadPS4's sceNetCtlGetInfo answers 0x80412108 (not connected) for every code while the console is not connected, before writing anything. Offline: code 14, the only code the executable asks for ( 0x00dfd2b9 , 0x00dfd445 , each printing the buffer only on a non-negative answer), answers "not connected" and writes nothing. Other codes stop by name (a disconnected console may still describe its device or link; no source settles it), and so does a missing structure (PS4Recomp checks it first, shadPS4 the connection first). sceNetCtlGetNatInfo(void *nat_info) { size, STUN status, NAT type, mapped address } , four 32-bit fields, 16 bytes; "not connected" is 0x80412108 (PS4Recomp's libSceNetCtl , used as facts). The guest writes 16 at offset 0 ( 0x01889417 ), reads back only offset 8, the NAT type, and only on 0 ( 0x01889436 ); on any other answer it takes NAT type 1 itself ( 0x0188942d ). Offline: answers "not connected" and writes nothing, so the guest's own fallback applies. A size other than 16 and a missing structure stop by name. 0 is the success value, the convention public SCE-family documentation states for these calls (the @return 0 on success lines in psp2/error.h of vita-headers). libSceNetCtl's own error codes have no public source, so no path in runtime/syslib/netctl.c returns one: a case that would need an error value stops the boot by name instead.
docs.title: Network connection state (libSceNetCtl, issue #41)

docs.text: eboot and libSceFios2.elf import scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate from libkernel , and eboot imports pthread_attr_setdetachstate from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ). Each source below establishes a different part: What the call does: POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate . A thread created with the attribute starts detached for PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED and joinable for PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE . Invalid detach state: POSIX and FreeBSD's pthread_attr(3) both make any other value EINVAL . Invalid attribute variable: POSIX leaves a null or uninitialised attribute undefined and only recommends EINVAL , and the FreeBSD manual lists no error for it. The behaviour comes from FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_setdetachstate ( lib/libthr/thread/thr_attr.c ), which returns EINVAL when the variable is null or holds no attribute object. The numbers: FreeBSD's <pthread.h> defines the two states as 0 and 1 . The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK header ( include/orbis/_types/pthread.h ) defines ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE and ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED with the same values. That header follows FreeBSD's text, so it corroborates the numbers rather than measuring them independently. As with the mutex functions ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ), the SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number, and the POSIX name returns the number itself. Still open: the detach state a fresh attribute starts with, and the one scePthreadAttrGet copies from a running thread. Both are values the system supplies. POSIX makes joinable the default, but nothing we can cite confirms what the PS4 reports. In FreeBSD libthr, _pthread_create ( thr_create.c ) uses that same default ( _pthread_attr_default ) when it is given no attribute variable or an empty one. The runtime treats both cases as the unknown default, so the outcome, a fatal, does not depend on the PS4 matching libthr there. How the runtime keeps that open: The attribute records a state only when one is set ( has_detach_state ). scePthreadAttrGet replaces the whole attribute, as libthr's pthread_attr_get_np does, so a state set before the copy is dropped. By convention, thread creation reads the state through rt_thread_attr_detach_state ( runtime/include/runtime/process.h ) and never from the field. A fresh attribute's field holds zero, which is the joinable value, so reading the field directly would assume joinable silently. For no variable, an empty variable, or a state nobody set, the reader stops the process ( rt_fatal ), names the call that asked, and says which of those cases it hit. What would settle it: an observed scePthreadAttrGetdetachstate result on a console, for a fresh attribute and for one filled by scePthreadAttrGet from the main thread. Guest call sites would also settle it: a thread created without a detach state being set, then joined or detached ( scePthreadJoin , pthread_join and scePthreadDetach are imported).
docs.title: Thread attribute detach state (scePthreadAttrSetdetachstate, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy from libScePosix ( symbols/imports.csv ), next to the libkernel SCE names the runtime already implements. They are the same calls with the POSIX error convention, as for the mutex and detach-state calls: pthread_self has no error return (POSIX), so it answers what scePthreadSelf answers: the calling thread's own variable value. With no guest thread registered on the host thread it stops by the name the guest used. pthread_attr_init allocates the attribute object and stores it in the variable; ENOMEM when it cannot (POSIX; FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_attr_init ). pthread_attr_destroy frees it and empties the variable; EINVAL for a missing or empty variable (libthr's _pthread_attr_destroy ). The POSIX names return the error number itself, the SCE names 0x80020000 plus it, and an object made under one name is freed under the other. A missing variable passed to pthread_attr_init is undefined in POSIX and unchecked in libthr. The runtime answers EINVAL under both names, as the SCE name already did; no PS4 source or call site says otherwise.
docs.title: POSIX names of the thread self and attribute calls (libScePosix, issue #34)

docs.text: A mutex belongs to the thread that locked it. FreeBSD libthr ( thr_mutex.c , the same in stable/9 and main) checks that for every mutex type: Unlocking a mutex the caller does not own is EPERM , whether it is free or another thread holds it ( mutex_unlock_common ); so is a condition wait with it ( _mutex_owned ). The owner locking again gets EDEADLK for the error-checking (default) and adaptive types, and waits forever for the normal type, on purpose ( mutex_self_lock ). Its trylock is EBUSY for all three ( mutex_self_trylock ). A recursive mutex counts one more level. The host (glibc) checks the owner only for its error-checking and recursive types, and its adaptive type waits forever when the owner locks again. So the runtime makes every non-recursive guest mutex an error-checking host mutex, and keeps the guest type for its own answers ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ): scePthreadMutexUnlock , pthread_mutex_unlock and the condition waits answer EPERM for a caller that does not own the mutex, for the normal and adaptive types too. The adaptive type locked again by its owner answers EDEADLK , as in libthr. The normal type locked again by its owner stops by the name the guest used ( scePthreadMutexLock or pthread_mutex_lock ): the system would wait forever, the host answers EDEADLK , and neither is useful to return. The SCE names return 0x80020000 plus the error number, the libScePosix names the number itself. One difference left: the adaptive type no longer spins before it sleeps, as libthr's and glibc's do; that changes timing only, not an answer.
docs.title: Mutex ownership (scePthreadMutexUnlock, issue #132)

docs.text: Each takes the lock variable and the most it may wait, in microseconds from now (OpenOrbis libkernel.h declares an OrbisKernelUseconds ; shadPS4 binds the three names to libthr's relative-time calls, pthread_mutex_reltimedlock_np and pthread_rwlock_reltimed*lock_np , facts only). The executable's lock wrappers take them for any timeout but -1, which uses the untimed call: 0x02484119 (mutex) tells EDEADLK , EINVAL , EAGAIN and ETIMEDOUT apart, and 0x0247f681 and 0x0247f411 (rwlock) EDEADLK , EINVAL and ETIMEDOUT . What the runtime does: - The wait ends with the lock, or with ETIMEDOUT once the time has passed, on the monotonic clock (as for scePthreadCondTimedwait ). - The owner asking again. With a timeout, libthr's mutex_self_lock sleeps the whole time and answers ETIMEDOUT for the error-checking, adaptive and normal types; a recursive mutex takes one more level. The kernel's umtx rwlock has no owner check, so a thread holding the write lock that asks again waits out the time too ( do_rw_rdlock , do_rw_wrlock ). The host would answer EDEADLK at once, so the runtime sleeps the time itself. - A destroyed lock or a missing variable is EINVAL , and the static initializers are set up on first use, as for the untimed calls.
docs.title: Timed locks (scePthreadMutexTimedlock, scePthreadRwlockTimedrdlock, scePthreadRwlockTimedwrlock, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize , sceKernelAllocateDirectMemory , sceKernelMapDirectMemory and sceKernelReleaseDirectMemory ( symbols/imports.csv ). Its first use is the startup heap, at 0x02481a80 : It asks for the size. It allocates 0x7400000 bytes, aligned to 0x200000 , anywhere from 0 to that size, with memory type 0. It maps the range read/write (protection 3) with flags 0, so the system picks the address, at the same alignment. If the map fails, it releases the range. On any failure it logs an error and builds its heap from a null base, so these calls have to succeed. The signatures match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h , as supporting evidence only. The pool. Direct memory is a host memory file. An allocation is a range of it and a map is a host mapping of that range, so two maps of one range see the same bytes. The size. sceKernelGetDirectMemorySize answers the size of that pool (5 GiB), a choice of the runtime . The PS4 's value is not established here. A title that sizes its allocations from the answer sizes them from the runtime 's pool. Allocation. It takes the lowest start at or above the search start that fits before the search end. GPU access. The executable maps with protection 3 and 0x33 , CPU and GPU read/write ( 0x10 and 0x20 in the public SDK list). The host mapping takes the CPU bits. Where a map goes. Without an address hint, the system chooses: A GPU-visible map goes at a fixed base ( 0x2000000000 ) plus its offset in the pool. Every such address is then a fixed distance from the same byte of the pool, which is how the renderer's GPU will reach guest memory: it gets the whole pool as one buffer ( runtime/gpu_memory.h , docs/RENDERER.md ). Other maps go anywhere free in the map window above that region. A second GPU-visible map of a range would need the same place, so it stops by name. A boot doesn't make one: every range it maps, it maps once. With a hint, a map goes where the hint says (below). What stops by name. Every case whose PS4 answer is not established stops with the function's name: lengths, starts or alignments that are not multiples of 16 KiB (the granularity the executable's calls use); memory types other than 0, 3 and 10; map flags other than no-overwrite ( 0x80 , shadPS4's kernel memory.h ). No-overwrite keeps a map off memory already mapped, and the runtime never replaces a mapping, so it changes nothing. The movie code ( 0x02d032b9 ) passes it with no address, to map part of its own direct memory a second time; protection other than CPU and GPU read and write; a range that does not fit or was not allocated; releasing part of a range or a mapped one; the error values. Measured with a local boot that let the libc affinity probe return (not committed): with these four calls the executable's heap setup succeeds and the boot reaches entry . It stops next at scePthreadRwlockInit .
docs.title: Direct memory (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: The existing sceKernelAllocateDirectMemory and sceKernelMapDirectMemory implementations validate lengths by subtraction after checking the starting address. This prevents a full-width length from wrapping an end address and passing the allocation or containment check. An allocation must fit wholly inside its end-exclusive search range; a map must fit inside one live allocation. Misaligned address hints still stop by the API name before mapping. test_direct_memory_bounds exercises the registered calls with exact boundaries, overlong and wrapping ranges, a misaligned hint and a valid writable map. These are host validation limits, without a claim about native error codes.
docs.title: Range arithmetic

docs.text: libc.elf is Sony's FreeBSD-derived libc, with HP libunwind for C++ exceptions. These call sites are in libc.elf unless marked; libSceFios2 imports from libSceLibcInternal . Data - __progname points at "eboot.bin" (shadPS4, the deadinside28 port). - _Stdout ( libSceLibcInternal ) is a 456-byte object, the size of libc.elf 's own _Stdout . libSceFios2 only passes its address to fflush . - Need_sceLibcInternal is an int holding 1. libSceFios2 stores its address and never reads it. No-ops and fixed answers - __pthread_cxa_finalize does nothing: there is no fork, so there are no atfork handlers. - _is_signal_return answers 0: no guest signals are delivered, so there is no signal trampoline (PS4Recomp agrees). - signal keeps each signal's disposition and answers the previous one, delivering nothing. libc's one call sets SIGKILL to SIG_DFL. A signal outside 1 to 128, or a handler other than SIG_DFL for SIGKILL or SIGSTOP, answers SIG_ERR with EINVAL (FreeBSD's rules). - __cxa_finalize ( libSceFios2 ) does nothing: the module registers no handlers. Output and files - _write writes descriptors 1 and 2 (stdio, +0x27362 ) to the host's standard output and error. Other descriptors stop by name. - fflush ( libSceFios2 ) flushes the host's standard output for &_Stdout , and every host stream for NULL. Other streams stop by name. - fstat is sceKernelFstat with -1 and errno (libunwind, +0x530ae ). Clocks and time - getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF) gives the host's process times in FreeBSD's 144-byte layout. libc's clock() ( +0x2ef13 ) reads them. - sceKernelGettimezone writes the standard offset in minutes east of UTC and the daylight saving minutes, for the host's zone. libc's localtime and mktime add both to UTC, which fixes the sign; shadPS4 fills them the same way. - localtime and mktime ( libSceLibcInternal ) use the same zone. mktime normalizes in place, or answers -1 and leaves the structure as it was. Memory - mmap . Anonymous private read-write maps ( +0x52fac and others) are flexible memory, rounded up to 16 KiB (shadPS4's posix_mmap , and a native port family). - EINVAL for a zero length, a descriptor other than -1, or a non-zero offset. - File maps, hints, and other flags or protections stop by name. - munmap is sceKernelMunmap with -1 and errno. - msync is libunwind's mapped-memory probe ( +0x541a5 ). The runtime asks the host and answers 0, or -1 with ENOMEM. A constant 0 would let libunwind read unmapped memory. - sceKernelMapNamedFlexibleMemory maps like sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory . No name answers 0x8002000e , and 32 or more characters 0x8002003f (shadPS4). - sceKernelMlock answers 0: host memory needs no locking. NULL, zero length or a wrapping range answer EINVAL. - malloc and free ( libSceLibcInternal ) use the host allocator, reached through libSceFios2 's default allocator. Process and input (maintainer's rulings, 2026-11-10) - getpid answers 1000, the fixed id of the bloodborne-native port family (facts only): runs stay reproducible, and the host's pid is not the guest's. libunwind passes it to sysctl . - _read on descriptor 0 (stdio, +0x2729a ) answers end of file, 0 bytes: a console title has no standard input. Other descriptors stop by name. - __stack_chk_guard (data) is the stack protector's canary, a fixed non-zero word, 0xdeadbeef54321abc (shadPS4's; droogie's and Astrr00's hosts also use fixed constants). Unbound, the import read a zeroed page. Exceptions - sceKernelDebugRaiseException and the OnReleaseMode variant. A non-zero second argument answers EINVAL. Otherwise the program stops by name with the code: abort() raises 0xa002000b . This is shadPS4's behaviour.
docs.title: What the title's C library imports (libc.elf and libSceFios2, issue #34)

docs.text: libc.elf's HP libunwind and FreeBSD's __cxa_finalize ask the system about modules and process memory ( runtime/syslib/kernel_unwind.c ). The runtime records every module it maps ( rt_process.modules , filled by runtime/boot.c from the loader : segments, PT_GNU_EH_FRAME , DT_INIT , DT_FINI ). sceKernelGetModuleInfoFromAddr(address, flags, info) fills the 0x1a8-byte structure shadPS4's module.h calls OrbisKernelModuleInfoEx : size, name (256 bytes), id, TLS fields (left 0: no caller reads them), init and fini, the exception frame index and the frames it points to with their sizes ( 0x148 - 0x15c ), and up to four segments {address, u32 size, s32 prot} with their count ( 0x160 , 0x1a0 ). The segments carry the program header's flags, as in shadPS4. libunwind asks with flags 1 ( +0x61d34 , then reads the index at 0x148 and checks its version byte); __cxa_finalize with flags 2. shadPS4's errors: flags 3 or more zero the structure and answer EINVAL , no structure EFAULT ( 0x8002000e ), an address in no module ESRCH ( 0x80020003 ). The frames' start is decoded from the index's DWARF pointer encoding (absolute or pc-relative, 4 or 8 bytes); other encodings, another version and frames after their index stop by name. __elf_phdr_match_addr(info, address) is FreeBSD libc's helper ( lib/libc/gen/elf_utils.c ): 1 when a segment with the execute flag holds the address, else 0 ( +0x2f39e ). __Ux86_64_setcontext(context) resumes at a landing pad. The layout is the one libc.elf's own getcontext writes ( +0x53cd0 , FreeBSD's ucontext_t with the machine context at 0x40 ). Every general register, the flags and the x87/SSE state ( fxrstor from 0x120 ) are restored; the return address is pushed below the new stack pointer and returned to, as libunwind's own setcontext does (maintainer's ruling). A context of another length or format, or a misaligned FXSAVE area, stops by name. sigreturn stops by name: the runtime delivers no guest signals and answers _is_signal_return with 0, so libunwind never takes that path (maintainer's ruling). sysctl answers {CTL_KERN, KERN_PROC, KERN_PROC_VMMAP, pid} (libunwind's process map query, +0x52f50 ) with -1 and ENOENT (maintainer's ruling); libunwind then probes with msync . Any other name stops by name. sceKernelPrintBacktraceWithModuleInfo writes a line on standard error and answers 0 (PS4Recomp and the deadinside28 port do the same).
docs.title: C++ exceptions and module information (sceKernelGetModuleInfoFromAddr, __Ux86_64_setcontext, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports sceKernelCreateSema , sceKernelDeleteSema , sceKernelWaitSema , sceKernelSignalSema and sceKernelPollSema ( symbols/imports.csv ). Its own calls are the evidence here. They include the audio wrappers at 0x0111ad10 – 0x0111adc0 and the wrappers at 0x0084ac20 – 0x0084ac83 : Create: (&handle, name, attr, initial, max, NULL) , with attr 1 or 2, initial 0 or passed through, and max 0xffff , 1, or passed through. Wait: (handle, 1, NULL) , with no timeout. Signal: (handle, 1) or a count passed through. Delete: (handle) . Results: every result is compared with 0. The signatures, and attr 1 = FIFO and 2 = priority wake order, match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK headers (supporting evidence only). What the runtime does. A semaphore is a runtime object behind the handle. Wait blocks until the units are there. Waiters are served in the order they arrived, or with attr 2 by thread priority: - the best priority goes first, which is the smallest number (OpenOrbis _types/user.h : 0x100 highest, 0x2FF lowest); - equal priorities are served in arrival order; - each waiter is placed by the priority its thread has when it starts to wait. The runtime records each guest thread's priority ( scePthreadSetprio , inherited at creation). shadPS4's semaphore ( threads/semaphore.cpp ) orders its wait list the same way. Signal adds units and wakes the waiters. What stops by name. Every case whose PS4 answer is not established stops with the function's name: - timeouts; - a missing semaphore, variable or name; - an option parameter, and attributes other than 1 and 2; - counts outside 0 <= initial <= max ; - signalling past the maximum; - a poll that cannot be satisfied now; - deleting a semaphore with waiters; - a wait for more than one unit behind another waiter (whether it may be passed is not established); - the error values. A local boot that let the affinity probe and the rwlocks through (not committed) stopped next at sceKernelCreateSema . With throwaway answers past it, the next stops were gettimeofday , then sceSysmoduleLoadModule for system module 0x00b4 .
docs.title: Kernel semaphores (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot imports gettimeofday from libScePosix , libc.elf imports it from libkernel , and libSceFios2.elf imports sceKernelGettimeofday ( symbols/imports.csv ). The executable's own call, at 0x024e2703 , passes a timeval on its stack and no timezone, and reads both fields as 64-bit values. That matches FreeBSD's amd64 struct timeval : seconds, then microseconds. The runtime answers the host's wall clock, under all three names, because the guest asks the system it runs on. It returns 0. Given no timeval, the POSIX names fill nothing and succeed, as FreeBSD's sys_gettimeofday does. What stops by name: - a timezone argument (obsolete in POSIX; what the PS4 fills in is not established); - a missing timeval for sceKernelGettimeofday (its error value is not established).
docs.title: Time of day (gettimeofday, sceKernelGettimeofday, issue #34)

docs.text: eboot loads system module 0x00b4 ( libSceAppContent in the OpenOrbis id list). It imports sceAppContentInitialize , sceAppContentAppParamGetInt and sceAppContentGetAddcontInfoList from it. The public toolchain header names these functions but gives no signatures, so the shapes come from the executable's own calls at 0x024261d8 – 0x0242622a : Initialize: sceAppContentInitialize(init, boot) . Both structures are zeroed first and the result is not checked. Parameters: sceAppContentAppParamGetInt(id, int32_t *value) for ids 0 to 4, each into a global, results not checked. Ids 1–4 are the title's USER_DEFINED_PARAM_1 – 4 from its own sce_sys/param.sfo . Id 0 is the SKU flag, which the system answers. Neither the boot parameter's contents, the SKU answer, the answer for a key the file lacks, nor the error values are public. Which answers this executable observes. A scan of every RIP-relative reference shows that the boot parameter and the outputs for ids 0, 2, 3 and 4 are only passed to these calls. Nothing reads them afterwards. Only id 1's output is read (at five sites). How the runtime answers. It answers only what the game's own data declares, in game/app_params.csv : - an id with source sfo gets its value from the user's own parameter file (read by tools/boot.py and passed as --app-param ID=VALUE ); - an id with source unread succeeds without being written; - boot set to unread lets the initialize call pass over the boot parameter. Anything else stops by name: an undeclared id, a boot parameter not declared unread, and a missing value variable. A local boot with the affinity probe and the rwlocks let through (not committed) loads the module, passes these calls, and stops next at pthread_cond_init ( libScePosix ). Add-ons ( sceAppContentGetAddcontInfoList ). It is called as sceAppContentGetAddcontInfoList(service label, list, capacity, &hits) and lists the title's add-ons (DLC). Each entry is {entitlement label[17], padding[3], status} , and status 4 means installed. - Answers: without a list it gives only the count. A service label above 7, or neither a list nor a count, answers 0x80D90002 , and a call before initialize 0x80D90001 . The facts come from shadPS4's libSceAppContent . - The title's call: it asks for the count first ( 0x023b67cf ). - What the runtime lists: an add-on is what the person running the runtime owns, the labels given to tools/boot.py --addcont LABEL (repeatable), each installed, under service label 0. None are listed by default. - Bloodborne's expansion: The Old Hunters is SPEXPANSIONDLC03 . Its data ships with patch 1.09 (another Bloodborne port's notes), so the entitlement is all it needs.
docs.title: Application content (libSceAppContent, issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadExit(void *value) ends the calling thread with value , as a return from its entry would: the value kept for a join, then the thread's key destructors, then the end (FreeBSD libthr's _pthread_exit , and shadPS4's posix_pthread_exit ). The runtime does not unwind the guest's frames, which were not built for the host's unwinder. Instead the thread's host side marks where it starts the guest's entry ( setjmp ), and an exit returns there ( longjmp ). It then ends exactly as a return does. Stops by name: an exit from inside a key destructor (libthr refuses it too), and an exit from the main thread, which the runtime runs the boot on.
docs.title: Ending a thread (scePthreadExit)

docs.text: The executable's thread wrapper ( 0x02a3b324 – 0x02a3b46e ) sets up each thread like this: It initializes an attribute. It sets the stack size: the caller's size, or 64 KiB by default. If that is refused, it retries with 16 KiB and reports a fatal error if that fails too. It sets detach state 0 and scheduling policy 1. It creates the thread with (&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) , comparing a failure with EPERM, EINVAL and EAGAIN as SCE codes. It destroys the attribute and sets the new thread's affinity to a mask of the six bits 0x3f . What the runtime does: scePthreadAttrSetstacksize and pthread_attr_setstacksize record the size. The stack's address is left to the system, as libthr keeps one address and size per attribute. Sizes below 16 KiB are refused with EINVAL. libthr refuses sizes below its minimum that way, and the executable's wrapper names the PS4 's minimum: its callers pass smaller sizes, and when one is refused it asks again for exactly 16 KiB ( 0x02a3b383 ). scePthreadAttrSetschedpolicy records one of FreeBSD's three policies (FIFO 1, OTHER 2, RR 3). libthr refuses any other with ENOTSUP, whose SCE value is not established, so another policy stops by name. A missing attribute answers EINVAL (as an SCE code under the SCE names).
docs.title: Thread attributes: stack size and scheduling policy (issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadCreate(&thread, &attr, entry, argument, name) runs the guest on a new host thread: The thread gets its own guest stack, of the attribute's size. It gets its own TLS block, a copy of the executable's template as the main thread's is, and its thread pointer goes in GS. It is registered, so scePthreadSelf answers the new thread's handle. entry(argument) is called with the guest's convention. A return ends the thread (POSIX). The attribute's detach state decides whether the host thread is joinable. The scheduling policy is recorded, but the host schedules the thread: guest priorities are not modelled. What stops by name: - no attribute, or no stack size or detach state on it (the PS4 defaults are not established); - a stack address the guest supplies; - the error values. scePthreadSetaffinity records the CPU mask. The executable sets it once per thread, within 0x3f . Scheduling is left to the host, because the host's CPUs say nothing about the PS4 's. An empty mask stops by name. scePthreadGetaffinity(thread, &mask) (imported by libSceFios2 ) answers the recorded mask, or all ones for a thread nobody set one on (maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10; shadPS4 answers the host thread's set, PS4Recomp 0x3f ). No thread answers ESRCH , as for the set; no variable stops by name. Stops on other threads. A worker thread can fault or reach an unimplemented import. The boot records the first such stop and wakes the main thread ( SIGUSR1 ) to make the usual report. Workers leave the timeout and that signal to the main thread. A local boot with the affinity probe and the rwlocks let through (not committed) reaches the threads milestone and stops next at sceUserServiceInitialize .
docs.title: Thread creation (scePthreadCreate, scePthreadSetaffinity, issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadJoin(thread, void **value) and scePthreadDetach(thread) are FreeBSD libthr's pthread_join and pthread_detach ( thr_join.c , thr_detach.c ; OpenOrbis libkernel.h shapes; shadPS4's JoinThread and posix_pthread_detach agree, facts only). The executable's join ( 0x02a3b6c5 ) tells ESRCH , EDEADLK and EINVAL apart. The other callers compare the answer with 0: libc.elf +0x6130 and +0x6174 , libSceFios2 +0x2ebde , and the POSIX pthread_join ( libScePosix ) at 0x00838793 and 0x008387f3 . In libthr's order: - join: no thread is EINVAL ; the calling thread itself EDEADLK ; a thread the runtime does not know, or one already collected, ESRCH ; a detached thread EINVAL ; a thread another thread waits to join ENOTSUP (45). Otherwise it waits for the end, stores the exit value through a non-null value , and collects the thread. - detach: no thread is EINVAL ; an unknown or collected thread ESRCH ; a detached thread, or one a thread waits to join, EINVAL . A detached thread is collected when it ends. - Stops by name: a join or detach of the main thread, on which the runtime runs the boot. POSIX names ( libScePosix ). They return the error number itself: - pthread_create(thread, attr, entry, argument) is scePthreadCreate without a name. The executable's job threads ( 0x00466674 , 0x004666df ) pass a detached attribute with a stack size and a priority. - pthread_exit(value) is scePthreadExit (one call, 0x004667e3 ). - pthread_attr_setschedparam is scePthreadAttrSetschedparam . The job threads take their priorities from a table of 256, 650, 700, 750 and 767 ( 0x02fc5480 ), inside the range the SCE name accepts. scePthreadAttrSetinheritsched(attr, inherit) chooses between PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED (4, libthr's default: a new thread starts at its creator's priority) and PTHREAD_EXPLICIT_SCHED (0: it starts at the attribute's priority), FreeBSD <pthread.h> 's numbers. libSceFios2 's thread helper ( +0x2eaa2 ) asks for explicit scheduling and then sets the priority. A variable without an attribute is EINVAL . Stops by name: another value (libthr's ENOTSUP , whose SCE value is not established, as for the policy), and explicit scheduling without a priority set (the attribute's default priority is not established). scePthreadOnce(once, init) runs init once per once variable (libthr thr_once.c ). The variable's first int is its state: 0 never done (the static initializer), 1 done, 2 in progress, 3 in progress with waiters. A caller that finds it in progress waits for the end; any other state is EINVAL . libc.elf calls it five times ( +0xad02 , +0x1b292 , +0x54ecb and two tail calls) with a static variable and a routine. Nothing cancels a guest thread, so a routine always runs to its end. scePthreadRename(thread, name) records a thread's name (OpenOrbis libkernel.h ; libthr's pthread_set_name_np , to which shadPS4 binds it, facts only). The executable's job threads rename themselves with it (a tail call at 0x00466834 ). The runtime keeps the first 31 bytes, as for the name scePthreadCreate takes, names the host thread with the first 15 (the host's limit; debuggers and the host's thread list show it), and answers 0. Stops by name: a thread the runtime does not know or has collected, and a missing name.
docs.title: Joining, detaching, explicit scheduling and once (issue #34)

docs.text: PlayGo lets a title start before all of its package is installed: the title asks which chunks of the package are present. On this runtime the whole title is always present, so every chunk is reported installed ( runtime/syslib/playgo.c ). Call Shape (from the executable's own calls) Runtime scePlayGoInitialize(params) a 16-byte block: a 2 MiB work buffer the title allocated, its size, 0 (calls at 0x023dd67a , 0x023de849 ); neither reads the result checks the buffer and answers 0 scePlayGoOpen(int32_t *handle, params) params is NULL ( 0x023deae4 ); 0 counts as opened writes handle 1, the runtime 's choice (the title only passes it back) scePlayGoGetChunkId(handle, uint16_t ids[], capacity, uint32_t *count) capacity 100 ( 0x023deb0f ); the result is not read the package's chunks, 0 to chunk_count - 1 , from chunk_count in the copy's sce_sys/playgo-manifest.xml (3 for this title; playgo-chunk.dat agrees) scePlayGoGetLocus(handle, const uint16_t ids[], count, int8_t loci[]) one byte per chunk ( 0x023de8d6 , 0x023deb30 ); non-zero counts as failure; the title treats 0 as not there, 2 as still arriving and polls again, any other value as ready 3 for every chunk, a ready value (the title can't tell the ready values apart) scePlayGoSetInstallSpeed(handle, speed) called through a function pointer ( 0x023dd891 ) with 1 (trickle) or 2 (full); 0 is suspended accepts it (everything is installed, so there is nothing to pace; nothing reads it back); an unknown handle 0x80B20009 , before initialize 0x80B20005 , another speed 0x80B20004 (shadPS4's libScePlayGo ) No public source declares these calls: the OpenOrbis toolchain has no PlayGo header. Stops by name: Open with parameters, an unknown handle, a chunk list longer than the space given, an unknown chunk ID, a missing manifest, and every error value.
docs.title: PlayGo (libScePlayGo)

docs.text: eboot imports sceUserServiceInitialize , sceUserServiceTerminate , sceUserServiceGetInitialUser and sceUserServiceGetLoginUserIdList , among others. The shapes match the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's UserService.h and _types/user.h (supporting evidence only): - the parameter block holds a uint32_t priority; - the login list is four user ids, an unused slot holding -1; - id 0xFF is the system's. The executable initializes the service twice: - once at 0x024e1e69 , with priority 0x2bc ; - again at 0x010ba1ac , where it accepts success or exactly 0x80960003 . So a second initialize answers 0x80960003 , the "already initialized" code. What the runtime does. It models one user, the person running it, logged in from the start: - GetInitialUser answers that user's id; - the login list holds it, then three -1 slots; - the id is a handle the runtime hands out, never -1 or 0xFF , because the PS4 's ids are the system's and a title only passes them back. What stops by name: a call before initialize, a missing argument, and the other error values. The user's name ( sceUserServiceGetUserName(int32_t, char *, const size_t) , in OpenOrbis UserService.h ; a name is at most 16 characters). The executable asks with 17 bytes ( 0x02561cd7 ) or a size it computed ( 0x0111bdfe ), and goes on only on 0. The name is the runtime 's choice, Hunter , written with its terminating zero. A user the runtime did not hand out, or a buffer too small for the name, stops by name. Login and logout events ( sceUserServiceGetEvent(OrbisUserServiceEvent *) , the event being a type, 0 login or 1 logout, and a user id; "no event" is 0x80960007 , OpenOrbis errors.h ). No user logs in or out during a run, so every call answers 0x80960007 and writes nothing. The executable's one caller ( 0x025628e4 ) is a polling thread: after any non-zero answer it sleeps 33 ms ( sceKernelUsleep(0x80e8) ) and asks again, and it handles a login or logout only when one comes. It never waits for the first user's login to be reported; whether the PS4 reports that login is not public.
docs.title: The user service's start-up calls (libSceUserService, issue #36)

docs.text: The runtime gives the host's local time, and keeps ticks as its own convention ( runtime/syslib/rtc.c ). Sources. - Signatures: OpenOrbis Rtc.h gives sceRtcGetCurrentClockLocalTime(date and time *) , sceRtcGetTick(const date and time *, uint64_t *) and sceRtcSetTick(date and time *, const uint64_t *) . It names sceRtcGetTickResolution without a signature; the executable's one call ( 0x010b70ea ) takes no argument and uses the int32_t answer as ticks per second, a negative one being a failure. - The date and time is six 16-bit fields (year, month, day, hour, minute, second), then a 32-bit microsecond at offset 12, 16 bytes in all. Rtc.h gives the microsecond 16 bits, which cannot hold 999999. The Vita homebrew SDK's SceDateTime , of the same library family, gives it 32 bits in a 16-byte structure, and the executable copies the whole structure as 16 bytes. - Ticks: the executable compares ticks, takes their differences and asks for the resolution. It holds no constant relating them to another epoch (neither the span from 0001 to 1970 in microseconds or seconds, nor its negation). About 60 sites ask for the local time; those reached pass it straight to sceRtcGetTick . What the runtime does. - The local time is the host's, in the time zone of the person running the runtime , as the console gives the one its owner set. A leap second shows as :59 . - A tick is the runtime 's own convention, the same in every call: microseconds since 0001-01-01 00:00:00 (proleptic Gregorian), 1000000 per second. sceRtcSetTick reverses sceRtcGetTick exactly. - Stops by name: a date out of range (including February 30 and February 29 of a non-leap century), a tick past the year 9999, a missing argument, and every error value. Day of the week: sceRtcGetDayOfWeek(year, month, day) ( 0x024ee2a9 , its answer packed into 3 bits) answers 0 for Sunday to 6 for Saturday. The PS4Recomp project's libSceRtc numbers the days so, and notes that a real PS4 's ticks count from year 1, as these do; both are used as facts only. (The PSP SDK documents 0 as Monday, for an older library.) A date out of range stops by name.
docs.title: The real-time clock (libSceRtc)

docs.text: These five calls relate ticks to Unix time and to UTC ( runtime/syslib/rtc.c , tests in test/syslib/rtc_time_zones.c ). Ticks and Unix time: a tick counts microseconds from year 1, so 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC is tick 62135596800000000. PS4Recomp's libSceRtc and shadPS4's rtc.cpp both relate them so (facts only). sceRtcSetTime_t(date and time *, time_t) ( 0x010b70a6 : seconds parsed from text, then sceRtcGetTick on the result, going on only on 0) gives the UTC date and time that many seconds after 1970. Both sources say the answer depends on the SDK the title was built with: before SDK 3.00 only the low 32 bits count, from 3.00 a negative count is an error. Counts from 0 to 0xffffffff mean the same either way; others stop by name. sceRtcConvertUtcToLocalTime(const tick *, tick *) and sceRtcConvertLocalTimeToUtc (11 and 2 call sites, such as 0x01969648 and 0x019696ae ; each passes a local copy of the tick and treats anything but 0 as no time) use the host's time zone, as the local time above does, with its daylight saving rule at that instant. A local time that the clock skips or shows twice at a daylight saving change stops by name, because the PS4 's choice there is not established. sceRtcFormatRFC2822LocalTime(char *, const tick *utc) ( 0x023e5ca9 , with no tick, which means now) writes RFC 2822 section 3.3's date and time in the host's local time, such as Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:05:09 +0100 : 31 characters and a NUL, the day of the month in two digits as both sources write it. sceRtcGetCurrentNetworkTick(tick *) ( 0x01086f50 , 0x010b70cf ; 0 is success, and the first treats a failure as no time) answers the current UTC tick from the host's clock, as both sources do. The host's wall clock stands for the network clock. Stops by name: a missing argument, and a time before year 1 or past the year 9999.
docs.title: Unix time, time zones, RFC 2822 and the network tick (issue #40)

docs.text: The runtime models one standard controller, the one user's, always connected ( runtime/syslib/pad.c ). Its state comes from the input backend ( runtime/input_host.h , runtime/input/ ): by default ( pbboot --input none , tools/boot.py --input none ) none is installed and the pad is at rest, so CI and recorded boots read the same state as before. With --input host the host's first gamepad and the window's keyboard drive it, and the title's vibration rumbles the gamepad. Sources. - Signatures and layouts: the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Pad.h , _types/pad.h and _types/errors.h . They give the 120-byte OrbisPadData (touch data at 0x34 : a count, seven reserved bytes, then two 8-byte touches of x, y and an id), the 28-byte OrbisPadInformation , the two-byte vibration block (large motor, then small), port type 0 (standard), and ALREADY_OPENED 0x80920004 . - Button bits: OpenOrbis' OrbisPadButton ; shadPS4's OrbisPadButtonDataOffset ( src/core/libraries/pad/pad.h ) agrees: L3 0x2 , R3 0x4 , options 0x8 , up 0x10 , right 0x20 , down 0x40 , left 0x80 , L2 0x100 , R2 0x200 , L1 0x400 , R1 0x800 , triangle 0x1000 , circle 0x2000 , cross 0x4000 , square 0x8000 , touch pad 0x100000 . - The executable's own calls agree: - before each scePadReadState ( 0x02a90168 , 0x02a91948 ) it clears exactly 120 bytes, and afterwards it tests connected at offset 0x4c ; - scePadGetControllerInformation gets a cleared 28-byte block. The title reads the touch resolution, dividing a non-zero touch point by it, and the stick deadzones: a stick within 0x80 ± the deadzone counts as centred; - scePadInit is called once ( 0x02fa6182 ), and the result is not read; - scePadOpen(initial user, 0, 0, NULL) keeps any handle ≥ 0, and the title closes before it opens again; - scePadSetVibration is called with the title's speeds ( 0x02a9c7c1 ) or with both 0 to stop ( 0x02a9c822 ), and 0 counts as success. - The DualShock 4: the touch pad is 1920 × 942 ( DS4_TOUCHPAD_WIDTH and _HEIGHT in the Linux kernel's drivers/hid/hid-playstation.c ); each stick axis is a byte, 0 at the left and at the top; a touch carries a 7-bit id that changes for each new touch; the left motor is the strong one (a force-feedback effect's strong magnitude goes to motor_left ). - SDL3: stick axes run -32768 (left, up) to 32767 (right, down) and triggers 0 to 32767 ( SDL_GetGamepadAxis ); touch fingers are 0..1 of the pad ( SDL_GetGamepadTouchpadFinger ); scancodes are USB HID keyboard usages ( SDL_scancode.h ); SDL_RumbleGamepad 's low-frequency motor is the left one. - The timestamp is the process time in microseconds when the state is read, as shadPS4 stamps it ( src/input/controller.cpp ); the title does not read it. Call Runtime scePadInit 0 scePadOpen handle 1, the runtime 's choice; a second open while it is open answers 0x80920004 scePadClose 0; the pad can be opened again scePadReadState the backend's buttons, sticks, triggers and touches, the timestamp, connected 1; no motion, identity orientation. At rest without a backend: no button, sticks 0x80 , triggers 0, no touch, timestamp 0 scePadGetControllerInformation touch pad 1920 × 942; stick deadzones 13 (the runtime 's choice); connected; a local pad scePadSetVibration 0; the speeds are kept ( rt_pad_vibration ) and passed to the backend: with --input host , the large motor to SDL's low-frequency rumble, the small one to the high-frequency rumble Host input ( pbboot --input host , tools/boot.py --input host ). It needs a build with SDL3 (the window's) and --display window , since the window's event loop reads the devices: SDL's events are pumped on the display's thread ( display_vulkan.c ), never from a guest thread, and after each pump rt_input_host_pump samples the gamepad and keyboard there ( runtime/input/input_host_sdl.c ). The state therefore changes once per presented frame. For example: Text Only python3 tools/boot.py --display window --audio host --input host The first connected SDL gamepad is used, and the next one when it is removed. Its buttons map by position: south cross, east circle, west square, north triangle, start options, back and the touch pad click the touch pad, the shoulders L1 and R1, the stick clicks L3 and R3, the D-pad the D-pad. A DualShock 4 or DualSense touch pad reports up to two touches. Stick bytes are the axis' top eight bits after the offset; the triggers are scaled to 0..255. The keyboard works with or without a gamepad; a key's stick direction overrides the gamepad's stick, both keys of an axis cancel out, and buttons combine. The default layout ( rt_default_keys , runtime/input/input.c ): Keys Pad W A S D left stick up, left, down, right (full deflection) arrow keys right stick I J K L D-pad up, left, down, right Return, Space cross Backspace circle R square F triangle Q / E L1 / R1 Z / C L2 / R2, fully pressed left Shift / Tab L3 / R3 Escape options T touch pad click The runtime 's choices: the L2 and R2 bits are set while their trigger is off zero; touch ids count 0..127 and wrap, down fingers listed first; a held vibration is sent to SDL again every 30 seconds, as SDL's rumble lasts at most about 65. Scripted input ( pbboot --input-script SPEC , tools/boot.py --no-record --input-script SPEC ). For unattended boots, a timed script plays the controller through the same backend interface ( runtime/input/input_script.c ); it works with any --display mode and cannot be combined with --input host . SPEC is the script, or @FILE to read it from a file. Events are separated by commas, semicolons or new lines, and # starts a comment. Each event is WHEN:CONTROLS[*HOLD] : WHEN is seconds since the process started ( 45 , 45.5s ) or frames presented by video out's first port ( 700f ). Frames follow the game's own progress, so they suit a slow boot; seconds need no display. CONTROLS are names joined by + : cross circle square triangle up down left right l1 r1 l2 r2 l3 r3 options touch , and the stick directions lstick-up lstick-down lstick-left lstick-right and rstick-up ... rstick-right at full deflection. A scripted trigger is fully pressed. The controls are held from WHEN for HOLD , on the same clock (default 0.25 s or 4 frames), then released; overlapping events combine. pbboot writes pbboot: input script: event N starts (S s, frame F) when the title first reads the pad during an event, so a run's log shows when each press landed. For example: Text Only python3 tools/boot.py --no-record --display headless --input-script "45:down,47:cross" A malformed event, an unknown control, a hold on the other clock, more than 256 events or a script file over 64 KiB is refused before the boot, naming the event. Fields the executable does not read are left zero. Not modelled: motion. The accelerometer and gyroscope are not forwarded, because the units and axes the system reports them in are not established here (shadPS4 scales SDL's m/s² by 0.098 without a source); acceleration and angular velocity stay 0 and the orientation the identity. Stops by name: a second initialize, a call before initialize, another user, port type, index or open parameters, an unknown handle, a missing argument, and the other error values. The motion settings (issue #36). scePadResetOrientation(handle) (OpenOrbis Pad.h ) makes the pad's present attitude the reference its orientation is reported from; scePadSetAngularVelocityDeadbandState(handle, bool) and scePadSetTiltCorrectionState(handle, bool) (named in Pad.h without a signature; shadPS4's pad.cpp declares (int32_t handle, bool enable) , used as a fact) switch the motion sensors' deadband and tilt correction. The executable calls each through a small wrapper ( 0x02a9082e , 0x02a90852 , 0x02a90882 ) with its open handle, and a bool for the two settings, and counts 0 as success. Since motion is not modelled, a reset leaves the reported orientation the identity, neither setting changes a reading with no motion, and each call answers 0 ( test/syslib/pad_motion_settings.c ). An unknown handle and a setting other than 0 or 1 stop by name.
docs.title: The controller (libScePad)

docs.text: Facts. OpenOrbis ImeDialog.h and _types/ime_dialog.h give: - the shapes: sceImeDialogInit(setting, extended) , GetStatus() , GetResult(result) and Term() ; - the statuses: NONE 0, RUNNING 1, STOPPED 2; - the result: an end status (OK 0, CANCEL 1, ABORT 2) followed by 12 reserved bytes. shadPS4's ime_dialog.cpp (facts only) gives the states: Init from NONE to RUNNING, Abort from RUNNING to finished with ABORT, and Term from finished to NONE. The executable's keyboard ( 0x02d03f80 ): - Opening. It fills a setting with a text buffer that holds the initial text, calls Init with no extended setting, and takes 0 as open. - Polling. Each frame, 0x02d03df0 asks GetStatus. On 2 it reads the result: end status 0 takes the buffer's text; 1 and 2 (or a failed GetResult) take none. - Closing. 0x02d03e70 then calls Term. 0x02d04300 calls Abort while the keyboard is open and takes 0 as closed. What the runtime does: - Cancel. Init opens the keyboard, and the first GetStatus finds it closed with CANCEL, as if the user backed out at once. The title takes no text, the buffer is left as given, and nothing is shown. - Abort and Term. Abort of an open keyboard closes it with ABORT, and Term closes the library. What stops by name: - Init without a setting, or while a keyboard is open or not yet terminated (shadPS4 answers busy, 0x80bc0001 ; this is not confirmed); - GetResult before the keyboard closed, or with no structure; - Abort when no keyboard is open; - Term before the keyboard closed. An extended setting is ignored.
docs.title: The on-screen keyboard, canceled (libSceImeDialog, issue #36)

docs.text: The runtime has no host mouse, so it answers as a console with no mouse plugged in ( runtime/syslib/mouse.c , tests in test/syslib/mouse_not_connected.c ). Sources. shadPS4's libSceMouse ( mouse.h , mouse.cpp , mouse_error.h ; facts only) gives the shapes: sceMouseInit(void) , sceMouseOpen(user, type, index, param) , sceMouseRead(handle, data, count) answering how many records it wrote (1 to 64 asked for), sceMouseClose(handle) , the 40-byte record { uint64_t timestamp, bool connected, uint32_t buttons, int32_t x, y, wheel, tilt, 8 reserved } and 0x80DF0004 for a mouse already open. With no mouse it answers one record, not connected, all zero. OpenOrbis Mouse.h only names the calls. The executable's calls agree. It loads the library's system module ( 0x02a8bce1 ), then calls Init (six sites, such as 0x02a8bcea ) and counts 0 as success. Two input objects each open the mouse with (the initial user, 0, 0, NULL) ( 0x02a8bf75 , 0x02a8c465 ), keep the answer as their handle only when it is above 0, and close a handle above 0 before opening again. Read ( 0x02a8c07f , 0x02a8c56f ) asks for one record into the 40 bytes the object clears: below 0 is a failure, and a record that is not connected ends the poll. What the runtime does. Init answers 0 every time, as shadPS4 does. Open gives handle 1 (the runtime 's choice; the title keeps only handles above 0) and 0x80DF0004 while it is open. Read writes one all-zero record (not connected) and answers 1. Close frees the handle. Stops by name: a call before Init, another user, type, index or open parameters, an unknown handle, a count outside 1 to 64, and a missing record.
docs.title: The mouse, not connected (libSceMouse, issue #36)

docs.text: sceCommonDialogInitialize is the only call eboot imports from libSceCommonDialog . It takes no arguments (OpenOrbis CommonDialog.h , as supporting evidence). The executable calls it twice: - at 0x024e1e8c , logging a failure; - at 0x02023fbb , accepting success or exactly 0x80b80002 . So the first call succeeds and a repeat answers 0x80b80002 , the "already initialized" code. No dialog is shown: each dialog library's own calls do that (next section).
docs.title: The common dialog's initialize (libSceCommonDialog, issue #40)

docs.text: The executable uses four of the console's common dialogs. It never reads a choice from three of them: the message, save data and commerce dialogs do not import GetResult . It reads the profile dialog's result but does not use it. So the runtime models each dialog as one the user closes at once. Facts: - Statuses and the base block. NONE 0, INITIALIZED 1, RUNNING 2, FINISHED 3, and the parameter block's base: 0x30 bytes, with a magic number 0xC0D1A109 at 0x2c (OpenOrbis _types/common_dialog.h ). Every call site stores the magic as 0xC0D1A109 plus the low 32 bits of the base's own address. - Errors and states. 0x80b80003 (not initialized) and 0x80b80004 (already initialized), and the states: Initialize from NONE, Open from INITIALIZED or FINISHED, Terminate back to NONE (shadPS4's commondialog.h , msgdialog.cpp , np_commerce.cpp and np_profile_dialog.cpp , facts only). The executable's uses: - Message dialog. One system message, mode 3 with type 2 (the PSN user-generated content restriction notice, built at 0x020233b3 ). Its start-up ( 0x02023e95 ) accepts 0 or exactly 0x80b80004 . It polls UpdateStatus while RUNNING ( 0x02023d6b ) and terminates on FINISHED. - Save data dialog. Shown when a save mount fails with 0x809f000a (no space, 0x02c425e7 ). It initializes, retrying while the answer is busy ( 0x80b80008 ), opens a system message (mode 3, size 0x98), polls while RUNNING and terminates. - Profile dialog. 0x010b85e0 opens a profile (mode 1, size 0x80) for an online id and polls. On FINISHED it reads the result, which it does not use, and then terminates. - Commerce dialog. 0x02040350 opens the PlayStation Plus offer (mode 5, size 0x80), ignoring Initialize's answer. 0x02040244 polls while RUNNING. Terminate's answer is ignored. What the runtime does: - Opening. Open checks the block (base size 0x30, the address-based magic, the library's own size field) and starts the dialog. - Closing. The first UpdateStatus after Open finishes it. Nothing is shown. - Terminating. A Terminate before any Initialize answers 0x80b80003 , which every caller ignores. - The profile result. It is result 0, user action 1 (canceled) and the caller's user data ( OrbisNpProfileDialogResult , 0x30 bytes, in shadPS4's np_profile_dialog.h ). What stops by name: an Open outside INITIALIZED or FINISHED; a NULL or malformed block; a profile result before FINISHED or with no structure. One dialog at a time (the console's busy answer, 0x80b80008 ) is not enforced: each runtime dialog finishes on its first status update.
docs.title: The common dialogs, closed at once (libSceMsgDialog, libSceSaveDataDialog, libSceNpProfileDialog, libSceNpCommerce, issues #35 and #40)

docs.text: sceSystemServiceHideSplashScreen() : the title tells the system it may take down the boot splash, because its own screens follow. It answers 0, and the runtime keeps the fact ( rt_splash_hidden ), a sign of how far a boot got. The executable calls it through a function pointer ( 0x01d5d995 ) and reads no result. sceSystemServiceGetStatus(status) : polled for system events. The status is {int32_t pending events, then one byte each: system UI overlaid, in background execution, CPU mode 7 normal, live streaming, out of the VR play area} , and a missing pointer answers 0x80A10003 . The runtime has no system UI and no system events, so the answer is: no events, nothing overlaid, in the foreground, CPU mode normal, not streaming, not in VR. Only these 9 bytes are written. Facts from shadPS4's libSceSystemService ( systemservice.cpp , systemservice.h , systemservice_error.h ).
docs.title: The splash screen and system status (sceSystemServiceHideSplashScreen, sceSystemServiceGetStatus)

docs.text: The executable calls it in three places and discards the answer each time. Each call passes a URL string and NULL; OpenOrbis SystemService.h names the function without a shape. The three places: - the official site link at 0x02437039 ; - a debug BROWSER_TEST command at 0x01d5eeeb , with the same URL; - a URL it builds at 0x02437112 . The runtime opens no browser, as if the user closed it at once. It notes the URL on stderr and answers 0 (shadPS4 also answers 0, facts only). No URL stops by name.
docs.title: The web browser, not opened (sceSystemServiceLaunchWebBrowser, issue #40)

docs.text: sceSystemServiceReceiveEvent(event *) takes the oldest pending system event. shadPS4's libSceSystemService answers 0x80A10003 for a missing pointer and 0x80A10004 ("no event", systemservice_error.h ) for an empty queue (facts only). The executable calls it only inside a loop bounded by the pending count sceSystemServiceGetStatus gave ( 0x01b8a433 , 0x02276aa3 ), and acts on an event only when the call answers 0. The runtime raises no system events, so it answers "no event" and writes nothing ( test/syslib/system_service_events.c ).
docs.title: System events (sceSystemServiceReceiveEvent, issue #40)

docs.text: sceSystemServiceParamGetInt(id, int32_t *value) reads a console system setting. The setting ids and the language codes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's _types/sys_service.h (id 1 is the language, and 1 there is English (United States)). All nine of the executable's call sites ask for id 1, into a variable preset to -1. They accept codes 0–20 and fall back to a default otherwise. What the runtime does. A setting is the console owner's choice, so the runtime answers what the person running it chose: - tools/boot.py passes --system-param ID=VALUE ; - it defaults the language to 1 (English, United States); - --system-param 1=18 , for example, chooses English (United Kingdom). What stops by name: a setting nobody gave a value, and a missing variable.
docs.title: System settings (sceSystemServiceParamGetInt, issue #40)

docs.text: Every one of these services is gated in the executable on the signed-in user's NpId or online ID, which sceNpGetNpId and sceNpGetOnlineId never give offline: - matchmaking setup: 0x010bcf70 ; - web API client: 0x010b4d90 ; - signaling and lookup setup: 0x010c0800 . So nothing beyond sceNpMatching2Initialize is reached, with one exception: the leaderboard object reaches sceNpScoreCreateRequest with title context 0, from the comment checks ( 0x010d07a8 , 0x010d0a39 ) and the jobs ( 0x010cdf63 , 0x010cf339 , 0x010d04ed ), and treats an answer below 1 as failure. The codes come from shadPS4's np_matching2.cpp , np_web_api.cpp , np_score.cpp , np_signaling.cpp and np_utility.cpp , with PS4Recomp where noted (facts only). The executable itself tests several of them ( 0x80550C06 , 0x80552701 / 04 / 05 , 0x8055080B , 0x80550707 ), which supports the numbering. Ids start at 1 everywhere. Matching2. Before initialize, every call answers 0x80550C03 . NULL pointers, and a context block other than 0x28 bytes, answer 0x80550C0A . An unknown context answers 0x80550C0B . ContextStart answers 0x804101E2 , the resolver timeout. shadPS4 notes this was confirmed on a disconnected console, and PS4Recomp agrees. So no context starts, and ContextStop answers 0x80550C08 . Calls that need a started context stop by name on a known context: the server id, request options, the room, lobby and signaling callbacks, and every room and lobby request. A NULL context callback also stops by name. Web API. Library contexts are ids below 0x8000 . User contexts carry their library in the upper 16 bits. Error answers: 0x80552902 for a NULL or empty argument; 0x80552903 for a library id of 0x8000 or more; 0x80552904 , 0x80552905 and 0x80552906 for an unknown library, user context or request; 0x8055290B and 0x8055290C for an unknown filter or callback. SendRequest answers 0x80552907 , not signed in (PS4Recomp agrees). The response calls on a known request, which was never sent, stop by name. So does UtilityParseNpId on a real argument; NULL arguments answer 0x80550003 . Leaderboards. CreateNpTitleCtx answers 0x80550006 , signed out. PS4Recomp and shadPS4's sign-in-checking variant agree; shadPS4's plain variant and one port hand out an id instead. So no title context or request exists. Every id answers 0x8055070E , and SetPlayerCharacterId first answers 0x80550704 for a negative character id. Signaling. Answers: 0x80552702 for a second initialize; 0x80552701 before initialize; 0x80552715 for NULL pointers; 0x80552705 for an unknown context. Connections: ActivateConnection answers 0x8055270B , network information not available (PS4Recomp). DeactivateConnection answers 0x8055270E . GetConnectionStatus writes inactive (0) and answers 0. Lookup. Answers: 0x8055070C for a NULL NpId; 0x8055070E for an unknown title context or request; 0x80550704 for an option block. sceNpLookupNpId starts the lookup. sceNpLookupPollAsync then answers 0 with result 0x80550705 , no login (PS4Recomp); before that it answers 1, still running (shadPS4).
docs.title: PSN services with no one signed in: matchmaking, web API, leaderboards, signaling, lookup (issue #41)

docs.text: The runtime is offline: the one user is signed out of PSN for the whole run, and nothing about that ever changes. The facts come from shadPS4's libSceNpManager , libSceNpMatching2 and libSceNpAuth ( np_manager.h , np_manager.cpp , np_types.h , np_types2.h , np_common.cpp , np_error.h , np_auth/np_auth.cpp , np_auth/np_auth.h ), checked against two other Bloodborne ports and PS4Recomp's libSceNp ( ps4_np.c ), which answer the same for a signed-out user. The code is the runtime 's own. Call Runtime sceNpRegisterStateCallback(callback, data) keeps it and never calls it: callbacks run only from sceNpCheckCallback when the sign-in state changes. A second registration answers 0x80550008 , no callback 0x80550003 . sceNpUnregisterStateCallback() 0, or 0x80550009 with none registered sceNpRegisterGamePresenceCallback(callback, data) keeps it (replacing any earlier one) and answers nothing; the caller ( 0x010b8386 ) reads no result sceNpGetState(user, uint32_t *state) 1, signed out (0 is not signed up, 2 signed in); a missing variable answers 0x80550003 , and a user the runtime did not hand out stops by name sceNpCheckCallback() 0, running nothing: offline nothing changes sceNpGetNpId(user, NP id *) , sceNpGetOnlineId(user, online id *) 0x80550006 (signed out), writing nothing: a signed-out user has no PSN identity. A missing variable answers 0x80550003 ; the invalid user (-1, whose answer depends on the system software version) and a user the runtime did not hand out stop by name. The callers ( 0x010bd072 , 0x010c0860 , 0x010b4666 , 0x010b4e5d , 0x010b8931 ) take their offline path. sceNpGetGamePresenceStatus(const online id *, int32_t *status) 0 with status 0 (offline; 1 is online) for every player; a missing argument answers 0x80550003 sceNpRegisterPlusEventCallback(callback, data) , sceNpUnregisterPlusEventCallback() the state callback's rules ( 0x80550003 , 0x80550008 , 0x80550009 ); kept and never called, since offline no PlayStation Plus event happens sceNpNotifyPlusFeature(const parameter *) 0: offline there is no one to tell. The callers ( 0x01d38ac9 , 0x02275873 , 0x022769e6 ) pass the 0x38-byte block of sceNpCheckPlus and read no result; a missing block stops by name. sceNpCreateAsyncRequest(const parameter *) a request id from 0x20000001 , at most 32 in use ( 0x80550013 ), a deleted one's slot reused. The block is 0x18 bytes {size, CPU affinity mask, thread priority} : no block 0x80550003 , another size 0x80550011 . The caller ( 0x02274f54 ) passes 0x18, 0x3f , 700. sceNpCheckNpAvailability(id, const online id *, reserved) , sceNpCheckPlus(id, const parameter *, result *) , sceNpGetParentalControlInfo(id, const online id *, int8_t *age, info *) the check completes at once: the call answers 0 and the request's result is 0x80550006 (signed out); nothing is written. A request id of 0 or a missing argument 0x80550003 , an id that is no request 0x80550014 , an aborted request 0x80550012 , a second check on one request 0x80550003 . sceNpCheckPlus 's 0x38-byte block {size, user, padding, features, 32 reserved} : another size 0x80550011 ; features outside 1–3, a non-zero reserved byte or the invalid user 0x80550003 ; another user stops by name. A third argument to the availability check other than the observed 0 stops by name. sceNpPollAsync(id, int32_t *result) 0 with the result once the check ran (always at once offline); no variable 0x80550003 , an id that is no request 0x80550014 , a request that ran no check 0x80550015 . The caller ( 0x022767b5 ) reads 0 as done, 1 as still running. A request aborted before its check stops by name. sceNpAbortRequest(id) , sceNpDeleteRequest(id) 0, or 0x80550014 for an id that is no request. Abort marks an unchecked request aborted and leaves a checked one alone; delete frees the id. sceNpAuthCreateAsyncRequest(const parameter *) ( libSceNpAuth ) a request id from 0x10000001 , at most 16 in use ( 0x80550305 ), a deleted one's id reused. The block is 0x18 bytes {size, CPU affinity mask, thread priority} : no block 0x80550301 , another size 0x80550302 . The caller ( 0x02275de5 ) passes 0x18, 0x3f , 700. sceNpAuthGetAuthorizationCode(id, const parameter *, code *, int32_t *issuer) 0x80550007 (user not found), writing nothing: the library looks up the user the online id belongs to, which cannot succeed signed out (shadPS4's note: a title cannot even obtain an online id then). The 0x20-byte block {size, online id *, client id *, scope} (caller 0x02276028 ): no block or code variable, or a missing online id, client id or scope 0x80550301 ; another size 0x80550302 . The request is not started. PS4Recomp answers 0x80550006 (signed out) here instead; the caller discards this answer either way and learns the outcome by polling. sceNpAuthPollAsync(id, int32_t *result) , sceNpAuthDeleteRequest(id) Poll: no variable or an id of 0 or below 0x80550301 , an id that is no request 0x80550306 , and otherwise 0x80550307 (invalid id): offline no request is ever started, so none has a result. Delete frees the id: 0, 0x80550301 or 0x80550306 as for poll. Callers 0x022752ca (only an id above 0; a negative answer is its failure state, 1 still running, 0 done) and 0x02276f43 . sceNpCmpOnlineId(a, b) , sceNpCmpNpId(a, b) ( libSceNpCommon ) 0 for the same identity, 0x80550609 (no match) otherwise, 0x80550003 for a missing one. Online ids compare their 16 characters as strncmp does; NP ids then compare their 8 option and 8 reserved bytes. Callers 0x010a28d1 and 0x010b4676 . sceNpMatching2Initialize(const parameter *) the 0x30-byte block carries its own size at 0x20 , and 0x30 or the older 0x28 is accepted. Anything else, or no block, answers 0x80550C0A ; a second initialize answers 0x80550C02 . The caller ( 0x010ba2d0 ) treats a negative answer as failure. sceNpMatching2Terminate() 0, or 0x80550C03 before initialize
docs.title: PSN offline: sign-in state, callbacks and matchmaking start-up

docs.text: sceNpSetNpTitleId(const title id *, const title secret *) registers the title's PSN title id (12 characters and a terminator, in a 16-byte block) and its 128-byte title secret, which the system would use to talk to PSN. A missing argument answers 0x80550003 (invalid argument). The facts come from shadPS4's libSceNpManager ( np_types.h , np_error.h ); the other ports answer 0 too. The executable's call ( 0x010ba192 ) treats only a negative answer as failure. Offline nothing talks to PSN, so the runtime keeps the title id ( rt_np_title_id , for later PSN-side calls such as trophies) and nothing of the secret.
docs.title: The PSN title id (sceNpSetNpTitleId)

docs.text: The executable creates a trophy context for the initial user (service label 0, options 0) and a handle at 0x02420524 , registers the context, and later unlocks trophies by id and reads the game and trophy info. The facts (sizes, limits, error values) come from shadPS4's libSceNpTrophy ( np_trophy.h , np_trophy.cpp , np_error.h ), checked against the other ports and PS4Recomp; the code is the runtime 's own ( runtime/syslib/np_trophy.c ). Call Runtime answer sceNpTrophyCreateContext(int32_t *context, user, label, options) contexts from 1, one per (user, label), at most 8; a second for the same pair 0x80551613 , the ninth 0x80551623 ; options other than 0 or no variable 0x80551604 sceNpTrophyCreateHandle(int32_t *handle) handles from 1, at most 4 ( 0x80551624 ) sceNpTrophyRegisterContext(context, handle, options) an unknown context 0x80551609 , an unknown handle 0x80551608 , a second registration 0x80551610 sceNpTrophyUnlockTrophy(context, handle, id, int32_t *platinum) ids 0 to 127 (others 0x8055160A ); records the unlock with its time; a repeat 0x8055160C ; *platinum is always -1; an unregistered context 0x8055160F sceNpTrophyGetGameInfo , sceNpTrophyGetTrophyInfo the recorded unlocks: the unlocked count, and per trophy whether and when it was unlocked; names empty, grades 0; each structure must carry its own size, else 0x80551604 The trophy definitions (names, grades, which count toward the platinum) live in the title's sce_sys/trophy/trophy00.trp , encrypted with a key the runtime does not hold, so it has none of them and never awards a platinum. Unlocks are kept per user in <savedata>/<user>/sce_trophy/unlocked , one id tick line each, and survive across runs when --savedata names a folder.
docs.title: Trophies, offline (libSceNpTrophy)

docs.text: The executable's only call, at 0x023b704f , passes a parameter block it built on its stack (an age from a table and a pointer to a restriction list), and it discards the result. The call tells the system which online content the title restricts. The offline runtime offers no online content, so there is nothing to record and it answers 0. A missing block stops by name.
docs.title: Content restriction (sceNpSetContentRestriction, issue #41)

docs.text: The executable keeps a thread variable's value in 40 bits. Its lock at 0x024368c0 records the owner as scePthreadSelf() masked with 0xffffffffff , then compares that with the whole answer. A thread object above 2^40 would never own a lock it had just taken, and would wait on itself (a local boot hung there). The host heap lies above 2^40, so the runtime allocates thread objects, the main thread's included, from a range it reserves below it, at 0xf000000000 .
docs.title: Thread variables fit in 40 bits (issue #34)

docs.text: sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory(void **address, size_t length, int32_t protection, int32_t flags) maps memory the system provides without a range of the direct memory pool. The signature is corroborated by the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h . The executable's only call, at 0x02481dbe : - presets the address to 0; - rounds the length up to 16 KiB; - passes protection 3 or 0x33 and flags 0; - on success, requires a non-null address. What the runtime does. It maps fresh zeroed host memory at an address it picks, with the CPU bits of the protection; GPU access is accepted, as for direct memory. The PS4 limits a title's flexible memory to a budget. The budget is not established and the runtime does not enforce it. What stops by name: - an address hint; - map flags; - other protection bits; - a length that is not whole 16 KiB pages; - a missing variable.
docs.title: Flexible memory (sceKernelMapFlexibleMemory, issue #34)

docs.text: Sockets are FreeBSD's socket calls under SCE names (shapes from OpenOrbis net.h and shadPS4's net.cpp , facts only). A failure answers 0x80410100 plus the error number, with the number in the network errno. The executable expects exactly that: it compares answers with 0x80410123 , 0x80410139 , 0x80410109 and 0x80410104 at 0x02f9a8d0 , and errno with 35 at 0x011c7c60 . A socket can be created, set up, bound and listened on, as FreeBSD 9 does with only its loopback interface. shadPS4, the droogie bbhost runtime and PS4Recomp also create sockets. A family of native ports refuses every socket call with ENETUNREACH instead, which breaks the executable's Havok code: its bind and listen checks test for -1. Nothing ever connects or arrives: - Connect and send. Connect, or a datagram to a non-loopback address, answers ENETUNREACH at once (FreeBSD 9's in_pcbladdr ). An unconnected stream socket answers ENOTCONN to send and receive. A datagram socket with no destination answers EDESTADDRREQ to send. - Accept and datagram receive. These answer EWOULDBLOCK on a nonblocking socket ( SO_NBIO ). A blocking socket waits until sceNetSocketAbort or sceNetSocketClose (EINTR), or until its accept or receive timeout option passes (EWOULDBLOCK, as shadPS4 does). An abort with no waiter answers ENOTBLK. - Bind and listen. Bind answers EINVAL when the socket is already bound, EADDRNOTAVAIL for an address other than any or loopback, and EADDRINUSE for a port another socket holds, unless the new one set SO_REUSEADDR or SO_REUSEPORT (FreeBSD 9's in_pcbbind ). Listen on a datagram socket answers EOPNOTSUPP. - Options. The executable's options are stored and read back. - Epoll sets. sceNetEpollControl adds a socket to a set (events 1 or 3) or removes it. Answers, from shadPS4: EINVAL for a bad operation or event; EBADF for an unknown set or socket, or for removing a socket the set does not hold; EEXIST for adding one twice. A closed socket leaves every set. Offline nothing ever becomes ready. The resolver. With no DNS server, a name other than localhost answers RESOLVER_ENODNS, 0x804101e1 (shadPS4's offline resolver). An IPv4 literal is converted unless flag 0x10000 is set. A pool that is not live, including the 0 that the HavokScript debugger ( 0x00dfd1b0 ) passes, answers EBADF. HTTP requests. The executable's HTTP manager ( 0x013d2740 ) builds a connection and a request, then sets the content length, timeout and waiting handle. Its state machine ( 0x013d2970 ) sends, and treats any error other than busy, again or timeout as failure. The runtime builds both, with ids from 1 that are never reused: - sceHttpSendRequest answers 0x80431063 (network). PS4Recomp and the native port family answer the same; shadPS4 sends in the background and then answers 0x80431065 . Either way, the job ends failed. - The response calls answer 0x80431065 . - Ids that are not live answer 0x80431100 , a missing URL 0x80433060 , and NULL results 0x804311fe (shadPS4's codes). What stops by name (each needs a maintainer ruling or a real network to settle): - type 6 peer-to-peer sockets and other families; - binding port 0 (the PS4 's ephemeral port is not known); - connect or datagrams to loopback (no loopback stack); - reading an option that was never set (the PS4 's defaults are not known); - asynchronous resolving, listening while unbound, and abort flags; - non-HTTP URLs, methods other than GET, POST and PUT, and full tables.
docs.title: Sockets, the resolver and HTTP requests, offline (libSceNet, libSceHttp, issue #41)

docs.text: Facts from shadPS4's libSceNet ( net.cpp , guest_net.cpp , net_error.h , net_types.h ) and from bbhost. The implementation is the runtime 's own. Errors: a failing call answers 0x80410100 plus a FreeBSD error number, and sets the calling thread's network errno, whose address sceNetErrnoLoc() gives. That errno is separate from the C library's. Offline: an epoll set exists, but no socket ever becomes ready on it, so a wait ends only by its timeout, an abort or a destroy. Call Runtime sceNetEpollCreate(name, flags) a new id from 1; flags other than 0 are EINVAL ( 0x80410116 ), a name over 31 characters ENAMETOOLONG ( 0x8041013f ). The caller ( 0x02b1575d ) keeps the id and reads the network errno on failure. sceNetEpollWait(id, events, max, timeout µs) 0 events after the timeout (negative waits for ever); EINTR ( 0x80410104 ) if an abort or destroy cuts it short; unknown id EBADF , no events or max < 1 EINVAL sceNetEpollAbort(id, flags) interrupts the waiters; with none, ENOTBLK ( 0x8041010f ), or with flag 1 the abort is kept and the next wait fails with EINTR at once; other flags EINVAL sceNetEpollDestroy(id) closes the set, interrupting its waiters; unknown id EBADF
docs.title: The network errno and epoll sets (sceNetErrnoLoc, sceNetEpoll*)

docs.text: The names and argument shapes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Net.h , which declares sceNetTerm as returning nothing; the executable reads its result. The behaviour comes from the executable's own calls: - sceNetInit . Seven subsystems each call it once, behind a flag of their own. One ( 0x011c7992 ) accepts success or exactly 0x80410110 , and then does not terminate the library itself. So a repeat initialize answers 0x80410110 , "already initialized". - sceNetTerm . Its callers ( 0x011c79d9 ) accept 0 or exactly 0x804101c8 . Which condition gives the second is not established, so terminating a library that is not initialized stops by name. - sceNetPoolCreate . Every call passes a name and flags 0, treats a negative result as failure, and keeps the result as a pool id it passes on. The runtime hands out ids from 1. The runtime is offline: initializing touches no network. A pool before initialize, without a name or size, or with flags stops by name.
docs.title: Network library start-up (sceNetInit, sceNetTerm, sceNetPoolCreate, issue #41)

docs.text: sceSslInit(size_t pool_size) and sceHttpInit(int32_t pool, int32_t ssl, size_t pool_size) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Ssl.h and Http.h declare them. The executable's HTTP manager ( 0x013d1fc0 and 0x013d2050 ): - creates a network pool; - then calls sceSslInit with a size; - then calls sceHttpInit with the pool id, the SSL result and the same size. It treats a negative result as failure, keeps each non-negative one as an id, and passes each id back on teardown. So each call answers a context id; offline, a context is only an id. What stops by name: an id the runtime did not hand out, and a size of 0.
docs.title: SSL and HTTP library start-up (sceSslInit, sceHttpInit, issue #41)

docs.text: sceHttpCreateTemplate(int32_t context, const char *user_agent, int32_t version, int32_t proxy) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it.
