Its version list has 1 for HTTP/1.0 and 2 for HTTP/1.1. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1d32 ) passes the HTTP context id, its user agent string, version 2 and proxy 1. It keeps the result as a template id and passes it straight to the next HTTP call. Offline, a template is only an id. What stops by name: - a context the runtime did not hand out; - no user agent; - a version other than HTTP/1.0 or 1.1; - a proxy value other than the observed 1 (its meaning is not public). sceHttpSetNonblock(id, enable) comes next. OpenOrbis names it without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only call ( 0x013d1d41 ): the new template id and 1, with the result discarded. The runtime records the choice and answers 0; offline, nothing ever blocks on a network. An unknown id, and a value other than 0 or 1, stop by name.
docs.title: HTTP templates (sceHttpCreateTemplate, sceHttpSetNonblock, issue #41)

docs.text: OpenOrbis names sceHttpCreateEpoll without a signature, so its shape comes from the executable's only use, a tail call at 0x013d1d82 . It passes the HTTP context id and the address of an eight-byte slot preset to 0, and its caller ( 0x023e4567 ) discards the result. A handle is an object the library allocates and the title only passes back, so the runtime allocates one per call and answers 0. What the title later does with it (waiting on requests) belongs to other calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: an HTTP context the runtime did not hand out, and a missing slot.
docs.title: HTTP waiting handles (sceHttpCreateEpoll, issue #41)

docs.text: The executable's HTTP manager tears down what it set up, each call only for an id it got, and none reads an answer: - its connection object ( 0x013d1d90 , 0x013d1e10 ) calls sceHttpAbortWaitRequest(handle) , sceHttpDestroyEpoll(HTTP context, handle) and sceHttpDeleteTemplate(template) ; - the manager ( 0x013d20d0 , 0x013d2120 , 0x013d2170 ) calls sceHttpTerm(HTTP context) , sceSslTerm(SSL context) and sceNetPoolDestroy(pool) . OpenOrbis' Http.h and Net.h give the int32_t id arguments of sceHttpTerm , sceHttpDeleteTemplate and sceNetPoolDestroy ; the others' come from these calls. The answers are facts from shadPS4's libSceHttp ( http.cpp , http_error.h ): Call Runtime sceHttpTerm(context) , sceHttpDeleteTemplate(template) 0, ending the id; 0x80431100 (invalid id) for one that is not live (never handed out, or already ended) sceHttpDestroyEpoll(context, handle) 0, freeing the handle; 0x80431100 for a context or handle that is not live, 0x804311fe (invalid value) for no handle sceHttpAbortWaitRequest(handle) 0; 0x804311fe for no handle, 0x80431100 for one that is not live. Every later sceHttpWaitRequest on the handle answers 0x80431080 (aborted). Offline no wait blocks, so there is no waiter to wake. sceSslTerm(context) , sceNetPoolDestroy(pool) 0, ending the id Ids are never reused. Using an ended pool or SSL context in sceHttpInit , an ended HTTP context in sceHttpCreateTemplate or sceHttpCreateEpoll , and an ended template in the template calls, stop by name as an unknown id does ( sceHttpsEnableOption and sceHttpsDisableOption answer 0x80431100 , as before). What stops by name: ending an SSL context or pool that is not live (no source gives the answer). shadPS4 answers 0x80431001 (before init) for the HTTP calls before any sceHttpInit ; the runtime does not model that state and answers 0x80431100 there, which the executable never reaches.
docs.title: Network, SSL and HTTP teardown (sceHttpTerm, sceSslTerm, sceNetPoolDestroy, issue #41)

docs.text: sceHttpsEnableOption(id, flags) and sceHttpsDisableOption(id, flags) set and clear HTTPS flags on a template. The facts come from shadPS4's and PS4Recomp's libSceHttp , which agree: - The flags: 0x01 verify the server, 0x02 verify the client, 0x04 check the common name, 0x08 and 0x10 check the not-after and not-before dates, 0x20 check for a known CA, 0x40 reuse sessions, 0x80 send SNI, and 0x2000 . - A new template's flags: server verification, the common-name and known-CA checks, and SNI ( 0xa5 ). - Errors: other bits answer 0x804311fe (invalid value); an id that is no template answers 0x80431100 (invalid id). The executable's one wrapper ( 0x013d1e90 ) enables or disables 0x01 on its template, and its caller ( 0x0227dade ) does not read the answer. Offline no request is sent, so each template keeps its flags for when one is ( rt_http_template_ssl_flags ).
docs.title: HTTPS options (sceHttpsEnableOption, sceHttpsDisableOption)

docs.text: sceHttpAddRequestHeader(id, name, value, mode) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's Http.h declares it. The executable's only call ( 0x013d1ed5 ) adds a header to its template with mode 0, and treats only 0 as success. A header only matters to a request the library sends. Offline, no request is ever sent, because every sending call stops by name. So the runtime checks the arguments and answers 0 without keeping the header. What stops by name: - an id that is not one of the runtime 's templates; - a missing name or value; - a mode other than the observed 0 (the modes are not public).
docs.title: HTTP request headers (sceHttpAddRequestHeader, issue #41)

docs.text: _sigprocmask(how, set, old) is FreeBSD's sigprocmask(2) : the calling thread's blocked signals. A FreeBSD sigset_t is four 32-bit words, with signal n at bit n - 1. how is SIG_BLOCK (1), SIG_UNBLOCK (2) or SIG_SETMASK (3), and is ignored when there is no new set. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can never be blocked, and are dropped silently. The bundled libc's setjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fcb0 ) reads the mask with SIG_BLOCK and no new set, and its longjmp ( libc.elf+0x2fd00 ) puts it back with SIG_SETMASK . What the runtime does. No signal is delivered to the guest yet. So the runtime keeps each guest thread's mask, a new thread starting with its creator's, and does not apply it to the host thread. What stops by name: an unknown how . Its error is reported through the guest's errno , which the runtime does not model. sigprocmask and sigfillset ( libc.elf imports both from libkernel). sigprocmask is the same call under its POSIX name (FreeBSD's libc sigprocmask is the system call itself); its thirteen calls include +0x53f84 , which blocks everything with SIG_SETMASK and a set from sigfillset and keeps the old mask. sigfillset(set) puts every signal in the set, each of the four words all ones (FreeBSD libc's sigsetops.c , POSIX), and answers 0. A missing set stops by name: POSIX defines no error for it.
docs.title: Signal masks (_sigprocmask, issue #34)

docs.text: scePthreadGetprio(thread, int32_t *priority) and scePthreadSetprio(thread, priority) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares them. What the executable does. Its only reader ( 0x02a3b59d ) reads the current priority before choosing a new one from a class. It sets priorities from 256 ( 0x100 ) to 767 ( 0x2ff ), at 0x02a3b63d and 0x0111ab46 . Where a thread's priority comes from: - The main thread. An executable may declare its main thread's settings in its process parameters ( sceUserMainThreadPriority and the like, which homebrew titles define). Without them the main thread runs at SCE_KERNEL_PRIO_FIFO_DEFAULT , 700 (libretro's public ps4_defines.h ). The executable passes the same 700 ( 0x2bc ) as a priority to sceUserServiceInitialize . - This executable's block holds no main thread settings: after relocation only the C library's parameter pointer ( +0x38 ) is set, and +0x18 to +0x37 are empty. - Created threads. A thread created without explicit scheduling inherits its creator's priority (FreeBSD libthr's default attribute, PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ). The executable sets none. What the runtime does. It records priorities. The host schedules the threads, so priorities change nothing else. What stops by name: - main thread settings in the process parameters (which slot is the priority is not established); - a priority outside 256–767; - a missing thread or variable.
docs.title: Thread priorities (scePthreadGetprio, scePthreadSetprio, issue #34)

docs.text: clock_gettime(clockid_t id, struct timespec *tp) is POSIX, with FreeBSD's clock numbers and amd64 struct timespec (two 64-bit fields, seconds and nanoseconds). The bundled libc's time() ( libc.elf+0x2f030 ) asks for clock 13 and returns its seconds. Clock 13 is FreeBSD's CLOCK_SECOND , which FreeBSD answers with the wall clock's whole seconds and 0 nanoseconds ( kern_clock_gettime ). What the runtime does. It answers the clocks whose meaning FreeBSD fixes and the host has: - CLOCK_REALTIME (0) and CLOCK_SECOND (13), from the host's wall clock; - CLOCK_MONOTONIC (4), from the host's monotonic clock. What stops by name: other clocks and a missing timespec. Their errors go through errno , which the runtime does not model. sceKernelClockGettime(id, tp) is the same call under its SCE name. It returns 0x80020000 plus the error number: EINVAL for another clock and EFAULT for a missing timespec, as FreeBSD answers them. The executable's call ( 0x0111a815 ) asks for clock 4, and treats anything but 0 as failure.
docs.title: clock_gettime and sceKernelClockGettime (libkernel, issue #34)

docs.text: uint64_t sceKernelGetProcessTime(void) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares it, is the time since the process started. Its unit is microseconds. The executable turns it into seconds by dividing by 1,000,000: - at 0x00e4fb6e , through the compiler's multiply by 0x431bde83 and shift by 50; - at 0x0252607e , through a division by the double 1000000.0. It also seeds a random generator with it ( 0x00835dba ). What the runtime does. It measures from its own start, on the host's monotonic clock.
docs.title: Process time (sceKernelGetProcessTime, issue #34)

docs.text: AJM decodes compressed audio in batches of jobs that the title builds in a buffer and hands over. The facts come from shadPS4's libSceAjm , checked against bbhost (a Bloodborne host, whose observations of the title's FMOD are noted) and PS4Recomp. The ATRAC9 configuration word's layout and tables are LibAtrac9's (MIT). The code is the runtime 's own. Contexts, codecs and instances. - Contexts: sceAjmInitialize(0, &context) and sceAjmFinalize(context) . - Codecs: sceAjmModuleRegister(context, codec, 0) and sceAjmModuleUnregister , with 0 MP3, 1 ATRAC9 and 2 AAC. - Instances: sceAjmInstanceCreate(context, codec, flags, &instance) gives an id that is the slot index with the codec at bit 14. Its flags hold a revision (bits 0–2, not 0), the channels (3–6), the sample format (7–9, 0 for 16-bit) and gapless looping (bit 10). - The title's instances: it creates ATRAC9 instances with flags 0x409 to 0x441 : revision 1, 1 to 8 channels, 16-bit, gapless looping ( 0x01118d9a ). Jobs and batches. - Building jobs: sceAjmBatchJobControlBufferRa and sceAjmBatchJobRunBufferRa write a job into the batch and return the next free position. - A job is a sequence of chunks, each with a 32-bit header: an identifier in bits 0–6 and a 20-bit payload. The chunks are the job itself (payload the instance), an optional return address, input and output buffers ( {header, size, pointer} ) and the flags. - Fixed sizes: a control job is 0x30 bytes (0x40 with a return address) and a run job 0x40 (0x50). The title's FMOD lays jobs out at those strides. - Starting and waiting: sceAjmBatchStartBuffer runs the batch (a size that is not a multiple of 8 is malformed, 0x80930011 ). sceAjmBatchWait waits with a timeout in ms; sceAjmBatchCancel and sceAjmBatchErrorDump round it out. Job flags: - run: bit 11 get codec info, bit 12 multiple frames; - control: bit 13 reset, bit 14 initialize, bit 15 resample; - sideband: bit 45 gapless, bit 46 format, bit 47 stream. A job's output control buffer starts with its result, then the stream result, format, gapless state, frame count and codec info, as its flags ask. The ATRAC9 codec info is {superframe bytes, frames per superframe, bytes left in the superframe, samples per frame} . What the runtime does. - When jobs run: when the batch is started, on the calling thread (bbhost does the same for this title). A wait finds the batch finished and frees its id; a cancel of a batch that has run does nothing. - Control jobs are modelled: initialize with the 4-byte ATRAC9 configuration word, reset, and gapless. So is the codec info, derived from the configuration word: 0xFE , a sample rate index, a channel configuration, a 0 bit, the frame bytes minus one, and a superframe index, read most-significant bit first. - Errors: context 0x80930002 , instance 0x80930003 , batch 0x80930004 , parameter 0x80930005 , no batch id left 0x80930006 , no instance left 0x80930007 , already registered 0x80930009 , not registered 0x8093000A , revision 0 0x8093000B . Decoding. ATRAC9 is decoded with LibAtrac9 (MIT, vendored unmodified in third_party/libatrac9 ), behind a small decoder interface ( runtime/ajm.h ). The decode loop answers as shadPS4's does: - Before each frame: too little output room answers "not enough room" ( 0x10 ), and less input than the rest of the superframe "partial input" ( 0x8 ). - Each frame: it drops the gapless skip and stops at the gapless total. A superframe's padding is skipped, and when the gapless window ends mid-superframe the rest of it is decoded and dropped. - Looping and repeats: an instance with gapless looping starts the window again. A job repeats frames only with "multiple frames". - Errors: a decoder error is fatal, with its code as the internal result. The tests use a stand-in decoder, because no ATRAC9 data may be in the repository, plus the real one on junk input. Stops by name: codecs other than ATRAC9, sample formats other than 16-bit, resampling, format inputs and outputs, and the statistics instance.
docs.title: Audio job manager (libSceAjm, issue #37)

docs.text: Microphone input. The executable's only user is FMOD's PS4 record driver: - Opening. Its record start ( 0x0111c050 ) opens a port with sceAudioInOpen(user, type 0/1/5, index 0, 256 samples, 16000 Hz, param 0 = 16-bit mono) at 0x0111c11d . A negative answer is an FMOD error. - Reading. Its update thread calls sceAudioInInput at 0x0111beee and uses the answer as a sample count to advance a ring buffer, so an open port must never answer an error there. - Closing. The port is closed at 0x0111c25b , and the answer is ignored. The facts come from shadPS4's audioin.cpp and audioin_error.h (facts only), whose codes match the PS Vita SDK's audioin.h : - A port opens without a device and reads silence. PS4Recomp and the droogie bbhost runtime agree; the bloodborne-native port family answers 0x80260109 (not opened) instead, so the majority answer is used. - The length must be 1 to 2048 samples ( 0x80260102 ), the frequency 16000 or 48000 ( 0x80260103 ), and the param 0 or 1, 16-bit mono or stereo ( 0x80260106 ). - An unknown handle is 0x80260101 , a NULL buffer 0x80260105 . What the runtime does with the microphone: - Open hands out handles from 1. - Input writes the port's samples of silence, waits for the time they last (length / frequency), and answers the sample count. - Close frees the handle. - Stops by name: a type other than 0, 1 and 5; an index other than 0; a full table. Voice chat. At 0x010c8000 the executable initializes the library ( sceVoiceInit(param, 100) ). It then creates a microphone port (type 0) and a speaker port (type 5) for the initial user. Its microphone loop ( 0x010c8a50 ) reads only while sceVoiceGetPortInfo reports bytes. Peer ports, connections, Start and the incoming packet path need an online peer. Teardown ignores every answer. shadPS4 ( voice.cpp , voice.h ), PS4Recomp ( ps4_voice.c ), the droogie bbhost runtime and the bloodborne-native port family all answer success with no audio behind it (facts only). The port info is 0x20 bytes: the byte count is at 0x10, and the frame size at 0x14 is 1 (shadPS4), which the incoming packet path divides by. Their error codes disagree (shadPS4 0x804e08xx , the PS Vita's; PS4Recomp 0x80233xxx ), so misuse stops by name. What the runtime does with voice chat: - Answers 0. Init; CreatePort, which hands out the lowest free id from 0; DeletePort, for any id, since the executable also deletes 0xff ; Connect, Disconnect, Start and Stop; End, which forgets every port. - GetPortInfo writes the type, frame size 1 and byte count 0. - ReadFromOPort reads 0 bytes, and WriteToIPort discards the data.
docs.title: No microphone and no voice chat (libSceAudioIn, libSceVoice, issue #37)

docs.text: The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's AudioOut.h declares int32_t sceAudioOutInit(void) and int32_t sceAudioOutOpen(user, port type, index, length, sample rate, param) . Its _types headers give: - port type 0 (main); - format 4 (float stereo); - the error codes 0x8026000E (already initialized) and 0x8026000F (not initialized). What the executable does: - Its only init call ( 0x0111b665 ) accepts success or exactly 0x8026000E . - Its only open ( 0x0111b69d ) passes user 0xff (the system user in the SDK's user types), the main port, index 0, 256 samples, 48000 Hz and a format. It keeps a non-negative result as the port handle. - The format is the executable's own evidence. Its output callback ( 0x0111b600 ) accepts 2 or 8 channels and passes 4 | (channels == 8) . So 4 is float stereo (as in the SDK) and 5 is float with eight channels. The boot opens eight channels. - A second open ( 0x0111b6fc ) passes port type 1 with the same settings, and does not check the result. The PS4 name of type 1 is not public; the sibling Vita SDK calls it BGM. - The movie player's sound gets a port of its own ( 0x02c225ae , 0x02c22842 ): 1024 samples at 48000 Hz. Its format comes from the movie's channel count: 0, 1 or 2 (16-bit mono, stereo, eight channels) for 48 kHz sound, and 3, 4 or 5 (float) otherwise. The SDK's _types/audio_out.h names 0, 1, 3 and 4; shadPS4's audioout.h adds 2 and 5 as the eight-channel forms. The 6-channel movies open format 2. With --audio host , 16-bit blocks are scaled to -1..1 for the host stream. What the runtime does. It records each open port and hands out handles from 1, the lowest one free, so a closed port's handle is handed out again (shadPS4 also reuses a closed port's slot). Sound output belongs to the output calls, which stop by name until they are implemented. What stops by name: any open other than the observed ones (256 float samples in formats 4 and 5, or 1024 samples in formats 0 to 5, at 48000 Hz), and running out of handles. int32_t sceAudioOutSetVolume(handle, flag, int32_t *volume) , as the SDK declares it, comes next. The executable's only call ( 0x0111b6d6 ) passes its new port, flag 0xff and eight volumes of 32768, and treats nonzero as failure. Flag bit n selects channel n, whose volume is volume[n] . What the runtime does. It records the volumes. What stops by name: - a handle it did not hand out; - a flag naming a channel the port does not have; - a missing array; - a volume outside 0–32768. int32_t sceAudioOutOutput(handle, const void *samples) , as the SDK declares it, hands a port sound. The executable's audio thread ( 0x0111b93c ) hands its port one block at a time ( length samples for every channel). It advances its ring buffer when the result is not negative, and loops with no wait of its own. So the call itself paces the thread: it returns once the port has room for the next block. What the runtime does. It plays nothing yet. - Each port takes one block per length / rate seconds (256 samples at 48000 Hz: 5.33 ms). - A call waits until the block before it would have finished playing, then answers 0 (the caller only checks the sign). - A port that falls behind starts again from now. - No block ( samples NULL) hands nothing over: the call waits until the port has room for the next block and answers 0, without moving the port's timeline on. shadPS4 ( audioout.cpp ) waits for the port's buffer to drain and copies nothing for a null pointer, returning 0 samples; PS4Recomp ( ps4_audioout.c ) waits for room and pushes nothing, returning 0. The movie player's sound thread calls it so when it has no sound to give (found during the opening movie). What stops by name: a handle the runtime did not hand out. int32_t sceAudioOutClose(handle) , as the SDK declares it, closes a port. The movie player's sound ends with it ( 0x02c2276f ): first no block ( sceAudioOutOutput with NULL, which waits for room), then the close, whose negative result it takes as failure. The runtime takes the port back once any output call on it has returned, closes its host stream and answers 0, as shadPS4's audioout.cpp does; the handle is free for the next open. A handle that names no open port stops by name (the error value is not established). int32_t sceAudioOutGetPortState(handle, void *state) , as the SDK declares it, reports a port's state. Its _types/audio_out.h gives the layout (32 bytes): a 16-bit output, an 8-bit channel count, a volume and a 64-bit flag. The executable's only call ( 0x0111bb41 ) asks about its second port, and reads only output, testing it for 0. What the runtime does. It plays nothing on the host, so no port is output anywhere. It answers output 0, and 0 in the fields whose encoding is not established. This must change when the runtime plays sound. What stops by name: an unknown handle, and a missing state. Sound on the host ( pbboot --audio host , tools/boot.py --audio host ). With this option, each port plays through SDL3 on the default playback device ( runtime/audio_host.h , runtime/audio/audio_host_sdl.c ). Without it, or in a build without SDL3, nothing is played and ports keep time on their own as before. Boots are silent by default. Each block: each channel is scaled by its volume (32768 is 0 dB, the level the title sets; until it sets one the port plays at 0 dB, the runtime 's choice) and queued on the port's stream. Pacing: the call returns once no more than four blocks wait to be played, so the title's audio thread runs at the device's pace. Channel order: the title's 8-channel float format (format 5) is passed in SDL's 7.1 order, as shadPS4's SDL backend does; the STD layouts, which are remapped, are not used by the title. Port state: a port playing on the host reports output 1 ( CONNECTED_PRIMARY , shadPS4's audioout.h ). Observed: with ATRAC9 decoding, a boot plays the game's own sound after about 17 seconds.
docs.title: Audio output (sceAudioOutInit, sceAudioOutOpen, sceAudioOutSetVolume, sceAudioOutOutput, issue #37)

docs.text: The title plays its movies ( /app0/.../movie/*.mp4 : H.264 video, AAC sound in several languages) through the console's movie player. One wrapper in the executable makes every call ( 0x02cfdf33 to 0x02d004a9 ): sceAvPlayerInit gets a 0x78-byte block with the title's memory callbacks and an event callback. The block has no file callbacks, auto start is 0 and the default language is none. sceAvPlayerPostInit gets decoder settings (video decoder type 3). sceAvPlayerAddSource gets the movie's path and sceAvPlayerSetLooping a flag. After the ready event the title counts the streams and reads each one's info. It enables one video stream and the audio stream its language setting picks, then calls sceAvPlayerStart . Each frame, a picture comes from sceAvPlayerGetVideoDataEx and sound from sceAvPlayerGetAudioData on the title's audio thread. The layouts, event numbers and error values are from shadPS4's libSceAvPlayer ( avplayer.h , avplayer_error.h , avplayer_state.cpp , avplayer_source.cpp ), checked against the OpenOrbis AvPlayer.h . The code is the runtime 's own ( runtime/syslib/avplayer.c ). Decoding uses FFmpeg on the host ( runtime/media/ , runtime/media_host.h ), when the runtime is built with it. Call What the title passes and reads Runtime answer sceAvPlayerInit(const InitData *) memory callbacks {allocate, deallocate, allocate texture, deallocate texture}, an event callback, no file callbacks a handle; file callbacks, auto start, a missing allocator or event callback stop by name sceAvPlayerPostInit(handle, data) decoder types and parameters 0 (they change how the console decodes, not the result) sceAvPlayerAddSource(handle, path) the movie under /app0 opens and probes it, sends event 2 (ready), 0; a movie the runtime cannot open stops by name sceAvPlayerStreamCount , sceAvPlayerGetStreamInfo the type (0 video, 1 audio), an audio stream's channels and rate the movie's video and audio streams, durations in ms sceAvPlayerEnableStream(handle, index) one video stream and one audio stream 0 sceAvPlayerStart event 3 (playing); the movie's clock starts sceAvPlayerGetVideoDataEx(handle, FrameInfoEx *) the picture's address, width, height and four crops; it lays the planes out from the width true once the clock reaches the next picture. The picture is NV12 in a buffer from the title's texture allocator (alignment 0x100), with pitch = width rounded up to 64 and height rounded up to 16, cropped back to the picture sceAvPlayerGetAudioData(handle, FrameInfo *) address, size in bytes, channels, rate true with up to 1024 interleaved 16-bit sample frames, handed out up to 0.1 s ahead of the clock sceAvPlayerIsActive , sceAvPlayerCurrentTime true until a movie that does not loop has handed out its last frame, then event 1 (stopped) once; the clock in ms, standing still while paused sceAvPlayerPause , sceAvPlayerResume , sceAvPlayerStop , sceAvPlayerClose events 4, 3 and 1; Close frees the buffers through the title's callbacks The runtime decodes a few frames ahead on a host thread of its own, so FFmpeg never runs on a guest thread's small stack. The guest calls only copy finished frames into the title's buffers. A looping movie starts again with its clock carried on. Without FFmpeg, opening a movie stops by name.
docs.title: The movie player (libSceAvPlayer)

docs.text: scePthreadAttrSetschedparam(attr, const struct sched_param *param) sets the priority ( sched_param 's one int) of a thread created with the attribute. OpenOrbis' libkernel.h gives the shape; libthr's _pthread_attr_setschedparam gives the semantics. What the executable does. Its thread wrapper ( 0x0111aafd ) sets it without explicit-scheduling inheritance. So under libthr's default ( PTHREAD_INHERIT_SCHED ), the new thread still starts at its creator's priority. The wrapper then sets the priority itself with scePthreadSetprio ( 0x0111ab46 ). What the runtime does. It records the priority on the attribute. A variable holding no attribute is EINVAL (libthr). What stops by name: a missing param, and a priority outside 256–767. scePthreadAttrSetaffinity(attr, uint64_t mask) is the wrapper's next call ( 0x0111ab0e ), with the CPU mask its caller chose. As for scePthreadSetaffinity , the runtime records the mask (the created thread takes it) and the host schedules. An empty mask stops by name, and a variable holding no attribute is EINVAL .
docs.title: Attribute priority and CPU mask (scePthreadAttrSetschedparam, scePthreadAttrSetaffinity, issue #34)

docs.text: The title's saves live in the host folder given to pbboot --savedata . tools/boot.py gives each run a new empty one, so boots start alike, unless --savedata DIR names a folder to keep them in. A mounted save appears to the title as /savedataN (N the lowest free of 16), through the same file calls as /app0 and /data , read-only or writable as mounted. Sources. shadPS4's libSceSaveData ( savedata.cpp , savedata.h , savedata_error.h , save_instance.cpp , save_memory.cpp ), checked against two other Bloodborne ports and the OpenOrbis headers. Where they disagree, shadPS4's answer is taken. The code is the runtime 's own. The title's SDK version decides some answers. The executable says SDK 0x02000071 (firmware 2.00), which the runtime reads through rt_compiled_sdk_version : - "not initialized" is 0x80960002 (it is 0x809F000B before 2.00 and 0x809F0001 from 2.50); - a directory search reports the total hits, the number set and the params (from 1.70); - a mount writes back only the mount point (before 4.50), and mode 0x20 (create or open) does not create; - terminating with saves mounted unmounts them (before 4.00). On the host. <savedata>/<user id>/<directory name>/ holds the title's files, with sce_sys/param.bin (the 1328-byte param) and sce_sys/icon0.png ; a save exists when its sce_sys does. The memory-backed save is <savedata>/<user id>/sce_sdmemory/memory.dat . These are the runtime 's own files, not a console's param.sfo . Call Runtime sceSaveDataInitialize(params) 0; the parameter block (a priority, 0x2bc from the caller at 0x02c3c50e ) is ignored, as the library does sceSaveDataTerminate() 0, unmounting any save still mounted; "not initialized" before initialize sceSaveDataMount(request, result) the 80-byte original request. Modes: 1 read-only, 2 read-write, 4 create, 8 destruct-off, 0x10 copy the package's icon. Answers: not there and no create 0x809F0008 ; create when it exists 0x809F0007 ; already mounted 0x809F0003 ; 16 mounted 0x809F000C ; user below 0 0x809F0011 ; a bad name (empty, unterminated, / , \ , leading . ) 0x809F0000 sceSaveDataUmount(mount point) 0, or 0x809F0008 for a mount point not mounted sceSaveDataSetParam(mount point, type, data, size) types 0 (whole param), 1 title, 2 subtitle, 3 detail, 4 user param, written to param.bin with the time; type 5 or more 0x809F0000 ; not mounted 0x809F0004 sceSaveDataSaveIcon(mount point, icon) writes the icon (the smaller of buffer and data size); read-only mount 0x809F000D sceSaveDataDirNameSearch(condition, result) the user's saves (folders with sce_sys/param.bin , not sce_* ), matched by an SQL-LIKE pattern without regard to case ( % , _ ), sorted by name, user param or time (blocks are alike here), ascending or descending; a key above 5 or an order above 1 0x809F0000 sceSaveDataSetupSaveDataMemory(user, size, param) creates or grows memory.dat to the size (never shrinks it); size 0 0x809F0000 sceSaveDataGet/SetSaveDataMemory(user, buffer, size, offset) reads or writes at the offset; before setup 0x809F0012 ; no buffer or a negative offset 0x809F0000 sceSaveDataDelete(request) the 64-byte request { user, padding, title id, directory name, unused, reserved }; removes the save's folder and everything in it, 0. Mounted 0x809F0003 ; no request, no name or a bad name 0x809F0000 ; user below 0 0x809F0011 . The executable's one caller ( 0x02c3e765 ) passes no title id and asks again while the answer is 0x809F0014 Stops by name (not modelled): another title's saves (a title id), the free-space check and its required-blocks answer, the backup copy and its "corrupted" marker, sort key 4, and a memory read or write past the size set up, a delete of a save that is not there (shadPS4 answers 0 then, which is not established for the console), and a host failure to remove a save. The save data dialog stays unbound until the boot reaches it.
docs.title: Save data (libSceSaveData)

docs.text: The title reads its own data under /app0 , the console's read-only mount of its package. The runtime serves /app0 from your own copy and never writes to it: - tools/boot.py --app0 DIR chooses the copy, defaulting to $BB_APP0 , then $BB_DATA_ROOT/merged . - pbboot takes it as --app0 . - A path under any other mount, and one with a .. component (which could leave the copy), stops by name. sceKernelStat(path, struct stat *) is FreeBSD's stat(2) under its SCE name, which returns 0x80020000 plus the error number. The PS4 's struct stat is FreeBSD 9's amd64 layout, 120 bytes (OpenOrbis' _types/kernel.h , OrbisKernelStat ). What the executable does. Its call at 0x02474519 asks whether /app0/dvdroot_ps4/sound/sprj_mixer.fev exists: - 0 means yes; - exactly 0x80020002 ( ENOENT ) means no; - anything else goes to its error path. What the runtime does. It fills the structure from the host file: - type, size, block count and size, link count and times; - the permission bits without write (the mount is read-only); - device and inode numbers as the host's (they only identify the file); - the birth time as the modification time (the host's stat has none); - owner, group, flags and generation 0. Errors. A missing file answers ENOENT , and a missing directory component ENOTDIR (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux). Any other host error stops by name. POSIX stat and errno . eboot also imports POSIX stat from libScePosix . The runtime gives it the same lookup and answer, the POSIX way: 0, or -1 with the calling thread's errno set to ENOENT (2) or ENOTDIR (20). The executable's one call ( 0x00465431 ) reads the access and modification times and the size on 0, and treats any other answer as no file. errno is libkernel's __error() , FreeBSD's int *__error(void) behind the errno macro. It is imported by eboot , libc and libSceFios2 . Each guest thread runs on its own host thread, so a thread-local int is that thread's errno ; it starts at 0, and success leaves it alone.
docs.title: The title's files: /app0, sceKernelStat, opening and reading (issue #35)

docs.text: sceKernelTruncate(path, length) (imported by eboot and libSceFios2 ) is FreeBSD's truncate(2) under its SCE name: 0, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The shape is OpenOrbis libkernel.h 's; the executable's wrapper ( 0x024733a4 ) passes a 64-bit length and turns each 0x8002xxxx answer into an engine error through a table ( 0x02473530 ). eboot also imports mkdir , rmdir and rename from libScePosix : 0, or -1 with errno set. The executable's calls ( 0x00df0bf4 , 0x00e03e68 , 0x00e03ddb and others) ignore the answer or only compare it with 0. ( sceKernelRename and sceKernelFtruncate are under "Opening and reading".) What the runtime does: - Paths resolve as for opening: /data , the mounted save data, and /app0 . - Errors are FreeBSD's numbers, never the host's: ENOENT , ENOTDIR , EEXIST , EISDIR , EINVAL and ENOTEMPTY (66 on FreeBSD, 39 on Linux). - rmdir of a mount's own root is EBUSY (the man page's "mount point for a mounted file system"). - rename across mounts is EXDEV , after the source and the target's folder are looked up, in FreeBSD's order (stable/9 vfs_syscalls.c , kern_renameat ). A directory over a non-empty one is ENOTEMPTY . - truncate with a negative length is EINVAL before the lookup ( kern_truncate ; Linux checks it first too); a directory is EISDIR . Growing a file fills with zero bytes. - A new directory's mode is mode & 0777 less the host's umask. The PS4 process's umask is not established. What stops by name: - no path; - any change under a read-only mount ( /app0 , save data mounted to read). FreeBSD answers EROFS , but only after lookups whose order the runtime does not model for each call, and the title's callers change only /data and its saves; - renaming a mount's root; - any other host error ( EACCES , ENOSPC , EIO and the rest).
docs.title: Truncating by name, and the POSIX mkdir, rmdir and rename

docs.text: sceKernelOpen , sceKernelRead , sceKernelPread , sceKernelLseek , sceKernelFstat and sceKernelClose are FreeBSD's open(2) , read(2) , pread(2) , lseek(2) , fstat(2) and close(2) under their SCE names. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares the shapes. Each returns a result, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. The executable opens its data with flags 0 ( O_RDONLY ) and mode 0555. What the runtime does: - Opening. It opens the host file read-only. A request to write, create, truncate or append answers EROFS , as FreeBSD does on a read-only mount. The lookup comes first: a missing file without O_CREAT is ENOENT . Other flag bits stop by name. - Descriptors. A descriptor is the runtime 's own number, from 3 up, standing for a host descriptor (the title only passes it back). One the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . - Seeking. A whence other than 0, 1 or 2 ( SEEK_SET , SEEK_CUR , SEEK_END , the same on FreeBSD and Linux), and a seek before the start, are EINVAL .
docs.title: Opening and reading

docs.text: sceKernelWrite(fd, buf, n) (imported by eboot and libSceFios2 ) and sceKernelPwrite(fd, buf, n, offset) (imported by libSceFios2 ) are FreeBSD's write(2) and pwrite(2) under their SCE names, with the shapes from the same libkernel.h . Each returns the number of bytes written, or 0x80020000 plus the error number. Writes reach files under the writable /data mount, which sceKernelOpen opens with the requested access mode. What the runtime does: - Order of checks. FreeBSD's order (stable/9 sys_generic.c , sys_write , sys_pwrite and kern_pwritev ): the size, then the descriptor, then the offset. - EBADF . write(2) answers it for a descriptor that is not open for writing: one the runtime did not hand out (0 to 2 included, as for reading), and one opened read-only, which is every /app0 file and a /data file opened with O_RDONLY . - EINVAL . A negative pwrite offset, as for pread ( pwrite(2) : "The offset value was negative"). - The position. A pwrite leaves the file position where it was. A write past the end leaves a hole that reads as zero bytes, as the host file system does. A zero count writes nothing and answers 0. - The count. The answer is the host's count, which can be short. Linux writes at most 0x7ffff000 bytes per call, so a request between that and INT_MAX comes back short where FreeBSD would write it all. What stops by name: - More than INT_MAX bytes. FreeBSD answers EINVAL above IOSIZE_MAX . That is INT_MAX while the debug.iosize_max_clamp sysctl is set (its default in FreeBSD 9; current FreeBSD defaults to 0), and SSIZE_MAX otherwise. The FreeBSD 9.0 write(2) page says INT_MAX . The PS4 's setting is not known. - No buffer for a non-zero count, as for reading. - A pwrite on a descriptor opened with O_APPEND . POSIX writes at the offset. FreeBSD's write(2) BUGS section says its pwrite appends instead, and Linux does the same. The PS4 's answer is not established. - Any host write error ( ENOSPC , EIO , EFBIG and the rest). What would settle the stops: guest call sites that pass these cases, or results observed on a console.
docs.title: Writing

docs.text: sceKernelFtruncate(fd, length) is FreeBSD's ftruncate(2) under its SCE name (shape from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ). The title reaches it after Play Offline, while it creates its save data: its file object cuts its file at its current position ( 0x02473290 ). The runtime passes the length to the host. A negative length, and a descriptor opened without write permission, are EINVAL (FreeBSD's truncate(2) ; Linux answers the same); one the runtime did not hand out is EBADF . Any other host error stops by name. sceKernelRename(from, to) is FreeBSD's rename(2) (shape from libkernel.h ); the title calls it ( 0x02474a85 ) while it creates its save data. The runtime renames the host file, replacing an existing to as rename(2) does. Paths on two different mounts are EXDEV ( rename(2) : "on different logical devices"); on the read-only /app0 EROFS , after the lookup; a missing file or directory component ENOENT or ENOTDIR . Any other host error stops by name.
docs.title: Truncating and renaming

docs.text: sceKernelGetdirentries(fd, buf, nbytes, basep) is FreeBSD's getdirentries(2) and sceKernelFsync(fd) FreeBSD's fsync(2) , under their SCE names (shapes from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ). eboot and libSceFios2 import the first, libSceFios2 the second. How the executable lists a directory. Its directory iterator opens the directory with sceKernelOpen(path, 0x20000, 0555) , that is O_DIRECTORY ( 0x024722d0 ), and treats a negative answer as no listing. Each step ( 0x02472480 ) takes st_blksize from the directory's sceKernelFstat as nbytes , then walks the FreeBSD 9 records: a 32-bit file number, the 16-bit record length, the type, the name length and the NUL-terminated name. It skips . and .. , adds / to a DT_DIR (4) name, and, when it stops partway through a buffer, seeks the descriptor back to *basep so that its next call reads the same records again. What the runtime does: - Opening. O_DIRECTORY alone opens a directory on either mount. A path that is not a directory is ENOTDIR ( open(2) ). - Listing. It lists the host directory in the host's order, as many whole records as fit, each rounded up to 4 bytes (FreeBSD 9's GENERIC_DIRSIZ ), and answers the byte count, 0 at the end. File numbers are the host's inode numbers (they only identify a file). The type is the host's: FreeBSD and Linux share the DT_ numbers. Where the host file system leaves it unknown, the runtime asks fstatat . - Positions. *basep (when not NULL) is the position before the call, and the position afterwards follows the last record listed. So a seek to *basep lists the same records again. A position is a count of entries, the runtime 's own number; FreeBSD's is a byte offset. The title only hands it back to sceKernelLseek , which on a directory accepts SEEK_SET and SEEK_CUR ; a position before the start is EINVAL . - Flushing. sceKernelFsync flushes the host file and answers 0. - Errors. A descriptor the runtime did not hand out is EBADF for both. What stops by name: O_DIRECTORY with any other flag; listing a descriptor that is not a directory, with no buffer, or into fewer than 512 bytes (a directory block: shadPS4 answers EINVAL , the PS4 's answer is not established); SEEK_END on a directory; a host fsync error. An entry added or removed between two calls can move the listing by one entry, as on any file system that lists by position.
docs.title: Directories and flushing

docs.text: sceKernelMkdir(path, mode) , sceKernelRmdir(path) and sceKernelUnlink(path) are FreeBSD's mkdir(2) , rmdir(2) and unlink(2) under their SCE names, 0 or 0x80020000 plus the error number. eboot and libSceFios2.elf import all three from libkernel ( symbols/imports.csv ). The shapes come from the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h ( int32_t sceKernelMkdir(const char *, OrbisKernelMode) , OrbisKernelMode a uint16_t like FreeBSD's mode_t ; int32_t sceKernelRmdir(const char *) , int32_t sceKernelUnlink(const char *) ), supporting evidence for the shapes only. No call site in the repository shows them yet. Under /data and a writable mount the host does the work, and its error is translated: - a missing file or directory component is ENOENT or ENOTDIR , and mkdir of an existing name EEXIST (the same numbers on FreeBSD and Linux); - rmdir of a directory with entries is ENOTEMPTY , 66 on FreeBSD (Linux's is 39), and of a path whose last component is . EINVAL ( rmdir(2) ; Linux answers the same); - unlink of a directory is EPERM . FreeBSD's unlink(2) page lists both EISDIR and EPERM for "the named file is a directory"; the kernel settles it: kern_unlinkat (stable/9) and kern_funlinkat (current) answer EPERM ("POSIX"), and turn the lookup's EINVAL for a last component . into EPERM too. Linux answers EISDIR for both, which the runtime translates. - Any other host error stops by name. The mode of mkdir . FreeBSD gives the new directory (mode & ACCESSPERMS) & ~umask ( kern_mkdirat , stable/9 and current), so bits above 0777 are dropped. The runtime passes mode & 0777 to the host, as sceKernelOpen does for a new file, and the host process's umask then applies. Not established: the PS4 process's umask, so the bits a later sceKernelStat shows are the host's answer, not a console's; and whether the console enforces those bits for the title (a folder made without the owner's write and search bits refuses files on the host, which then stop by name). On a read-only mount ( /app0 , a save mounted read-only) nothing changes, and the answers follow FreeBSD's lookup order ( vfs_lookup.c , stable/9 and current): - a missing component of the path prefix is ENOENT or ENOTDIR first; - mkdir of an existing name is EEXIST (the read-only check is not made for a name that exists), of a new name EROFS ; - rmdir and unlink of an existing name, file or directory, are EROFS , before rmdir 's ENOTDIR and ENOTEMPTY and unlink 's EPERM for a directory; - a last component . is refused by the lookup before that: rmdir EINVAL , unlink EPERM . Stops by name , besides the path checks every file call shares (no path, a path outside the mounts, a .. component, a path longer than the runtime 's buffer): rmdir of a mount point itself ( /data , /app0 , /savedataN ). FreeBSD's rmdir(2) answers EBUSY for the root of a mounted file system, but whether /data is one on the console is not established, and the host would remove the runtime 's own folder.
docs.title: Directories and removing files

docs.text: The disc map tells the file library whether part of a file is already on the hard disk or still only on the disc ( runtime/syslib/disc_map.c ). Shape: sceDiscMapIsRequestOnHDD(const char *path, int64_t offset, int64_t bytes, int32_t *on_hdd) , as shadPS4's disc_map.cpp declares it (a fact only). The caller: the bundled file library's one call ( libSceFios2.elf+0x2d71c ) passes a variable preset to 0. On 0 it takes a nonzero variable as on the hard disk; on any other answer it treats the request as not mapped and remembers that the map is unavailable. The answer: the runtime serves the title from host files with no disc, so there is no disc bitmap. It answers 0x81100004 ("no bitmap info", numbered in shadPS4's disc_map_codes.h ), as shadPS4 does, and writes nothing. A missing path or variable stops by name. The unnamed import ioKMruft1ek . Its name is not public, so it is registered by its NID with RT_SYSLIB_NID ( runtime/include/runtime/syslib.h ): the loader matches the import's hash directly, and tools/runtime_issues.py checks the row ioKMruft1ek#A#B . The file library calls it as (path, offset, bytes, int *, int *, int *) ( libSceFios2.elf+0x29c6f , +0x2a381 ) and takes any non-zero answer as "no map". It answers 0x81100004 and writes nothing, as shadPS4 and the bloodborne-native ports do (PS4Recomp answers 0x80820001 ); the maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10 picked 0x81100004 . A missing path or variable stops by name.
docs.title: The disc map (sceDiscMapIsRequestOnHDD, issue #35)

docs.text: sceKernelQueryMemoryProtection(void *address, void **start, void **end, int32_t *protection) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares it, gives the protection of the mapping that holds an address. What the executable does. Its helpers ( 0x02abad98 , 0x02abadf8 ) pass no start or end. They test the protection's CPU read bit (1) and GPU read bit ( 0x10 ), on memory the game mapped itself. Another ( 0x02d031df , reached once the movie player runs) passes a start and an end and reads only the protection. What the runtime does. It records every direct and flexible mapping with the protection the guest asked for, GPU bits included, and answers that. A start gets the mapping's start, and an end the address one past its last byte (exclusive), as shadPS4's MemoryManager::QueryProtection and PS4Recomp's ps4_direct_mem.c both answer. What stops by name: - an address outside those mappings (other memory is not tracked yet); - a missing variable.
docs.title: Memory protection queries (sceKernelQueryMemoryProtection, issue #34)

docs.text: Graphics are rebuilt at the engine level (issue #39), so the GNM calls answer what the engine expects back; the GPU is not emulated. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's GnmDriver.h only names this call. The executable's only call ( 0x02ad3fb4 ) takes a 64-bit address and maps 128 KiB of direct memory there, for the GPU's tessellation factors: sceKernelMapDirectMemory with that address as a hint, protection 0x33 , alignment 0x10000 . What the runtime does. The PS4 answers a fixed address of its own. The runtime answers one it reserves for this, 0xfe00000000 : below 2^40, and clear of the executable, modules and thread objects. It is the runtime 's choice, not the PS4 's value: the engine only maps it and hands it back to the GPU calls. For this, sceKernelMapDirectMemory now takes an address hint as FreeBSD's mmap does without MAP_FIXED : the map goes there when the range is free. A hint in use (where the system then maps is not established) and one off the alignment stop by name.
docs.title: GNM: the tessellation factor ring (sceGnmGetTheTessellationFactorRingBufferBaseAddress, issue #39)

docs.text: sceKernelVirtualQuery(address, flags, info *, size) , as the OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h and _types/kernel.h ( OrbisKernelVirtualQueryInfo ) declare it, describes the mapping that holds an address. The answer is a 0x48-byte structure: Offset Field 0x00 , 0x08 start and end 0x10 the direct memory offset 0x18 protection 0x1c memory type 0x20 flag bits: flexible 1, direct 2, stack 4, pooled 8, committed 0x10 0x24 a 32-byte name What the executable does. Every call passes flags 0 and size 0x48, and reads the start, the offset or the direct bit: - 0x02d0328c works out an address's place in direct memory as offset + (address - start) ; - 0x02ad3f5e , 0x02ad4066 and 0x02ad423e release the direct memory at the offset. What the runtime does. It answers from its record of direct and flexible mappings: start, offset, protection as asked for, memory type, flexible or direct, committed, and no name. No call reads the end, and whether it is inclusive is not established; the runtime writes the address just past the mapping. What stops by name: - flags other than 0; - a size other than 0x48; - an address outside those mappings (other memory is not tracked yet); - a missing structure.
docs.title: Virtual memory queries (sceKernelVirtualQuery, issue #34)

docs.text: The shapes are OpenOrbis libkernel.h 's: sceKernelMunmap(address, length) , sceKernelMprotect(address, length, protection) and sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType(start, &type, &range_start, &range_end) . What the executable does: - It frees a direct map with sceKernelMunmap and then sceKernelReleaseDirectMemory ( 0x024826fd , 0x0248270c ), the order the release needs. - 0x02d03214 wraps sceKernelMprotect and answers whether the result was 0. - 0x02abae74 passes the pool offset sceKernelVirtualQuery gave for an address to sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType and only tests whether the type is 3 (write-combined garlic). What the runtime does: - Munmap is FreeBSD's munmap(2) . A zero length is EINVAL (FreeBSD's sys_munmap ; shadPS4's sceKernelMunmap answers the same, facts only). As in FreeBSD the range may span several mappings, reserved space and holes: every mapping the runtime made inside it goes (a direct map no longer holds its range, which can then be released), reserved space inside it is given back, and holes stay as they are. A GPU-visible range can be mapped again at its GPU address. The address is not handed out again for other maps. - Mprotect is FreeBSD's mprotect(2) : the mapping takes the new protection, the CPU bits on the host and the GPU bits recorded, as for a map. The queries answer the new protection. - GetDirectMemoryType answers the memory type of the allocated range that holds the pool offset, and that range's start and end (just past it, as for sceKernelVirtualQuery ). What stops by name: - part of a mapping; for munmap, a start off the 16 KiB page, or a range outside the runtime 's map window that touches nothing it mapped or reserved; for mprotect, more than one mapping or memory the runtime did not map (other memory is not tracked yet); - an offset outside every allocated range (shadPS4 answers ENOENT ; no public source settles it); - protection beyond CPU and GPU read and write; - a missing variable.
docs.title: Unmapping, protecting and typing memory (sceKernelMunmap, sceKernelMprotect, sceKernelGetDirectMemoryType, issue #34)

docs.text: The executable's block allocator ( 0x02d01eb0 ) builds one contiguous view of blocks it got separately. It reserves room for all of them ( sceKernelReserveVirtualRange , flags 0x80 , no overwrite, alignment 0); for each block it asks sceKernelVirtualQuery where the block lies in direct memory, then maps an alias of every block at its place in the reserved range in one sceKernelBatchMap . To free the view (or after a failed batch) it turns every entry into an unmap, runs the batch again, and unmaps the whole reserved range, which by then is holes. sceKernelReserveVirtualRange(&address, length, flags, alignment) reserves inaccessible space in the runtime 's map window (shadPS4 maps it with no access). EINVAL ( 0x80020016 ) for no variable, a length that is 0 or not whole 16 KiB pages, and an alignment that is not 0 or a power-of-two multiple of 16 KiB up to 2 GiB (shadPS4's checks, shared by the bloodborne-native ports). An address hint and flags other than no overwrite stop by name. sceKernelBatchMap(entries, count, &processed) runs 32-byte operations (start 0x00 , offset 0x08 , length 0x10 , protection 0x18 , type 0x19 , operation 0x1c ; shadPS4's memory.h ) in order until one fails, and writes how many succeeded when processed is given. Each map is placed at its start exactly: shadPS4, the bloodborne-native ports and droogie's host agree on the implicit MAP_FIXED . No list, a zero length or an operation above 4 answers EINVAL . Map direct (0) maps the pool range over reserved space, with the CPU bits. Unmap (1) is the munmap above. Protect (2) is sceKernelMprotect . Stops by name: a map outside reserved space (what a fixed map replaces is not modelled), an aliased map with GPU access (the GPU reaches each pool range at one address, runtime/gpu_memory.h ), and the flexible-map and type-protect operations (3, 4), which the executable does not use. sceKernelReleaseFlexibleMemory(address, length) unmaps (maintainer's ruling of 2026-11-10; the bloodborne-native ports and droogie's host unmap, shadPS4 keeps the mapping and drops its pages). The allocator frees whole flexible blocks with it ( 0x02482721 ). EINVAL for no address, a zero length or one that is not whole 16 KiB pages; direct memory in the range stops by name.
docs.title: Reserving address space and mapping into it (sceKernelReserveVirtualRange, sceKernelBatchMap, sceKernelReleaseFlexibleMemory, issue #34)

docs.text: sceGnmSetVsShader and sceGnmUpdateVsShader take (command buffer, dwords, registers, modifier); sceGnmSetPsShader and sceGnmUpdatePsShader take (command buffer, dwords, registers). The argument order is shadPS4's libSceGnmDriver ( gnmdriver.cpp ). A boot shows the registers argument holding the shader's register block (7 words for a vertex shader, 12 for a pixel shader; see Paleblood's docs/RENDERER.md ). Detail Answer The reserved space one PM4 NOP packet, as for the other command-buffer writers The shader handed to the renderer, placed at the command-buffer address ( runtime /renderer.h); nothing without the display The vertex shader's modifier replaces PGM_RSRC1 's SGPR count (bits 6-9) and input VGPR count (bits 24-25): ( PGM_RSRC1 & 0xfcfffc3f ) OR the modifier, as shadPS4 applies it. The game's vertex shaders pass one (they call a fetch shader). A modifier with any other bit stops by name A null pixel shader block no pixel shader (a depth-only pass): recorded as such, and a draw with it stops in the renderer No vertex shader registers stops by name
docs.title: GNM: binding vertex and pixel shaders (sceGnmSetVsShader, sceGnmSetPsShader, issue #39)

docs.text: Compute queues. sceGnmMapComputeQueueWithPriority maps as sceGnmMapComputeQueue . The runtime runs no GPU queues, so the priority changes nothing (shadPS4, the deadinside28 port and droogie bbhost ignore it too). sceGnmUnmapComputeQueue(id) (teardown at 0x0148c81c , answer ignored) forgets the queue and answers 0. A later map takes the freed slot first. An id that names no mapped queue stops by name. sceGnmAreSubmitsAllowed answers 1. The console refuses submissions only while the system holds the GPU (shadPS4: "no submission lock held"; bbhost answers 1). sceGnmFlushGarlic is a memory fence. The runtime 's GPU reads the CPU's memory. sceGnmGetEqEventType(event) answers the kevent's data field (offset 16; shadPS4 and deadinside28 agree). A NULL event stops by name. sceGnmSetGsRingSizes(esgs, gsvs) answers 0 for sizes from 4 to 8 MiB in whole MiB, and 0x08000000 otherwise (shadPS4's check). No geometry shader stage runs. The mip statistics report follows shadPS4. Setup answers 0x80000001 for no buffer or one not 64-byte aligned. shadPS4 also refuses addresses past 40 bits, the console GPU's range; the runtime 's memory is the host's, so that check is left out. Setup answers 0x80000002 for a size under 0x1040 or one not 0x40 past a 2 KiB multiple. Otherwise setup zeroes the buffer, writes 0x40 to its first word and answers 0. Request and Disable answer 0. The Razor capture tools exist only on development kits. The retail answers (shadPS4): sceRazorIsLoaded and sceGnmDriverCaptureInProgress answer 0; sceGnmDriverTriggerCapture answers 0x80d15001 ; the four sceRazorCapture* calls answer 0x80d1500f . The last six (maintainer's rulings of 2026-11-10). Five of them are unreachable in the stock game: no instruction or relocated pointer in the executable reaches their wrappers ( 0x01489a40 , 0x01489a50 , 0x01489a70 , 0x01489b40 , 0x01489b70 ). - sceGnmAddEqEvent(queue, id, udata) and sceGnmDeleteEqEvent(queue, id) register and remove a graphics-core event (filter -14) whose ident and data are the id (shadPS4). The GPU's completion step raises it, after the work before the packet, on the renderer's thread (or at once with the display off). This happens when an EVENT_WRITE_EOP or RELEASE_MEM asks for an interrupt (select bits 24 and up: 1 interrupt only, 2 after the write, 3 for RELEASE_MEM ). Graphics submissions raise id 0x40 , the end of pipe. A compute queue's buffers raise its pipe number, 0 to 6 (shadPS4's interrupt numbers). No queue answers EBADF ( 0x80020009 ). Deleting an event that is not registered, an EOP select of 3 and a compute pipe above 6 stop by name. Event queues gained rt_equeue_remove ( runtime/include/runtime/equeue.h ). The renderer is untouched: the step is gnm.c's own. - sceGnmRequestFlipAndSubmitDone(command buffer, bytes, handle, index, mode, argument) takes shadPS4's six-argument shape (droogie's host takes four; the GNM header and the workload variant agree on six). Fewer than 0x100 bytes answers 0x80d11001 (not enough resources). Otherwise it writes one NOP over the first 0x100 bytes and submits them with the flip as the step after them, as sceGnmSubmitAndFlipCommandBuffers does. - sceGnmGetEqTimeStamp and sceGnmDebugHardwareStatus answer 0 and write nothing. shadPS4 (no arguments) and droogie's host (a pointer they write through) agree on the answer, not on the arguments. - sceGnmLogicalCuIndexToPhysicalCuIndex(shader engine, index) and sceGnmLogicalCuMaskToPhysicalCuMask(shader engine, mask) map by identity. The performance counter set-up ( 0x01482804 and eleven more; 0x014818fa , 0x01481eb4 ) passes the shader engine first and reads back a byte and a 16-bit mask, only when sceGnmIsUserPaEnabled is on, which it never is.
docs.title: GNM: queries, debug calls and freeing compute queues (issue #39)

docs.text: OpenOrbis' GnmDriver.h only names this call, so its shape comes from the engine's wrapper ( 0x01489a80 , called from its compute queue setup at 0x0148c7b0 ). What the engine does: - The wrapper passes the pipe and queue from the queue object, the ring buffer, its size in dwords, and the address of the GPU's read pointer. - A negative result is failure. Otherwise the wrapper keeps the result as the queue's id, and sets the read pointer to 0. - The setup then reports success only when that id is not 0. What the runtime does. It does not run the GPU, so the ring is never read. It records each queue for the engine-level graphics layer, and answers ids from 1. What stops by name: mapping the same pipe and queue twice, and a missing ring or read pointer. The renderer and compute queues. sceGnmDingDong completes each indirect buffer the ring points to (the temporary stand-in in runtime/syslib/gnm.c ), then hands it to the renderer, which drops its recorded calls without running them ( rt_renderer_skip ): compute queues do not run on the renderer yet. Dropping them matters because a shader bound in a command buffer is recorded by its address. A compute queue's buffer is never submitted to the graphics queue, so before this its bindings stayed waiting, and a graphics buffer later built in the same memory picked them up: on the main menu after Play Offline, a stale compute shader replaced the one the graphics buffer had just bound.
docs.title: GNM: compute queues (sceGnmMapComputeQueue, issue #39)

docs.text: The PS4 kernel is FreeBSD's, whose kqueue delivers struct kevent : ident (64-bit), filter (16-bit), flags (16-bit), fflags (32-bit), data (64-bit) and udata (a pointer), 32 bytes on amd64. The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's libkernel.h declares create and delete; its _types/kernel.h lists the filters (display -13, graphics core -14, ...). What the executable does. Right after asking video out for a flip, it waits with room for one event, a variable for how many came back, and no timeout ( 0x015e41b6 , 0x02ad6f26 ). So the wait blocks until the flip is done. What the runtime does: - The queue is a list of registrations, added and triggered by the runtime 's own event sources ( runtime/include/runtime/equeue.h ; video out is the first). - A wait returns the triggered events, oldest first, and clears them, so each is reported once per trigger. - An event's flags and fflags are 0: what the PS4 sets there is not established, and no caller reads them. What stops by name: - a timeout (no call passes one); - deleting a queue a thread is waiting on; - an event array or count that does not fit; - the error values.
docs.title: Kernel event queues (sceKernelCreateEqueue, sceKernelWaitEqueue, sceKernelDeleteEqueue, issue #34)

docs.text: The OpenOrbis homebrew SDK's VideoOut.h declares the calls. Its _types/video.h gives: - the 40-byte buffer attribute: format, tiling mode, aspect, width, height, pitch in pixels; - the 64-byte flip status: flip count, two times, the flip argument, pending counts, current buffer; - flip rates (0: 60 Hz, 1: 30 Hz, 2: 20 Hz) and flip modes (1: vsync, 2: hsync). What the executable does. It sets video out up twice, in the same order ( 0x015e488e and 0x02ad61d4 ): 1. open, with (0, 0, 0, no parameter); 2. flip rate 0; 3. an event queue with a flip event; 4. a buffer attribute (format 0x80000000 ; 1920 × 1080 in the first); 5. its buffers. Each frame, it submits a flip with mode 2 and waits on the queue ( 0x015e419a , then 0x015e41b6 ). Its other loop ( 0x02ad6ee9 ) reads the flip status until the flip argument reaches the frame it submitted. What the runtime does. It has no display yet. It keeps each port's buffers and status, and an hsync flip completes at once: - the current buffer and flip argument change, and the flip count grows; - the port's flip events are triggered. The flip event's ident is 0, and its data the flip argument. The PS4 's values are not established, and no caller reads them. What stops by name: - a vsync flip, and other flip modes or rates; - a flip status before the first flip (its initial argument is not established); - other open arguments; - errors. The buffer-attribute setter and buffer registration share the 40-byte rt_video_out_buffer_attribute layout. The setter copies all six input DWORDs without interpreting them and clears the 16 reserved bytes; unaligned output is supported. The public API is void. The independently examined native leaf also leaves the zero-extended pitch in RAX, which this implementation preserves for callers that observe it. A null output stops by the API name before any store.
docs.title: Video out (libSceVideoOut, issue #38)

docs.text: Implement the established contract and test the RT_SYSLIB entry through its library and symbol name. Keep target-specific values separate from host values. When an argument, ID, return value, or error case is unknown, fail loudly with the call name and leave the question open; never choose a value to make tools/boot.py advance.
docs.title: Implementation rule

docs.text: Boot assigns TLS module IDs in mapped-object order, beginning at one, and prepares all nonempty templates before module entry. The executable reuses its static TLS block: the base is the thread pointer minus its rounded allocation size. Other blocks copy the relocated initialization bytes, zero-fill the rest and respect alignment. Lookup allocates nothing. Each context belongs to its host thread; unbinding and rebinding retain values, and destruction preserves borrowed storage. scePthreadCreate installs static executable TLS but no module context, so module lookups on those threads stop as __tls_get_addr .
docs.title: Module TLS (__tls_get_addr)

docs.text: The libkernel library SHA-256 is b3e13917da667d01a353ccf49025d6b1308a32cf86f3f351f96b3a13cd5c7c2f . Its __tls_get_addr export, NID vNe1w4diLCs , begins at ELF address 0x289c0 . The body reads a two-word 64-bit module/offset index, consults TCB/DTV and linker state, masks a slot to 48 bits and adds the full offset without a bounds check. Invalid states can diagnose and execute INT 0x44 . Generation updates, lazy allocation, alternate modes and linker helpers remain unsupported. Adjacent helpers at 0x2a9a0 and 0x2aca0 do not establish a general allocation-residue rule. The title libc template has virtual-address residue 8, while LibcInternal has zero; this implementation aligns the block base to the template's declared alignment. Paleblood accepts full-width IDs and offsets through the template's logical size, including a one-past pointer. Unknown IDs, larger offsets and absent contexts stop by name. These bounds are runtime support limits, not native error behavior. There is no native DTV layout, lazy loading or unloading. The initialization model follows the TLS ABI and Oracle linker documentation . No other PS4 runtime implementation was used.
docs.title: Evidence and limits

docs.text: The loader rejects duplicate headers, initialized size beyond logical size, out-of-file bytes, inconsistent segment aliases, invalid alignment and templates outside the mapped image. Zero alignment becomes one; TBSS need not be readable. Boot checks allocation arithmetic and allocates aligned storage. test_module_tls checks the registry, initialization, owned 256- and 4096-byte alignment, zero-fill, stable writes, borrowed storage, separate threads, full-width requests and named stops. test_module_tls_boot.py runs synthetic AMD64 fixtures through boot, checking static/dynamic main-block aliasing, rounded sizes, module-ID relocations, relocated pointers, constructor persistence and rejected IDs. Loader tests cover malformed metadata.
docs.title: Validation

docs.text: POSIX clock_gettime and clock definitions POSIX getpid Older POSIX gettimeofday specification RFC 2822 section 3.3, date and time specification ; PS4Recomp libSceRtc and shadPS4 rtc.cpp (facts only: the year-1 tick epoch, the SDK-dependent sceRtcSetTime_t , the two-digit day, the network tick answered from the clock) FreeBSD getpagesize(3) ELF ABI, program headers and p_align (loadable segments must be congruent modulo the page size; p_align is the alignment the loader honors) FreeBSD AMD64 param.h (stock PAGE_SIZE 4096) and Sony's open-source page for the PS4 FreeBSD clock_gettime(2) and gettimeofday(2) Linux getpagesize(2) , getpid(2) , clock_gettime(2) , and gettimeofday(2) PSP2SDK sceNetHtonl / sceNetHtons / sceNetNtohl / sceNetNtohs declarations FreeBSD htonl(3) / htons(3) / ntohl(3) / ntohs(3) POSIX sched_yield , FreeBSD sched_yield(2) and FreeBSD pthread_yield(3) ; Linux pthread_yield(3) for the int -returning form ISO C (N1570 draft) 7.24.2.1 memcpy and 7.24.6.1 memset FreeBSD usleep(3) and SUSv2 usleep POSIX sleep , FreeBSD sleep(3) and FreeBSD libc sleep.c (the INT_MAX split and the rounded-up remainder) POSIX nanosleep , FreeBSD nanosleep(2) and FreeBSD kern_time.c ( kern_nanosleep in stable/9, kern_clock_nanosleep in main: the EINVAL check, the zero or negative time, when rmtp is written) FreeBSD 9.0 write(2) and current write(2) ( write and pwrite : EBADF , EINVAL for the size and a negative offset, the O_APPEND note in BUGS), and FreeBSD stable/9 sys_generic.c ( sys_write , sys_pwrite , kern_pwritev : the order of the checks) POSIX pthread_rwlock_rdlock , pthread_rwlock_wrlock , pthread_rwlock_unlock , pthread_rwlock_destroy / init ; FreeBSD libthr thr_rwlock.c and thr_private.h ( THR_RWLOCK_DESTROYED ); FreeBSD kernel kern_umtx.c ( do_rw_rdlock , do_rw_wrlock , do_rw_unlock ) LSB Core __stack_chk_fail and FreeBSD libc libc_stack_protector.c ( __stack_chk_fail , __fail ) POSIX pthread_cond_wait , pthread_cond_signal , pthread_cond_destroy / pthread_cond_init ; FreeBSD libthr thr_cond.c , thr_mutex.c ( _mutex_owned , _mutex_cv_unlock , mutex_unlock_common , mutex_self_lock , mutex_self_trylock ) and thr_private.h ( THR_COND_DESTROYED ); for pthread_cond_timedwait , POSIX pthread_cond_timedwait (the CLOCK_REALTIME default, ETIMEDOUT , EINVAL ), pthread_condattr_getclock , libthr thr_cond.c ( _pthread_cond_timedwait in stable/9 and main, cond_init ) and thr_init.c ( _pthread_condattr_default ) vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/net/netctl.h - PS Vita, a different operating system: shape of the SceNetCtl declarations, never a PS4 value PSP2SDK psp2/net/netctl.h file reference and vitasdk SceNetCtl user group - the same declarations, with no prose describing any return value in this group vitasdk/vita-headers psp2/error.h - 0 on success as the documented SCE-family return convention OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain Sysmodule.h and _types/sysmodule.h - the sceSysmoduleLoadModule , sceSysmoduleIsLoaded and sceSysmoduleUnloadModule declarations and return convention, and the system module ids (after psdevwiki, "Libraries" ) POSIX pthread_attr_setdetachstate - the detach state semantics, the invalid-value error, and the recommended EINVAL for an uninitialised attribute POSIX pthread_self and pthread_attr_init / pthread_attr_destroy FreeBSD pthread_attr(3) , libthr thr_attr.c ( _pthread_attr_setdetachstate , _pthread_attr_get_np ), thr_create.c ( _pthread_create : the default attribute for a null or empty variable) and include/pthread.h ( PTHREAD_CREATE_JOINABLE , PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED ) OpenOrbis include/orbis/_types/pthread.h - the PS4 homebrew SDK's ORBIS_PTHREAD_CREATE_* values, which follow FreeBSD's FreeBSD 9.0 mkdir(2) , rmdir(2) , unlink(2) and current unlink(2) ; FreeBSD vfs_syscalls.c (stable/9 and main: kern_mkdirat and its mode, kern_rmdirat / kern_frmdirat , kern_unlinkat / kern_funlinkat and EPERM for a directory) and vfs_lookup.c (stable/9 and main: the read-only checks and the . check, and their order); OpenOrbis libkernel.h and _types/kernel.h ( OrbisKernelMode ) for the shapes
docs.title: References

docs.text: Runtime system-call notes What each runtime system call is for, what it must do, what the game was seen to do with it, and how Paleblood's runtime answers. At a glance Covers Calls from runtime issue #34 , the files from #35 , the start-up services from #36 and #40 , sound and movies from #37 , the controller, the clock, save data, trophies and the offline PSN calls, the network from #41 , and the graphics calls from #39 . Since 10 November every issue but #34 is closed, and #34 lists only calls contributors have claimed ( below ). A generated list of every registered call is near the end; the runtime call reference has the full notes and sources for each call. Status implemented : the runtime answers the call. unresolved : no established answer, so the runtime has no implementation or stops by name. observed : seen in a real boot, not yet implemented. How to read Each group starts with a status table, then explains the calls. PRs, citations, call-site addresses and "what would settle it" notes are in the collapsibles. Caution A platform manual describes that platform; it does not prove every detail of the PS4 implementation. These notes separate documented behavior from what remains unknown for the target. Two rules the runtime follows Most calls below share the same shape, so it helps to know it first. Stopping by name. When the PS4 's answer to a call is not established, the runtime does not guess. It stops the process (a "fail-loud diagnostic") and names the call the guest made. A registry entry that stops like this is not an implementation. Two error conventions. Many calls exist under an SCE name ( scePthread… ) and a POSIX name ( pthread_… ). As with the mutex functions ( runtime/syslib/kernel_mutex.c ), the SCE name returns 0x80020000 plus the error number, and the POSIX name returns the number itself. Time and process Call Status What the runtime does getpagesize implemented (maintainer's ruling) Answers 16384 (16 KiB), the value every PS4 runtime and port uses and the alignment of every segment in the game's files ( #528 ). getpid implemented (maintainer's ruling) Answers a fixed id, 1000, so runs stay reproducible; the host's process id is not the guest's ( #528 ). clock_gettime , sceKernelClockGettime implemented FreeBSD's clocks 0 (wall clock), 4 (monotonic) and 13 (wall-clock seconds) from the host's clocks; other clocks stop or answer EINVAL . sceKernelGetProcessTime implemented Microseconds since the runtime started. gettimeofday , sceKernelGettimeofday implemented The host's wall clock; a timezone argument stops by name. time ( libSceLibcInternal ) implemented Seconds since the Epoch, from the same clock as clock_gettime(13) , also stored through a non-null pointer, as FreeBSD's time.c does ( #296 , by @EzequielRindello ). The game's file module is its only caller. gmtime , gmtime_s , printf , vprintf , vsnprintf ( libSceLibcInternal ) implemented For the bundled file library: UTC calendar time in ISO C's nine-field struct tm (the PS4 's is 36 bytes, measured from the library's own copy), and formatted output through the host's formatter after each format is checked; wide-character conversions stop by name ( #468 ). What the calls are for getpagesize Takes no arguments and returns the system's memory page size in bytes. The number is platform-specific. It is not in current POSIX; portable code uses sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE) . getpid Takes no arguments and returns a pid_t for the calling process. POSIX defines no error return. What a process ID means, and how long it lives, is platform-specific. clock_gettime Reads the clock chosen by clock_id into a struct timespec : seconds ( tv_sec ) and nanoseconds ( tv_nsec , from 0 through 999,999,999). POSIX returns 0 on success, and -1 with errno on failure; an unsupported clock ID is EINVAL . gettimeofday Reads wall time into a struct timeval : seconds since the Epoch and microseconds ( tv_usec from 0 through 999,999). Wall time can jump, so it is not a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time. POSIX.1-2024 removed the interface. What the game does with them The executable imports getpagesize and gettimeofday from libScePosix . The game's bundled libc.elf imports clock_gettime , getpagesize , getpid , and gettimeofday from libkernel . These imports tell us which names are needed, not every argument or how the PS4 behaves. The frame limiter reads the time with gettimeofday and passes null for the timezone argument. A separate verified game helper calls sceKernelClockGettime with clock ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC . The bundled C library's time() calls clock_gettime with clock ID 13 and keeps only the seconds. That is FreeBSD's CLOCK_SECOND , whose answer is the wall clock in whole seconds. Clock ID numbers are implementation-defined. The PS4 's kernel descends from FreeBSD, and both observed IDs fit FreeBSD's numbering, so the runtime answers FreeBSD's realtime (0), monotonic (4) and second (13) clocks from your computer's clocks ( #164 , #165 ). Any other ID stops by name, or answers EINVAL under the SCE name. Working out the page size The page size is a good example of how far file evidence goes, and where it stops. getpagesize is the only page-size query the game has: nothing imports sysconf . Observed in the game files. Every loadable segment of the eight images is aligned to 0x4000 , and each segment's file offset and address differ by exactly 0x4000 . Three call sites use the result the same way: they accept it only if it is a power of two and cache it next to three fixed sizes ( 0x10000 , 0x40000 , 0x200000 ). Byte order Network protocols send integers big-endian ("network order"); the CPU may store them the other way round ("host order"). Paleblood imports four integer conversion calls from libSceNet in eboot : sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . Their public SCE declarations use unsigned 32-bit and 16-bit integer arguments and results. The documented contract converts between host order and big-endian network order; the reverse direction uses the same operation. For the project's AMD64 guest ABI, this is byte reversal. The four calls are pure value conversions and do not require socket or online state. This evidence supports only these four conversions. It does not establish behavior for libSceNet sockets, name resolution, epoll, or offline-state queries. Those imports remain unimplemented until their own evidence is available. IPv4 text to binary ( sceNetInetPton ) inet_pton turns an address written as text, such as dotted decimal, into its binary form. The game was seen calling it in four places, each passing address-family value 2 (AF_INET) and using the result as an IPv4 address. For that observed path, the implementation parses dotted-decimal text into four network-order bytes, returns 1 for a valid address and 0 for malformed text, and performs no network I/O. The original call sites support the family and output use; the parser's accepted text forms come from the public BSD inet_pton(3) contract. A game keeps many threads busy at once: loading, audio, rendering, the game's own logic. These calls let the game start those threads and make them wait for one another. Starting a thread. The game describes a thread with an attribute object (stack size, scheduling policy, whether anyone will wait for it to finish), then creates it. The runtime gives each guest thread its own stack and its own copy of the game's thread-local data, then runs the game's entry function on a new host thread.
