The runtime serves /data from a writable folder of its own choosing ( pbboot --data ); tools/boot.py gives each run a new, empty one, so every boot starts alike and nothing the game writes outlives the run. The executable also asks for file details through POSIX stat , which reports an error through errno instead of its result. The runtime answers from the same lookup, and keeps a separate errno for each of the game's threads, as the C library expects ( #376 ). Files: PRs and what stops by name PRs #170 and #376 (POSIX stat and errno ; the executable's one stat call is at 0x00465431 ). Stops by name: any folder other than /app0 , a .. in a path, and host errors other than a missing file or folder.
docs.title: Reading the game's files

docs.text: Call Status What the runtime does sceVideoOutOpen , sceVideoOutClose implemented Opens the game's video output. sceVideoOutSetFlipRate , sceVideoOutAddFlipEvent implemented Records the rate, and which event queue hears about each flip. sceVideoOutSetBufferAttribute , sceVideoOutRegisterBuffers implemented Describes and keeps the game's frame buffers (1920 × 1080). The attribute keeps all six values the game gives, uninterpreted, and clears its reserved bytes ( #229 , by @evill33t ). sceVideoOutSubmitFlip , sceVideoOutGetFlipStatus implemented Flips to the next buffer (an hsync flip at once, a vsync flip at the next 60 Hz tick) and tells the waiting game it is done; before the first flip the status is all zero. Each frame the game asks video out to show one of its frame buffers, then waits on an event queue until the console reports that the flip happened, or reads the flip status until it catches up. The runtime keeps the buffers and answers every flip straight away, so the game's frame loop can run. Each buffer also has a frame on your side, which the flip shows: in a window with --display window (SDL3 and Vulkan), or written to image files with --display-capture DIR ( #313 ). Since #369 the runtime 's own renderer draws into those frames when the game submits its GPU work, and since 6 November 2026 the maintainer's local runs show the studio logos and the title screen there ( #441 , #442 ). With the display off they are not drawn. Video out: PRs and call sites PR #180 , built on the event queues of #179 ; claimed on #38 . The two setups are at 0x015e488e and 0x02ad61d4 ; the flip loops at 0x015e419a and 0x02ad6ee9 . The game's frame loop flips with vsync (mode 1) through sceGnmSubmitAndFlipCommandBuffers ( #310 ); the other flips use mode 2 (hsync).
docs.title: Showing frames: video out

docs.text: Call Status What the runtime does sceGnmGetTheTessellationFactorRingBufferBaseAddress implemented Answers an address the runtime reserves; the game maps its tessellation memory there. sceGnmValidateCommandBuffers implemented Answers "validation is not available" ( #297 ): Paleblood has no GPU validation layer, and that is the one answer the game's start-up probe checks for. sceGnmDispatchInitDefaultHardwareState , sceGnmDrawInitDefaultHardwareState200 implemented Write nothing and answer 0 words ( #299 ): there is no GPU state to set up. sceGnmSetCsShader implemented Fills the space the game reserved with a single no-op packet and reports success ( #299 ). sceGnmIsUserPaEnabled implemented Answers "off" ( #299 ): Paleblood has no GPU performance-analysis mode. sceGnmSet{Es,Gs,Hs,Ls,Ps,Vs}Shader , sceGnmUpdate{Gs,Hs,Ps,Vs}Shader , the marker calls, sceGnmInsertWaitFlipDone implemented Fill the space the game reserved with one no-op packet ( #310 ). The vertex, pixel and compute shader calls also hand the shader to the renderer ( #412 , #418 ). sceGnmSubmitCommandBuffers , sceGnmSubmitAndFlipCommandBuffers , sceGnmSubmitDone implemented (temporary stand-in) Complete a frame's GPU work: "work done" values are written, waits are checked, the other packets are skipped; then the frame is flipped ( #310 ). With the display on, the renderer also runs the drawing calls recorded for each submitted buffer ( #369 ); since #488 the call returns at once and the renderer's own thread runs the work in submission order, with each "work done" value, wait and flip placed after the work before it. Any number of buffers per call ( #504 : character creation submits 70). sceGnmMapComputeQueue implemented Records a GPU compute queue and gives it an ID; the GPU itself is not run. sceGnmDingDong implemented (temporary stand-in) Completes submitted compute work at once ( #302 ): no shaders run, but each job's "work done" value is written and the queue is freed. Since #470 the renderer takes each buffer's recorded calls and drops them, so their shader bindings cannot leak into a later graphics buffer in the same memory. Paleblood does not emulate the PS4 's graphics chip. It will rebuild the graphics at the level of the game engine's own drawing interface, so the graphics-driver calls only need to answer what the engine expects back. The first one asks where the GPU keeps its tessellation factors (the data it uses to split surfaces into finer triangles); the engine then maps memory at that address. The PS4 answers a fixed address of its own; the runtime answers one it reserves, because nothing but the engine's own graphics code ever uses it. The next call validates a command buffer, and the engine treats one particular error code as "this console cannot validate". Paleblood has no validation layer, so it gives that answer ( #297 ). The temporary GPU stand-in. The game hands work to the GPU through compute queues: it writes a pointer to each finished command buffer into a ring, then rings a "doorbell" ( sceGnmDingDong ). Each command buffer the game sent during start-up holds the same few steps: set shader registers, run a compute shader, then write a "work done" value to memory, which the CPU waits for. Until the engine's own renderer replaces this layer, the doorbell completes the work at once ( #302 ): it follows each buffer, skips the shader steps (nothing is drawn or computed), writes the "work done" value and moves the queue's read position on. Any other kind of step stops by name. This keeps start-up moving; it does not make anything appear on screen. What the stand-in skips safely. As the boot went further, the frame's command buffers held more kinds of packets. The stand-in skips only those that change nothing it would have to model: an empty constant-buffer entry ( #375 ), a memory read that only warms the GPU's cache and the size of an index ( #377 ), and an indexed draw's packets ( #395 ). Any other form still stops by name. The renderer alongside it. The drawing itself does not happen here. When the game binds a shader through sceGnmSetVsShader , sceGnmSetPsShader or sceGnmSetCsShader , the runtime also hands the shader's registers to Paleblood's renderer ( #412 , #418 ), and the game's own GPU library functions report its draws (see The renderer ). At each submit the renderer runs what was recorded for that buffer on your GPU, and the stand-in still writes the "work done" values the game waits for. Where the engine meets the GPU. Every one of the game's 50 graphics-driver imports is reached through one thin engine wrapper, with one or two callers each, and none of them draws anything. Bloodborne builds its GPU command buffers itself, with the graphics library compiled into the game, and only hands finished buffers to the system to run and to put on screen. So the runtime cannot take over drawing at the system-call boundary: the graphics have to be rebuilt above it, in the engine's own renderer (its GX graphics framework). The full map is on issue #39 . Graphics: PRs and call sites PRs #176 and #178 (compute queues); claimed on #39 . The tessellation ring is mapped at 0x02ad3fda with protection 0x33 (CPU and GPU read and write). The runtime 's address is 0xfe00000000 . The validation check is at 0x02abb950 : the engine compares the result with 0x80d13fff . The compute submit is at 0x0148c830 and its ring-packet writer at 0x0148b330 ; the stand-in handles the packet kinds a boot found there: NOP, SET_SH_REG, DISPATCH_DIRECT and RELEASE_MEM (AMD's public PM4 format). Since then: #375 (empty constant entries, from the second submit caller at 0x0149bf3a ), #377 ( DMA_DATA into CP_DMA_READ_TAGS , INDEX_TYPE ), #395 ( INDEX_BASE , INDEX_BUFFER_SIZE , DRAW_INDEX_2 , DRAW_INDEX_OFFSET_2 ), #412 (vertex and pixel shaders handed to the renderer; a vertex shader's modifier is applied to its register block) and #418 (compute shaders).
docs.title: Graphics: the first calls

docs.text: On 10 November the runtime answered every system import the boot can reach. Each call follows the executable's own call sites; where the PS4 's answer is not public, the maintainer ruled on it, using what other PS4 runtimes and ports agree on as facts (never their code). The generated list below and the runtime call reference have every call. Group What the runtime does Pull request Directories and flushing Opens a directory, lists it as FreeBSD 9 records the engine's directory walker reads, and flushes files. #498 Message, save data, profile and commerce dialogs Each opens and finishes at once, as a dialog the user closed; the game never reads a choice from them. Nothing is shown. #500 On-screen keyboard, web browser The keyboard opens and is found cancelled at the first status query; the browser is not opened. #502 Microphone and voice chat A console with no microphone or headset: the record port opens and gives silence, voice chat answers success with no audio. #506 GNM queries and debug calls The answers of a retail console with no capture tool attached. #506 PSN matchmaking, web API, leaderboards, signaling, lookup Signed out: every service is gated on the user's online id, which a signed-out console has not got. #507 Sockets, resolver, HTTP requests A console with no connection: sockets can be created and bound as with only loopback, anything that would leave the machine fails at once. Nothing is ever sent. #509 What the game's C library imports The calls and data the bundled C library and file library take from the kernel (C++ exception support, standard output, the heap, local time). #513 , #521 The maintainer's kernel and file rulings Page size, process id, the stack canary, standard input at end of file, the process-map query, resuming at an exception landing pad, module information, reserving address space and batches of maps. #528 The last graphics calls Graphics events raised when the GPU's completion step performs a write that asks for one; flip requests; the remaining queries. #532 Sound ports A movie's sound port closes when the movie ends, and its handle is used again. #490 File paths Kept off the game's small thread stacks; one boot in five overflowed the save thread's stack while creating the save. #512 The last three of the executable's imports, sceKernelMkdir , sceKernelRmdir and sceKernelUnlink , were implemented by @EzequielRindello in #455 , merged on 11 November as #555 . The bundled C library's scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (below) is claimed by @evill33t in #239 .
docs.title: 10 November: the rest of the checklist

docs.text: Call Status What the runtime does scePthreadAttrGetaffinity observed Left unbound; since #207 the C library no longer calls it. The boot of 19 October stopped here; the boot of 4 November passes it. A thread's CPU affinity mask says which CPU cores it may run on, one bit per core. The boot of 19 October stopped when the bundled libc.elf asked for the main thread's mask. What the caller does. It is understood from the hash-pinned module: Copy the attributes. It copies the current thread's attributes. Ask for the mask. It passes the attribute variable and an eight-byte zeroed slot: two pointers, not FreeBSD's three-argument form with a size. Count the cores. It ignores the result, counts the set bits in the slot, and stores that count. Synthetic runs of that original caller with scripted imports confirm this. They are not observations of PS4 affinity. Why the runtime does not answer yet. Returning success with a guessed mask would change the CPU count the C library stores without implementing the query. So the import stays unbound until the main thread's real mask, the exact output width and the error contract are established. Issue #34 tracks it. BluePinetree has claimed the work: a way for the runtime to replace a function inside a bundled module such as libc.elf , so this probe can be answered there. How it was answered ( #207 , by BluePinetree, merged 3 November 2026). The runtime can now replace a function inside a bundled module before any of its code runs: it writes a jump at the function's start to a small stub just past the module's image. Two replacements are listed in game/module_hooks.csv for the pinned libc.elf : the thread-count probe described above returns at once, so scePthreadAttrGetaffinity is never called and the stored core count stays as it was (no mask is invented); std::thread::hardware_concurrency , which would read that count, stops the run by name if the game ever calls it, the same way an unimplemented import stops it. Since #456 (also by BluePinetree) each entry also lists the function's first bytes, and pbboot compares them with the loaded module before patching: a different libc.elf build is refused by name before any game code runs, instead of patching the middle of another function. The boot recorded on 4 November 2026 ( #295 ) confirms it: merged main now passes this point; later the same day ( #300 ) it reaches the video out milestone. The hooks only cover these two functions, and their offsets fit only the pinned libc.elf . scePthreadAttrGetaffinity: declaration source OpenOrbis libkernel.h has the affinity declaration. It is corroboration, not a measured PS4 contract.

docs.text: Implement only behavior supported by public documentation, independent reverse engineering, or observed behavior. Keep unresolved target behavior visible; do not fabricate a return value to make tools/boot.py advance. Add cases for each established behavior and error path in a test file of the group's own, test/syslib/<group>.c , as SYSLIB_TEST(name) { ... } blocks ( #407 ; test/syslib/np_trophy.c is an example), so parallel pull requests do not edit the same lines. Cases already in test/test_syslib.c may be updated there. Runtime-only contributions do not need a game dump, captures , or function-level verify.py results; CI builds and runs the runtime and syslib tests.

docs.text: Runtime Paleblood is building a runtime of its own. A runtime is the software that loads a program and provides the system services it expects. At a glance Works An ELF loader and boot harness load the executable and bundled modules, bind imports and run the entry point. Since 6 November 2026 Paleblood's own renderer draws the studio logos and the title screen ("Play Online / Play Offline") natively ( #441 , #442 ). With scripted input ( #447 ) the maintainer's local runs go on past the title: save data is created, the main menu appears, and New Game reaches the first-run Brightness and Controls screens, the opening cinematic in 3D and, on 10 November, character creation, with pull requests still in review applied ( Milestones ). The logos and title run at the game's own 30 frames a second ( #472 ). The runtime checklist is done: every system import the boot reaches is answered, all but three of the executable's are bound in the record of 10 November, and those three, by contributor @EzequielRindello , merged the next day ( #555 ). Stops at Nowhere, since 6 November 2026 ( #408 ): no system call stops the boot, and the game keeps running until the harness 's time limit. Without input it waits at the title screen. In local runs with input, the next stops are in the renderer: each new scene needs drawing features the renderer stops on by name until they are added ( #457 , #471 , and the 3D work of 10 November below). Full game Still runs on a third-party host scaffold; the project-owned runtime has not replaced it. Evidence The boot result below is a saved run, not a live measurement: the latest, #536 on 10 November, runs with the display off and no input. The logos, the title screen and everything after it are the maintainer's local runs with the display on. The project has an ELF loader and boot harness that can load the game's executable and bundled system modules, bind imports, and run the entry point until it reaches a call the current runtime does not implement. That is different from running the full game. Full native game runs still use a third-party host scaffold for the broader execution environment, system-library coverage, and Vulkan rendering. Since 4 November 2026 Paleblood targets macOS as well as Linux ( #292 ): graphics are rebuilt on Vulkan on Linux and on Metal on macOS. Linux stays the primary platform and the one CI tests; macOS support is in progress. On 10 November two pieces of the runtime that only compiled on Linux became portable, by @evill33t : sound and video pacing now wait on the monotonic clock with plain POSIX nanosleep , rechecking the deadline after every wake ( #538 ), and file details read macOS's own timestamp fields while keeping the guest's layout ( #541 ). Both have their own tests and native macOS CI on ARM64 and Intel; the game's behaviour does not change. Paleblood supplies a project-owned hook plug-in and host interface, but the project-owned runtime has not replaced that host or passed equivalent full-run checks. What works in Paleblood's runtime ELF loading and boot diagnostics. runtime/loader.c maps the executable and bundled modules, applies relocations, and binds known imports. runtime/boot.c and tools/boot.py run the entry point and record how far it gets. System calls. In the boot recorded on 10 November ( #536 ) the runtime itself implements 464 of the 686 system imports and the bundled modules supply 219 more; three were unbound: sceKernelMkdir , sceKernelRmdir and sceKernelUnlink . Contributor @EzequielRindello implemented them in #455 , merged on 11 November as #555 ; they count at the next recorded boot. The bundled C library's one remaining import, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , is claimed by @evill33t in #239 . That closes the runtime checklist: the issues for files, input and users, audio, video out, GNM , system services and the network ( #35 to #41 ) are closed, and the kernel issue ( #34 ) lists only the claimed calls. The calls cover threads, locks and semaphores, memory, clocks, the console's start-up services, the controller, save data and trophies, the network, HTTP and PSN libraries offline, sound and movies, and reading the game's own files. On 10 November a batch added file renames, truncation and folders ( #449 , #458 ), deleting a save ( #459 ), thread join, detach and once ( #460 ), timed locks ( #464 ), unmapping and protecting memory ( #467 ), signal masks and thread names ( #469 ), time zones and RFC 2822 dates ( #466 ), the formatted output the file library uses ( #468 ), the pad's motion settings and an unplugged mouse ( #462 ), and more offline PSN and network answers ( #450 , #451 , #461 , #465 ). Later that day a second batch answered what was left: listing directories and flushing files ( #498 ), the message, save data, profile and commerce dialogs, which the game opens and the runtime closes at once ( #500 ), the on-screen keyboard, cancelled, and the web browser, not opened ( #502 ), no microphone and no voice chat ( #506 ), the remaining PSN services and the sockets, resolver and HTTP requests of a console with no connection ( #507 , #509 ), what the game's own C library imports ( #513 , #521 ), the maintainer's rulings for the last kernel and file calls (page size, process id, the stack canary and others, #528 ), the last graphics calls, with graphics events raised when the GPU finishes work ( #532 ), closing a sound port when a movie ends ( #490 ), and file paths kept off the game's small thread stacks, which crashed one boot in five while creating the save ( #512 ). The runtime system-call notes explain each group, and end with a list of every call the runtime answers, generated from the code on every sync. Where the PS4 's behaviour is not established, the runtime does not guess: it stops and names the call. It never contacts a network. It decodes the game's sound and can play it ( #398 , #406 ), plays the game's movies ( #419 , #420 ), reads a real controller and keyboard ( #431 ), and draws the game's logos, title screen, menus and 3D scenes with its own renderer (see The renderer ). Three kernel details followed on 6 November, each found by a boot that stopped there: a semaphore created for priority order now wakes its most urgent waiter first instead of stopping when a second thread waits ( #426 ; before, some boots stopped there and others did not, depending on thread timing); a memory-protection query also answers the mapping's start and end ( #422 ); and a second map of the same memory with the "no-overwrite" flag is accepted ( #423 ). The movie code needs the last two. Movies. The game plays its movies through the console's movie player library. The runtime answers all 16 of its calls ( #419 ) and decodes the movies with FFmpeg on your computer, on a thread of its own a few frames ahead; the game receives finished pictures and sound on the movie's clock. The movie's sound port (1024 samples, 16-bit, up to 8 channels) followed in #420 . FFmpeg is optional when building: without it, opening a movie stops by name. Controller input. With --input host (and a window, --display window ) the runtime reads your first gamepad and the keyboard through SDL3 and fills in the game's controller state: buttons, sticks, triggers, touch pad and vibration ( #431 ). The default is --input none : one controller at rest, so recorded boots and CI see the same state every time. For unattended runs, --input-script plays timed button presses ( #447 ). In the maintainer's local runs it selects "Play Offline" on the title screen and the game creates its save data. That needs sceKernelWrite , which contributor @EzequielRindello is implementing in #444 (merged on 10 November; the earlier local runs applied it from review), then sceKernelFtruncate and sceKernelRename ( #449 ). Function replacements and hooks . The project's plug-in receives the guest image and a hook -install callback, then registers its function replacements. Paleblood now also provides a small implementation of the version-1 hook callback: it checks the requested function range; it writes a jump to the replacement. A synthetic executable-memory test confirms the patched entry reaches the replacement. The callback is not connected to the full game-run scaffold, and the test does not run the game. Recent loader work (by evill33t, 3–4 November 2026): the loader also accepts the separate read-only-after-relocation segments some system modules carry ( PT_SCE_RELRO , #217 ; none of the game's own files has one), and guest memory is reserved at its address without replacing anything already mapped there ( #220 ). For macOS, the runtime 's table of system calls can now also be built in the Mach-O format macOS uses ( #216 ), and the loader can rewrite thread-pointer loads to a non-zero offset ( #218 ), which the macOS thread-data work needs. That thread-data library now builds in the normal macOS configuration ( #214 ), and a standalone Metal unit that draws offscreen is the start of the Mac display ( #318 , from #213). Both are by @evill33t and are compile-tested on macOS in CI. The runtime 's own boot harness can now load the decompilation's replacements too ( #225 , by @evill33t ): pbboot takes --game-lib with the compiled game library and runs its set-up before the game's first code, so finished replacements run in place of the originals during a boot. Without the option the boot runs the original code only, as before. Runtime System imports provided 683 of 686 (99.56%): 219 by the game's own modules, 464 by the runtime ; 3 remaining Furthest boot milestone first flip (8 of 8) Boot stops at the run's time limit, still running (no call stopped it) Last recorded run: 2026-11-10. This is saved evidence, not a live measurement. Generated by tools/sync_progress.py from the code repo. Do not edit. The table above is generated from the saved Paleblood boot record. Its date identifies the last recorded run; changing runtime code does not refresh the result by itself. How far a boot gets 10 November 2026: the cinematic and character creation (local runs). With the renderer's 3D work below, the opening cinematic plays on in the maintainer's local runs, lit and with its subtitles, its movie's sound ending and its port closing ( #490 ), and the game reaches character creation: the contract screen with name, gender, age, origin, appearance and starting attributes. That screen hands the GPU 70 command buffers in one call, which the stand-in had capped at 64 ( #504 ). These are local observations with renderer work then still in review applied, not saved records. The boot recorded on merged main the same evening ( #536 , display off, no input, 30 seconds) still reports the first flip, 243 imports called and nothing stopping it, because without input the game waits at its title. 6 to 10 November 2026: past the title (local runs). With scripted input ( #447 ) and the display on, the maintainer's local runs select "Play Offline". The game creates its save data (with #444 , then in review and since merged, applied for sceKernelWrite , and #449 ), and after the renderer learned 8- and 16-bit buffer formats ( #457 ) it shows its main menu (New Game, System, Log In) for over a thousand frames. Choosing New Game needed depth and stencil tests that read the buffer ( #471 ); with it, and with #470 (compute queues' buffers, in review) also applied, the boot reaches the first-run Brightness screen and then Controls, and runs on waiting for input. Scripted on past Controls, the next scene's draws needed image descriptors loaded behind a branch ( #474 ), two-channel 8-bit images ( #476 ) and samplers with anisotropy fields but plain filters ( #477 ); with them the game's opening cinematic, its first 3D scene, draws. These are local observations, not saved records; the frames are on the Milestones page. 6 November 2026: the logos and the title screen. Later the same day, Paleblood's own renderer began drawing what the game asks for (see The renderer ). In the maintainer's local runs (display on, with the game library from the decompilation), the boot shows the three studio logos, "Sony Computer Entertainment presents", "JAPAN Studio" and "FROM SOFTWARE", and reaches the title screen with its "Play Online / Play Offline" menu at about frame 480, with no stop within 90 seconds ( #441 , #442 ). Compared with reference frames captured locally from another PS4 runtime , the JAPAN Studio and FROM SOFTWARE frames are pixel-identical, and the title frame differs in 0.7% of its pixels, by at most 13 levels, where the menu's highlight is animated. These are local observations, not a saved record; the frames are on the Milestones page. The boot recorded on merged main afterwards ( #443 ) runs with the display off: first flip, 243 imports called, 234 of them answered by the runtime , and nothing stops it. Earlier on 6 November: no call stops the boot ( #408 ). The boot recorded on merged main calls 243 imports, 218 of them answered by the runtime , and keeps running until the harness 's 30-second limit. The round of runtime work merged on 5 and 6 November answered every call between the first flip and the game's main loop: the install service (PlayGo, #370 ): every part of the game is installed; the user's name and events ( #372 ), and one controller at rest ( #373 ); the clock and calendar ( #378 , #379 ); the offline PSN calls: the title id, sign-in state, matchmaking start-up, NAT and HTTPS options, network waits ( #380 , #381 , #382 , #385 , #386 ); file details and the error variable ( #376 ), thread exit ( #389 , #399 ), add-on content ( #392 ), the boot splash and system status ( #396 ); save data in a folder you choose ( #402 ), and trophies, kept offline with your save data ( #405 ); the graphics packets the stand-in skips safely ( #375 , #377 , #395 ); sound ( #398 , #406 ). The game's audio is ATRAC9, decoded with LibAtrac9 (MIT, by Alex Barney, included unmodified in Paleblood), and with --audio host it plays through your computer's sound output. In the maintainer's local runs with the display on, the game's main loop then runs at its own 30 frames a second, and its music and sounds start after about 17 seconds. These are observed local runs; the saved boot record shows only that nothing stops the run. At that point the frames were still black; the renderer work merged later that day draws them. Earlier, 4 November. The boot recorded on 4 November 2026 ( #304 ) reached the video out milestone, 6 of 8: the game's threads, its files, input and its sound system start, and it opens its display. Its first GPU work now goes through a temporary stand-in ( #302 ), its network worker polls offline ( #303 ), and it calls 135 imports. Its scratch files go to a writable /data folder ( #308 ). Since #310 it gets through all eight milestones : it hands its first frame's work to the GPU and flips it to the display, then carries on to the PS4 's install service (PlayGo), calling 170 imports. Nothing is drawn: the GPU work goes through the temporary stand-in described below. The boot before it (19 October) stopped much earlier, at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity inside the game's bundled C library. #207 replaced the C library's probe that made that call, so the call is no longer made ( Runtime syscalls ), and the runtime work merged since covers everything up to the graphics. Before this, the maintainer used local discovery boots that stood in for the missing pieces (the affinity query and the reader-writer locks) without committing them, to see which call comes next. On 30 October 2026 a local discovery boot: started the game's threads, its HTTP client (offline) and its sound system; found and read its first data file, sprj_mixer.fev , from the person's own copy; stopped at the first graphics-driver call whose answer is not established ( sceGnmValidateCommandBuffers ). Each call it passed through was then implemented and merged with its own evidence (the runtime system-call notes list them), and the genuine boot of 4 November now reaches the same point on merged main alone. Capture and replay Paleblood has a local capture writer and replay verifier. Saved cases carry function and run identifiers and use stable buffer ordering. Replay checks reject a case for a different function or address. The version-1 production hook interface does not observe function returns or describe pointer buffers, and current replacements do not call the recorder. A separate test adapter proves that explicitly described synthetic inputs can be serialized and replayed. This checks the case format and verifier path only. It does not capture real game calls, prove a replacement against a real recording, or supply production run inputs. tools/promote.py consumes existing recorded cases and generated edge cases ; it does not create captures . The merged differential tools can now replay fixtures, observe supported guest instruction memory accesses, collect bounded control-flow coverage, minimize mismatches, and coordinate an opt-in candidate workflow. Unsupported instructions and skipped host-call bodies reject the trace; synthetic automation tests establish tool behavior only. The Architecture verification guide explains what is observed and which stages still require original-game evidence and human review. Boot history and the current blocker The latest genuine boot trace was recorded with merged Paleblood main in #536 (10 November 2026, after the runtime checklist and the renderer's 3D work). Latest trace (10 November, #536) 6 November (#443) Earlier on 6 November (#408) 4 November (#310) Earlier on 4 November (#300) 19 October (#92) Imports resolved 683/686: 219 bundled, 464 implemented by the runtime , 3 unbound 453/686: 219 bundled, 234 implemented by the runtime 437/686 (218 runtime ) 368/686 (149 runtime ) 344/686 (125 runtime ) 252/686 (33 runtime ) Import calls reached 243 243 243 170 133 seven Stopped at nothing: still running at the 30-second limit nothing: still running at the 30-second limit nothing: still running at the 30-second limit scePlayGoInitialize (install service) sceGnmDingDong (compute-queue doorbell) scePthreadAttrGetaffinity in libc.elf Milestone first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) video out (6/8) loaded (0/8) Between 11 and 19 October (PR #63 to #92) only the supplied-import count rose; startup did not advance. Between 19 October and 4 November it advanced six milestones. The generated status above is synchronized from the latest run. The GPU, for now. The first graphics calls are answered honestly for a runtime with no GPU ( #297 , #299 ): there is no debug-validation layer, no hardware state to set up, and the reserved command space is filled with no-op packets. When the game first hands work to the GPU ( sceGnmDingDong ), a temporary stand-in ( #302 ) completes it at once. It runs no shaders and draws nothing: it only writes each job's "work done" value, which is what the CPU waits for, and frees the queue. This was a maintainer decision of 4 November 2026, so that start-up can continue while the engine's own renderer (its GX framework) is rebuilt to replace it (issue #39). See Runtime syscalls . Scratch files. The engine maps its temp: and title: drives to /data and creates a fresh cache file there at start-up. The runtime now serves /data as a writable folder of its own choosing ( #308 ): each boot gets a new, empty one, so runs start alike. Memory the GPU can reach. The game stores GPU buffer addresses in a shortened form that only holds addresses below a fixed limit (the GPU's 40-bit address space). Memory the runtime placed higher lost its top bits there and crashed the game, so the runtime now places the memory it chooses an address for below that limit ( #310 ). The first frame. The game's first frame hands the GPU shader settings, draws, cache steps, waits and "work done" markers. The temporary stand-in performs the "work done" writes, checks the waits already hold, and skips the rest, then flips at the next 60 Hz tick ( #310 ). At the time nothing was drawn; the renderer now runs the drawing work alongside it (see below). What blocks it now. No system call does: since #408 the boot runs until its time limit, and since #442 the maintainer's local runs draw the title screen. With scripted input ( #447 ) those runs now get past it, through the menus, the settings screens and the opening cinematic to character creation (see above). What stops them next is the renderer: each new scene uses drawing features it does not have yet, and it stops by name on them. The saved boot record runs without input, so it waits at the title and does not show any of this. The temporary stand-in described above still answers the GPU's "work done" values; with the display on, the renderer also runs the drawing work. The renderer Bloodborne draws through its own engine renderer (the GX framework) and Sony's GPU helper library compiled into the game. Its shaders ship as compiled AMD GPU code. On 4 November 2026 the maintainer chose how Paleblood draws them: - Draws: the game's own drawing functions are hooked like the rest of the decompilation, and send their work to Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. - Shaders: each one is translated from AMD's code to Vulkan's or Metal's shader language when it loads, on your machine. The translator is written from AMD's public instruction-set manuals, not from any emulator. Nothing translated is published. - Ruled out: replaying the finished GPU commands, which would be GPU emulation. Where it stands (6 November 2026). The renderer now draws the game's logos and its title screen. When the game's GPU library sets up a draw, the call is reported to Paleblood's renderer, which translates the shaders involved and draws on a PC GPU with Vulkan. In the maintainer's local runs this produces the three studio logos and the title screen, and the title frame matches a reference capture to within 0.7% of pixels ( #442 ). It needs the display on ( --display headless or window ) and the game library built from the decompilation ( --game-lib ), because the reports come from its replacements. Since then the menus after the title draw too in local runs with scripted input: the main menu after #457 (8- and 16-bit buffer formats) and the Brightness and Controls screens after #471 (depth and stencil tests that read the buffer, stencil steps, a depth target larger than the colour target). Past them, the opening cinematic's first 3D frames draw too ( #474 , #476 , #477 ), and with the 3D work of 10 November (below) the cinematic plays on to character creation. The playable game has not run yet. The work comes in four phases (Paleblood's docs/RENDERER.md ): Display (done, #313 ): every frame buffer the game registers gets a frame of its own, and each flip shows it, in a window (SDL3 and Vulkan) or captured to image files for tests. Since 6 November the renderer draws into them. Shader translator (begun, #316 ): a decoder for GFX7, the PS4 GPU's instruction set, names every instruction. Its opcode table is generated from AMD's manual and LLVM's AMDGPU assembler, which must agree. A census of your own copy's shaders shows the game uses only 175 distinct instructions, and the decoder knows all of them. The first translation to Vulkan shaders works ( #319 ): simple compute shaders (arithmetic, compares, conversions, buffer and constant reads and writes) run on a real GPU and give exactly the results AMD's manual defines. Since #330 it also handles branches, loops and GCN 's active-lane mask: only the lanes that are switched on write results or touch memory, as on the console. Since #332 it also reads and writes typed buffers, which nearly half of the game's shaders use. Every typed access in the game uses plain 32-bit floats, so those translate exactly; any other format is refused rather than guessed. Since #333 it translates vertex and pixel shaders too: their outputs (positions, values passed down to pixels, colours) and the pixel shader's blended inputs. A translated pair already draws a test triangle on the GPU with every pixel checked, and most of the game's vertex shaders now translate completely. A batch of arithmetic instructions followed in #334 (24-bit multiplies, bit fields, carries, sine and cosine, exponent and logarithm), each checked on the GPU. Since #343 a vertex shader's extra position outputs work too: in this game they always carry two clip distances, which the GPU uses to cut triangles off at a plane. With them, most of the game's vertex shaders translate completely. Texture sampling followed on 6 November ( #433 ), with the rest of what the title screen needs (see below). On macOS the same translated shaders become Metal shaders through SPIRV-Cross; since #331 macOS CI converts every test shader and compiles it with Apple's Metal compiler. evill33t's Metal unit ( #318 , from #213) is the start of the Mac display, and since 11 November an offscreen Metal draw executor, also by @evill33t , plays recorded draws through the same translated shaders behind the renderer's common interface ( #518 ): render targets, viewports, shaders, user data and triangle-list draws, checked by its own macOS CI. Engine draw hooks (working for the logos and title screen; begun in #335 ): route the game's render targets, clears, shader binding, textures and draws to the renderer, starting with the title screen's 2D passes. A first map found Sony's GPU helper library, compiled into the game, in one block of about 230 small functions: everything the game asks of the GPU passes through it, and the engine writes no GPU commands of its own. The library's draw functions and about 60 of its state setters are identified, along with the engine code that calls the draws. The game keeps its GPU state only in the commands those setters write, so the hooks will sit on the setters and draws themselves: each setter hands its value to the renderer, and each draw becomes a Vulkan or Metal draw. The library's key functions are identified ( #341 ): its draw call, setRenderTarget , setViewport , the depth target and the user-data writers. Several are already decompiled in @evill33t 's pull requests, as replacements verified to write exactly the original commands. The renderer will observe those replacements rather than change them. The shader files in the game's archive turned out to carry each shader's GPU register settings, and those settings were checked against the shaders' own code. They say where a shader's code lives, which inputs it gets, and what its extra outputs carry. On the runtime side, the renderer now keeps its own record of these calls for each command buffer ( #342 , #344 , #345 ): render targets, viewports, shaders, their data and draws, ready to play back when the game submits the buffer. The next piece is the draw executor, which plays those calls back on a PC GPU. Its first step is done ( #346 , #348 ). Game shaders find memory by the PS4 's addresses, so the runtime now keeps the game's GPU-visible memory at fixed places, and the translator adds one fixed offset to every address a shader forms. That lets the whole memory pool be handed to the GPU as a single buffer. A test on an RTX 3070 shows this works, at the cost of holding the 5 GiB pool in RAM while graphics run. Its second step works too ( #368 ): given a written-down list of drawing calls, the executor runs them on a Vulkan GPU. It translates the shaders the calls name, finds or makes the picture they draw into, and draws. In a test with real PS4 -style shaders, every pixel comes out right. Since #369 it is wired into the running game: with the display on, the calls run when the game submits its drawing work, and a flip shows what was drawn instead of a black frame. Until the game's drawing functions report their calls, nothing visible changes. Since #401 the record also keeps the GPU register values the game sets (blending, depth, primitive type, colour masks and the like), and the executor checks them before it draws: anything it cannot draw faithfully yet stops by name rather than drawing something wrong. Since 6 November the GPU library's decompiled replacements, by @evill33t ( #411 , from #233), report their calls to the renderer ( #414 ), and a few library functions without replacements are observed where they are called ( #416 ). Textures and 3D (under way): the texture formats and tiled layouts the title screen uses work ( #427 , #428 , #441 , #442 ), and since 10 November so do the opening cinematic's 3D scenes and character creation in local runs (see the last step below). The playable game's areas, with their meshes, materials and post-processing, are still to come. From black frames to the title screen All of this was merged on 6 November 2026. Each step removed the next thing the boot stopped at by name; the renderer never draws something it cannot draw faithfully, it stops and says what is missing. Draw reports and hooks ( #411 , #412 , #414 , #415 , #416 ): the GPU library's replacements tell the renderer which shaders are bound, the render targets, the shaders' data and each draw. setRenderTarget and the user-data writers are observed where they are called. Rectangle-list draws, which the game uses for full-screen passes, work. Compute ( #418 , #421 , #424 ): the game's compute passes run on the GPU, including the ones that clear the screen and build its colour lookup tables. They read and write buffers in the formats their descriptors name, and images. A shader that needs something not translated yet stops the run by name while it runs. Pixel shaders ( #425 ): a pixel's own screen position as an input, and the GPU's whole-quad mode. Textures and tiling ( #427 , #428 , #432 ): the PS4 stores most images tiled, not row by row. The renderer knows the tiled layouts the game uses (linear, 1D and 2D thin), loads images from the game's memory in those layouts, and reads image descriptors the shaders load from memory. Sampling ( #433 ): shaders read textures through the game's samplers (filtering and clamping). This gave the first frame that was not black: a flat grey from the game's colour-correction pass. Blending, depth and vertex fetch ( #434 , #435 , #436 , #437 , #438 ): blending, depth and stencil targets, triangle strips, vertex shaders that call fetch shaders to read their vertices, and GPU state that carries over from one command buffer to the next. Indexed draws and the logos ( #439 , #440 , #441 ): indexed draws, render targets that keep the game's memory up to date so later passes can read them, vertex colours and block-compressed (BC) textures. This drew the first logo, "Sony Computer Entertainment presents". Speed ( #442 ): render targets are copied back to the game's memory only when something may read them, and unchanged images are not loaded again. In the maintainer's local runs a 90-second boot went from 66 frames to about 1,445, enough to reach the title screen at about frame 480. A shader reading data the game never set now stops by name. Draws still waited for the GPU one at a time. Since #463 (10 November) each submitted command buffer's draws and dispatches go to the GPU as one batch, and the CPU waits only where it reads what the batch produced; on the logos and title this alone changed nothing measurable: the limit there was the CPU's own tiling copies of the render targets. #472 moved those copies to a compute shader on the GPU, and in the maintainer's local runs the logos and title now run at the game's own 30 frames a second (about 14 before); the JAPAN Studio frame is still pixel-identical. Beside the game, and into 3D (10 November): submissions now return at once and the renderer runs them on a thread of its own in the order the game submitted them, as on the PS4 ; anything the game can observe (a "work done" value, a wait, a flip) happens only after the work before it has run ( #488 ). Compute queues' buffers are taken and dropped, so their shader bindings no longer leak into graphics buffers ( #470 ). For the cinematic and character creation the renderer learned depth-only passes ( #519 ), depth target slices ( #522 ), mip chains and mip-mapped images sampled at the level the derivatives pick or the shader gives ( #516 , #523 , #526 , #549 ), stencil replace with a fixed value ( #524 ), several render targets in one draw ( #533 ), the pixel shader's front-face input ( #537 ), anisotropic sampler filters ( #554 ), render targets cleared by a compute shader ( #539 ), more image formats ( #476 , #492 , #503 ) and float formats, stored and as render targets ( #525 , #530 , #534 : the character creation preview draws into float targets), more shader instructions, among them the cube-map ones, with cube images in pixel shaders ( #495 , #501 , #548 , #551 ), and buffer accesses checked against their descriptor's range, as the GPU does, with an invalid-format (unbound) buffer reading zeros and writing nothing ( #556 , #494 , #505 , #508 , #540 ), and descriptors that arrive as part of a wider load, as the character creation preview's pixel shader loads them ( #547 ), or that come from the user data even when the program writes those registers later, past a forward branch ( #553 ). Contributor @evill33t tightened the executor's checks: indexed-draw packets keep their raw fields and are validated before they draw ( #452 ), and a user-data range that wraps around is refused ( #493 ). Boot history fields (PR #51) PR #51 extended new symbols/boot_history.csv rows with the run outcome, execution phase, unresolved-import return site, and guest-fault location, signal, and address. A changed failure location is recorded even when import counts and the blocking symbol stay the same. Existing rows remain readable. After relevant changes merge, compare the history fields added by PR #51 against the saved failure location and trace. Decompilation progress The runtime is developed alongside the decompilation. The verified -function counts below come from Paleblood's function table; see the progress dashboard for the generated breakdown. With function families Functions (of target) Bytes (of target) Members of 19 function families 18,019 (11.42%) 62,426 (0.15%) Replaced, with family members 18,258 (11.57%) 163,393 (0.38%) Edge- verified , with family members 18,258 (11.57%) 163,393 (0.38%) Family members are tiny functions (one to a few bytes each) that share one replacement per family: they add far more to the function count than to the bytes. Do not edit. Roadmap Loader and boot harness : project-owned and independently tested. Kernel, threads, and memory: done for the boot: merged main boots through all eight milestones and keeps running, passing its GPU work through a temporary stand-in; no system call stops it ( #408 ), and since #528 only contributor-claimed calls are left in #34 . Files, audio, network start-up: the game reads its own files read-only and keeps save data and trophies in a folder you choose; its sound is decoded and can play on your computer; its HTTP client and PSN calls answer offline. GNM and shaders: the logos and title screen draw natively in the maintainer's local runs ( #441 , #442 ). The renderer hooks the game's own drawing layer and translates its shaders, rather than emulating the GPU (see The renderer ). In local runs with scripted input the menus, the opening cinematic and character creation draw as well ( #457 , #471 , #488 and the 3D work above). Next: the first playable area, with its meshes, materials and post-processing (the logos and title already reach the game's 30 fps cap in local runs, #472 ). Movies and input: the game's movies decode with FFmpeg ( #419 , #420 ); a real controller and keyboard work with --input host ( #431 ). Capture integration: add a return-aware, ABI-described observation boundary before connecting recordings to production hooks . Synthetic tests are not a substitute for real captures . System-library work is tracked separately from boot milestones, in one issue per group: kernel ( #34 ), files ( #35 ), input and users ( #36 ), audio ( #37 ), video out ( #38 ), GNM ( #39 ), system services ( #40 ) and network ( #41 ). All but the kernel issue are closed, and it lists only calls contributors have claimed. The network group covers the byte-order and IPv4 helpers (both directions since #465 ), offline network control, the offline start-up and teardown of the network, SSL and HTTP libraries ( #451 ), and the PSN identity, Plus and authorization checks of a signed-out console ( #450 , #461 ), the remaining PSN services ( #507 ) and sockets, resolvers and HTTP requests that find no connection ( #509 ). Nothing is ever sent. See Paleblood's runtime queue and runtime issues . Network-group pull requests Merged PR #60 makes the registry and coverage tools preserve that distinction: unresolved diagnostics are excluded from implemented counts while still producing useful failure messages when called. Merged PR #63 adds the documented IPv4 text conversion for Bloodborne's observed AF_INET calls. Full-run dependency and replacement path The current full-game path retains an external GPL-2.0-or-later scaffold and its required host, system-library, and graphics dependencies. Paleblood's new hook callback covers only one host responsibility; it is not yet integrated into the full game-run path. Paleblood's own pbboot harness builds and tests without that scaffold, but it does not yet provide equivalent full-game loading, services, rendering, or route checks. The scaffold and its required attribution stay in the code repository until a project-owned replacement passes the same native game-run checks.
docs.title: Runtime

docs.text: Paleblood is building a runtime of its own. A runtime is the software that loads a program and provides the system services it expects. At a glance Works An ELF loader and boot harness load the executable and bundled modules, bind imports and run the entry point. Since 6 November 2026 Paleblood's own renderer draws the studio logos and the title screen ("Play Online / Play Offline") natively ( #441 , #442 ). With scripted input ( #447 ) the maintainer's local runs go on past the title: save data is created, the main menu appears, and New Game reaches the first-run Brightness and Controls screens, the opening cinematic in 3D and, on 10 November, character creation, with pull requests still in review applied ( Milestones ). The logos and title run at the game's own 30 frames a second ( #472 ). The runtime checklist is done: every system import the boot reaches is answered, all but three of the executable's are bound in the record of 10 November, and those three, by contributor @EzequielRindello , merged the next day ( #555 ). Stops at Nowhere, since 6 November 2026 ( #408 ): no system call stops the boot, and the game keeps running until the harness 's time limit. Without input it waits at the title screen. In local runs with input, the next stops are in the renderer: each new scene needs drawing features the renderer stops on by name until they are added ( #457 , #471 , and the 3D work of 10 November below). Full game Still runs on a third-party host scaffold; the project-owned runtime has not replaced it. Evidence The boot result below is a saved run, not a live measurement: the latest, #536 on 10 November, runs with the display off and no input. The logos, the title screen and everything after it are the maintainer's local runs with the display on. The project has an ELF loader and boot harness that can load the game's executable and bundled system modules, bind imports, and run the entry point until it reaches a call the current runtime does not implement. That is different from running the full game. Full native game runs still use a third-party host scaffold for the broader execution environment, system-library coverage, and Vulkan rendering. Since 4 November 2026 Paleblood targets macOS as well as Linux ( #292 ): graphics are rebuilt on Vulkan on Linux and on Metal on macOS. Linux stays the primary platform and the one CI tests; macOS support is in progress. On 10 November two pieces of the runtime that only compiled on Linux became portable, by @evill33t : sound and video pacing now wait on the monotonic clock with plain POSIX nanosleep , rechecking the deadline after every wake ( #538 ), and file details read macOS's own timestamp fields while keeping the guest's layout ( #541 ). Both have their own tests and native macOS CI on ARM64 and Intel; the game's behaviour does not change. Paleblood supplies a project-owned hook plug-in and host interface, but the project-owned runtime has not replaced that host or passed equivalent full-run checks.

docs.text: ELF loading and boot diagnostics. runtime/loader.c maps the executable and bundled modules, applies relocations, and binds known imports. runtime/boot.c and tools/boot.py run the entry point and record how far it gets. System calls. In the boot recorded on 10 November ( #536 ) the runtime itself implements 464 of the 686 system imports and the bundled modules supply 219 more; three were unbound: sceKernelMkdir , sceKernelRmdir and sceKernelUnlink . Contributor @EzequielRindello implemented them in #455 , merged on 11 November as #555 ; they count at the next recorded boot. The bundled C library's one remaining import, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , is claimed by @evill33t in #239 . That closes the runtime checklist: the issues for files, input and users, audio, video out, GNM , system services and the network ( #35 to #41 ) are closed, and the kernel issue ( #34 ) lists only the claimed calls. The calls cover threads, locks and semaphores, memory, clocks, the console's start-up services, the controller, save data and trophies, the network, HTTP and PSN libraries offline, sound and movies, and reading the game's own files. On 10 November a batch added file renames, truncation and folders ( #449 , #458 ), deleting a save ( #459 ), thread join, detach and once ( #460 ), timed locks ( #464 ), unmapping and protecting memory ( #467 ), signal masks and thread names ( #469 ), time zones and RFC 2822 dates ( #466 ), the formatted output the file library uses ( #468 ), the pad's motion settings and an unplugged mouse ( #462 ), and more offline PSN and network answers ( #450 , #451 , #461 , #465 ). Later that day a second batch answered what was left: listing directories and flushing files ( #498 ), the message, save data, profile and commerce dialogs, which the game opens and the runtime closes at once ( #500 ), the on-screen keyboard, cancelled, and the web browser, not opened ( #502 ), no microphone and no voice chat ( #506 ), the remaining PSN services and the sockets, resolver and HTTP requests of a console with no connection ( #507 , #509 ), what the game's own C library imports ( #513 , #521 ), the maintainer's rulings for the last kernel and file calls (page size, process id, the stack canary and others, #528 ), the last graphics calls, with graphics events raised when the GPU finishes work ( #532 ), closing a sound port when a movie ends ( #490 ), and file paths kept off the game's small thread stacks, which crashed one boot in five while creating the save ( #512 ). The runtime system-call notes explain each group, and end with a list of every call the runtime answers, generated from the code on every sync. Where the PS4 's behaviour is not established, the runtime does not guess: it stops and names the call. It never contacts a network. It decodes the game's sound and can play it ( #398 , #406 ), plays the game's movies ( #419 , #420 ), reads a real controller and keyboard ( #431 ), and draws the game's logos, title screen, menus and 3D scenes with its own renderer (see The renderer ). Three kernel details followed on 6 November, each found by a boot that stopped there: a semaphore created for priority order now wakes its most urgent waiter first instead of stopping when a second thread waits ( #426 ; before, some boots stopped there and others did not, depending on thread timing); a memory-protection query also answers the mapping's start and end ( #422 ); and a second map of the same memory with the "no-overwrite" flag is accepted ( #423 ). The movie code needs the last two. Movies. The game plays its movies through the console's movie player library. The runtime answers all 16 of its calls ( #419 ) and decodes the movies with FFmpeg on your computer, on a thread of its own a few frames ahead; the game receives finished pictures and sound on the movie's clock. The movie's sound port (1024 samples, 16-bit, up to 8 channels) followed in #420 . FFmpeg is optional when building: without it, opening a movie stops by name. Controller input. With --input host (and a window, --display window ) the runtime reads your first gamepad and the keyboard through SDL3 and fills in the game's controller state: buttons, sticks, triggers, touch pad and vibration ( #431 ). The default is --input none : one controller at rest, so recorded boots and CI see the same state every time. For unattended runs, --input-script plays timed button presses ( #447 ). In the maintainer's local runs it selects "Play Offline" on the title screen and the game creates its save data. That needs sceKernelWrite , which contributor @EzequielRindello is implementing in #444 (merged on 10 November; the earlier local runs applied it from review), then sceKernelFtruncate and sceKernelRename ( #449 ). Function replacements and hooks . The project's plug-in receives the guest image and a hook -install callback, then registers its function replacements. Paleblood now also provides a small implementation of the version-1 hook callback: it checks the requested function range; it writes a jump to the replacement. A synthetic executable-memory test confirms the patched entry reaches the replacement. The callback is not connected to the full game-run scaffold, and the test does not run the game. Recent loader work (by evill33t, 3–4 November 2026): the loader also accepts the separate read-only-after-relocation segments some system modules carry ( PT_SCE_RELRO , #217 ; none of the game's own files has one), and guest memory is reserved at its address without replacing anything already mapped there ( #220 ). For macOS, the runtime 's table of system calls can now also be built in the Mach-O format macOS uses ( #216 ), and the loader can rewrite thread-pointer loads to a non-zero offset ( #218 ), which the macOS thread-data work needs. That thread-data library now builds in the normal macOS configuration ( #214 ), and a standalone Metal unit that draws offscreen is the start of the Mac display ( #318 , from #213). Both are by @evill33t and are compile-tested on macOS in CI. The runtime 's own boot harness can now load the decompilation's replacements too ( #225 , by @evill33t ): pbboot takes --game-lib with the compiled game library and runs its set-up before the game's first code, so finished replacements run in place of the originals during a boot. Without the option the boot runs the original code only, as before. Runtime System imports provided 683 of 686 (99.56%): 219 by the game's own modules, 464 by the runtime ; 3 remaining Furthest boot milestone first flip (8 of 8) Boot stops at the run's time limit, still running (no call stopped it) Last recorded run: 2026-11-10. This is saved evidence, not a live measurement. Generated by tools/sync_progress.py from the code repo. Do not edit. The table above is generated from the saved Paleblood boot record. Its date identifies the last recorded run; changing runtime code does not refresh the result by itself.
