docs.text: 10 November 2026: the cinematic and character creation (local runs). With the renderer's 3D work below, the opening cinematic plays on in the maintainer's local runs, lit and with its subtitles, its movie's sound ending and its port closing ( #490 ), and the game reaches character creation: the contract screen with name, gender, age, origin, appearance and starting attributes. That screen hands the GPU 70 command buffers in one call, which the stand-in had capped at 64 ( #504 ). These are local observations with renderer work then still in review applied, not saved records. The boot recorded on merged main the same evening ( #536 , display off, no input, 30 seconds) still reports the first flip, 243 imports called and nothing stopping it, because without input the game waits at its title. 6 to 10 November 2026: past the title (local runs). With scripted input ( #447 ) and the display on, the maintainer's local runs select "Play Offline". The game creates its save data (with #444 , then in review and since merged, applied for sceKernelWrite , and #449 ), and after the renderer learned 8- and 16-bit buffer formats ( #457 ) it shows its main menu (New Game, System, Log In) for over a thousand frames. Choosing New Game needed depth and stencil tests that read the buffer ( #471 ); with it, and with #470 (compute queues' buffers, in review) also applied, the boot reaches the first-run Brightness screen and then Controls, and runs on waiting for input. Scripted on past Controls, the next scene's draws needed image descriptors loaded behind a branch ( #474 ), two-channel 8-bit images ( #476 ) and samplers with anisotropy fields but plain filters ( #477 ); with them the game's opening cinematic, its first 3D scene, draws. These are local observations, not saved records; the frames are on the Milestones page. 6 November 2026: the logos and the title screen. Later the same day, Paleblood's own renderer began drawing what the game asks for (see The renderer ). In the maintainer's local runs (display on, with the game library from the decompilation), the boot shows the three studio logos, "Sony Computer Entertainment presents", "JAPAN Studio" and "FROM SOFTWARE", and reaches the title screen with its "Play Online / Play Offline" menu at about frame 480, with no stop within 90 seconds ( #441 , #442 ). Compared with reference frames captured locally from another PS4 runtime , the JAPAN Studio and FROM SOFTWARE frames are pixel-identical, and the title frame differs in 0.7% of its pixels, by at most 13 levels, where the menu's highlight is animated. These are local observations, not a saved record; the frames are on the Milestones page. The boot recorded on merged main afterwards ( #443 ) runs with the display off: first flip, 243 imports called, 234 of them answered by the runtime , and nothing stops it. Earlier on 6 November: no call stops the boot ( #408 ). The boot recorded on merged main calls 243 imports, 218 of them answered by the runtime , and keeps running until the harness 's 30-second limit. The round of runtime work merged on 5 and 6 November answered every call between the first flip and the game's main loop: the install service (PlayGo, #370 ): every part of the game is installed; the user's name and events ( #372 ), and one controller at rest ( #373 ); the clock and calendar ( #378 , #379 ); the offline PSN calls: the title id, sign-in state, matchmaking start-up, NAT and HTTPS options, network waits ( #380 , #381 , #382 , #385 , #386 ); file details and the error variable ( #376 ), thread exit ( #389 , #399 ), add-on content ( #392 ), the boot splash and system status ( #396 ); save data in a folder you choose ( #402 ), and trophies, kept offline with your save data ( #405 ); the graphics packets the stand-in skips safely ( #375 , #377 , #395 ); sound ( #398 , #406 ). The game's audio is ATRAC9, decoded with LibAtrac9 (MIT, by Alex Barney, included unmodified in Paleblood), and with --audio host it plays through your computer's sound output. In the maintainer's local runs with the display on, the game's main loop then runs at its own 30 frames a second, and its music and sounds start after about 17 seconds. These are observed local runs; the saved boot record shows only that nothing stops the run. At that point the frames were still black; the renderer work merged later that day draws them. Earlier, 4 November. The boot recorded on 4 November 2026 ( #304 ) reached the video out milestone, 6 of 8: the game's threads, its files, input and its sound system start, and it opens its display. Its first GPU work now goes through a temporary stand-in ( #302 ), its network worker polls offline ( #303 ), and it calls 135 imports. Its scratch files go to a writable /data folder ( #308 ). Since #310 it gets through all eight milestones : it hands its first frame's work to the GPU and flips it to the display, then carries on to the PS4 's install service (PlayGo), calling 170 imports. Nothing is drawn: the GPU work goes through the temporary stand-in described below. The boot before it (19 October) stopped much earlier, at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity inside the game's bundled C library. #207 replaced the C library's probe that made that call, so the call is no longer made ( Runtime syscalls ), and the runtime work merged since covers everything up to the graphics. Before this, the maintainer used local discovery boots that stood in for the missing pieces (the affinity query and the reader-writer locks) without committing them, to see which call comes next. On 30 October 2026 a local discovery boot: started the game's threads, its HTTP client (offline) and its sound system; found and read its first data file, sprj_mixer.fev , from the person's own copy; stopped at the first graphics-driver call whose answer is not established ( sceGnmValidateCommandBuffers ). Each call it passed through was then implemented and merged with its own evidence (the runtime system-call notes list them), and the genuine boot of 4 November now reaches the same point on merged main alone.
docs.title: How far a boot gets

docs.text: Paleblood has a local capture writer and replay verifier. Saved cases carry function and run identifiers and use stable buffer ordering. Replay checks reject a case for a different function or address. The version-1 production hook interface does not observe function returns or describe pointer buffers, and current replacements do not call the recorder. A separate test adapter proves that explicitly described synthetic inputs can be serialized and replayed. This checks the case format and verifier path only. It does not capture real game calls, prove a replacement against a real recording, or supply production run inputs. tools/promote.py consumes existing recorded cases and generated edge cases ; it does not create captures . The merged differential tools can now replay fixtures, observe supported guest instruction memory accesses, collect bounded control-flow coverage, minimize mismatches, and coordinate an opt-in candidate workflow. Unsupported instructions and skipped host-call bodies reject the trace; synthetic automation tests establish tool behavior only. The Architecture verification guide explains what is observed and which stages still require original-game evidence and human review.
docs.title: Capture and replay

docs.text: The latest genuine boot trace was recorded with merged Paleblood main in #536 (10 November 2026, after the runtime checklist and the renderer's 3D work). Latest trace (10 November, #536) 6 November (#443) Earlier on 6 November (#408) 4 November (#310) Earlier on 4 November (#300) 19 October (#92) Imports resolved 683/686: 219 bundled, 464 implemented by the runtime , 3 unbound 453/686: 219 bundled, 234 implemented by the runtime 437/686 (218 runtime ) 368/686 (149 runtime ) 344/686 (125 runtime ) 252/686 (33 runtime ) Import calls reached 243 243 243 170 133 seven Stopped at nothing: still running at the 30-second limit nothing: still running at the 30-second limit nothing: still running at the 30-second limit scePlayGoInitialize (install service) sceGnmDingDong (compute-queue doorbell) scePthreadAttrGetaffinity in libc.elf Milestone first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) first flip (8/8) video out (6/8) loaded (0/8) Between 11 and 19 October (PR #63 to #92) only the supplied-import count rose; startup did not advance. Between 19 October and 4 November it advanced six milestones. The generated status above is synchronized from the latest run. The GPU, for now. The first graphics calls are answered honestly for a runtime with no GPU ( #297 , #299 ): there is no debug-validation layer, no hardware state to set up, and the reserved command space is filled with no-op packets. When the game first hands work to the GPU ( sceGnmDingDong ), a temporary stand-in ( #302 ) completes it at once. It runs no shaders and draws nothing: it only writes each job's "work done" value, which is what the CPU waits for, and frees the queue. This was a maintainer decision of 4 November 2026, so that start-up can continue while the engine's own renderer (its GX framework) is rebuilt to replace it (issue #39). See Runtime syscalls . Scratch files. The engine maps its temp: and title: drives to /data and creates a fresh cache file there at start-up. The runtime now serves /data as a writable folder of its own choosing ( #308 ): each boot gets a new, empty one, so runs start alike. Memory the GPU can reach. The game stores GPU buffer addresses in a shortened form that only holds addresses below a fixed limit (the GPU's 40-bit address space). Memory the runtime placed higher lost its top bits there and crashed the game, so the runtime now places the memory it chooses an address for below that limit ( #310 ). The first frame. The game's first frame hands the GPU shader settings, draws, cache steps, waits and "work done" markers. The temporary stand-in performs the "work done" writes, checks the waits already hold, and skips the rest, then flips at the next 60 Hz tick ( #310 ). At the time nothing was drawn; the renderer now runs the drawing work alongside it (see below). What blocks it now. No system call does: since #408 the boot runs until its time limit, and since #442 the maintainer's local runs draw the title screen. With scripted input ( #447 ) those runs now get past it, through the menus, the settings screens and the opening cinematic to character creation (see above). What stops them next is the renderer: each new scene uses drawing features it does not have yet, and it stops by name on them. The saved boot record runs without input, so it waits at the title and does not show any of this. The temporary stand-in described above still answers the GPU's "work done" values; with the display on, the renderer also runs the drawing work.
docs.title: Boot history and the current blocker

docs.text: Bloodborne draws through its own engine renderer (the GX framework) and Sony's GPU helper library compiled into the game. Its shaders ship as compiled AMD GPU code. On 4 November 2026 the maintainer chose how Paleblood draws them: - Draws: the game's own drawing functions are hooked like the rest of the decompilation, and send their work to Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. - Shaders: each one is translated from AMD's code to Vulkan's or Metal's shader language when it loads, on your machine. The translator is written from AMD's public instruction-set manuals, not from any emulator. Nothing translated is published. - Ruled out: replaying the finished GPU commands, which would be GPU emulation. Where it stands (6 November 2026). The renderer now draws the game's logos and its title screen. When the game's GPU library sets up a draw, the call is reported to Paleblood's renderer, which translates the shaders involved and draws on a PC GPU with Vulkan. In the maintainer's local runs this produces the three studio logos and the title screen, and the title frame matches a reference capture to within 0.7% of pixels ( #442 ). It needs the display on ( --display headless or window ) and the game library built from the decompilation ( --game-lib ), because the reports come from its replacements. Since then the menus after the title draw too in local runs with scripted input: the main menu after #457 (8- and 16-bit buffer formats) and the Brightness and Controls screens after #471 (depth and stencil tests that read the buffer, stencil steps, a depth target larger than the colour target). Past them, the opening cinematic's first 3D frames draw too ( #474 , #476 , #477 ), and with the 3D work of 10 November (below) the cinematic plays on to character creation. The playable game has not run yet. The work comes in four phases (Paleblood's docs/RENDERER.md ): Display (done, #313 ): every frame buffer the game registers gets a frame of its own, and each flip shows it, in a window (SDL3 and Vulkan) or captured to image files for tests. Since 6 November the renderer draws into them. Shader translator (begun, #316 ): a decoder for GFX7, the PS4 GPU's instruction set, names every instruction. Its opcode table is generated from AMD's manual and LLVM's AMDGPU assembler, which must agree. A census of your own copy's shaders shows the game uses only 175 distinct instructions, and the decoder knows all of them. The first translation to Vulkan shaders works ( #319 ): simple compute shaders (arithmetic, compares, conversions, buffer and constant reads and writes) run on a real GPU and give exactly the results AMD's manual defines. Since #330 it also handles branches, loops and GCN 's active-lane mask: only the lanes that are switched on write results or touch memory, as on the console. Since #332 it also reads and writes typed buffers, which nearly half of the game's shaders use. Every typed access in the game uses plain 32-bit floats, so those translate exactly; any other format is refused rather than guessed. Since #333 it translates vertex and pixel shaders too: their outputs (positions, values passed down to pixels, colours) and the pixel shader's blended inputs. A translated pair already draws a test triangle on the GPU with every pixel checked, and most of the game's vertex shaders now translate completely. A batch of arithmetic instructions followed in #334 (24-bit multiplies, bit fields, carries, sine and cosine, exponent and logarithm), each checked on the GPU. Since #343 a vertex shader's extra position outputs work too: in this game they always carry two clip distances, which the GPU uses to cut triangles off at a plane. With them, most of the game's vertex shaders translate completely. Texture sampling followed on 6 November ( #433 ), with the rest of what the title screen needs (see below). On macOS the same translated shaders become Metal shaders through SPIRV-Cross; since #331 macOS CI converts every test shader and compiles it with Apple's Metal compiler. evill33t's Metal unit ( #318 , from #213) is the start of the Mac display, and since 11 November an offscreen Metal draw executor, also by @evill33t , plays recorded draws through the same translated shaders behind the renderer's common interface ( #518 ): render targets, viewports, shaders, user data and triangle-list draws, checked by its own macOS CI. Engine draw hooks (working for the logos and title screen; begun in #335 ): route the game's render targets, clears, shader binding, textures and draws to the renderer, starting with the title screen's 2D passes. A first map found Sony's GPU helper library, compiled into the game, in one block of about 230 small functions: everything the game asks of the GPU passes through it, and the engine writes no GPU commands of its own. The library's draw functions and about 60 of its state setters are identified, along with the engine code that calls the draws. The game keeps its GPU state only in the commands those setters write, so the hooks will sit on the setters and draws themselves: each setter hands its value to the renderer, and each draw becomes a Vulkan or Metal draw. The library's key functions are identified ( #341 ): its draw call, setRenderTarget , setViewport , the depth target and the user-data writers. Several are already decompiled in @evill33t 's pull requests, as replacements verified to write exactly the original commands. The renderer will observe those replacements rather than change them. The shader files in the game's archive turned out to carry each shader's GPU register settings, and those settings were checked against the shaders' own code. They say where a shader's code lives, which inputs it gets, and what its extra outputs carry. On the runtime side, the renderer now keeps its own record of these calls for each command buffer ( #342 , #344 , #345 ): render targets, viewports, shaders, their data and draws, ready to play back when the game submits the buffer. The next piece is the draw executor, which plays those calls back on a PC GPU. Its first step is done ( #346 , #348 ). Game shaders find memory by the PS4 's addresses, so the runtime now keeps the game's GPU-visible memory at fixed places, and the translator adds one fixed offset to every address a shader forms. That lets the whole memory pool be handed to the GPU as a single buffer. A test on an RTX 3070 shows this works, at the cost of holding the 5 GiB pool in RAM while graphics run. Its second step works too ( #368 ): given a written-down list of drawing calls, the executor runs them on a Vulkan GPU. It translates the shaders the calls name, finds or makes the picture they draw into, and draws. In a test with real PS4 -style shaders, every pixel comes out right. Since #369 it is wired into the running game: with the display on, the calls run when the game submits its drawing work, and a flip shows what was drawn instead of a black frame. Until the game's drawing functions report their calls, nothing visible changes. Since #401 the record also keeps the GPU register values the game sets (blending, depth, primitive type, colour masks and the like), and the executor checks them before it draws: anything it cannot draw faithfully yet stops by name rather than drawing something wrong. Since 6 November the GPU library's decompiled replacements, by @evill33t ( #411 , from #233), report their calls to the renderer ( #414 ), and a few library functions without replacements are observed where they are called ( #416 ). Textures and 3D (under way): the texture formats and tiled layouts the title screen uses work ( #427 , #428 , #441 , #442 ), and since 10 November so do the opening cinematic's 3D scenes and character creation in local runs (see the last step below). The playable game's areas, with their meshes, materials and post-processing, are still to come.
docs.title: The renderer

docs.text: All of this was merged on 6 November 2026. Each step removed the next thing the boot stopped at by name; the renderer never draws something it cannot draw faithfully, it stops and says what is missing. Draw reports and hooks ( #411 , #412 , #414 , #415 , #416 ): the GPU library's replacements tell the renderer which shaders are bound, the render targets, the shaders' data and each draw. setRenderTarget and the user-data writers are observed where they are called. Rectangle-list draws, which the game uses for full-screen passes, work. Compute ( #418 , #421 , #424 ): the game's compute passes run on the GPU, including the ones that clear the screen and build its colour lookup tables. They read and write buffers in the formats their descriptors name, and images. A shader that needs something not translated yet stops the run by name while it runs. Pixel shaders ( #425 ): a pixel's own screen position as an input, and the GPU's whole-quad mode. Textures and tiling ( #427 , #428 , #432 ): the PS4 stores most images tiled, not row by row. The renderer knows the tiled layouts the game uses (linear, 1D and 2D thin), loads images from the game's memory in those layouts, and reads image descriptors the shaders load from memory. Sampling ( #433 ): shaders read textures through the game's samplers (filtering and clamping). This gave the first frame that was not black: a flat grey from the game's colour-correction pass. Blending, depth and vertex fetch ( #434 , #435 , #436 , #437 , #438 ): blending, depth and stencil targets, triangle strips, vertex shaders that call fetch shaders to read their vertices, and GPU state that carries over from one command buffer to the next. Indexed draws and the logos ( #439 , #440 , #441 ): indexed draws, render targets that keep the game's memory up to date so later passes can read them, vertex colours and block-compressed (BC) textures. This drew the first logo, "Sony Computer Entertainment presents". Speed ( #442 ): render targets are copied back to the game's memory only when something may read them, and unchanged images are not loaded again. In the maintainer's local runs a 90-second boot went from 66 frames to about 1,445, enough to reach the title screen at about frame 480. A shader reading data the game never set now stops by name. Draws still waited for the GPU one at a time. Since #463 (10 November) each submitted command buffer's draws and dispatches go to the GPU as one batch, and the CPU waits only where it reads what the batch produced; on the logos and title this alone changed nothing measurable: the limit there was the CPU's own tiling copies of the render targets. #472 moved those copies to a compute shader on the GPU, and in the maintainer's local runs the logos and title now run at the game's own 30 frames a second (about 14 before); the JAPAN Studio frame is still pixel-identical. Beside the game, and into 3D (10 November): submissions now return at once and the renderer runs them on a thread of its own in the order the game submitted them, as on the PS4 ; anything the game can observe (a "work done" value, a wait, a flip) happens only after the work before it has run ( #488 ). Compute queues' buffers are taken and dropped, so their shader bindings no longer leak into graphics buffers ( #470 ). For the cinematic and character creation the renderer learned depth-only passes ( #519 ), depth target slices ( #522 ), mip chains and mip-mapped images sampled at the level the derivatives pick or the shader gives ( #516 , #523 , #526 , #549 ), stencil replace with a fixed value ( #524 ), several render targets in one draw ( #533 ), the pixel shader's front-face input ( #537 ), anisotropic sampler filters ( #554 ), render targets cleared by a compute shader ( #539 ), more image formats ( #476 , #492 , #503 ) and float formats, stored and as render targets ( #525 , #530 , #534 : the character creation preview draws into float targets), more shader instructions, among them the cube-map ones, with cube images in pixel shaders ( #495 , #501 , #548 , #551 ), and buffer accesses checked against their descriptor's range, as the GPU does, with an invalid-format (unbound) buffer reading zeros and writing nothing ( #556 , #494 , #505 , #508 , #540 ), and descriptors that arrive as part of a wider load, as the character creation preview's pixel shader loads them ( #547 ), or that come from the user data even when the program writes those registers later, past a forward branch ( #553 ). Contributor @evill33t tightened the executor's checks: indexed-draw packets keep their raw fields and are validated before they draw ( #452 ), and a user-data range that wraps around is refused ( #493 ). Boot history fields (PR #51) PR #51 extended new symbols/boot_history.csv rows with the run outcome, execution phase, unresolved-import return site, and guest-fault location, signal, and address. A changed failure location is recorded even when import counts and the blocking symbol stay the same. Existing rows remain readable. After relevant changes merge, compare the history fields added by PR #51 against the saved failure location and trace.

docs.text: Loader and boot harness : project-owned and independently tested. Kernel, threads, and memory: done for the boot: merged main boots through all eight milestones and keeps running, passing its GPU work through a temporary stand-in; no system call stops it ( #408 ), and since #528 only contributor-claimed calls are left in #34 . Files, audio, network start-up: the game reads its own files read-only and keeps save data and trophies in a folder you choose; its sound is decoded and can play on your computer; its HTTP client and PSN calls answer offline. GNM and shaders: the logos and title screen draw natively in the maintainer's local runs ( #441 , #442 ). The renderer hooks the game's own drawing layer and translates its shaders, rather than emulating the GPU (see The renderer ). In local runs with scripted input the menus, the opening cinematic and character creation draw as well ( #457 , #471 , #488 and the 3D work above). Next: the first playable area, with its meshes, materials and post-processing (the logos and title already reach the game's 30 fps cap in local runs, #472 ). Movies and input: the game's movies decode with FFmpeg ( #419 , #420 ); a real controller and keyboard work with --input host ( #431 ). Capture integration: add a return-aware, ABI-described observation boundary before connecting recordings to production hooks . Synthetic tests are not a substitute for real captures . System-library work is tracked separately from boot milestones, in one issue per group: kernel ( #34 ), files ( #35 ), input and users ( #36 ), audio ( #37 ), video out ( #38 ), GNM ( #39 ), system services ( #40 ) and network ( #41 ). All but the kernel issue are closed, and it lists only calls contributors have claimed. The network group covers the byte-order and IPv4 helpers (both directions since #465 ), offline network control, the offline start-up and teardown of the network, SSL and HTTP libraries ( #451 ), and the PSN identity, Plus and authorization checks of a signed-out console ( #450 , #461 ), the remaining PSN services ( #507 ) and sockets, resolvers and HTTP requests that find no connection ( #509 ). Nothing is ever sent. See Paleblood's runtime queue and runtime issues . Network-group pull requests Merged PR #60 makes the registry and coverage tools preserve that distinction: unresolved diagnostics are excluded from implemented counts while still producing useful failure messages when called. Merged PR #63 adds the documented IPv4 text conversion for Bloodborne's observed AF_INET calls.

docs.text: The current full-game path retains an external GPL-2.0-or-later scaffold and its required host, system-library, and graphics dependencies. Paleblood's new hook callback covers only one host responsibility; it is not yet integrated into the full game-run path. Paleblood's own pbboot harness builds and tests without that scaffold, but it does not yet provide equivalent full-game loading, services, rendering, or route checks. The scaffold and its required attribution stay in the code repository until a project-owned replacement passes the same native game-run checks.

What this page can and cannot claim Every claim in this section is labelled by the kind of evidence behind it. Label Meaning observed Seen during play or in a recording, with its context: starting state, player position and actions, the visible change, and whether it repeats. inferred A conclusion drawn from code or tests, stated with the scope that evidence covers. unknown Not yet traced. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. Absence is not a claim about the game. A missing profile describes the project's research, not what the game contains. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels evidence.

docs.text: Enemy AI & Behavior Players can watch an enemy move, react, attack, or return to an earlier behavior. That sequence does not reveal the code that selected it; this page explains what is known and how a behavior claim gets supported. At a glance What is verified ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 steps the shared Havok AI world at 1/30 second. What is unmapped The world update at 0x021cdad0 , its group/object structure, and each enemy's decisions. Not proven Target acquisition, attack selection, cooldowns, navigation, or randomness. Profiles No individual enemy AI profile is supported by the current evidence. The verified boundary The verified function ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 : steps the shared Havok AI world at 1/30 second; conditionally copies matrices; conditionally runs debug drawing. The world update it calls, at 0x021cdad0 , its group/object structure, and each enemy's decisions remain unmapped. So the verified wrapper does not prove target acquisition, attack selection, cooldowns, navigation, or randomness. Read the AI system page for its structures and open questions. How behavior claims will be supported Internal AI claims need an identified entity and a traceable path through the game's update logic. Keep a reproducible observation separate from an implementation result. docs.text: 6 October 2026: from an empty repository to the frame loop The first day: the target was prepared, the repositories and tooling were set up, and the first Ghidra export and verified frame-loop replacements were completed, from the clock up to the function that runs every frame. The target Both packages extracted without keys and merged. The update's param.sfo reports the 1.09 app version. All eight executables (the eboot and seven PRX modules) were fake-signed SELFs with no encrypted segments, and converting them to ELF only unwrapped them. Hashes are on the Target page. Repositories and tooling progress.py derives every number from symbols/ in the code repository. verify.py runs the original code and a replacement side by side, outside the game, on the same inputs, and compares everything they do (more on that below). The pre-commit hooks refuse game data, local notes and stale progress numbers. The converted eboot has no section headers, so there is no .text to measure. The progress denominator is the set of functions Ghidra finds in executable blocks, tied to the hash of the committed export. The first Ghidra export Ghidra 12.0.3 with the GhidraOrbis loader imported the eboot and finished full auto-analysis in about 26 minutes. It found 157,757 functions in .text , 42,487,347 bytes, not counting 9,302 thunks . All 671 imports resolved to names through the NID database. The loader decides where .text ends with a heuristic, and on a small module it put almost all the code into .rodata , where nothing gets analyzed. So the export needed a check that does not depend on Ghidra at all: the unwind table. It lists 162,959 functions. 155,000 of them are functions in the export, and the other 7,959 are all thunks , which the export skips on purpose. Ghidra also found 2,757 functions that have no unwind entry. The gap is fully accounted for. That is the size of the job: about 158 thousand functions and 42 MB of code. The first function: a millisecond clock 0x0111a7f0 turned out to be a monotonic millisecond clock: it asks the system for CLOCK_MONOTONIC , keeps the seconds of its first call in a shared state object, and returns the milliseconds since then. The C++ replacement does the same, down to the 32-bit arithmetic that wraps. To check the checker, deliberately broken versions of each replacement are run through verify.py ; each must fail. Then the game runs with the hook installed, the replacement records its real inputs as it goes, and those recordings are compared too: over 30,000 calls in 90 seconds here, and the game reached the title menu exactly as it does without the hook . Two bugs were caught before anything was marked verified : the recording code dropped half of each clock value, and the tester counted cases from two runs as one when they shared names. With the monitors off, the desktop throttles a game window to one frame a second. A virtual display ( Xvfb ) fixes that for test runs, at about 15 frames a second on the title screen. Finding the frame limiter The plan was to walk outward from the millisecond clock to the frame limiter. But the clock and its two neighbours have 52 callers, all in one stretch of the executable and none touched by any frame-rate patch: a separate subsystem, not the frame loop. The frame-rate patches by Kyo (and Lance McDonald for the uncapped one) were written by people who already found the limiter. Mapping every patched address to its function, then keeping the functions that both read the clock and sleep, left one that every frame-rate patch edits: 0x02434770 , now frame_timing_pace_frame . The frame limiter article explains how it works. The limiter, replaced , and the first option The replacement follows the original instruction by instruction, down to how it converts between integers and floating point and how each comparison treats NaN. Twenty-six hand-written cases cover every mode; four deliberately wrong versions all fail, after two of them first got through and showed the cases had blind spots. In-game recordings, with the community patches off so the original is the real one, all match. The spinning wait broke the first recording: frames with more than 20,000 clock reads were dropped, which removed exactly the frames that spin. Runs of clock reads are now stored as one series. BB_TARGET_FPS set to 30 , 60 or uncapped changes the limiter in code, the way the community patches change it with byte edits. Unset, nothing changes. It covers only the limiter: the patches also fix many places where the game assumes 30 frames a second, and those still need the patch until they are replaced too. BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep makes the limiter sleep instead of spinning while it waits. Both wait for a measurement on a real screen. The frame step and the flipper frame_timing_frame_step is the function the main loop calls once per frame. It asks the window object whether the game is still running, creates the frame-pacing object on the first frame, runs the limiter, runs the game's task update, and asks two more objects whether the player has asked to quit. Four of those questions are virtual calls, so it was the first function whose inputs are objects: the recordings now describe each object as a small stand-in whose table slot points at the real function the game called. It matched on every recorded frame. frame_timing_flipper_init builds the frame-pacing object. It reads the config value Game.FlipMode twice through the game's own string class; the shipped config leaves it unset, which is why the game runs the 30 FPS mode. Verified on the recorded call and nine edge cases . The microsecond time helper the frame-rate patches edit is replaced too, but the game never calls it before the title menu, so it waits for a run that gets further. The frame-rate option, corrected A function nothing calls turned out to be a code cave: the time helper the frame-rate patches edit is never called in the stock game, and the patches overwrite it with their own code. That led to a closer look at what the patches do to the functions we did replace, by disassembling each with and without the patch. They do more than the limiter: they also make the frame step hand the game the measured frame time instead of a fixed 1/30 s. Our hooked frame step had switched that off, so the first version of BB_TARGET_FPS=60 would have run the game logic twice as fast. The test harness can now apply a patch to the original code, so each part of the option is checked against the patch itself: all edge cases , every deliberately wrong version caught, and frames recorded at 60 FPS in the game match. A real-screen measurement waits for the display plug. Counting calls, and three more functions Of the 59 functions the frame-rate patches touch outside frame timing, 12 turned out to be dead code and 47 live. To find which of the live ones the game actually runs, the runtime can now count calls to original functions without replacing them: a short jump at each entry to a counter that then runs the original. One gameplay run in Iosefka's Clinic showed 13 of them running, several every frame. Nine of the others are small state methods that advance an owner by a fixed 1/30 s step; they are built next to the game's Chalice Dungeon singleton and do not run in the clinic. They are replaced and checked against the 60 FPS patch, and wait for a save that reaches the Chalice Dungeons. A per-frame task that hands the frame time to its parts is replaced and verified , including what the uncapped patch does to it through a code cave. And the engine's condition variable wait is the first function of a new system, the engine's kernel layer: the patches put a return over its timed wait that would crash if it ran, and every wait the game made was untimed. One trap on the way: Ghidra treats the engine's fatal error as a call that never returns, so it hides the instructions right after it. The game's code does continue there, and a replacement written from the listing alone got one path wrong until the bytes were read directly. Workflow The work no longer waits on the maintainer between steps: a target queue, a standing procedure, a smoke test of the whole pipeline at the start of each session, a lock that keeps two projects off the GPU at the same time, and one game run records inputs for every replaced function at once. Checking the limiter's recordings used to keep a core busy for four minutes; with a native answer for the clock reads, the executable loaded once and low priority, it takes under one. Replacements may start from a draft of the decompiler's output, kept on the maintainer's machine and never committed. What is committed is the renamed, readable, verified version. This wiki The site theme and the one-post-per-day devlog were established alongside the project's documentation. Next The live functions the 60 FPS patches edit, starting with the frame-time descriptor family. The other places the frame-rate patches edit.

The test harness can now apply a patch to the original code, so each part of the option is checked against the patch itself: all edge cases , every deliberately wrong version caught, and frames recorded at 60 FPS in the game match. A real-screen measurement waits for the display plug.
docs.title: The frame-rate option, corrected

docs.text: Of the 59 functions the frame-rate patches touch outside frame timing, 12 turned out to be dead code and 47 live. To find which of the live ones the game actually runs, the runtime can now count calls to original functions without replacing them: a short jump at each entry to a counter that then runs the original. One gameplay run in Iosefka's Clinic showed 13 of them running, several every frame. Nine of the others are small state methods that advance an owner by a fixed 1/30 s step; they are built next to the game's Chalice Dungeon singleton and do not run in the clinic. They are replaced and checked against the 60 FPS patch, and wait for a save that reaches the Chalice Dungeons. A per-frame task that hands the frame time to its parts is replaced and verified , including what the uncapped patch does to it through a code cave. And the engine's condition variable wait is the first function of a new system, the engine's kernel layer: the patches put a return over its timed wait that would crash if it ran, and every wait the game made was untimed. One trap on the way: Ghidra treats the engine's fatal error as a call that never returns, so it hides the instructions right after it. The game's code does continue there, and a replacement written from the listing alone got one path wrong until the bytes were read directly.
docs.title: Counting calls, and three more functions

docs.text: The work no longer waits on the maintainer between steps: a target queue, a standing procedure, a smoke test of the whole pipeline at the start of each session, a lock that keeps two projects off the GPU at the same time, and one game run records inputs for every replaced function at once. Checking the limiter's recordings used to keep a core busy for four minutes; with a native answer for the clock reads, the executable loaded once and low priority, it takes under one. Replacements may start from a draft of the decompiler's output, kept on the maintainer's machine and never committed. What is committed is the renamed, readable, verified version.

docs.text: 7 October 2026: a new direction, our own runtime Paleblood opened its code to contributors and began building a clean-room runtime of its own. This entry combines the day's runtime work and decompilation progress. Runtime and boot progress Earlier that day, the former runtime ran the game at 60 FPS through Iosefka's Clinic. The project then began removing that borrowed runtime and its graphics dependency. Paleblood's new loader maps the executable byte for byte and its verification harness reproduced the earlier function results. At this point the new runtime did not run the game; its system-library work stopped at an unimplemented import. The roadmap still included threads and memory, files, input, audio, video out, and graphics. Decompilation and verified functions The frame-loop work included the pad manager's step, reference-counted render updates, present/ vblank handling, YEBIS sample parameters, six task-manager functions, a physics constructor, the Havok AI manager, and a character update. Existing cases cover per-frame work and 19 physics constructions. The AI manager's branches and idle paths use explicit test fixtures. Tests caught floating-point edge cases , stack arguments, thread-local state, shared patch data, and object memory that the harness needed to describe. Tooling and automation The verification harness learned to pass and return floating-point values, model stack arguments and thread-local state, apply the frame-rate patch to the original, and count calls without replacing functions. Deliberately incorrect replacements were used to check that the cases caught known mistakes. The project also introduced a readable-code review gate and a contributor route based on claimed work and pull-request evidence. Documentation and website changes The public Paleblood repository opened with contribution guidance and protected pull requests. The runtime roadmap and clean-room boundary were documented alongside the new loader . Tests and validation The verification harness ran existing recorded and edge cases , and deliberately wrong versions exposed several test gaps. The new loader reproduced the same verification results. These checks validated function behavior; they did not demonstrate full game execution on the project-owned runtime . Blockers and next steps At the time, the new runtime still needed its system imports and execution layers before it could boot the game. The decompilation continued independently, with every replacement requiring recorded inputs where available, edge cases , readable code, and matching verification evidence.

docs.text: 9 October 2026: a path for runtime contributors Runtime-only contributors can implement a documented syscall without access to a game dump or recorded captures . This day's work prepared the issue #34 contribution route and clarified what the current boot evidence does and does not establish. Runtime and boot progress The runtime still stopped at its first unresolved system call. The maintainer's boot check runs locally after a runtime pull request merges; a contributor does not need proprietary files or captures to implement and test a runtime -only change. Decompilation and verified functions No function replacement or verification status changed in this milestone. The frame limiter's clock calls pass a null timezone to gettimeofday ; a separate sceKernelClockGettime call uses clock ID 4 , but the IDs passed to the imported clock_gettime are still unknown. Those gaps remain open instead of being filled with assumed return values. Tooling and automation The issue #34 workflow uses a claim-and-branch process, small related changes, and a concise evidence report. Paleblood PR #44 , merged at ef1989e , prepared the contributor checks. Runtime-only pull requests use the compiler matrix, system-library tests, and policy checks. Decompilation and mixed changes retain the full session report and verification gates. Shared Git hooks dispatch through the active worktree, so linked worktrees use their own installed checks. The devlog moved to one post per day: new milestones are added to that day's post under fixed sections, and repeat updates replace their own entry instead of adding a second one. The publishing script keeps the Paleblood source it builds from separate from the public site. This is workflow only; the game did not get further. Paleblood PR #51 makes the boot history record where each run stopped (the phase, the unresolved import and where the game faulted), even when only that location changes between runs. This improves diagnostics; it is not boot progress. Documentation and website changes The syscall notes distinguish public contracts for getpagesize , getpid , clock_gettime , and gettimeofday from target-specific behavior not yet established. The loading map records the bundled Fios module while leaving archive access, PlayGo flow, and target-specific error paths as open questions. Progress was synchronized from merged Paleblood sources. Paleblood PR #52 notes that running the full game still depends on the old borrowed runtime until Paleblood has its own equivalent checks. Byrgenwerth removed the pages, test-run media and build hook left over from that runtime , and added checks so they don't come back. Tests and validation The issue #34 workflow added no replacement and no verification result. Runtime-only CI checks run without game data; pull-request CI validates the changed code and policy before the local post-merge boot check. The shared hook changes were exercised in linked worktrees. Blockers and next steps The first unresolved import and the target-specific behavior listed above still need evidence. The next runtime change should implement one documented call or a tightly related group, keep unknown behavior explicit, and include deterministic tests and its source basis. Nine functions are checked against hand-written edge cases , but none of them has matching recordings from the game yet, so none could be promoted to verified . Issue #34 is still claimed by a contributor and is still the earliest boot blocker. Issues #35–#40 are open, but they don't yet describe the system calls well enough to implement them safely. docs.text: 10 October 2026: recorded verification and runtime foundations This day improved capture reliability, verified one function from existing recorded calls, and added four deterministic network byte-order imports. The tooling work did not itself advance game execution. Runtime and boot progress Paleblood PR #50 , merged at 816ea96 , added sceNetHtonl , sceNetHtons , sceNetNtohl , and sceNetNtohs . These implement fixed-width host/network byte-order conversions; socket, resolver, epoll, and online behavior remain uncovered. The saved boot result still stopped at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity (238/686 system imports provided), within contributor-owned issue #34. No boot run was made for this change. Paleblood PR #55 adds Paleblood's own version of the callback that redirects a game function to its replacement. A synthetic test confirms the redirect works. The full game run still uses the old runtime , which doesn't call this yet. Decompilation and verified functions Paleblood PR #48 promoted frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ) using its existing evidence: 585/585 recorded calls and 26/26 edge cases . Its approved independent review remained in place. PR #49 refreshed generated public documentation from the merged verification result; it added no runtime behavior or new cases. The verified function count reached 21. Tooling and automation Paleblood PR #46 made capture output stable, recorded function/run provenance, refused unsafe paths and existing case files, and kept older schema-1 cases replayable. PR #47 added an isolated typed adapter proof with explicit signature and memory descriptors. Synthetic fixtures passed capture , serialization, replay, and verification; unsupported signatures and missing descriptors failed closed. Production replacements still do not call this adapter, so these tests produced no real game captures . Paleblood PR #53 lets the runtime issue counts see implemented system calls without waiting for a boot run. That corrected issue #41 : its network group now shows the four byte-order helpers from PR #50, 4/175 implemented. Paleblood PR #54 adds a test that checks how Paleblood talks to the old runtime : version checks, handing over the game image, registering redirects and passing errors back. It guards against regressions; nothing new runs. PR #55 also made the repository's Git hook tests more robust: they respect the configured temporary directory and stop cleanly if their test copy can't be made. The tests confirm that the hooks refuse game code and block a push when a required check fails. Documentation and website changes The frame-timing page and generated progress data were refreshed from merged Paleblood revision 816ea96 . The public site was published at 21e1d26 . The runtime notes keep the production observer and capture integration explicitly unfinished. Public source documents the synthetic limits alongside the results. All 30 public wiki pages were reviewed against the current Paleblood source, and the Runtime, Architecture and CI Setup pages were updated; the Runtime page now lists the four network byte-order helpers. Automatic syncing from Paleblood stays off until it can run with safe, limited credentials. The first Workshop article explains the verified per-frame character points update ( 0x01cbdb20 ): how it keeps fractional amounts between frames, its limits, and the evidence behind it, with a diagram. Calling it "stamina" is still a guess, and the article says so. A redesign put the wiki's pages into seven themed, collapsible menu groups that remember which ones you opened and work as a drawer on phones. The homepage got the hunter artwork chosen by the maintainer (SteamGridDB, by r_dsgnd ) in place of a product image. The redesign went live at public site commit 975ec0c . Every page loaded, the search index was up to date, and the phone menu opened, closed and moved focus correctly. The sidebar menu was repaired and the artwork moved into it, above Home, with its credit beneath. Section headings line up and no longer wrap, submenus sit along a guide line, only one section opens at a time, and short windows scroll instead of squeezing the menu. The homepage now opens with Master Willem's words. The repaired menu went live at public site commit 6b16b45 , with the artwork in the sidebar and no longer on the homepage. Tests and validation The capture changes passed GCC and Clang builds and all 11 CTest suites. The verification promotion used the 585 recorded calls plus 26 edge cases . The four network helpers passed registry tests with known byte patterns, zero, maximum-width values, and round trips; both compiler builds and all 11 CTest suites passed. Clean-room, policy, hook , and session audits also passed. Blockers and next steps No production capture integration or game execution advanced. 0x02713870 still has no matching recorded inputs and remains blocked. The earliest saved boot blocker remains the issue #34 affinity import; synthetic capture tests are not substitutes for matching recorded cases or production ABI evidence. None of it establishes a new verified function or startup milestone. Runtime and boot progress Catching up on 11–15 October. @clee 's merged PR #66 makes getpagesize stop by name under both import names instead of guessing. The game's own executables bound the answer to a divisor of 16384 (4096, 8192 or 16384), and no public source says which one the PS4 reports, so only a console observation can settle it. The entries do not count as implemented. @EzequielRindello 's merged PR #62 compares guest thread handles, and PR #72 supplies the documented sched_yield path. scePthreadYield stays unresolved because its PS4 return signature is unknown. The registry tests are synthetic. No boot was run for this audit; the saved result still stops at scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , before the first startup milestone. merged #82 runtime : implement memcpy and memset (libSceLibcInternal) , by @EzequielRindello . docs.text: merged #102 tools: skip byte scans of unchanged harness snapshots , by @evill33t . Merged 2026-10-28. Findings: Skip Python byte-by-byte scanning when the before/after writable snapshots are identical. Changed snapshots continue through the existing difference extraction. merged #98 tools: prepare extracted backups without copying assets , by @evill33t . Merged 2026-10-28. docs.text: Week of 2 November 2026: first flip, no call stops the boot, and the title screen The boot reached first flip on merged main, then ran with no system call stopping it; Paleblood's own renderer drew the studio logos and the title screen, and local runs with scripted input reached the main menu. Contributions by @evill33t, @EzequielRindello, @BluePinetree and @gabee12; no new function was verified . Runtime and boot progress The week in brief: from the October stop to the title screen. Advances game execution. 3–4 November: @BluePinetree 's #207 removed the boot's October stop ( scePthreadAttrGetaffinity inside the bundled C library). Recorded boots of merged main then climbed from milestone audio (5 of 8, #295 ) and video out (6 of 8, #300 ) to first flip, 8 of 8 ( #310 , 4 November): the game hands its first frame to the screen. 5–6 November: a round of runtime work answered every call between the first flip and the game's main loop: PlayGo #370 , the user service #372 , one controller at rest #373 , the clock #378 , #379 , PSN and network offline #380 , #381 , #382 , #385 , #386 , file details and errno #376 , thread exit #389 , #399 , add-ons #392 , the splash screen #396 , save data #402 , trophies #405 , and sound: ATRAC9 decoded with LibAtrac9 and played on the host #394 , #398 , #406 . The recorded boot after it ( #408 ) is the first that no system call stops : it calls 243 imports and keeps running to the time limit. Movies play through the console's movie player, decoded with FFmpeg #419 , #420 ; a real gamepad and keyboard work with --input host #431 ; scripted input lets unattended runs press buttons on a timetable #447 . Kernel details found by boots: priority-ordered semaphores #426 , memory-protection ranges #422 , no-overwrite maps #423 ; later file and network calls #448 , #449 , #450 , #451 . Contributors: @EzequielRindello implemented time , sleep , nanosleep , thread keys, pthread_cond_timedwait and mutex ownership #241 , #296 , #298 , #315 , #351 , #353 ; @evill33t landed loader and macOS groundwork and loading the decompilation's replacements in the runtime 's own boot harness #214 , #215 , #216 , #217 , #218 , #220 , #224 , #225 , #226 , #227 , #229 . The boot recorded after the renderer work ( #443 ): first flip, 243 imports called, 234 of them answered by the runtime , still running at the limit. It runs with the display off and no input. Maintainer's local runs (not saved records): the title screen draws (below), and with scripted input and the then-open #444 the game takes "Play Offline", creates its save data and shows its main menu (6 November). Frames: Milestones . The renderer: from black frames to the title screen. Advances game execution (in local runs with the display on). Phase 1, the display: every frame buffer gets a window or captured image #313 . Phase 2, the shader translator from AMD's GCN code to Vulkan's SPIR-V, written from AMD's manuals: the decoder and a census of the game's 175 instructions #316 , straight-line compute #319 , branches #330 , typed buffers #332 , vertex and pixel shaders #333 , arithmetic #334 , clip distances #343 , guest addresses #346 ; macOS CI compiles every test shader as Metal #331 . Phase 3, hooking the game's own drawing layer: the GPU library's packet writers and key entry points mapped #335 , #341 , a record of its calls per command buffer #342 , #344 , #345 , #401 , and the draw executor that plays them on a Vulkan GPU #349 , #368 , #369 . 6 November, #411 – #442 : @evill33t 's verified GPU-library replacements ( #411 , from #233) report the game's draws to the renderer #414 ; compute passes, tiled textures, sampling, blending, depth, fetch shaders, indexed draws and BC textures followed. Results in the maintainer's local runs: the first non-black frame ( #433 ), the first logo ( #441 ), then the JAPAN Studio and FROM SOFTWARE cards and the title screen once #442 made the renderer about 22 times faster (66 to about 1,445 frames in a 90-second boot). merged #207 runtime : replace functions inside mapped modules before they run , by @BluePinetree . Merged 2026-11-03. Findings: my own dump now boots to milestone audio (was libc.elf+0x81ad5). merged #241 runtime : answer EPERM to a non-owner of a normal or adaptive mutex , by @EzequielRindello . Merged 2026-11-03. System calls: scePthreadMutexUnlock; scePthreadMutexLock; scePthreadCondWait; scePthreadCondTimedwait; pthread_mutex_unlock; pthread_mutex_lock (and 1 more). Tests: 3 synthetic runtime test(s); the effect on the real boot is measured after merge, so this is not a boot result. Left unresolved: normal mutex locked again by its owner stops by name (the system would wait forever); cond waiters counted until the mutex is retaken: destroy after broadcast can answer EBUSY (recorded, unchanged). merged #297 runtime : answer sceGnmValidateCommandBuffers with "validation not available" , by @ThisIsAkill . Merged 2026-11-04. System calls: sceGnmValidateCommandBuffers. Tests: 2 synthetic runtime test(s); the effect on the real boot is measured after merge, so this is not a boot result. docs.text: The week in brief: from the October stop to the title screen. Advances game execution. 3–4 November: @BluePinetree 's #207 removed the boot's October stop ( scePthreadAttrGetaffinity inside the bundled C library). Recorded boots of merged main then climbed from milestone audio (5 of 8, #295 ) and video out (6 of 8, #300 ) to first flip, 8 of 8 ( #310 , 4 November): the game hands its first frame to the screen. 5–6 November: a round of runtime work answered every call between the first flip and the game's main loop: PlayGo #370 , the user service #372 , one controller at rest #373 , the clock #378 , #379 , PSN and network offline #380 , #381 , #382 , #385 , #386 , file details and errno #376 , thread exit #389 , #399 , add-ons #392 , the splash screen #396 , save data #402 , trophies #405 , and sound: ATRAC9 decoded with LibAtrac9 and played on the host #394 , #398 , #406 . The recorded boot after it ( #408 ) is the first that no system call stops : it calls 243 imports and keeps running to the time limit. Movies play through the console's movie player, decoded with FFmpeg #419 , #420 ; a real gamepad and keyboard work with --input host #431 ; scripted input lets unattended runs press buttons on a timetable #447 . Kernel details found by boots: priority-ordered semaphores #426 , memory-protection ranges #422 , no-overwrite maps #423 ; later file and network calls #448 , #449 , #450 , #451 . Contributors: @EzequielRindello implemented time , sleep , nanosleep , thread keys, pthread_cond_timedwait and mutex ownership #241 , #296 , #298 , #315 , #351 , #353 ; @evill33t landed loader and macOS groundwork and loading the decompilation's replacements in the runtime 's own boot harness #214 , #215 , #216 , #217 , #218 , #220 , #224 , #225 , #226 , #227 , #229 . The boot recorded after the renderer work ( #443 ): first flip, 243 imports called, 234 of them answered by the runtime , still running at the limit. It runs with the display off and no input. Maintainer's local runs (not saved records): the title screen draws (below), and with scripted input and the then-open #444 the game takes "Play Offline", creates its save data and shows its main menu (6 November). Frames: Milestones . The renderer: from black frames to the title screen. Advances game execution (in local runs with the display on). Phase 1, the display: every frame buffer gets a window or captured image #313 . Phase 2, the shader translator from AMD's GCN code to Vulkan's SPIR-V, written from AMD's manuals: the decoder and a census of the game's 175 instructions #316 , straight-line compute #319 , branches #330 , typed buffers #332 , vertex and pixel shaders #333 , arithmetic #334 , clip distances #343 , guest addresses #346 ; macOS CI compiles every test shader as Metal #331 . Phase 3, hooking the game's own drawing layer: the GPU library's packet writers and key entry points mapped #335 , #341 , a record of its calls per command buffer #342 , #344 , #345 , #401 , and the draw executor that plays them on a Vulkan GPU #349 , #368 , #369 . 6 November, #411 – #442 : @evill33t 's verified GPU-library replacements ( #411 , from #233) report the game's draws to the renderer #414 ; compute passes, tiled textures, sampling, blending, depth, fetch shaders, indexed draws and BC textures followed. docs.text: Tests and validation. Every runtime call above carries synthetic tests (CI); these test the runtime 's answers, not the real boot. The title screen and everything after it are the maintainer's local observations, compared locally with reference frames.

docs.text: Week of 9 November 2026: past the title to character creation In local runs with scripted input the game now gets past its title: save data, the main menu, the Brightness and Controls screens, the opening cinematic in 3D, and character creation; the logos and title run at 30 fps. The runtime checklist is done, function families replace thousands of tiny functions at once (a large share by count, a very small one by bytes), and every function is tagged with its likely source file. Work by @EzequielRindello, @BluePinetree, @evill33t and a lead from @sweetbbak; no new function was verified . This post grows through the week. Runtime and boot progress So far this week: past the title, to character creation (local runs). Advances game execution in the maintainer's local runs; the boot recorded on merged main ( #536 , display off, no input) still waits at the title, as expected without input. With scripted input, the maintainer's local runs take "Play Offline", create the save data, show the main menu and, after New Game, the first-run Brightness and Controls screens; scripted on, the game's opening cinematic draws in 3D, lit, and plays to its end, and the game reaches character creation (the contract screen). Frames: Milestones . The runtime checklist is done. Every system import the boot reaches is answered; the boot record of 10 November ( #536 ) shows 683 of the 686 bound (219 by the game's own modules, 464 by the runtime ). The last three, sceKernelMkdir , sceKernelRmdir and sceKernelUnlink , are @EzequielRindello 's in #455 , merged on 11 November as #555 ; the C library's affinity query is @evill33t 's in #239 . Issues #35 to #41 are closed. Contributors: @EzequielRindello 's sceKernelWrite and sceKernelPwrite ( #444 ), the save code's first writes after "Creating save data", and _exit ( #454 ); @BluePinetree 's check of a module hook 's first bytes before patching, so another libc.elf build is refused by name ( #456 ). A first batch of runtime calls merged on 10 November, each with its own tests: renaming, truncating and folders #458 ; deleting a save and the disc map #459 ; thread join, detach, explicit scheduling and once #460 ; timed mutex and reader-writer locks #464 ; unmapping, protecting and typing memory #467 ; signal masks and thread names #469 ; time zones, RFC 2822 dates and the network tick, and no system events #466 ; the C library's calendar and formatted output for the file library #468 ; the pad's motion settings and an unplugged mouse #462 ; offline PSN authorization and the IP address query #461 ; IPv4 address to text #465 . A second batch answered the rest: directories and flushing #498 ; the four common dialogs, closed at once #500 ; the on-screen keyboard, cancelled, and the browser, not opened #502 ; no microphone, no voice chat, and GNM queries and debug calls #506 ; the remaining PSN services, signed out #507 ; sockets, resolver and HTTP requests with no connection #509 ; the C library's imports from the kernel #513 , #521 ; the maintainer's rulings for page size, process id, the stack canary, exception landing pads, module information and reserved address space #528 ; the last graphics calls, with graphics events raised from the GPU's completion step #532 ; a movie's sound port closing #490 ; file paths kept off small thread stacks, which crashed one boot in five #512 . Audio output with no block: the movie player's sound thread can pass none when it has nothing to give, which stopped a slower run during the opening movie; the call now waits for room and hands nothing over ( #481 ). Renderer: what the menus, the cinematic and character creation need. Advances game execution in local runs. 8- and 16-bit buffer formats, and stops that name the shader ( #457 ): with them the main menu draws. Depth and stencil tests that read the buffer, stencil steps and a depth target larger than the colour target ( #471 ): choosing New Game needed all three; the boot then reaches the Brightness screen. Image descriptors loaded behind a branch ( #474 ), two-channel 8-bit images ( #476 ) and samplers with anisotropy fields but plain filters ( #477 ): the next scene after Controls, the opening cinematic, draws. Speed: one GPU batch per submitted command buffer ( #463 , no measurable change by itself), then the render targets' tiling copies moved to the GPU ( #472 ): the logos and title run at the game's 30 fps cap in local runs, up from about 14, with the JAPAN Studio frame still pixel-identical. Submissions run beside the game, in order ( #488 ): a submit returns at once and the renderer's own thread runs the work, with every "work done" value, wait and flip after the work before it. Compute queues' buffers are taken and dropped ( #470 ). For the rest of the cinematic and character creation: depth-only passes #519 , depth target slices #522 , mip chains and mip-mapped images sampled at the right level #516 , #523 , #526 , stencil replace #524 , several render targets in one draw #533 , the front-face input #537 , targets cleared by a compute shader #539 , more image and float target formats #534 , #492 , #503 , #525 , #530 , more instructions #495 , #501 , buffer accesses checked against their descriptors #494 , #505 , #508 , #540 , and 70 command buffers in one submit #504 . merged #458 runtime : truncate by name, and the POSIX mkdir, rmdir and rename , by @ThisIsAkill . Merged 2026-11-10. System calls: sceKernelTruncate; mkdir; rmdir; rename. Tests: 3 synthetic runtime test(s); the effect on the real boot is measured after merge, so this is not a boot result. docs.title: Week of 9 November 2026: past the title to character creation

docs.text: In local runs with scripted input the game now gets past its title: save data, the main menu, the Brightness and Controls screens, the opening cinematic in 3D, and character creation; the logos and title run at 30 fps. The runtime checklist is done, function families replace thousands of tiny functions at once (a large share by count, a very small one by bytes), and every function is tagged with its likely source file. Work by @EzequielRindello, @BluePinetree, @evill33t and a lead from @sweetbbak; no new function was verified . This post grows through the week.
docs.title: Week of 9 November 2026: past the title to character creation

docs.text: So far this week: past the title, to character creation (local runs). Advances game execution in the maintainer's local runs; the boot recorded on merged main ( #536 , display off, no input) still waits at the title, as expected without input. With scripted input, the maintainer's local runs take "Play Offline", create the save data, show the main menu and, after New Game, the first-run Brightness and Controls screens; scripted on, the game's opening cinematic draws in 3D, lit, and plays to its end, and the game reaches character creation (the contract screen). Frames: Milestones . The runtime checklist is done. Every system import the boot reaches is answered; the boot record of 10 November ( #536 ) shows 683 of the 686 bound (219 by the game's own modules, 464 by the runtime ). The last three, sceKernelMkdir , sceKernelRmdir and sceKernelUnlink , are @EzequielRindello 's in #455 , merged on 11 November as #555 ; the C library's affinity query is @evill33t 's in #239 . Issues #35 to #41 are closed. Contributors: @EzequielRindello 's sceKernelWrite and sceKernelPwrite ( #444 ), the save code's first writes after "Creating save data", and _exit ( #454 ); @BluePinetree 's check of a module hook 's first bytes before patching, so another libc.elf build is refused by name ( #456 ). A first batch of runtime calls merged on 10 November, each with its own tests: renaming, truncating and folders #458 ; deleting a save and the disc map #459 ; thread join, detach, explicit scheduling and once #460 ; timed mutex and reader-writer locks #464 ; unmapping, protecting and typing memory #467 ; signal masks and thread names #469 ; time zones, RFC 2822 dates and the network tick, and no system events #466 ; the C library's calendar and formatted output for the file library #468 ; the pad's motion settings and an unplugged mouse #462 ; offline PSN authorization and the IP address query #461 ; IPv4 address to text #465 . A second batch answered the rest: directories and flushing #498 ; the four common dialogs, closed at once #500 ; the on-screen keyboard, cancelled, and the browser, not opened #502 ; no microphone, no voice chat, and GNM queries and debug calls #506 ; the remaining PSN services, signed out #507 ; sockets, resolver and HTTP requests with no connection #509 ; the C library's imports from the kernel #513 , #521 ; the maintainer's rulings for page size, process id, the stack canary, exception landing pads, module information and reserved address space #528 ; the last graphics calls, with graphics events raised from the GPU's completion step #532 ; a movie's sound port closing #490 ; file paths kept off small thread stacks, which crashed one boot in five #512 . Audio output with no block: the movie player's sound thread can pass none when it has nothing to give, which stopped a slower run during the opening movie; the call now waits for room and hands nothing over ( #481 ). Renderer: what the menus, the cinematic and character creation need. Advances game execution in local runs. 8- and 16-bit buffer formats, and stops that name the shader ( #457 ): with them the main menu draws. Depth and stencil tests that read the buffer, stencil steps and a depth target larger than the colour target ( #471 ): choosing New Game needed all three; the boot then reaches the Brightness screen. Image descriptors loaded behind a branch ( #474 ), two-channel 8-bit images ( #476 ) and samplers with anisotropy fields but plain filters ( #477 ): the next scene after Controls, the opening cinematic, draws. Speed: one GPU batch per submitted command buffer ( #463 , no measurable change by itself), then the render targets' tiling copies moved to the GPU ( #472 ): the logos and title run at the game's 30 fps cap in local runs, up from about 14, with the JAPAN Studio frame still pixel-identical. Submissions run beside the game, in order ( #488 ): a submit returns at once and the renderer's own thread runs the work, with every "work done" value, wait and flip after the work before it. Compute queues' buffers are taken and dropped ( #470 ). For the rest of the cinematic and character creation: depth-only passes #519 , depth target slices #522 , mip chains and mip-mapped images sampled at the right level #516 , #523 , #526 , stencil replace #524 , several render targets in one draw #533 , the front-face input #537 , targets cleared by a compute shader #539 , more image and float target formats #534 , #492 , #503 , #525 , #530 , more instructions #495 , #501 , buffer accesses checked against their descriptors #494 , #505 , #508 , #540 , and 70 command buffers in one submit #504 . merged #458 runtime : truncate by name, and the POSIX mkdir, rmdir and rename , by @ThisIsAkill . docs.text: The Great Ones The research map for boss encounters. Paleblood has not yet identified any boss's internal decision tree or phase code. Profiles Boss Directory What evidence an individual boss profile needs. Read Behavior Boss AI & Phases Visible encounter changes versus the unverified state machines that may cause them. Read Combat Boss Mechanics Attacks, damage, stagger, and arena interactions without turning an impression into a code claim. Read What a boss encounter is made of A boss fight brings together many systems that are studied separately elsewhere: an entity's updates, animation, attack effects, collision, damage, arena events, and the player's response. Start with the evidence we have AI. Paleblood has verified a wrapper that steps the shared Havok AI world. Its internal world update and individual enemy decisions remain unknown. The AI system page explains exactly what that wrapper proves. Other shared systems. The Character , Event , and Physics pages describe other verified pieces that could eventually intersect a boss encounter. They do not yet identify boss-specific behavior. What this page can and cannot claim Every claim in this section is labelled by the kind of evidence behind it. Label Meaning observed Seen during play or in a recording, with its context: starting state, player position and actions, the visible change, and whether it repeats. inferred A conclusion drawn from code or tests, stated with the scope that evidence covers. unknown Not yet traced. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. Absence is not a claim about the game. A missing profile describes the project's research, not what the game contains. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels evidence.

docs.text: Boss AI & Phases A boss can visibly change its movement, attacks, or presentation mid-fight. This page explains what is known about the code behind that, and how a visible change becomes a code-level explanation. At a glance What is verified ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 advances the shared Havok AI world by a fixed 1/30-second step. What is open The AI world update at 0x021cdad0 , its groups and objects, and individual enemy behavior. Boss-specific No state machine, phase trigger, attack choice, or cooldown has been reverse engineered. What the verified wrapper does Each frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 : advances the shared Havok AI world by a fixed 1/30-second step; conditionally copies matrices; conditionally draws debug information. Its tests and recordings establish the wrapper's behavior, not the AI world's internal decisions. The update inside it, at 0x021cdad0 , is where boss decisions would live, and it is still unmapped ( AI system findings ). Observation is not implementation A visible change cannot, by itself, tell us whether a threshold, event, timer, distance check, or random choice caused it. A phase boundary seen in a video, for example, does not establish the field or branch that controls it. To record an encounter for a future study, write down: Record Example of what to note Starting state Where the fight was when the sequence began Player position and actions What the player was doing Visible transition What changed on screen Repeatability Whether it happens again under the same conditions Keep that as an observation. Do not turn it into a claim about a hidden threshold or probability without source evidence. What decompilation must establish To explain a boss phase in implementation terms: Find the entity and the update path that runs it. Trace the transition condition and the data it reads. Verify any claimed timing or attack selection. Cite the exact merged source revision and relevant tests or review records. If only the transition is observable, label it as observed and leave its cause unknown. The Boss Directory has the full profile requirements.
