docs.text: AI The game runs a shared Havok AI world, owned by the SprjHkAiManager singleton. This page covers the once-a-frame update that steps that world and draws its debug display. At a glance Scope The per-frame AI manager update: the world step and the AI debug drawing. Verified ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 steps the AI world by a fixed 1/30 s and gates the debug drawing behind flags. Open The world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, and how individual enemies decide what to do. Summary The game steps a shared Havok AI world through SprjHkAiManager (singleton 0x059401a0 ). The verified wrapper does not establish which enemy or NPC decisions that world supplies. What one frame does Once a frame, ai_hk_frame_update_0222bc10 ( 0x0222bc10 ): Steps the Havok AI world with a fixed time step of 1/30 s. Checks its second flag. It is always set in the recordings. When it is set, the update: copies the frame object's matrices to the manager's view object; resets the render manager's debug state to its defaults and runs the AI debug display and drawing, made of the pieces below. Piece What it uses Debug position the camera's position, or the player character's when the character manager exists Debug marks (not yet detailed) Draw descriptor every AI object in the owner's groups, or the whole manager Axis frames ids looked up in the manager's id map Boxes the box mode at +0x2c68 The time step is a constant, not the measured frame time. Every frame moves the AI world on by 1/30 s however long the frame really took. That is why the frame-rate patches have to change it (see Patch points ). In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic the update resets its three groups, copies the matrices and draws each AI object; the debug display, axis frames, boxes and the manager-wide draw stay off. Scope still to map: the AI world step itself ( 0x021cdad0 ), the groups and objects, the behaviour of individual enemies. What this wrapper does not tell us This verified wrapper establishes how the AI manager is stepped and how its debug drawing is gated. It does not reveal an individual enemy's decisions, attack timing, or boss phases. The current source and evidence contain no basis for those profiles yet; gameplay observations alone will be labeled as observations until their implementation is traced. The AI objects sit two levels down: the owner holds groups, each group holds elements, and each element holds a list of objects. docs.text: Audio The audio system covers sound playback, mixing and music. The game uses the FMOD sound engine; the first of its functions are mapped. At a glance Scope Sound playback, mixing, music. Verified Three FMOD functions are edge-verified against constructed cases: the thread affinity lookup ( 0x0111a8c0 ) and two output callbacks ( 0x0111b060 , 0x0111b0b0 ). Open Playback, mixing and music themselves. Summary FMOD's threads The game plays sound through FMOD, a commercial sound engine. FMOD runs its own threads (mixer, streaming, loading and others), and before it starts one it asks the game which CPU cores that thread may use. audio_fmod_thread_affinity_lookup ( 0x0111a8c0 ) answers: it compares the thread's name against eight known FMOD thread names in a fixed order (the non-blocking one by its first 23 characters only) and copies the matching slot's settings; for any other name it changes nothing and returns 0. How the lookup was verified By @evill33t in #106, brought up to date with main and merged in #272 : its 21 constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it. Several neighbouring helpers in the same address range (string comparisons, the recursive mutex and semaphore wrappers) are FMOD's too; they are described on the Engine and Kernel pages. FMOD's output device FMOD learns about the PS4 's audio output through a table of callbacks the game installs (at 0x0111aed0 ). Two of them are mapped and replaced : audio_fmod_output_driver_count ( 0x0111b060 ) reports one output driver. audio_fmod_output_defaults ( 0x0111b0b0 ) fills in the output's defaults, each only when FMOD asked for it: a setting word, then what looks like a 48 kHz sample rate and FMOD's 5.1 speaker mode. Those two meanings are hypotheses from the values, not yet confirmed from FMOD's use of them. How the callbacks were verified By @evill33t in #114 : both match the original on constructed edge cases (every combination of present and missing outputs), and an independent review approved it. They are edge-verified , not yet verified against recorded game runs. docs.text: The game plays sound through FMOD, a commercial sound engine. FMOD runs its own threads (mixer, streaming, loading and others), and before it starts one it asks the game which CPU cores that thread may use. audio_fmod_thread_affinity_lookup ( 0x0111a8c0 ) answers: it compares the thread's name against eight known FMOD thread names in a fixed order (the non-blocking one by its first 23 characters only) and copies the matching slot's settings; for any other name it changes nothing and returns 0. How the lookup was verified By @evill33t in #106, brought up to date with main and merged in #272 : its 21 constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it. Several neighbouring helpers in the same address range (string comparisons, the recursive mutex and semaphore wrappers) are FMOD's too; they are described on the Engine and Kernel pages.

docs.text: Camera The follow camera: how it turns the stick, the character's movement and a lock-on target into a camera position each frame, how it keeps out of walls, and where its field of view comes from. At a glance Scope Camera update, targeting and lock-on, collision with the world, field of view. Verified The whole follow-camera update, camera_update_follow (20 KB), and the pitch and yaw getters are replaced and edge-verified , each with an independent review. Our option BB_TARGET_FPS (30, 60, uncapped) reproduces what the frame-rate patches change in the update. Open Who calls the update and sets its requests, the parameter table's other fields, and what the camera looks like in the running game. Summary What the follow camera does each frame camera_update_follow ( 0x0183ac60 ) takes the camera, the character it follows (the subject ), a world to cast spheres against, and the frame's time step. It works in stages: Parameters. It picks a row from the lock-camera parameter table and eases the camera toward it: distance, lowest pitch, lock-on pitch shift, height above the subject and vertical field of view. The row's key is the map's ID, replaced in turn by an event ID, a boss ID while a boss lock is requested, and an explicit override, whichever are set; failing that, key 0. It also sets rotation speeds from an option rate (squared, between a minimum and a maximum). With no subject the update stops here. Carry-along. It moves last frame's camera and subject points by a stored velocity and turns them by a stored angular velocity around a pivot that it reaches through the subject. Stick. It reads a stick vector from the subject, or a default one. Stick input marks the camera as hand-controlled. Once the stick is released, a wait and then a release time hand control back. Target. It chases the subject's position and places the target point at the subject plus the parameter row's offset. The camera's pivot ( fulcrum ) and its first position guess (the candidate ) move with the subject. Angles. Exactly one of these sets pitch and yaw: reset: stored reset angles, or level pitch and the subject's heading; lock-on: aim at the lock target (below); front lock: turn smoothly to the subject's heading for up to a set time. It ends when the time runs out, when the angles come within a small tolerance, or on stick input. (The name is ours; we take it to be "reset the camera behind the character".) free: stick input times the rotation speed. Pitch stays between a minimum and a maximum. Pushing the stick hard up or down past a set angle ramps into a faster rotation that also moves pitch directly toward its limit. Afterwards, unless the camera is locked on or in front lock, pitch drifts back toward a target pitch. 6. Placement and collision. It builds the look direction from the angles and keeps the fulcrum at its distance from the target. Sideways movement of the subject shortens that distance, between a minimum and a maximum rate. Then it avoids walls in one of two ways (see Keeping out of walls ). 7. Chase. The final position eases toward the candidate. Up and down chase at one rate, the ground plane at another, and both depend on how far the direction has swung: below a minimum angle only the height follows, above a maximum angle both follow fully. Right after stick rotation the camera follows at once. 8. Orientation and checks. It builds the camera's axes and casts a sphere from the target to the final position. It clears the one-frame requests (reset, lock, boss lock, front lock). If any axis or the position is not a number, it restores the whole previous frame. Then it pushes the camera out of territories (below) and pulls it a safety margin toward the target. Targeting and lock-on While a lock is requested, the camera aims from its orbit point at a stored lock-target point. The pitch is raised by a shift that grows with the field of view and the row's lock-pitch-shift ratio, plus an angle from the distances involved. The pitch limits blend from the lock-on limits to the normal limits as the height difference to the target grows. The angles chase the goal at a lock rotation rate. Inside a dead angle the camera does not move. If lock adjustment is enabled, the stick nudges pitch and yaw up to a set maximum. The update does not choose the target: it only reads the point and the request flags. Keeping out of walls A global byte ( 0x05527a94 , which we call the wall camera mode) picks one of two methods: Zero: pull in. A sphere is cast from the target to the fulcrum, then to the candidate. On a hit the point moves to where the sphere stopped, but no closer than a minimum. Non-zero: swing away. Two wing spheres are cast at a set angle to each side of the camera's line to the target. If exactly one hits, an escape yaw builds up and turns the camera away from that side. It builds at a strong rate while the hit is close, easing toward a weak rate as the hit lies farther along the probe. The swing is speed-limited, fades when nothing new is hit, and switches the chase rates to escape rates, which ease back afterwards. Stick input, lock-on, front lock and reset switch the swing off. In both modes the final position gets one more sphere cast (step 8). Territories are spheres in a list the update reaches through a global ( 0x0593e858 ). Each has a centre and a one-byte radius. If the camera is inside an enabled one, it moves back along its view axis to the sphere's surface, then a sphere cast checks the new position. A debug flag draws them. Field of view The vertical field of view ( +0x50 , radians) eases toward the parameter row's value in degrees. Below a minimum the row's value is replaced by a fixed minimum. Above a maximum it is capped at 48°. A flag raises the target point toward the height that half the view angle covers at the current distance, going halfway to it, so the subject stays in frame. Which way the follow camera looks The follow camera keeps its orientation as a direction it is looking along. Two small functions turn that into angles: camera_follow_pitch ( 0x0183fad0 ) gives the up-down angle, from the direction's height against its length across the ground (an atan2 ), negated; camera_follow_yaw ( 0x0183fb20 ) gives the left-right angle, from the direction's two ground components. When the direction has no length to measure (both components zero), each falls back to the angle it stored last time instead of computing a meaningless one. How these were verified camera_update_follow : by @evill33t in #112, merged in #489 (commit 9786f4b9 ). 72 constructed edge cases pass against the original on stock code and under each BB_TARGET_FPS option (30, 60, uncapped) against the matching patch: 72/72 in all four runs. The cases cover both wall modes, the reset, lock and front-lock flags, chase limits, the safety margin, parameter selection with no subject, territories and their debug drawing, frame-time edge values, sphere-cast hits and misses, and callbacks that change the camera mid-update. An independent review rebuilt the change, reran every case and checked that deliberately planted mistakes are caught. It approved the change. camera_follow_pitch and camera_follow_yaw : by @evill33t in #109, merged in #280 . 32 and 30 edge cases pass, including not-a-number directions, and an independent review approved them. All three are edge-verified only. No camera behaviour has been recorded in the running game. The field names describe what the update does with each field; they are ours, not the game's. Offset Fields +0x10 , +0x50 , +0x60 camera transform (axes and position); vertical field of view (radians); subject transform +0xa0 – +0x110 points: target reference, target, cast origin, orbit origin, fulcrum, candidate, chased position; velocity +0x13c – +0x15c reset requests; pitch and yaw ( +0x140 , read by the getters); target pitch; hand control +0x180 – +0x234 distances, sphere radius, safety margin; chase rates and angles (normal, escape, lock-on); pitch limits; rotation speeds +0x240 – +0x288 lock-on: rotation rate, dead angle, pitch shift, target point ( +0x250 ), requests ( +0x260 – +0x262 ), front-lock timer and angles, stick adjustment +0x28c – +0x2e0 wall escape (mode, yaw, rates, wing shape, hit fractions); territory flags and working transform +0x320 – +0x344 parameter IDs (override, event, boss lock, map) and chase rate; stick source; raise target with the field of view Lock-camera parameter row: camera distance ( +0x0 ), lowest pitch in degrees ( +0x4 ), lock-pitch shift ratio ( +0x8 ), height above the subject ( +0xc ), vertical field of view in degrees ( +0x14 ). The table hangs off the solo parameter repository ( 0x05940340 ), at +0x9c0 (present when +0x9b8 is non-zero). The update reads three of its storage formats. Globals: one-shot event and boss-lock IDs ( 0x05956678 , +0x14 and +0x18 ), cleared every update; the wall camera mode ( 0x05527a94 ); the territory list ( 0x0593e858 ); the default stick vector ( 0x04b38000 ). The world sphere cast is 0x01c090e0 . Patch points The frame-rate patches edit camera_update_follow . While our replacement is installed, its original bytes never run, so a patch line inside it does nothing. BB_TARGET_FPS rebuilds the same changes in code (see Frame timing ): Where Original 30 FPS++ / option 30 60 FPS++ , Uncap FPS++ / options 60, uncapped 12 sites ( 0x0183ae75 , 0x0183af8c , 0x0183ba97 , 0x0183bc9b , 0x0183c30f , 0x0183c784 , 0x0183cef0 , 0x0183e2b2 , 0x0183e7da , 0x0183e964 , 0x0183f97e , 0x0183fa9f ) fixed per-frame rates (parameters, distance, subject and target chase, lock and front-lock rotation, target-pitch drift, direct pitch, escape easing) unchanged each rate is rescaled from the measured frame time, capped at 1/60 s (1/30 s for parameter and escape easing) 0x0183dc96 , 0x0183dcfe when both wings miss, the escape mode becomes 1; with the wall mode off, only the escape mode is cleared mode 0; with the wall mode off, the chase rates switch to the escape rates same 0x04d25e94 (constant) escape easing step 1/15 1/30 0x04d25e68 (constant) camera-distance easing rate 0.1 0.1 The two constants lie outside the function, so those patch lines still apply with the replacement installed: the option runs together with the patch, which supplies them, as it does for the other functions the option covers. 90 FPS++ and 120 FPS++ edit the same sites; we have no option for them. Three other kinds of patch edit the function too, and also do nothing while it is replaced ; none has a matching option. Disable Camera Auto Rotation via Movement blanks four instructions ( 0x0183c6e8 , 0x0183c870 , 0x0183c984 , 0x0183dde6 ). Increased camera distance , Smaller Hunter and Smallest Hunter jump out at 0x0183ae68 (the last two also at 0x0183aeef ); the first appears to scale the target camera distance by 1.5. Open questions Who calls camera_update_follow , and who sets the lock target, the lock and front-lock requests and the wall camera mode? Does the front lock really match the "camera behind the character" button? Is the wall mode a menu option? The other fields of the parameter row ( +0x10 is skipped) and the parameter file's identity. What the carry-along pivot is (a moving platform or a mount, for example). Its velocity fields are set elsewhere. Which of the 12 frame-rate sites carries which rate: the table matches them by count, not site by site. Which stage the auto-rotation patch's four sites belong to. 0x0183a0e0 , just before the update, is edited by the distance, Hunter-size and frame-rate patches. It is not mapped. What the camera does in the running game: nothing has been recorded beyond constructed cases.

docs.text: Character Every character instance in the game is updated once a frame. This page covers one of those updates: throw events, the regeneration of a points stat, and the hand-off of frame time to the character's modules. At a glance Scope character_frame_update_01cbdb20 , one of the per-frame updates of a character instance. Verified character_frame_update_01cbdb20 is verified : the throw event, the points regeneration with its fractional carry, and the frame-time hand-off. Open Whether the points stat is stamina, whether the update belongs only to the player, and the rest of the instance layout. Summary Character instances ( ChrIns in FromSoftware's engine) are updated once a frame through virtual calls on each instance. character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 ) is one of these updates. What the update does Fires a pending throw animation event ( W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef ) and clears the request. Regenerates a points stat that floors at -50 and caps at a maximum (see below). It reads like stamina. Hands the frame time to the character's modules , copies a few parameters, and builds (then drops) a wide string of the character's name with the thread's allocator. Nothing reads the string; it looks like the remains of debug code. In the recordings from Iosefka's Clinic the name string is never built. How the points stat regenerates The regeneration rate is a product of four terms: Text Only rate = parameter byte × 0.01 × per-character multiplier × virtual factor The multiplier lives at +0x16c on the instance, and the last rate is kept at +0x39c . Each frame the update: multiplies the rate by the frame time (read from +0xe0 ); adds the whole part of the result to the points (data module +0x134 ), capped at the maximum ( +0x138 ); keeps the fraction at +0x168 and adds it in on the next frame. Carrying the fraction means a rate too small to add a whole point in one frame still adds up over several frames instead of being rounded away. Two switches stop the stat from dropping: bit 7 of the data module's +0x200 , and the debug flag 0x0593e88a next to the WorldChrManDbg singleton. Points, stamina and the player The source calls this value points . Its relationship to stamina, and whether this update belongs only to the player, are not established. The current evidence-backed account is in Stats & Progression . Scope still to map: the character instance layout, the modules ( +0x3b0 ), the parameters, the other per-frame updates. docs.text: Engine The engine's shared plumbing that every system leans on: its fatal error report, its check for missing singletons, its reference-counted objects, and small helpers such as writing a line to the standard error stream. At a glance Scope Engine-wide helpers in Paleblood's game/engine/ : the fatal error report and singleton check, reference counting, and replaced engine utility functions. Verified engine_write_stderr , the string helpers (comparisons, appends, case changes), wide-string set-up, owner storage, a word-and-product store and a handle-table lookup are edge-verified against constructed cases. Open Who calls the stderr writer during play, and with what text. Summary What every system shares Most replaced functions lean on a few engine-wide pieces: The fatal error report ( 0x024b55b0 ) takes a source file, a line and a message. In the shipped game it logs and returns , so the code after it keeps running; Ghidra wrongly treats it as never returning (see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks ). The singleton check. Many systems are singletons ( FrpgNetMan , SprjEventFlagMan , ...). Code that needs one reports it by name through the fatal error report when it is missing, then reads it again and uses whatever is there. Reference-counted objects ( DLReferenceCountObject ). An object counts its holders; dropping the last reference destroys it through its first virtual function, and dropping one more than it has is reported as an invalid unref. The render frame update and the Chalice Dungeon gate's handle share this code ( #185 ). Writing to standard error engine_write_stderr ( 0x0111a740 ) writes a text to the standard error stream: it reads the C library's stderr once, passes the text to fputs , ignores the result, and returns 0. How the stderr writer was verified By @evill33t in #113, brought up to date with main and merged in #205 . Its 28 constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it; no frame-rate patch edits it. It has not been checked on frames recorded from a real game run. Comparing strings Two byte-string comparisons compare signed bytes and return the difference at the first mismatch: engine_compare_signed_strings ( 0x011c4970 ) runs to the end of the strings, and engine_compare_signed_prefix ( 0x011c4990 ) stops after a length, still comparing the first byte when the length is zero or negative. All their callers are in FMOD's code (see Audio ). More string helpers Since 4 November the engine's small C-string helpers are mapped too, by @evill33t : engine_string_length ( 0x011c47f0 , a strlen whose result is cut to 32 bits, #288 ), engine_ascii_to_upper_in_place and engine_ascii_to_lower_in_place ( 0x011c4910 , 0x011c4940 : change letters in place and return the string, #281 ), and engine_compare_ascii_ignoring_case ( 0x011c49c0 , compares two strings ignoring letter case, #282 ). Three more followed on 5 and 6 November, also by @evill33t : engine_string_append ( 0x011c4870 ) appends one zero-terminated string to another, a strcat that returns the destination ( #337 , from #118); engine_string_append_counted ( 0x011c48b0 ) appends at most a given number of bytes, counting only the low 32 bits of the count, and ends the result with a zero; a count of zero touches neither string ( #337 ); engine_ascii_to_lower ( 0x011c48f0 ) lowercases a single character: it changes A - Z to a - z , leaves every other byte as it is, and returns the byte as a signed 32-bit value ( #125 ). Wide strings and owned storage engine_wide_string_destroy ( 0x02a44140 ) releases a wide (16-bit character) string, and engine_initialize_static_wide_string_0217ffb0 sets up one static wide string the first time it is needed, guarded so it happens once ( #284 ). engine_release_owner_storage and engine_resize_owner_storage ( 0x0132c590 , 0x0132c6c0 ) free an object's storage block through its allocator, or replace it with a new 16-byte-aligned block of the requested size ( #285 ). What kind of object owns the block is not known yet; its only known caller is 0x02713870 . Storing a word and a product engine_store_word_product ( 0x011c4510 ) stores two 32-bit fields of an object: one input as it is at offset 0x18 , and the product of two other inputs times four at offset 0x1c , then returns 0 ( #336 , from #115 by @evill33t ). What the two fields mean is not known yet; it is called from 0x01111bb0 and through slot 1 of the function table at 0x0500ae48 . Looking up a table entry by handle engine_entry_manager_resolve ( 0x01314320 ) turns a handle into an entry: it checks that the table is enabled, rejects the all-ones handle, uses the handle's low 32 bits as an index checked against the table's capacity, and rejects an empty entry. Its callers are a family of functions at 0x02717f30 - 0x02718c80 and 0x0210f5a0 ; what the table holds is not known yet. How these were verified By @evill33t : the comparisons in #107, merged in #274 (18 and 24 cases), and the lookup in #110, merged in #276 (25 cases). Each was brought up to date with main , its constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it. The appends ( #337 , 32 and 48 cases), the word-and-product store ( #336 , 32 cases) and the single-character lowercase ( #125 , 291 generated cases) are edge-verified : their constructed cases pass against the original. None was checked on recorded game runs. docs.text: Event The event system keeps the game's event entries, runs its Lua event scripts and stores its event flags. This page covers how an event entry is found or added, and how one event flag bit is written. At a glance Scope SprjEmkSystem (event entries), SprjLuaEventMan (Lua event scripts) and SprjEventFlagMan (event flags). Verified event_emk_add is verified ; event_flag_write is edge-verified against constructed cases. Open What the two entry lists hold, what the ids mean, and what any real flag ID means in play. Summary The game's event system is three managers working together: Manager What it keeps SprjEmkSystem event entries, kept in keyed lists SprjLuaEventMan the Lua event scripts SprjEventFlagMan event flags Adding an event entry event_emk_add ( 0x016efd00 ) is the way into the entry lists: It looks for an event entry by id and sub-id in two linked lists. If there is none, it allocates, constructs and inserts one in key order. It advances a new entry once by a fixed 1/30 s step. It runs hundreds of times in a minute of gameplay in Iosefka's Clinic. Writing an event flag event_flag_write ( 0x017cfcc0 ) changes one stored bit. Flags are stored in groups, so the function first works out which group holds the flag, then which bit in that group: It divides the flag ID by the store's configured flags-per-group value. It finds an exact matching group in a keyed tree. It selects either a direct storage pointer or a stride-based offset into shared storage. It sets or clears the bit. Within a byte, flags are numbered from the most significant bit; a nonzero enabled argument sets the selected bit and zero clears it while retaining its neighbors. A missing group, unsupported storage kind, or null storage pointer leaves memory unchanged. Reading a flag follows the same path. Since #199 the store's layout and lookup are shared code, also used to read flags: an ID that is negative as a signed 32-bit number, a missing group or missing storage reads as a clear flag. The game itself inlines this read where it needs it; one such place is the Chalice Dungeon gate state's level creation (see Frame timing ). This replacement is edge-verified , not fully verified : it matches the original on constructed edge cases , not on recorded gameplay. How the flag write was verified The merged source and layout and verification record report matching original-instruction results on 14 constructed edge fixtures. Those cover tree search paths, byte boundaries, set/clear operations, missing groups, and storage selection. Since #199 the write uses the shared store code and was recorded again on 15 fixtures, one more with a group size that is not a power of two. What the fixtures do not establish They do not identify a real flag ID's gameplay meaning, establish a zero group-size contract, or replace recorded gameplay cases. No fixture was rerun for this article. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x016efd00 368 event_emk_add verified SprjEmkSystem: find or add an event entry in two keyed lists; first advance with the 1/30 s step (1/60 s in the 60 FPS patches) 0x017cfcc0 177 event_flag_write edge-verified finds an exact event-flag group in a tree and sets or clears one bit Structs and globals Event entry (0xe0 bytes): Offset Field +0x0 vtable; slot +0x10 advances the entry by a frame-time descriptor +0x28 id +0x2c sub-id (16-bit) +0x70 next entry Patch points 60 FPS++ , 60FPS (no deltatime) and 90 FPS++ change the first advance's 1/30 s step to 1/60 s in 0x016efd00 ; BB_TARGET_FPS=60 does the same. The patches are described in Frame timing . Open questions What the two lists hold (pending and active entries?), and what the ids are.

This replacement is edge-verified , not fully verified : it matches the original on constructed edge cases , not on recorded gameplay. How the flag write was verified The merged source and layout and verification record report matching original-instruction results on 14 constructed edge fixtures. Those cover tree search paths, byte boundaries, set/clear operations, missing groups, and storage selection. Since #199 the write uses the shared store code and was recorded again on 15 fixtures, one more with a group size that is not a power of two. What the fixtures do not establish They do not identify a real flag ID's gameplay meaning, establish a zero group-size contract, or replace recorded gameplay cases. No fixture was rerun for this article.

docs.text: Frame timing How the game paces its frames: a frame step that runs once a frame, a frame limiter that waits out each frame's budget, and a task manager that runs the frame's work. At a glance Scope Frame pacing, delta time, vsync and the main loop's time step. Verified The frame step, the frame limiter, the flipper constructor and the task manager's frame path are replaced and verified . Our option BB_TARGET_FPS does in code what the community frame-rate patches do in these functions. Open A few limiter fields, the owner of the 0x0111a... clock layer, and most functions the 60 FPS patches edit. Summary next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work The frame step frame_timing_frame_step ( 0x02418d20 ) runs once per frame. In order, it: checks that the SprjWindow is running; creates the SprjFlipper singleton on first use ( frame_timing_flipper_init , 0x02434520 ); runs the frame limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ), a method of that flipper; runs the task update with a small 1/30 s descriptor; asks a quit gate and a quit query, and returns whether the game keeps running. Both the limiter and the frame step are replaced and verified . The frame limiter Each frame the limiter does four things. It applies the flip mode. The constructor reads the mode from the config value Game.FlipMode . A pending mode at +0xc replaces the current one at +0x8 when +0x276 is set. The mode chooses the sync interval (stored at +0x10 ) and the frame interval (a float at +0x18 ): Flip mode Sync interval Frame interval 0 and 1 2 1/30 s 2 1 1/60 s 3 and 4 1 1/30 s It reads the time with gettimeofday , in microseconds. It waits out the frame's budget , shortened when recent frames ran late. A switch in the build ( 0x013e3980 , always 1) selects the spinning wait, which polls the clock without sleeping (hundreds of thousands of reads in a long frame). A sleeping wait is compiled in but unused. It keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring (index at +0x260 ) and derives a frame rate from their average ( +0x2b8 ). Which clock the game reads gettimeofday supplies wall time, so it is not guaranteed to be monotonic. The frame limiter's confirmed call passes a null timezone pointer. The game's separate verified clock helper invokes sceKernelClockGettime with ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC ; that does not establish the IDs accepted by the imported libc clock_gettime wrapper. See the runtime system-call notes . Two other clock functions are easy to mistake for part of the limiter: 0x004632d0 is a small gettimeofday helper in microseconds that the stock game never calls: nothing calls it directly, and no relocated pointer (vtable or table slot) points at it. The frame-rate patches overwrite it and its neighbours with their own code (a code cave), so it is not replaced . The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 ( replaced too, edge-verified , by @evill33t in #103 ) and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 (now replaced , see below) are not on the limiter's path. They look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem. Correction (2026-10-06): the 0x0111a... clocks are a separate layer The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. All 52 of their callers sit in one region ( 0x0110e... - 0x0121b... ) that shares its own helpers, and no frame-rate patch touches any of them: they look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem (unidentified; possibly middleware). Their system label may move once that subsystem is known. The fixed-step state methods Many small objects in the game advance in fixed steps of 1/30 s, whatever the real frame time is. The community "60 FPS++" patch changes those steps to 1/60 s, so knowing exactly which functions it edits, and what each belongs to, is part of running the game faster than 30 FPS. Paleblood has replaced a growing set of them in game/frame_timing/fixed_step_states.cpp . The latest belong to the Chalice Dungeon gate , the object behind the ritual altar: Its steps have names. The gate ( SprjDungeonGateIns ) keeps a table of 24 steps whose names are in the executable. They give its states their meaning: loading a channel, no chalice, a local or online ritual, a local or online dungeon, and an error display. Finding the gate. The game finds the current gate through SprjHolygrail . The highest of seven event flags, 9020 to 9026, picks one of eight gate slots; with none set, it uses the last slot. Waiting for it. Two methods advance the gate while it is busy and are done once it is idle. Two more wait until it is idle in a dungeon mode, or in a ritual mode. Leaving a mode. One method, held by an object that points to the gate, takes the gate out of a ritual or dungeon mode (request 7) and out of the error mode (request 10), around a check on the gate that reads the online manager, and reports when the check passes in the online dungeon mode. What its caller does with that answer is not known: the caller ignores it. The check itself. It passes only when the gate is idle in mode 1 (no Holy Chalice), four bytes of the online manager ( FrpgNetMan ) allow it (one set, three clear; what they mean is not known), and the id it is given is set. It then looks up an object for that id and keeps it as the gate's handle, a reference-counted pointer: the engine counts how many holders an object has and destroys it when the last one lets go, so swapping the handle drops the old object's count and takes one on the new. Finally, if the gate is still idle, it gives the gate request 6 and reports success. That the id names an online session is a guess. Its sibling, the entry check. It opens with the same gates, then searches a list for the first entry with a given key that holds an object, and keeps that object as the gate's handle in the same way, with request 4 instead of 6. When the gate becomes busy while the old handle is let go, it stops and reports failure rather than trying the next entry. Letting the handle go again. In a ritual mode a third method resets the handle. In the local ritual mode it always may; in the server ritual mode only when the online manager's bytes allow it and a flag bit in the handled object is clear. It clears one word of that object, hands the handle to a routine not yet analyzed ( 0x01e9cb80 ), and gives the gate request 8. A fourth method does the same under the same rules but first gathers the gate's sixteen slots: each active one goes into a short list (its key, its number, and a value the caller supplies for it), built on one of the engine's memory heaps. With no active slot it does nothing; otherwise it hands the handle and the list on ( 0x01e9cd20 , not yet analyzed), gives request 8, and then frees the list's memory. Passing the handle on. A readiness check lets the gate go on when it is idle in a ritual or dungeon mode and the online manager allows it; in the server modes the handled object must also have one word at zero. Two methods that differ only in a "kind" number (1 or 2) run that check, clear two words of the handled object, hand the handle on with the kind (to one routine in the local modes, another in the server modes, neither analyzed yet), and give request 9. Creating the handle. Two methods make the handle in the first place, both only while the gate is idle in mode 1. One drops the old handle, builds a new handled object from two blocks of data, a block of the online manager and a name (the current name entry's, or a default), and gives request 3. The other reads four "levels" from event flags: for each of four base flags, the highest level from 9 down to 1 whose flag is set (flag numbers 6228 to 6287, every seventh one belonging to the same column). It builds the handled object from those four levels and gives request 5. What the levels and the flags stand for in the game is not known yet. The millisecond sleep wrapper ( 0x0111a880 ), which is not on the limiter's path, is replaced too. It converts the engine's millisecond delay to the kernel's microseconds. It multiplies in 32 bits, as the original does, so very large delays wrap, and it always reports success. Fixed-step methods: PRs, contributors and evidence #104 by @evill33t : the millisecond sleep wrapper. #138 : five SprjDungeonGateIns methods that step the gate's state ( 0x01eb5390 , 0x01eb5490 , and the event handlers at 0x01eb9020 , 0x01ebb090 , 0x01ebf060 ). #141 : four methods that find the gate through SprjHolygrail ( 0x0200f970 , 0x020118f0 , 0x01f03210 , 0x01f03680 ). #182 : the method that leaves the gate's modes around the check 0x01ea5280 ( 0x01ec3ef0 , eleven 60 FPS++ edits). #186 : the check itself ( 0x01ea5280 , one 60 FPS++ edit), using the engine's shared reference counting from #185 . #188 : the entry check ( 0x01ea4a10 , one 60 FPS++ edit). Part of it sits in bytes the decompiler leaves out after an error report; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks . #192 : the ritual handle reset ( 0x01ea5670 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #194 : the ritual slot reset ( 0x01ea5850 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #196 : the readiness check ( 0x01ea5c90 ) and the two pass-on methods ( 0x01ea5e20 , 0x01ea6080 ; one 60 FPS++ edit each). #198 : the handle creation ( 0x01ea47a0 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #199 : the level creation ( 0x01ea4cb0 , one 60 FPS++ edit), with the event-flag store shared with the event system. Status: replaced , not verified . Each was compared with the original function on authored edge cases , stock and with the 60 FPS++ edits, and wrong variants were rejected. None was checked on frames recorded from a real game run. Small clocks, waits and stopwatches Nine small helpers that read the time or sleep are replaced and edge-verified (Paleblood #514 ). None of them is on the limiter's path: Time of day. frame_timing_time_of_day_us ( 0x02e61140 ) gives the time of day in microseconds; frame_timing_time_of_day_ticks ( 0x01088550 ) divides it by an owner's own tick length; frame_timing_time_seed_words ( 0x02e61280 ) returns four seed words, the time itself and the time plus a counter that steps by two on every call, so two calls in the same microsecond still differ. Random state. frame_timing_thread_random ( 0x02c6d580 ) returns the calling thread's random number state (a thread-local variable), seeding it the first time from the low 32 bits of the time in microseconds. About sixty callers fetch it. Stopwatch. frame_timing_stopwatch_start ( 0x01448580 ) stores the seconds since the game started, only when the stopwatch reads exactly zero; frame_timing_stopwatch_stop ( 0x01448620 ) adds the time since that start to two running totals. The task frame brackets work with them. Waiting for a job. frame_timing_job_wait ( 0x024bdd40 ) polls a background job's state until it is finished, sleeping 1 ms between polls; frame_timing_job_take_result ( 0x024bd150 ) takes a job's result, polling, waiting or taking at once depending on its mode, and counts one more holder of the result under a lock all jobs share. Sleep. frame_timing_posix_sleep_ms ( 0x00466810 ) sleeps through the POSIX usleep and always reports success. The community Performance Patch turns the stopwatch into a no-op and shortens the job waits' poll to 0.1 ms. Those byte edits do nothing while these functions are replaced , and there is no option for them yet. How these were verified Each function's edge cases pass against the original (10 to 55 cases each), deliberately wrong versions fail, and an independent review approved all nine. They are edge-verified : none has been recorded in a game run. Frame time in game logic The frame step also passes time into character updates. One verified update accumulates a per-frame points value using that time and retains fractional progress between frames. Its evidence and unresolved stat identity are documented in Stats & Progression . The task manager's frame Each frame, the frame step hands the frame's work to FD4::FD4TaskManager (singleton 0x058b2e30 ). The path is a good example of how an engine brackets its work so that nothing runs twice or half-finished: 0x024512a0 fetches the task manager and runs every task group ( 0x01388c60 , mask -1 ). 0x01388c70 refuses to start while a frame is already running (a busy flag at +0x38 ). It flushes the task queue that collected work since the last frame ( 0x0143e490 : lock, run each queued object, destroy and free it, empty the list, unlock), steps the worker threads' queues ( 0x014400a0 ), and publishes the frame's value ( 0x0143f9f0 copies a float from the frame's information to a global). With the busy flag set, it calls the dispatcher ( +0x40 , virtual +0x30 ), which runs the frame's tasks; then it clears the flag, flushes the second queue and steps the workers again. The dispatcher ( 0x0138a370 ) is the last link: when its group record asks for it, it wakes every registered task (76 in Iosefka's Clinic), then fills a job with the record, the task table and the group mask and runs it through the same five steps as the workers. Each of those tasks is a piece of the game's own per-frame work, the next layer to map. Every override is skipped: the reset flag ( +0x2c4 ), the two override counters ( +0x2bc , +0x2c0 ) and the two clear flags ( +0x271 , +0x272 ). At the end the sync interval ( +0x10 ) is kept on late frames instead of zeroed. Frame step ( 0x02418d20 ): the frame time passed to the task update starts at 1/60 s (30: 1/30 s), and when the flipper's interval is not 1/30 s it becomes the measured frame time ( +0x264 ) clamped to [interval, 1/30 s]. This is the patches' delta time: the game logic advances by how long the frame really took. The patch drops the SprjTask check to make room. Flipper constructor ( 0x02434520 ): the first interval is 1/60 s (60 and 90). They also edit 59 other functions; 12 of them are dead code in the stock game (no caller, no relocated pointer). Many of the rest pass the same 1/30 s frame-time descriptor to an owner object, which the 60 FPS patches change to 1/60 s. The patches also rewrite dozens of shared constants in the data segment (the 1/30 s step at 0x04d29170 becomes 1/60 s, 1/90 s or, uncapped, 1/60 s), which code we have not replaced reads too. BB_TARGET_FPS covers only the replaced functions, so it is meant to run together with the patch; option checks run both sides on the patched image for that reason. How the patch edits were mapped tools/patch_overlap.py maps every patch line to the function it falls in, and lists the patches that do nothing while our hooks are installed. Our option: BB_TARGET_FPS BB_TARGET_FPS=30 , 60 or uncapped does in code what 30 FPS++ , 60 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ do in the three functions above. Unset keeps the original behaviour exactly. The option has to cover the frame step as well as the limiter. A faster limiter alone would still tell the game logic that every frame lasts 1/30 s; the delta time comes from the frame step (see the patch points above). The other functions the patches edit are not replaced yet, so a 60 FPS game would still need the community patch for them; its edits inside our three functions do not run, and our option does their part. A second option, BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep , makes the limiter use the sleeping wait the game carries but never selects: it sleeps until about 5 ms before the frame's end and spins the rest, so a fast machine does not keep a core busy waiting. How the option is checked against the patches Each part is checked against the patch itself: tools/verify.py run --patch FILE:NAME --env BB_TARGET_FPS=... runs the original with the patch's bytes applied against our replacement with the option, on the edge cases and on frames recorded in the game at 60 FPS. Recorded frame times at 60 FPS (October 7) A saved October 7 measurement with the external host scaffold, all replacements hooked, and BB_TARGET_FPS=60 reports a median frame time of 16.67 ms and p99 of 16.69 ms. That historical result is recorded in Paleblood's status evidence ; it is not a real-display result from Paleblood's project-owned boot path. History: the first version changed only the limiter An earlier version only changed the limiter. Because the hooked frame step no longer ran the patches' delta-time code, at 60 FPS the game logic would still have been told every frame lasts 1/30 s; checking against the patches found that, and that the limiter's own settings differed. Open questions What +0x14 and the counters at +0x268 / +0x26c mean (the latter set how many recent late frames the catch-up sums). Which subsystem the 0x0111a... clock layer belongs to. What each live function the 60 FPS patches edit belongs to, and which run in gameplay.
docs.title: Frame timing

docs.text: How the game paces its frames: a frame step that runs once a frame, a frame limiter that waits out each frame's budget, and a task manager that runs the frame's work. At a glance Scope Frame pacing, delta time, vsync and the main loop's time step. Verified The frame step, the frame limiter, the flipper constructor and the task manager's frame path are replaced and verified . Our option BB_TARGET_FPS does in code what the community frame-rate patches do in these functions. Open A few limiter fields, the owner of the 0x0111a... clock layer, and most functions the 60 FPS patches edit.
docs.title: Frame timing

docs.text: next frame frame_timing_frame_step 0x02418d20 · once per frame SprjWindow running? else the game ends frame_timing_flipper_init 0x02434520 · first frame: Game.FlipMode frame_timing_pace_frame 0x02434770 · the frame limiter wait out the frame gettimeofday spin (1/30 or 1/60 s) task update 0x024512a0 · the game's frame of work
docs.title: Summary

docs.text: frame_timing_frame_step ( 0x02418d20 ) runs once per frame. In order, it: checks that the SprjWindow is running; creates the SprjFlipper singleton on first use ( frame_timing_flipper_init , 0x02434520 ); runs the frame limiter, frame_timing_pace_frame ( 0x02434770 ), a method of that flipper; runs the task update with a small 1/30 s descriptor; asks a quit gate and a quit query, and returns whether the game keeps running. Both the limiter and the frame step are replaced and verified .
docs.title: The frame step

docs.text: Each frame the limiter does four things. It applies the flip mode. The constructor reads the mode from the config value Game.FlipMode . A pending mode at +0xc replaces the current one at +0x8 when +0x276 is set. The mode chooses the sync interval (stored at +0x10 ) and the frame interval (a float at +0x18 ): Flip mode Sync interval Frame interval 0 and 1 2 1/30 s 2 1 1/60 s 3 and 4 1 1/30 s It reads the time with gettimeofday , in microseconds. It waits out the frame's budget , shortened when recent frames ran late. A switch in the build ( 0x013e3980 , always 1) selects the spinning wait, which polls the clock without sleeping (hundreds of thousands of reads in a long frame). A sleeping wait is compiled in but unused. It keeps the last 32 frame times in a ring (index at +0x260 ) and derives a frame rate from their average ( +0x2b8 ).
docs.title: The frame limiter

docs.text: gettimeofday supplies wall time, so it is not guaranteed to be monotonic. The frame limiter's confirmed call passes a null timezone pointer. The game's separate verified clock helper invokes sceKernelClockGettime with ID 4 , identified as CLOCK_MONOTONIC ; that does not establish the IDs accepted by the imported libc clock_gettime wrapper. See the runtime system-call notes . Two other clock functions are easy to mistake for part of the limiter: 0x004632d0 is a small gettimeofday helper in microseconds that the stock game never calls: nothing calls it directly, and no relocated pointer (vtable or table slot) points at it. The frame-rate patches overwrite it and its neighbours with their own code (a code cave), so it is not replaced . The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 ( replaced too, edge-verified , by @evill33t in #103 ) and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 (now replaced , see below) are not on the limiter's path. They look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem. Correction (2026-10-06): the 0x0111a... clocks are a separate layer The millisecond clock frame_timing_get_monotonic_ms ( 0x0111a7f0 ), its microsecond twin 0x0111a760 and the sleep wrapper 0x0111a880 are not on the limiter's path. All 52 of their callers sit in one region ( 0x0110e... - 0x0121b... ) that shares its own helpers, and no frame-rate patch touches any of them: they look like the timing layer of a separate subsystem (unidentified; possibly middleware). Their system label may move once that subsystem is known.
docs.title: Which clock the game reads

docs.text: Many small objects in the game advance in fixed steps of 1/30 s, whatever the real frame time is. The community "60 FPS++" patch changes those steps to 1/60 s, so knowing exactly which functions it edits, and what each belongs to, is part of running the game faster than 30 FPS. Paleblood has replaced a growing set of them in game/frame_timing/fixed_step_states.cpp . The latest belong to the Chalice Dungeon gate , the object behind the ritual altar: Its steps have names. The gate ( SprjDungeonGateIns ) keeps a table of 24 steps whose names are in the executable. They give its states their meaning: loading a channel, no chalice, a local or online ritual, a local or online dungeon, and an error display. Finding the gate. The game finds the current gate through SprjHolygrail . The highest of seven event flags, 9020 to 9026, picks one of eight gate slots; with none set, it uses the last slot. Waiting for it. Two methods advance the gate while it is busy and are done once it is idle. Two more wait until it is idle in a dungeon mode, or in a ritual mode. Leaving a mode. One method, held by an object that points to the gate, takes the gate out of a ritual or dungeon mode (request 7) and out of the error mode (request 10), around a check on the gate that reads the online manager, and reports when the check passes in the online dungeon mode. What its caller does with that answer is not known: the caller ignores it. The check itself. It passes only when the gate is idle in mode 1 (no Holy Chalice), four bytes of the online manager ( FrpgNetMan ) allow it (one set, three clear; what they mean is not known), and the id it is given is set. It then looks up an object for that id and keeps it as the gate's handle, a reference-counted pointer: the engine counts how many holders an object has and destroys it when the last one lets go, so swapping the handle drops the old object's count and takes one on the new. Finally, if the gate is still idle, it gives the gate request 6 and reports success. That the id names an online session is a guess. Its sibling, the entry check. It opens with the same gates, then searches a list for the first entry with a given key that holds an object, and keeps that object as the gate's handle in the same way, with request 4 instead of 6. When the gate becomes busy while the old handle is let go, it stops and reports failure rather than trying the next entry. Letting the handle go again. In a ritual mode a third method resets the handle. In the local ritual mode it always may; in the server ritual mode only when the online manager's bytes allow it and a flag bit in the handled object is clear. It clears one word of that object, hands the handle to a routine not yet analyzed ( 0x01e9cb80 ), and gives the gate request 8. A fourth method does the same under the same rules but first gathers the gate's sixteen slots: each active one goes into a short list (its key, its number, and a value the caller supplies for it), built on one of the engine's memory heaps. With no active slot it does nothing; otherwise it hands the handle and the list on ( 0x01e9cd20 , not yet analyzed), gives request 8, and then frees the list's memory. Passing the handle on. A readiness check lets the gate go on when it is idle in a ritual or dungeon mode and the online manager allows it; in the server modes the handled object must also have one word at zero. Two methods that differ only in a "kind" number (1 or 2) run that check, clear two words of the handled object, hand the handle on with the kind (to one routine in the local modes, another in the server modes, neither analyzed yet), and give request 9. Creating the handle. Two methods make the handle in the first place, both only while the gate is idle in mode 1. One drops the old handle, builds a new handled object from two blocks of data, a block of the online manager and a name (the current name entry's, or a default), and gives request 3. The other reads four "levels" from event flags: for each of four base flags, the highest level from 9 down to 1 whose flag is set (flag numbers 6228 to 6287, every seventh one belonging to the same column). It builds the handled object from those four levels and gives request 5. What the levels and the flags stand for in the game is not known yet. The millisecond sleep wrapper ( 0x0111a880 ), which is not on the limiter's path, is replaced too. It converts the engine's millisecond delay to the kernel's microseconds. It multiplies in 32 bits, as the original does, so very large delays wrap, and it always reports success. Fixed-step methods: PRs, contributors and evidence #104 by @evill33t : the millisecond sleep wrapper. #138 : five SprjDungeonGateIns methods that step the gate's state ( 0x01eb5390 , 0x01eb5490 , and the event handlers at 0x01eb9020 , 0x01ebb090 , 0x01ebf060 ). #141 : four methods that find the gate through SprjHolygrail ( 0x0200f970 , 0x020118f0 , 0x01f03210 , 0x01f03680 ). #182 : the method that leaves the gate's modes around the check 0x01ea5280 ( 0x01ec3ef0 , eleven 60 FPS++ edits). #186 : the check itself ( 0x01ea5280 , one 60 FPS++ edit), using the engine's shared reference counting from #185 . #188 : the entry check ( 0x01ea4a10 , one 60 FPS++ edit). Part of it sits in bytes the decompiler leaves out after an error report; see Ghidra & PS4 Quirks . #192 : the ritual handle reset ( 0x01ea5670 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #194 : the ritual slot reset ( 0x01ea5850 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #196 : the readiness check ( 0x01ea5c90 ) and the two pass-on methods ( 0x01ea5e20 , 0x01ea6080 ; one 60 FPS++ edit each). #198 : the handle creation ( 0x01ea47a0 , one 60 FPS++ edit). #199 : the level creation ( 0x01ea4cb0 , one 60 FPS++ edit), with the event-flag store shared with the event system. Status: replaced , not verified . Each was compared with the original function on authored edge cases , stock and with the 60 FPS++ edits, and wrong variants were rejected. None was checked on frames recorded from a real game run.
docs.title: The fixed-step state methods

docs.text: Nine small helpers that read the time or sleep are replaced and edge-verified (Paleblood #514 ). None of them is on the limiter's path: Time of day. frame_timing_time_of_day_us ( 0x02e61140 ) gives the time of day in microseconds; frame_timing_time_of_day_ticks ( 0x01088550 ) divides it by an owner's own tick length; frame_timing_time_seed_words ( 0x02e61280 ) returns four seed words, the time itself and the time plus a counter that steps by two on every call, so two calls in the same microsecond still differ. Random state. frame_timing_thread_random ( 0x02c6d580 ) returns the calling thread's random number state (a thread-local variable), seeding it the first time from the low 32 bits of the time in microseconds. About sixty callers fetch it. Stopwatch. frame_timing_stopwatch_start ( 0x01448580 ) stores the seconds since the game started, only when the stopwatch reads exactly zero; frame_timing_stopwatch_stop ( 0x01448620 ) adds the time since that start to two running totals. The task frame brackets work with them. Waiting for a job. frame_timing_job_wait ( 0x024bdd40 ) polls a background job's state until it is finished, sleeping 1 ms between polls; frame_timing_job_take_result ( 0x024bd150 ) takes a job's result, polling, waiting or taking at once depending on its mode, and counts one more holder of the result under a lock all jobs share. Sleep. frame_timing_posix_sleep_ms ( 0x00466810 ) sleeps through the POSIX usleep and always reports success. The community Performance Patch turns the stopwatch into a no-op and shortens the job waits' poll to 0.1 ms. Those byte edits do nothing while these functions are replaced , and there is no option for them yet. How these were verified Each function's edge cases pass against the original (10 to 55 cases each), deliberately wrong versions fail, and an independent review approved all nine. They are edge-verified : none has been recorded in a game run.
docs.title: Small clocks, waits and stopwatches

docs.text: The frame step also passes time into character updates. One verified update accumulates a per-frame points value using that time and retains fractional progress between frames. Its evidence and unresolved stat identity are documented in Stats & Progression .
docs.title: Frame time in game logic

docs.text: Each frame, the frame step hands the frame's work to FD4::FD4TaskManager (singleton 0x058b2e30 ). The path is a good example of how an engine brackets its work so that nothing runs twice or half-finished: 0x024512a0 fetches the task manager and runs every task group ( 0x01388c60 , mask -1 ). 0x01388c70 refuses to start while a frame is already running (a busy flag at +0x38 ). It flushes the task queue that collected work since the last frame ( 0x0143e490 : lock, run each queued object, destroy and free it, empty the list, unlock), steps the worker threads' queues ( 0x014400a0 ), and publishes the frame's value ( 0x0143f9f0 copies a float from the frame's information to a global). With the busy flag set, it calls the dispatcher ( +0x40 , virtual +0x30 ), which runs the frame's tasks; then it clears the flag, flushes the second queue and steps the workers again. The dispatcher ( 0x0138a370 ) is the last link: when its group record asks for it, it wakes every registered task (76 in Iosefka's Clinic), then fills a job with the record, the task table and the group mask and runs it through the same five steps as the workers. Each of those tasks is a piece of the game's own per-frame work, the next layer to map.

Field +0x10 : the seconds of the first clock call (32-bit), written once by the first call of either clock wrapper and read by every later call. The rest of the object is not documented. The SprjFlipper fields named on this page, gathered in one place: Offset Meaning +0x8 Current flip mode +0xc Pending flip mode +0x10 Sync interval +0x14 Unknown +0x18 Frame interval (float) +0x260 Index into the ring of recent frame times +0x264 Measured frame time +0x268 , +0x26c Set how many recent late frames the catch-up sums (meaning open); the patches zero the vblank word at +0x268 +0x271 , +0x272 Clear flags +0x276 Apply the pending flip mode +0x2b8 Frame rate derived from the ring's average +0x2bc , +0x2c0 Override counters +0x2c4 Reset flag
docs.title: Structs and globals

docs.text: The community frame-rate patches (Kyo; Lance McDonald and Kyo for Uncap FPS++ ) edit three of our functions; disassembling the limiter with and without each patch shows exactly what they do: Limiter ( 0x02434770 ): the flip-mode switch always takes one entry (mode 2 for 30 and 60, mode 0 for uncapped) with patched values: interval 1/30 s (30), 1/60 s (60) or 1/240 s (uncapped), and a zero vblank word ( +0x268 ). Every override is skipped: the reset flag ( +0x2c4 ), the two override counters ( +0x2bc , +0x2c0 ) and the two clear flags ( +0x271 , +0x272 ). At the end the sync interval ( +0x10 ) is kept on late frames instead of zeroed. Frame step ( 0x02418d20 ): the frame time passed to the task update starts at 1/60 s (30: 1/30 s), and when the flipper's interval is not 1/30 s it becomes the measured frame time ( +0x264 ) clamped to [interval, 1/30 s]. This is the patches' delta time: the game logic advances by how long the frame really took. The patch drops the SprjTask check to make room. Flipper constructor ( 0x02434520 ): the first interval is 1/60 s (60 and 90). They also edit 59 other functions; 12 of them are dead code in the stock game (no caller, no relocated pointer). Many of the rest pass the same 1/30 s frame-time descriptor to an owner object, which the 60 FPS patches change to 1/60 s. The patches also rewrite dozens of shared constants in the data segment (the 1/30 s step at 0x04d29170 becomes 1/60 s, 1/90 s or, uncapped, 1/60 s), which code we have not replaced reads too. BB_TARGET_FPS covers only the replaced functions, so it is meant to run together with the patch; option checks run both sides on the patched image for that reason. How the patch edits were mapped tools/patch_overlap.py maps every patch line to the function it falls in, and lists the patches that do nothing while our hooks are installed.
docs.title: Patch points

docs.text: BB_TARGET_FPS=30 , 60 or uncapped does in code what 30 FPS++ , 60 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ do in the three functions above. Unset keeps the original behaviour exactly. The option has to cover the frame step as well as the limiter. A faster limiter alone would still tell the game logic that every frame lasts 1/30 s; the delta time comes from the frame step (see the patch points above). The other functions the patches edit are not replaced yet, so a 60 FPS game would still need the community patch for them; its edits inside our three functions do not run, and our option does their part. A second option, BB_LIMITER_WAIT=sleep , makes the limiter use the sleeping wait the game carries but never selects: it sleeps until about 5 ms before the frame's end and spins the rest, so a fast machine does not keep a core busy waiting. How the option is checked against the patches Each part is checked against the patch itself: tools/verify.py run --patch FILE:NAME --env BB_TARGET_FPS=... runs the original with the patch's bytes applied against our replacement with the option, on the edge cases and on frames recorded in the game at 60 FPS. Recorded frame times at 60 FPS (October 7) A saved October 7 measurement with the external host scaffold, all replacements hooked, and BB_TARGET_FPS=60 reports a median frame time of 16.67 ms and p99 of 16.69 ms. That historical result is recorded in Paleblood's status evidence ; it is not a real-display result from Paleblood's project-owned boot path. History: the first version changed only the limiter An earlier version only changed the limiter. Because the hooked frame step no longer ran the patches' delta-time code, at 60 FPS the game logic would still have been told every frame lasts 1/30 s; checking against the patches found that, and that the limiter's own settings differed.

docs.text: Input The input system handles the controller pads. This page covers the once-a-frame step of FD4PadManager, the manager that keeps a map of pad entries, and the pad vibration and mouse setup functions. At a glance Scope Pad polling, mapping, dead zones, vibration, mouse and input buffering. Mapped so far: the per-frame step of the FD4PadManager pad map, pad vibration and the mouse device's setup. Verified The pad step is verified ; the vibration setter, the mouse device constructor and its two opens are edge-verified . Open What the two entries and the owner are; where the pad is polled; mapping, dead zones and input buffering. Summary FD4PadManager (singleton 0x058b31f0 ) keeps a map of pad entries. Once a frame, input_pad_step_01972900 ( 0x01972900 ): Marks two pad entries , keyed by the addresses of two globals ( 0x059464a8 , 0x059566c4 ). Checks whether its owner is ready : +0xc4 is 1, +0xc8 is 0 and +0xd0 is set. Advances that owner with a frame-time descriptor, when it is ready. While the hunter stands in Iosefka's Clinic the advance branch stays idle. Scope still to map: pad polling, mapping, dead zones, input buffering. What the game asks the system for The executable's imports show which input libraries it uses, and which calls from each: Library Calls the game imports What that tells us libScePad scePadInit , scePadOpen , scePadClose , scePadReadState , scePadGetControllerInformation , scePadSetVibration , scePadResetOrientation , scePadSetAngularVelocityDeadbandState , scePadSetTiltCorrectionState The game reads the pad's latest state once per poll ( scePadReadState ), not the buffered history ( scePadRead is not imported). It drives vibration and sets up the motion sensor. libSceMouse sceMouseInit , sceMouseOpen , sceMouseClose , sceMouseRead A mouse path exists, set up by the mouse device functions around 0x02a8c000 (below). libSceUserService sceUserServiceInitialize , sceUserServiceGetInitialUser , sceUserServiceGetLoginUserIdList , sceUserServiceGetUserName , sceUserServiceGetEvent , sceUserServiceTerminate Pads and the mouse are opened for a user, starting with the user who launched the game. libSceImeDialog sceImeDialogInit , sceImeDialogGetStatus , sceImeDialogGetResult , sceImeDialogAbort , sceImeDialogTerm Typed text (the character name, for example) goes through the system keyboard dialog; there is no keyboard library. What the game's pad calls show. Paleblood's runtime answers these calls ( #373 , #431 ; see Runtime system calls ), and the executable's own calls fix their shapes: before each scePadReadState ( 0x02a90168 , 0x02a91948 ) it clears the 120-byte state block, and afterwards it tests the "connected" byte at offset 0x4c ; it reads the touch pad's resolution and the sticks' deadzones from scePadGetControllerInformation , and treats a stick within 0x80 ± that deadzone as centred; scePadInit is called once ( 0x02fa6182 ) and its result is not read; vibration is set at 0x02a9c7c1 and stopped at 0x02a9c822 . With --input host the runtime feeds a real gamepad and the keyboard into these calls. That is the runtime 's side; the game code that reads the state is not decompiled yet. Vibration and the mouse Four small device functions are replaced and edge-verified (Paleblood #520 ): Vibration. input_pad_set_vibration ( 0x02a9c790 ) sets both motors of an open pad with scePadSetVibration , and answers false when the pad is not open or the call fails. Its second argument drives the small motor and its third the large one (the order of ScePadVibrationParam is large, then small). Its one caller is 0x01395ca5 . The mouse device. input_mouse_construct ( 0x02a8c210 ) builds a mouse device on top of the input devices' shared base constructor ( 0x02a8d2b0 ): it loads the mouse system module (id 0xa9 ), initialises the mouse library and opens the mouse through the device's own virtual open. If any step fails, the device keeps handle 0. Opening for the initial user. That open, input_initialize_mouse_for_initial_user ( 0x02a8c420 , named by @gabee12 in #270 ), asks the user service for the user who started the game, closes the previous connection when its handle is positive, and opens the mouse for that user (type 0, index 0). It is true when the new handle is positive. A second mouse device class has an identical open, input_mouse_b_open_for_initial_user ( 0x02a8bf30 ), with its handle at +0x128 instead of +0x168 . How these were verified Each function's edge cases pass against the original (9, 10, 11 and 11 cases), deliberately wrong versions fail, and an independent review approved all four. No community patch edits them. They are edge-verified : none has been recorded in a game run. What the functions around the two scePadReadState calls ( 0x02a90168 , 0x02a91948 ) keep of each state (the start of pad polling). Pad mapping and input buffering have not been studied yet. The sticks' dead zones are applied by the game's own code, from the deadzone the controller information reports (only the motion sensor's deadband is set through the library). Whether the mouse path is used by anything in the shipped game: the mouse device's constructor has two callers ( 0x02558eb3 , 0x02558fb6 ), not yet mapped, and nothing calls either open directly (only their vtable slots point at them). What the shared input device base constructor ( 0x02a8d2b0 , six callers) sets up, and which other device classes use it.

docs.text: Kernel The engine's core library: thin wrappers around the PS4 kernel for threads, mutexes and condition variables, which report every unexpected result through one fatal error function. At a glance Scope Dantelion2's kernel layer ("ClassLibrary/Core/Kernel" in its source paths), and the kernel and libc calls the executable imports. Verified kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ), the condition-variable wait the frame-rate patches edit. Open Which objects the condition waits made each frame belong to. Summary What the kernel layer is Dantelion2 is the engine's core library. Its kernel classes wrap the PS4 kernel's threads, mutexes and condition variables. Each wrapper checks the result of the call it makes, and any unexpected result goes to the engine's fatal error function ( 0x024b55b0 ), which takes a file, a line and a message. The current thread kernel_thread_self ( 0x0111a8a0 ) stores the calling thread's handle from scePthreadSelf through its pointer argument and returns 0. It is reached only through a function pointer. By @evill33t in #105, merged in #203 : its 7 constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it. Reading files Four small wrappers handle the engine's file access ( #283 , by @evill33t ): kernel_file_open ( 0x0111a620 ) opens a file read-only and reports its size (from the system's file-status record) and its descriptor; kernel_file_close , kernel_file_read_count and kernel_file_seek_absolute ( 0x0111a6b0 , 0x0111a6e0 , 0x0111a720 ) close, read and seek. Each was checked on constructed edge cases against the original and approved by an independent review. FMOD's semaphores and recursive mutexes FMOD (the sound engine; see Audio ) wraps the kernel's semaphores and mutexes in small functions of its own, and these are the first of them mapped: Semaphores ( #271 ): create ( 0x0111ad10 ) makes an empty first-in-first-out semaphore with room for 0xffff units and stores its handle only if the kernel succeeds; destroy ( 0x0111ad80 ), wait ( 0x0111ada0 , one unit, no time limit) and signal ( 0x0111adc0 , one unit) pass the handle on. Recursive mutexes ( #275 ): create ( 0x0111abb0 ) allocates the mutex from FMOD's memory pool (or uses one shared static slot), sets it up as recursive and hands it back only after every step succeeded; destroy, lock and unlock ( 0x0111ac80 , 0x0111acd0 , 0x0111acf0 ) pass it on, and lock and unlock do nothing for a null mutex. All of them turn any kernel error into 0x21 (a failed allocation gives 0x2b ). By @evill33t in #111 and #108: each was brought up to date with main , its constructed edge cases pass against the original on current main , and an independent review approved it. How a condition wait works kernel_condition_wait ( 0x02483e80 ) waits on a condition variable. It has two paths: Timeout of -1 : it waits forever (an untimed wait). Any other timeout : it makes a timed wait, and returns -3 if the time runs out. It is called about 40 times a frame in gameplay. Every wait recorded in gameplay is untimed, which matters for the frame-rate patches (see Patch points ). Imports are not implementations The executable and its bundled libc import POSIX-like calls such as getpagesize , getpid , clock_gettime and gettimeofday . An import only says the game can call something; it does not mean Paleblood implements it. For implementation status and evidence limits, see the runtime system-call notes . Two clock details are established so far: The frame limiter passes null as gettimeofday 's timezone argument. Numeric clock ID 4 is confirmed for sceKernelClockGettime , not for the imported clock_gettime wrapper. getpagesize: why it stops by name In the current runtime , both getpagesize entries are registered as fail-loud unresolved diagnostics because the PS4 page-size value is not established, as recorded in merged Paleblood PR #66 . Runtime thread-call implementations These are Paleblood runtime services, not newly decompiled game functions: the runtime answers some thread and timing calls itself. Two rules run through them: A call is implemented only when its guest-visible contract is known. Where the PS4 's exact behaviour is not established, the call stays a fail-loud diagnostic that stops by name. The SCE names and the POSIX names of the same call differ in their errors: the POSIX names return the FreeBSD error number, where the SCE names return 0x80020000 plus it. The former boot stop, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , is no longer reached: since Paleblood #207 the bundled C library's probe that called it returns at once. The boots recorded on merged main since then pass through these thread calls, and since #408 no system call stops the boot at all. Later thread work includes ending a thread early with scePthreadExit ( #389 ) and semaphores that wake their waiters by thread priority ( #426 ); the runtime system-call notes explain them. What each runtime change implements (PRs #62, #72, #81, #94, #95, #97) Merged PR #62 implements scePthreadEqual by comparing the object pointers used as guest thread handles. Its synthetic registry tests cover one handle compared with itself, distinct handles in both argument orders, and null; the public FreeBSD pthread_equal(3) contract supports zero for unequal and nonzero for equal, but the PS4 's exact nonzero value is unknown. Merged PR #72 implements imported sched_yield by yielding the host thread and returning zero, following POSIX and FreeBSD's documented contract. Unit tests check the result but cannot show that another host thread actually ran. Later runtime merges extend the same thread and timing group: PR #81 adds the detach-state setters for thread attributes under both the SCE and POSIX names. Reading a detach state that the system itself supplies still stops by name, because the PS4 default is not established. PR #95 registers the POSIX names pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy . They return the FreeBSD error number where the SCE names return 0x80020000 plus it. PR #94 sleeps the host thread for sceKernelUsleep , the call the verified frame limiter and swap-chain present functions make, and for usleep below one second. PR #97 ends the program by name on __stack_chk_fail . These are runtime services checked by synthetic registry tests, not decompiled game functions. scePthreadYield answers zero The similarly named scePthreadYield yields the same way and answers zero (Paleblood #308). Its PS4 signature is unpublished: FreeBSD's pthread_yield returns void , Linux's analogue returns int . Zero is right under either, and all 26 direct call sites in the executable ignore the result. translate nonzero low32 close status to 19; synthetic wire edge cases only 0x0111a6e0 60 kernel_file_read_count edge-verified Publish uint32 transferred bytes after kernel buffer writes; full64 received count controls errors and short reads 0x0111a720 22 kernel_file_seek_absolute edge-verified Forward the full opaque descriptor and zero-extended unsigned32 absolute offset; full64 seek result sign maps to 0 or 19; synthetic wire edge cases only 0x0111a8a0 26 kernel_thread_self edge-verified Copy the complete opaque current-thread handle to the output and return zero 0x0111abb0 207 kernel_mutex_create edge-verified Create a recursive mutex in static or allocated storage; the FPS patches put a ret on the timed path Structs and globals Not documented yet. Patch points 30 FPS++ , 60 FPS++ , 90 FPS++ and Uncap FPS++ write a return over the timed-wait call in 0x02483e80 . If that path ever ran, the return would jump to a garbage address. Every wait recorded in gameplay is untimed, so it never does. Our replacement keeps the original behaviour. Open questions Which objects the ~40 condition waits per frame belong to (job queues, the render thread?).
