The former boot stop, scePthreadAttrGetaffinity , is no longer reached: since Paleblood #207 the bundled C library's probe that called it returns at once. The boots recorded on merged main since then pass through these thread calls, and since #408 no system call stops the boot at all. Later thread work includes ending a thread early with scePthreadExit ( #389 ) and semaphores that wake their waiters by thread priority ( #426 ); the runtime system-call notes explain them. What each runtime change implements (PRs #62, #72, #81, #94, #95, #97) Merged PR #62 implements scePthreadEqual by comparing the object pointers used as guest thread handles. Its synthetic registry tests cover one handle compared with itself, distinct handles in both argument orders, and null; the public FreeBSD pthread_equal(3) contract supports zero for unequal and nonzero for equal, but the PS4 's exact nonzero value is unknown. Merged PR #72 implements imported sched_yield by yielding the host thread and returning zero, following POSIX and FreeBSD's documented contract. Unit tests check the result but cannot show that another host thread actually ran. Later runtime merges extend the same thread and timing group: PR #81 adds the detach-state setters for thread attributes under both the SCE and POSIX names. Reading a detach state that the system itself supplies still stops by name, because the PS4 default is not established. PR #95 registers the POSIX names pthread_self , pthread_attr_init and pthread_attr_destroy . They return the FreeBSD error number where the SCE names return 0x80020000 plus it. PR #94 sleeps the host thread for sceKernelUsleep , the call the verified frame limiter and swap-chain present functions make, and for usleep below one second. PR #97 ends the program by name on __stack_chk_fail . These are runtime services checked by synthetic registry tests, not decompiled game functions. scePthreadYield answers zero The similarly named scePthreadYield yields the same way and answers zero (Paleblood #308). Its PS4 signature is unpublished: FreeBSD's pthread_yield returns void , Linux's analogue returns int . Zero is right under either, and all 26 direct call sites in the executable ignore the result.

docs.text: Loading How the game reads its files: the file interfaces the executable imports from the PS4 kernel, the C library and the bundled Fios module, and the PlayGo calls for chunk and install state. At a glance Scope File access, Fios file and directory handles, PlayGo chunks, and the archive and mount layers above them. Verified Seven functions directly above the file imports (kernel files, Fios handles, C streams) are replaced and edge-verified . Open Which calls run during a load, and in what order. The boot now reads files from your copy, its scratch folder and its saves, but the game's loading code itself is not mapped. Summary Four interfaces to the file system The executable's file interface is split across imports from four places: Provider What it offers Example imports libSceFios2 (bundled) File and directory handles, plus sceFiosOp* operations sceFiosFHOpenSync , sceFiosFHReadSync , sceFiosOpWait libkernel Low-level file calls sceKernelOpen , sceKernelRead , sceKernelClose libc Standard C file streams fopen , fread , fclose libScePlayGo Chunk and install state scePlayGoGetChunkId , scePlayGoGetLocus The bundled Fios module ships with the game and is mapped as guest code. Its exports provide imports used by both the executable and the bundled C library. What the import table can and cannot tell you These rows describe link dependencies, not a trace of calls made during a load. The import list shows what the game can call; it does not show which calls run, their arguments, or their results. What a boot on Paleblood's runtime reads The boot recorded on merged main passes the file milestone and runs until its time limit ( #408 , #443 ). What the runtime serves, as the runtime system-call notes describe: /app0 , your own copy of the game, read-only. The first file the game looks for and reads is sprj_mixer.fev , its sound mixer description. Its movies are read from there too ( #419 ). /data , a scratch folder: the engine maps its temp: and title: drives there and creates a fresh cache.bin at start-up. /savedataN , a mounted save, kept in a host folder you choose ( #402 ). PlayGo reports every chunk installed ( #370 ). This is the runtime 's side. Apart from the seven small functions below, the game's own archive, mount and load-screen code above these calls has not been mapped, so which assets it loads, and in what order, is not documented here yet. The first loading functions Seven small functions on the file path are replaced and edge-verified (Paleblood #517 ). They sit directly on the imports above, one per interface: Kernel files. The loader 's platform layer keeps a file as a descriptor and an "open" bit. loading_kernel_file_open ( 0x02a70890 ) turns the caller's mode bits into FreeBSD open flags: read and write pick read-only, write-only or read-write; then the first of create-exclusive, create-and-truncate and create that is set adds O_CREAT with O_EXCL or O_TRUNC (a lone truncate bit adds O_TRUNC ). A new file gets permissions 0777 when it is writable and 0555 when it is opened only to read. This is the call that creates the start-up temp:/cache.bin . loading_kernel_file_read ( 0x02a70920 ) reads through the descriptor and hands back the count. Both answer 0 or -1; the kernel's own error code is dropped. Fios handles. loading_fios_open_file ( 0x00857cd0 ) and loading_fios_open_file_read ( 0x0085cda0 ) open a file with sceFiosFHOpenSync and wrap the handle in a small engine object allocated from the calling thread's allocator. loading_fios_directory_delete ( 0x0084d5a0 ) is the directory object's deleting destructor: it closes the directory handle, frees the listing and two path strings, and returns the object to the thread allocator. C streams. loading_stdio_stream_open ( 0x00464b90 ) opens a stream with fopen in one of six binary modes ( rb , r+b , wb , w+b , ab , a+b ) picked by mode bits, rewinds it, and turns a failure's errno into the engine's own codes: not found 0x1001 , denied ( EACCES or EPERM ) 0x1002 , no space 0x1004 , anything else 0x1003 . loading_stdio_close_files ( 0x02e67d20 ) closes three streams together, last first. How these were verified Each function's edge cases pass against the original (72, 19, 15, 14, 11, 30 and 9 cases), with deliberately wrong versions failing, and an independent review approved all seven. No community patch edits them. None has been recorded in a game run yet, so they are edge-verified , not verified . docs.text: Physics The game's rigid bodies live in one physics world: shared tables of bodies, motions and constraints that other objects index into, and listeners that hear when a body changes. At a glance Scope The physics world reached through the physics manager, and the objects that own bodies in it. Verified The physics-instance constructor physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 ( 0x01c0c2b0 ). Fixed step An instance's controller steps at 1/30 s; the 60 FPS patches and BB_TARGET_FPS=60 make it 1/60 s. Open What kind of object a physics instance is, and what the manager's two special modes mean. Summary The physics world The game keeps its rigid bodies in a physics world reached through the physics manager ( 0x0593d700 → +0x28 → +0x8 ). The world holds tables that everything else indexes into: Table Offset in the world Entry size (bytes) Bodies +0x20 0x90 Motions +0xe0 0x80 Constraints +0x128 0x38 Listeners (told when a body changes) +0x538 list How a physics instance is built physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 ( 0x01c0c2b0 ) is the constructor of a physics instance : an object that owns a set of bodies in that world (a ragdoll or a breakable object would look like this; which one is still open). Reading it is a good lesson in how a constructor wires a new object into shared tables: It asks the body-set constructor for its bodies, then moves every active body (flags +0x40 & 3 ) by the offset it was given. It writes a 16-byte back-link for each of its bodies and constraints, and points the world's tables at them, so the world can find the instance from any body. It copies the set's shape table ( 0x30 bytes per shape) into a buffer from a dedicated heap, handing it to a shape object, and builds a controller whose fixed frame step is 1/30 s and whose transform starts at the root body. Unless the physics manager is in one of its two special modes (as it is while Iosefka's Clinic loads), it rescales each active body's four 16-bit motion values and tells the world's listeners about each body, removing listeners that are flagged for removal. Last, it creates its own listener and a tracker, and collects the distinct motion types above 4 of its bodies. How the motion values are rescaled The four values are stored as the top halves of 32-bit floats (the format known as bfloat16): 16 bits holding a float's sign, exponent and the top of its mantissa. Step 4 above works like this: Widen. Each value goes back to a float by putting it in the upper half of a float's bit pattern. Scale. The first three are multiplied by 0.2, and all four by 1.00390625. Narrow. Only the top 16 bits of each result are kept again (an arithmetic shift of the bit pattern, then a saturating pack). It is a compact way to store floats at half the size, and an example of why a replacement has to reproduce the exact instructions: the truncation works on the float's bits, not its value. Key functions Address Size Name Status Notes 0x01c0c2b0 3222 physics_instance_construct_01c0c2b0 verified physics instance constructor over a body set: back-links, shape copy, controller (step 1/30 s; 60 FPS patches 1/60), motion rescale, listeners Structs and globals Object Field Meaning Physics manager ( 0x0593d700 ) +0x28 → +0x8 The world +0x274 , +0x275 Special-mode flags World +0x20 Body table +0xe0 Motion table +0x128 Constraint table +0x538 Listener list (a tagged pointer: the low two bits are flags) Body ( 0x90 bytes) +0x30 Position +0x40 Flags +0x68 Motion index +0x88 Back-link Instance +0x38 Body set +0x70 / +0x78 Back-links +0x88 Shape object +0x90 Controller (frame step at +0x60 ) +0x128 Own listener Patch points The controller's frame step is 1/30 s; 60 FPS++ (and 90 FPS++ , 60FPS (no deltatime) ) make it 1/60 s. BB_TARGET_FPS=60 does the same. Open questions What kind of object is a physics instance: ragdolls, breakables, or both? What do the physics manager's two special modes mean? Both are on while the clinic loads.

docs.text: The four values are stored as the top halves of 32-bit floats (the format known as bfloat16): 16 bits holding a float's sign, exponent and the top of its mantissa. Step 4 above works like this: Widen. Each value goes back to a float by putting it in the upper half of a float's bit pattern. Scale. The first three are multiplied by 0.2, and all four by 1.00390625. Narrow. Only the top 16 bits of each result are kept again (an arithmetic shift of the bit pattern, then a saturating pack). It is a compact way to store floats at half the size, and an example of why a replacement has to reproduce the exact instructions: the truncation works on the float's bits, not its value.

docs.text: Render The render system draws each frame and presents it to the screen. This page covers the per-frame render update, the pacing of each present, one helper from the YEBIS post-processing middleware, and the GPU helper library compiled into the game: its command writers, state setters, swap chain and shader uploads, and how they now report to Paleblood's renderer. At a glance Scope render_frame_update_02377bd0 , render_swap_chain_present , render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters , and the GPU helper library's command writers, state setters, swap chain and shader uploads. Verified All three: the reference-counted object list, the vblank pacing of the present, and the blur sample counts. Open What the listed objects and the two children are; the engine's own drawing code above the GPU library, materials and post-processing. Many GPU library functions are mapped and edge-verified ; they now tell Paleblood's renderer what they set. Summary The per-frame update render_frame_update_02377bd0 ( 0x02377bd0 ) runs once a frame: It walks a list of reference-counted objects and updates each one. An object whose update says it is finished loses its reference (destroyed at the last one; an underflow is reported as "DLReferenceCountObject: Invalid Unref() call"), and its node is unlinked and freed. It updates a RendMan -side child ( RendMan : singleton 0x05940298 ). It steps another child by a frame time of 1/30 s, or 0 while that child is held. Pacing the present render_swap_chain_present ( 0x025b2fb0 , the graphics framework's GXSwapChainCtrl ) paces each present: It waits until the requested number of 60 Hz vblanks has passed since the last present. It sleeps until 17 ms before that time, then polls the clock. It maps the interval to a flip mode. It presents. In Iosefka's Clinic the game presents with interval 1 and does not wait here; the frame limiter sets the pace. Blur sampling (YEBIS) render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters ( 0x00fbc3e0 ) belongs to YEBIS, the post-processing middleware. Its GPUTexUtil_GetRecursiveSampleParameters works out: how many recursive passes a blur needs; how many samples the last one takes; how far apart the first one samples. It carries the middleware's own assertions. Scope still to map: the engine's draw submission above the GPU library, materials and post-processing. The game's shaders ship as compiled AMD GPU code in its shader bundles. A census tool in the code repository decodes the shaders in your own copy and counts the instructions they use, for Paleblood's shader translator (Paleblood #316). It prints counts only; no shader code leaves your machine. Writing GPU commands and presenting The engine builds the GPU's command buffers itself (see Runtime syscalls ), as AMD " PM4 " packets: each packet is a header word naming the operation, followed by its arguments. The first of the engine's own packet writers are mapped, all by @evill33t : The command buffer. One shared structure describes it: where it begins and ends, the cursor where the next word goes, and a callback the engine calls to get more room when it runs out. render_command_prepare_submission ( 0x014784a0 ) reserves 64 words before a submission, and render_command_emit_counter_operation ( 0x01477b30 ) writes a seven-word packet that makes the GPU wait on a value in memory ( PM4 WAIT_REG_MEM ) ( #208 ). The pool counter. render_read_present_pool_counter ( 0x0247eb80 ) reads a 64-bit counter atomically, with a locked compare-and-exchange loop ( #279 ). Present records. render_present_record_consume ( 0x02ab5a70 ) turns a pending present record into commands: it classifies the record, clamps its range, copies its payload and writes the final fields ( #286 ). Building present records. render_build_present_source_record ( 0x0256e1d0 ) builds the record for a present, by mode, keeping partial output, unsigned divisions and the packed auxiliary requirements as the original does; render_choose_record_constructor_selector ( 0x02ab7a20 ), render_combine_record_parameters ( 0x02ab7ab0 ) and render_reduce_record_parameter ( 0x02ab7e40 , a four-entry scale table, zero past its end) pick and combine its constructor choices ( #473 , from #268; edge-verified on synthetic cases). A record test. render_record_auxiliary_predicate ( 0x02abb4f0 ) answers yes or no for a record's selector: always yes for two selector values, a flag bit for the next two, no otherwise ( #293 , from #266). Presenting a swap-chain image. render_swap_chain_present_mode ( 0x02ad5dd0 ) waits until the display has flipped far enough and picks the flip mode, and render_swap_chain_submit ( 0x02ad6e50 ) submits the frame, advances the frame counter and checks its owner again ( #287 ). They use the public layouts of the video-out flip status and kernel events. Depth and stencil clears. render_emit_present_preparation_scalar ( 0x01473590 ) and render_emit_present_preparation_byte ( 0x014735f0 ) write the depth and stencil clear values (AMD's DB_DEPTH_CLEAR and DB_STENCIL_CLEAR registers) #325 , from #210. The last record's depth settings. render_emit_present_last_record_packet ( 0x014769e0 ) writes DB_RENDER_CONTROL . Two setters turn its depth and stencil compression off or on ( 0x01485070 , 0x01485080 ), one replaces two packed indices ( 0x014721d0 ), and render_reset_present_preparation_dirty ( 0x02ad2c30 ) writes only the clear values that changed and remembers them #326 , from #211. Resource records. A record describes a GPU resource's layout. The reviews tie its fields to AMD's public tiling and format fields, though the full meaning is still open. The mapped parts: mapping: render_pack_record_mapping_word ( 0x01471310 ) packs its mapping word and render_read_record_mapping_word ( 0x01486cf0 ) reads one back #321 , from #212; encoding: three lookups decode the encoding byte's metadata, component arrangement and category ( 0x01471730 , 0x014717a0 , 0x014719a0 ), and render_record_set_encoding ( 0x01486540 ) stores it #327 , from #261; parameters: render_record_apply_parameter_tuple ( 0x0149c850 ) picks a record parameter from a normalisation table, with its classification helpers ( 0x0149e900 – 0x0149ea70 ) #322 , from #223; sizes: render_calculate_second_auxiliary ( 0x0149e570 ) works out the size and alignment of a second auxiliary area #323 , from #228; fields: seven setters ( 0x01486520 – 0x01486800 ) replace one field each, keeping the rest of the word #324 , from #236; construction: render_record_constructor ( 0x01485f90 ) clears a record's 44-byte prefix and fills in the record and its auxiliary outputs, returning a packed 64-bit result; render_record_constructor_pack_pair ( 0x01471600 ) packs a selector pair into an encoding, and two optional steps ( 0x0149e2d0 , 0x0149e400 ) align paired components and work out the geometry, writing their outputs even when a helper reports an error #478 , from #246 ( edge-verified on synthetic cases); normalisation: render_record_normalize_mode2 , …mode3 and …mode4 ( 0x025710a0 , 0x025711d0 , 0x02571340 ) bring a record's input into one normalised form, copying the words they do not interpret unchanged and keeping each helper's writes and failure codes in order, and render_record_translate_selector ( 0x02ab7310 ) maps a record selector to one output word, answering status 12 for a selector it does not support #249 ( edge-verified on synthetic cases). Setting GPU state and drawing The GPU helper library keeps no state of its own: each setter writes its value straight into the command buffer as a register packet, and the GPU reads it from there. A large group of setters and draw writers was mapped and replaced by @evill33t , each verified to write exactly the original packets: Blending and colour output #411 (from #233): render_set_cb_blend_control ( 0x01473090 , one colour buffer's blend equation, CB_BLENDn_CONTROL ), render_set_cb_color_control ( 0x01473320 , the colour output mode and raster operation, CB_COLOR_CONTROL ) and render_set_cb_target_mask ( 0x01472fd0 , which colour components each target writes, CB_TARGET_MASK ). Depth and stencil #411 : render_set_db_depth_control ( 0x014733a0 , the depth and stencil tests and writes) and render_set_db_stencil_control ( 0x01473400 , the front- and back-face stencil operations). What is drawn #411 : render_set_vgt_primitive_type ( 0x01473fe0 , triangles, strips, rectangles and so on), render_emit_num_instances ( 0x01475370 , how many copies a draw makes), render_emit_draw_index_auto ( 0x014741b0 , a draw of consecutive vertices) and render_emit_event_write ( 0x01475da0 , a GPU event such as a cache flush), with two record helpers ( 0x01485390 , 0x014853f0 ) and the one call that asks the system whether the GPU's performance-analysis mode is on ( 0x01489c40 ). Where on screen #364 (from #232): render_configure_viewport ( 0x014765e0 , the viewport's scale, offset and depth range), render_configure_screen_scissor ( 0x01476790 ), render_set_screen_offset ( 0x01473650 ), the guard-band clip and discard adjustments ( 0x014736d0 , 0x01473750 ) and the viewport-transform controls ( 0x01476980 , 0x01485220 ). A present's context section #365 (from #231): render_emit_present_context_section ( 0x01472870 ) reserves room and writes the context registers a present needs. Command buffers, swap chain and shader uploads Command buffers #360 (from #256): render_command_buffer_init ( 0x01471270 ) sets up a command buffer's pointers and its "need more room" callback. render_command_submit_batch ( 0x02ab0ce0 ), render_command_submit_snapshot ( 0x02ab0e30 ) and render_command_submit_present ( 0x02aafb30 ) hand finished regions to the system's submit call, with the waits the GPU needs. The room check that every packet writer makes before writing is now shared code #291 . The swap chain #361 (from #254): render_setup_swap_chain ( 0x02ad5e90 ) allocates and registers the swap chain's frame buffers with video out and sets up its cached resource data and tone curves; two cleanups release the curve and the cached record ( 0x02571c60 , 0x02572290 , #359 , from #244). The last present record #354 (from #260): render_present_last_record_consume ( 0x02ab6810 ) consumes the final record of a present, or only updates its tracking when the commands do not fit. Shaders #263 , #363 (from #251): render_flush_shader_preparation ( 0x02ab9850 ) flushes a pending barrier before a shader event, and render_allocate_shader_upload ( 0x02aaddc0 ) finds room of at most 64 KiB for a shader's code, reclaiming once if none is free. Resource descriptors #357 (from #255), #358 (from #222): the records that describe a texture's layout, its mip levels and their offsets ( 0x014a1e80 , 0x014a2c40 ), its encoding ( 0x014712d0 , 0x01471770 , 0x01489910 - 0x01489960 ) and its tiling ( 0x0149cc60 , which converts a tile-mode table index), and how its parameters are derived ( 0x02abaf10 , 0x0149cb30 ). Render targets, descriptors and the present path (10 November) Forty-five more of the library's functions were replaced on 10 November, all @evill33t 's work, brought up to date with main and merged as #482 , #485 , #486 , #487 and the batch #489 : Render targets #489 : render_set_render_target ( 0x014738b0 ) writes a colour target's register block, or switches the target off when there is no descriptor; render_set_depth_render_target ( 0x014739b0 ) does the same for the depth target. render_restore_color_target_from_bank and render_restore_depth_target_from_bank ( 0x02ad1e30 , 0x02ad1e70 ) put a saved target back from one of two banks, and render_present_slot_emit ( 0x01473840 ) writes a colour target's two clear words. Rasterizer state #489 : render_configure_viewport_and_guard_band ( 0x01496f60 ) sets the viewport and the guard band, the region outside the screen where triangles are kept rather than clipped; render_set_pa_sc_mode_cntl_0 ( 0x01477150 ) switches multisampling and the viewport scissor. Linking shaders #489 : render_build_shader_link_words ( 0x014873a0 ) matches a vertex shader's outputs to a pixel shader's inputs and builds the words that connect them; render_emit_shader_link_words ( 0x01475000 ) writes them. render_configure_record_shader , its secondary path and render_finish_record_shader ( 0x02ace1e0 , 0x02ace5e0 , 0x02acfc20 ) set up and finish a recorded shader's state. Descriptor geometry #482 , #485 , #486 , #489 (from #237, #247, #238): building a resource descriptor and the requirements it adds up ( render_prepare_resource_descriptor , 0x02fa6af0 ), the two- and three-part record descriptors and their size ( 0x01487ee0 , 0x01488590 , 0x01488370 , 0x014a27c0 , 0x01471a40 ), converting a constructor's record ( 0x01488d90 ), and render_record_geometry ( 0x0149ce10 ) with its helpers ( 0x0149c4e0 - 0x0149ed30 ), which work out an image's dimensions and alignment for the record constructor. The swap chain's resources #487 , #489 (from #245): render_initialize_swap_chain_resource ( 0x02565f90 ) checks a frame buffer's parameters, prepares its storage and wraps it; render_prepare_swap_chain_resource_info ( 0x02571d60 ) allocates that storage and publishes its descriptor. Finishing a present #489 : the chain that closes a frame's command lists and hands them on. render_finish_present_commands ( 0x02aaf700 ) finishes pending lists and submits the pending snapshot when there is room ( render_submit_present_finish_snapshot , 0x02ab0b00 ; render_managed_present_capacity , 0x02aaf030 ); a pool of present buffers is claimed and released ( 0x02ad3b80 , 0x02ad3c80 , 0x02ad3d40 , 0x02aaa5a0 ); the release packets that tell the GPU a buffer may be reused are written ( 0x014778f0 , 0x02abb6d0 ); and the present's sources are prepared and their state flushed ( 0x02ad1eb0 , 0x02ad1f80 ), with the encoding helpers 0x02564ed0 and 0x02565130 and the context finisher 0x02568530 . How the renderer learns what the game draws Paleblood does not replay the finished GPU commands. Instead, the GPU library's replacements, with their packets unchanged, also tell Paleblood's renderer what they set, and the renderer draws that on your GPU (see Runtime: the renderer ): Observer calls in replacements #414 : the blend, colour, depth, stencil, primitive-type, instance-count, viewport and draw replacements above each report the same value they write, with the place in the command buffer where they wrote it. Under the verification harness the calls do nothing. The depth and stencil clear values and DB_RENDER_CONTROL replacements report too #435 . Observed functions without replacements yet #416 , #418 , #435 , #441 : where a library function has no replacement, the runtime watches its arguments at its entry and lets the original run. These were setRenderTarget ( 0x014738b0 ) and the depth target ( 0x014739b0 ), now replaced (above), and still are the stencil references ( 0x01473190 , 0x014731f0 ), the shaders' user-data writers ( 0x014761a0 - 0x014764a0 ), the indexed-draw setters and draw ( 0x01475270 - 0x01475320 , 0x01474420 ) and two compute dispatch writers ( 0x01474c50 , 0x0148a350 ). The compute command buffer's user data #510 : that buffer's six user-data writers ( 0x0148aad0 - 0x0148ada0 ) take no stage argument and were not observed, so a compute pass ran with whatever user data the record held from before; one colour lookup-table pass read another pass's table. They now report through the same observers as the stage writers. This needs the game library built from the decompilation ( tools/boot.py --game-lib ). In the maintainer's local runs it was enough to draw the studio logos and the title screen #441 . How the library functions were verified Each replacement above was checked against the original instructions on constructed edge cases , which also caught deliberately broken variants; none was checked on recorded game frames. All are edge-verified . They are @evill33t 's work, brought up to date with main and merged from the PRs named in brackets; #362 adds cases for the shader preparation's reset modes (from #350) and #352 derives the packet tests' addresses from the harness . The observer calls were added afterwards and leave the packets unchanged. The functions of 10 November ( #482 , #485 - #487 , #489 ) were checked the same way and are edge-verified ; #489 lists each one's cases in its session report. Structs and globals The update's owner Offset Field +0x10 list sentinel (next +0x0 , prev +0x8 , object +0x10 ) +0x18 count +0x20 allocator (frees nodes through vtable slot +0x70 ) +0x70 child, stepped through vtable slot +0x40 +0x80 child +0x8c the held flag +0x98 a byte copied into the +0x70 child each frame Reference-counted objects : vtable slot 0 destroys, count at +0x8 (atomic). The engine shares this reference counting across systems since #185 ; the frame update was re- verified unchanged on all its recorded and edge cases . Patch points The frame-rate patches are described in Frame timing . Uncap FPS++ makes the +0x70 child's step the flipper's measured frame time ( +0x264 ) whatever the held flag says, through a small code cave inside the function, and drops the RendMan check. The 1/30 s it reads otherwise is the shared constant at 0x04d29170 , which the 60, 90 and uncapped patches rewrite in the data segment. Uncap FPS++ presents with flip mode 0 (no vblank sync) at the end of 0x025b2fb0 . Every frame-rate patch removes the first assertion of 0x00fbc3e0 (at least 3 base samples): at higher frame rates the blur gets fewer samples. Open questions What the reference-counted objects in the per-frame list are, and what the two children are. The engine's own drawing code above the GPU library, its materials and post-processing have not been studied yet. Which GCN descriptor kinds the user-data writers' NOP markers ( 0x68750004 , 0x68750005 , 0x68750006 ) name. What the fifth argument of the dispatch writers' relatives ( 0x01474d10 , 0x0148a410 ) selects.
docs.title: Render

docs.text: The render system draws each frame and presents it to the screen. This page covers the per-frame render update, the pacing of each present, one helper from the YEBIS post-processing middleware, and the GPU helper library compiled into the game: its command writers, state setters, swap chain and shader uploads, and how they now report to Paleblood's renderer. At a glance Scope render_frame_update_02377bd0 , render_swap_chain_present , render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters , and the GPU helper library's command writers, state setters, swap chain and shader uploads. Verified All three: the reference-counted object list, the vblank pacing of the present, and the blur sample counts. Open What the listed objects and the two children are; the engine's own drawing code above the GPU library, materials and post-processing. Many GPU library functions are mapped and edge-verified ; they now tell Paleblood's renderer what they set.
docs.title: Render

docs.text: render_frame_update_02377bd0 ( 0x02377bd0 ) runs once a frame: It walks a list of reference-counted objects and updates each one. An object whose update says it is finished loses its reference (destroyed at the last one; an underflow is reported as "DLReferenceCountObject: Invalid Unref() call"), and its node is unlinked and freed. It updates a RendMan -side child ( RendMan : singleton 0x05940298 ). It steps another child by a frame time of 1/30 s, or 0 while that child is held.
docs.title: The per-frame update

docs.text: render_swap_chain_present ( 0x025b2fb0 , the graphics framework's GXSwapChainCtrl ) paces each present: It waits until the requested number of 60 Hz vblanks has passed since the last present. It sleeps until 17 ms before that time, then polls the clock. It maps the interval to a flip mode. It presents. In Iosefka's Clinic the game presents with interval 1 and does not wait here; the frame limiter sets the pace.
docs.title: Pacing the present

docs.text: render_yebis_get_recursive_sample_parameters ( 0x00fbc3e0 ) belongs to YEBIS, the post-processing middleware. Its GPUTexUtil_GetRecursiveSampleParameters works out: how many recursive passes a blur needs; how many samples the last one takes; how far apart the first one samples. It carries the middleware's own assertions. Scope still to map: the engine's draw submission above the GPU library, materials and post-processing. The game's shaders ship as compiled AMD GPU code in its shader bundles. A census tool in the code repository decodes the shaders in your own copy and counts the instructions they use, for Paleblood's shader translator (Paleblood #316). It prints counts only; no shader code leaves your machine.
docs.title: Blur sampling (YEBIS)

docs.text: The engine builds the GPU's command buffers itself (see Runtime syscalls ), as AMD " PM4 " packets: each packet is a header word naming the operation, followed by its arguments. The first of the engine's own packet writers are mapped, all by @evill33t : The command buffer. One shared structure describes it: where it begins and ends, the cursor where the next word goes, and a callback the engine calls to get more room when it runs out. render_command_prepare_submission ( 0x014784a0 ) reserves 64 words before a submission, and render_command_emit_counter_operation ( 0x01477b30 ) writes a seven-word packet that makes the GPU wait on a value in memory ( PM4 WAIT_REG_MEM ) ( #208 ). The pool counter. render_read_present_pool_counter ( 0x0247eb80 ) reads a 64-bit counter atomically, with a locked compare-and-exchange loop ( #279 ). Present records. render_present_record_consume ( 0x02ab5a70 ) turns a pending present record into commands: it classifies the record, clamps its range, copies its payload and writes the final fields ( #286 ). Building present records. render_build_present_source_record ( 0x0256e1d0 ) builds the record for a present, by mode, keeping partial output, unsigned divisions and the packed auxiliary requirements as the original does; render_choose_record_constructor_selector ( 0x02ab7a20 ), render_combine_record_parameters ( 0x02ab7ab0 ) and render_reduce_record_parameter ( 0x02ab7e40 , a four-entry scale table, zero past its end) pick and combine its constructor choices ( #473 , from #268; edge-verified on synthetic cases). A record test. render_record_auxiliary_predicate ( 0x02abb4f0 ) answers yes or no for a record's selector: always yes for two selector values, a flag bit for the next two, no otherwise ( #293 , from #266). Presenting a swap-chain image. render_swap_chain_present_mode ( 0x02ad5dd0 ) waits until the display has flipped far enough and picks the flip mode, and render_swap_chain_submit ( 0x02ad6e50 ) submits the frame, advances the frame counter and checks its owner again ( #287 ). They use the public layouts of the video-out flip status and kernel events. Depth and stencil clears. render_emit_present_preparation_scalar ( 0x01473590 ) and render_emit_present_preparation_byte ( 0x014735f0 ) write the depth and stencil clear values (AMD's DB_DEPTH_CLEAR and DB_STENCIL_CLEAR registers) #325 , from #210. The last record's depth settings. render_emit_present_last_record_packet ( 0x014769e0 ) writes DB_RENDER_CONTROL . Two setters turn its depth and stencil compression off or on ( 0x01485070 , 0x01485080 ), one replaces two packed indices ( 0x014721d0 ), and render_reset_present_preparation_dirty ( 0x02ad2c30 ) writes only the clear values that changed and remembers them #326 , from #211. Resource records. A record describes a GPU resource's layout. The reviews tie its fields to AMD's public tiling and format fields, though the full meaning is still open. The mapped parts: mapping: render_pack_record_mapping_word ( 0x01471310 ) packs its mapping word and render_read_record_mapping_word ( 0x01486cf0 ) reads one back #321 , from #212; encoding: three lookups decode the encoding byte's metadata, component arrangement and category ( 0x01471730 , 0x014717a0 , 0x014719a0 ), and render_record_set_encoding ( 0x01486540 ) stores it #327 , from #261; parameters: render_record_apply_parameter_tuple ( 0x0149c850 ) picks a record parameter from a normalisation table, with its classification helpers ( 0x0149e900 – 0x0149ea70 ) #322 , from #223; sizes: render_calculate_second_auxiliary ( 0x0149e570 ) works out the size and alignment of a second auxiliary area #323 , from #228; fields: seven setters ( 0x01486520 – 0x01486800 ) replace one field each, keeping the rest of the word #324 , from #236; construction: render_record_constructor ( 0x01485f90 ) clears a record's 44-byte prefix and fills in the record and its auxiliary outputs, returning a packed 64-bit result; render_record_constructor_pack_pair ( 0x01471600 ) packs a selector pair into an encoding, and two optional steps ( 0x0149e2d0 , 0x0149e400 ) align paired components and work out the geometry, writing their outputs even when a helper reports an error #478 , from #246 ( edge-verified on synthetic cases); normalisation: render_record_normalize_mode2 , …mode3 and …mode4 ( 0x025710a0 , 0x025711d0 , 0x02571340 ) bring a record's input into one normalised form, copying the words they do not interpret unchanged and keeping each helper's writes and failure codes in order, and render_record_translate_selector ( 0x02ab7310 ) maps a record selector to one output word, answering status 12 for a selector it does not support #249 ( edge-verified on synthetic cases).
docs.title: Writing GPU commands and presenting

docs.text: The GPU helper library keeps no state of its own: each setter writes its value straight into the command buffer as a register packet, and the GPU reads it from there. A large group of setters and draw writers was mapped and replaced by @evill33t , each verified to write exactly the original packets: Blending and colour output #411 (from #233): render_set_cb_blend_control ( 0x01473090 , one colour buffer's blend equation, CB_BLENDn_CONTROL ), render_set_cb_color_control ( 0x01473320 , the colour output mode and raster operation, CB_COLOR_CONTROL ) and render_set_cb_target_mask ( 0x01472fd0 , which colour components each target writes, CB_TARGET_MASK ). Depth and stencil #411 : render_set_db_depth_control ( 0x014733a0 , the depth and stencil tests and writes) and render_set_db_stencil_control ( 0x01473400 , the front- and back-face stencil operations). What is drawn #411 : render_set_vgt_primitive_type ( 0x01473fe0 , triangles, strips, rectangles and so on), render_emit_num_instances ( 0x01475370 , how many copies a draw makes), render_emit_draw_index_auto ( 0x014741b0 , a draw of consecutive vertices) and render_emit_event_write ( 0x01475da0 , a GPU event such as a cache flush), with two record helpers ( 0x01485390 , 0x014853f0 ) and the one call that asks the system whether the GPU's performance-analysis mode is on ( 0x01489c40 ). Where on screen #364 (from #232): render_configure_viewport ( 0x014765e0 , the viewport's scale, offset and depth range), render_configure_screen_scissor ( 0x01476790 ), render_set_screen_offset ( 0x01473650 ), the guard-band clip and discard adjustments ( 0x014736d0 , 0x01473750 ) and the viewport-transform controls ( 0x01476980 , 0x01485220 ). A present's context section #365 (from #231): render_emit_present_context_section ( 0x01472870 ) reserves room and writes the context registers a present needs.
docs.title: Setting GPU state and drawing

docs.text: Command buffers #360 (from #256): render_command_buffer_init ( 0x01471270 ) sets up a command buffer's pointers and its "need more room" callback. render_command_submit_batch ( 0x02ab0ce0 ), render_command_submit_snapshot ( 0x02ab0e30 ) and render_command_submit_present ( 0x02aafb30 ) hand finished regions to the system's submit call, with the waits the GPU needs. The room check that every packet writer makes before writing is now shared code #291 . The swap chain #361 (from #254): render_setup_swap_chain ( 0x02ad5e90 ) allocates and registers the swap chain's frame buffers with video out and sets up its cached resource data and tone curves; two cleanups release the curve and the cached record ( 0x02571c60 , 0x02572290 , #359 , from #244). The last present record #354 (from #260): render_present_last_record_consume ( 0x02ab6810 ) consumes the final record of a present, or only updates its tracking when the commands do not fit. Shaders #263 , #363 (from #251): render_flush_shader_preparation ( 0x02ab9850 ) flushes a pending barrier before a shader event, and render_allocate_shader_upload ( 0x02aaddc0 ) finds room of at most 64 KiB for a shader's code, reclaiming once if none is free. Resource descriptors #357 (from #255), #358 (from #222): the records that describe a texture's layout, its mip levels and their offsets ( 0x014a1e80 , 0x014a2c40 ), its encoding ( 0x014712d0 , 0x01471770 , 0x01489910 - 0x01489960 ) and its tiling ( 0x0149cc60 , which converts a tile-mode table index), and how its parameters are derived ( 0x02abaf10 , 0x0149cb30 ).
docs.title: Command buffers, swap chain and shader uploads

docs.text: Forty-five more of the library's functions were replaced on 10 November, all @evill33t 's work, brought up to date with main and merged as #482 , #485 , #486 , #487 and the batch #489 : Render targets #489 : render_set_render_target ( 0x014738b0 ) writes a colour target's register block, or switches the target off when there is no descriptor; render_set_depth_render_target ( 0x014739b0 ) does the same for the depth target. render_restore_color_target_from_bank and render_restore_depth_target_from_bank ( 0x02ad1e30 , 0x02ad1e70 ) put a saved target back from one of two banks, and render_present_slot_emit ( 0x01473840 ) writes a colour target's two clear words. Rasterizer state #489 : render_configure_viewport_and_guard_band ( 0x01496f60 ) sets the viewport and the guard band, the region outside the screen where triangles are kept rather than clipped; render_set_pa_sc_mode_cntl_0 ( 0x01477150 ) switches multisampling and the viewport scissor. Linking shaders #489 : render_build_shader_link_words ( 0x014873a0 ) matches a vertex shader's outputs to a pixel shader's inputs and builds the words that connect them; render_emit_shader_link_words ( 0x01475000 ) writes them. render_configure_record_shader , its secondary path and render_finish_record_shader ( 0x02ace1e0 , 0x02ace5e0 , 0x02acfc20 ) set up and finish a recorded shader's state. Descriptor geometry #482 , #485 , #486 , #489 (from #237, #247, #238): building a resource descriptor and the requirements it adds up ( render_prepare_resource_descriptor , 0x02fa6af0 ), the two- and three-part record descriptors and their size ( 0x01487ee0 , 0x01488590 , 0x01488370 , 0x014a27c0 , 0x01471a40 ), converting a constructor's record ( 0x01488d90 ), and render_record_geometry ( 0x0149ce10 ) with its helpers ( 0x0149c4e0 - 0x0149ed30 ), which work out an image's dimensions and alignment for the record constructor. The swap chain's resources #487 , #489 (from #245): render_initialize_swap_chain_resource ( 0x02565f90 ) checks a frame buffer's parameters, prepares its storage and wraps it; render_prepare_swap_chain_resource_info ( 0x02571d60 ) allocates that storage and publishes its descriptor. Finishing a present #489 : the chain that closes a frame's command lists and hands them on. render_finish_present_commands ( 0x02aaf700 ) finishes pending lists and submits the pending snapshot when there is room ( render_submit_present_finish_snapshot , 0x02ab0b00 ; render_managed_present_capacity , 0x02aaf030 ); a pool of present buffers is claimed and released ( 0x02ad3b80 , 0x02ad3c80 , 0x02ad3d40 , 0x02aaa5a0 ); the release packets that tell the GPU a buffer may be reused are written ( 0x014778f0 , 0x02abb6d0 ); and the present's sources are prepared and their state flushed ( 0x02ad1eb0 , 0x02ad1f80 ), with the encoding helpers 0x02564ed0 and 0x02565130 and the context finisher 0x02568530 .
docs.title: Render targets, descriptors and the present path (10 November)

docs.text: Paleblood does not replay the finished GPU commands. Instead, the GPU library's replacements, with their packets unchanged, also tell Paleblood's renderer what they set, and the renderer draws that on your GPU (see Runtime: the renderer ): Observer calls in replacements #414 : the blend, colour, depth, stencil, primitive-type, instance-count, viewport and draw replacements above each report the same value they write, with the place in the command buffer where they wrote it. Under the verification harness the calls do nothing. The depth and stencil clear values and DB_RENDER_CONTROL replacements report too #435 . Observed functions without replacements yet #416 , #418 , #435 , #441 : where a library function has no replacement, the runtime watches its arguments at its entry and lets the original run. These were setRenderTarget ( 0x014738b0 ) and the depth target ( 0x014739b0 ), now replaced (above), and still are the stencil references ( 0x01473190 , 0x014731f0 ), the shaders' user-data writers ( 0x014761a0 - 0x014764a0 ), the indexed-draw setters and draw ( 0x01475270 - 0x01475320 , 0x01474420 ) and two compute dispatch writers ( 0x01474c50 , 0x0148a350 ). The compute command buffer's user data #510 : that buffer's six user-data writers ( 0x0148aad0 - 0x0148ada0 ) take no stage argument and were not observed, so a compute pass ran with whatever user data the record held from before; one colour lookup-table pass read another pass's table. They now report through the same observers as the stage writers. This needs the game library built from the decompilation ( tools/boot.py --game-lib ). In the maintainer's local runs it was enough to draw the studio logos and the title screen #441 . How the library functions were verified Each replacement above was checked against the original instructions on constructed edge cases , which also caught deliberately broken variants; none was checked on recorded game frames. All are edge-verified . They are @evill33t 's work, brought up to date with main and merged from the PRs named in brackets; #362 adds cases for the shader preparation's reset modes (from #350) and #352 derives the packet tests' addresses from the harness . The observer calls were added afterwards and leave the packets unchanged. The functions of 10 November ( #482 , #485 - #487 , #489 ) were checked the same way and are edge-verified ; #489 lists each one's cases in its session report. How these were verified Each was checked against the original instructions on constructed edge cases by an independent review, which also caught deliberately broken variants; none was checked on recorded game frames. #279, #286 and #287 were brought up to date with main from #209, #259 and #267, and

docs.text: The frame-rate patches are described in Frame timing . Uncap FPS++ makes the +0x70 child's step the flipper's measured frame time ( +0x264 ) whatever the held flag says, through a small code cave inside the function, and drops the RendMan check. The 1/30 s it reads otherwise is the shared constant at 0x04d29170 , which the 60, 90 and uncapped patches rewrite in the data segment. Uncap FPS++ presents with flip mode 0 (no vblank sync) at the end of 0x025b2fb0 . Every frame-rate patch removes the first assertion of 0x00fbc3e0 (at least 3 base samples): at higher frame rates the blur gets fewer samples.

docs.text: The Hunter's Workshop Player-facing mechanics, matched to the systems Paleblood can verify in source. Each guide starts with what a player can notice, then shows what source or test evidence exists. Combat Combat & Damage Separating visible outcomes from unverified formulas. Read Weapons Weapons & Transformations A research map for weapon state and transition behavior. Read Movement Movement & Stamina Movement evidence and the unresolved identity of the verified points value. Read Physics Hitboxes & Collision Shared physics findings and the missing link to combat volumes. Read Verified Stats & Progression The verified per-frame points update, its evidence, and its limits. Read What the current evidence covers The evidence is narrow: Verified piece What it gives the workshop One character update A per-frame points value A frame-step path Timing A physics constructor Rigid bodies wired into shared tables These findings do not yet establish a damage formula, weapon implementation, player stamina identity, or combat hitboxes. How to read a finding Each guide begins with what a player can notice, then states what source or test evidence exists. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence; a link to one does not automatically prove the others. When a mechanic's implementation is unknown, the page says what a future trace must establish. What this page can and cannot claim Every claim in this section is labelled by the kind of evidence behind it. Label Meaning observed Seen during play or in a recording, with its context: starting state, player position and actions, the visible change, and whether it repeats. inferred A conclusion drawn from code or tests, stated with the scope that evidence covers. unknown Not yet traced. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. Absence is not a claim about the game. A missing profile describes the project's research, not what the game contains. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels evidence.

docs.text: Stats & Progression One verified per-frame character update changes a bounded value the source calls points . It is a concrete example of how a game stat can be driven by the frame loop. At a glance Function character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 ), called from two character update loops. What it does Accumulates fractional recovery between frames, applies a character-specific rate, and clamps the result between -50 and a per-character maximum. Status Verified against recorded original-game calls and generated edge cases , with independent review. Not established That points is the player's stamina, that it belongs only to the player, or how it fits the wider progression system. This article describes one function and its tested behavior. It is not a complete account of combat, weapon costs, attributes, leveling, or save data. The per-frame update character_frame_update_01cbdb20 ( 0x01cbdb20 , 979 bytes) is called from two character update loops. In order, it: reads the character's frame time; handles a pending throw animation event when the animation-event manager is ready; updates the points value (below); passes time into a character module step; runs other module calls and copies data used by the character and animation systems. The Character page lists the observed fields and remaining layout questions. How points change each frame Check the flag. If the character parameter flag disables regeneration, return without changing the stat. Work out the rate. Multiply the parameter byte by 0.01 , the character multiplier, and a factor returned through the character's virtual table. The result is the per-second rate. Add this frame's share. Save the rate truncated toward zero, then calculate frame time × rate + saved fraction . Split whole and fraction. Apply the whole-number portion to the current points value and keep the fractional remainder for the next update. Guard and clamp. If the change would lower points, skip it when the data flag or observed debug flag disables drops. Otherwise clamp the value to at least -50 and at most the character's maximum. Why keep the fraction? It stops each frame from discarding the part of the recovery smaller than one point. A slower update can therefore accumulate several fractional contributions before the integer stat changes. Per-frame points update A character update checks regeneration flags, calculates a rate from parameters and a virtual factor, accumulates fractional frame-time progress, conditionally applies the whole points change, and clamps it to minus fifty through the character maximum. .points-box{fill:#171511;stroke:#8b6d4c;stroke-width:2;rx:10} .points-text{fill:#f0e8d5;font:20px sans-serif;text-anchor:middle} .points-small{fill:#c9bda5;font:16px sans-serif;text-anchor:middle} .points-arrow{fill:none;stroke:#8b6d4c;stroke-width:3;marker-end:url(#points-arrow)} Character frame update uses this instance's frame time Check regeneration flags disabled regeneration exits early Calculate per-second rate parameter × 0.01 × character and virtual factors Accumulate this frame frame time × rate + saved fraction Apply whole points change retain fractional remainder; no-drop flags can skip decreases Clamp to the observed range −50 through this character's maximum Static-analysis summary of the verified character update. The points field's game-facing identity is unresolved. Frame-time variants The update normally uses the frame time stored on the character. The community frame-rate patches substitute their own: Mode Frame time the update uses Original timing The frame time stored on the character Community 30 FPS patch 1/27 second Community 60 FPS patch 1/54 second Uncapped patch The stored time Paleblood's BB_TARGET_FPS option mirrors those substitutions in this function. See Frame timing for the main loop and the broader patch comparison. Those constants explain the code path; they do not establish why the patch authors selected them or how the resulting rate feels in every game state. How we know The replacement is marked verified in Paleblood's function table. It was compared against two kinds of evidence, in each of four runs (original timing, 30 FPS, 60 FPS, uncapped): Recorded cases: previously captured original-game calls. Edge cases: generated boundary cases. Each comparison reported zero failures, and an independent review approved the readable refactor after rerunning all recorded and edge cases . These results support equivalence over those recorded inputs and generated cases. They do not prove every possible state, identify the points value as stamina, or establish that an enemy or boss uses this exact update. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels different kinds of evidence. Verification record and source links The verification record, dated 2026-10-07 with source digest b243fddb1ca6589a , reports 457/457 recorded cases and 39/39 edge cases for each of four runs: original timing, 30 FPS, 60 FPS, and uncapped. Each comparison reported zero failures. An independent review record says the readable refactor was approved and all recorded and edge cases were rerun. Why do the frame-rate patches use 1/27 and 1/54 second rather than exact display-frame intervals? Until those links are supported by source analysis or recorded evidence, “stamina” remains a hypothesis rather than the name of this mechanic. It stays an open question, with the evidence needed next. Observation is not implementation. An animation, health-bar change, phase transition, hit reaction, movement, or line of dialogue can be observed. On its own it does not identify an entity ID, function, data field, condition, timer, probability, script, or internal state. No guessing. Nothing is filled in from genre convention, a gameplay impression, animation timing, or a displayed bar. Visually similar actions are not assumed to share code. No guessed names, IDs, catalogs, or numerical tables are published. What a source claim needs. The entity, the function and address, the data or state it reads, the result it produces, public Paleblood source at the exact merged revision, tests, and independent review. Evidence kinds differ. Recorded original-game behavior, static analysis, synthetic Paleblood tests, and verified replacements are different kinds of evidence. A link to one does not prove the others. Tests have a scope. Passing tests support equivalence on the cases they cover, not untested gameplay situations. Timing and probability claims need measurements or directly verified logic, not a single encounter. Shared systems are not specific actors. The verified AI, Character, Event, and Physics findings do not yet identify any particular boss, enemy, NPC, weapon, or attack. Absence is not a claim about the game. A missing profile describes the project's research, not what the game contains. See Evidence & Media Review for how this wiki labels evidence.

docs.text: Weapons & Transformations A transformed weapon is a visible change in how an equipped weapon looks and is used. That change is a starting point for research, not proof of the internal state layout, attack table, or transition function. At a glance What is verified Nothing about weapon instances, transformation states, weapon-specific attack selection, or the functions that switch forms. Easy to misread The character update can fire W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef throw-animation events. That is not transformation evidence. Not published No weapon catalog or numerical attack table without verified evidence. The throw-animation event The verified character update can fire a pending throw-animation event named W_ThrowAtk or W_ThrowDef .
